paras: This is a short interview, first published by the Vietnamese outlet Nhân Dân (People's Daily online) on 14 April 2025. Its Beijing correspondent interviews Pan Jin'e, a professor at the Academy of Marxism, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and a specialist on Vietnam, during Xi Jinping's state visit. Pan argues that making Vietnam the first destination of the year shows how highly China values Vietnam and bilateral relations.

The interview moves through four topics: Xi's repeated visits and the priority given to neighbourhood diplomacy; economic and trade cooperation; people-to-people exchanges; and cooperation between the two ruling parties.

Pan notes that this is Xi's fourth visit to Vietnam as both Party General Secretary and state president since 2015. In Pan's account, neighbourhood diplomacy is a priority for China, and Vietnam is a priority within it, because both countries are socialist states led by communist parties. Pan expects progress under the "six more" framework, especially in practical cooperation. Pan cites 2024 trade figures above US$260 billion by Chinese statistics and above US$200 billion by Vietnamese ones, and points to potential in supply chains, border roads, railways and ports. On the party side, Pan holds that party relations have long set the direction of state relations.

Pan concludes that cooperation should deepen in each area. Pan proposes using shared revolutionary heritage sites and new media to reach young people, strengthening exchanges between party leaders on the international situation and development paths, and translating each side's leaders' works. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic view of how China's Vietnam policy was framed during the April 2025 visit.
quoteEn: Achieving closeness between the two peoples' hearts is a very important and also the highest goal of diplomacy, because only then can connectivity in every area, including infrastructure and economic and trade relations, be realised.
quoteZh: 做到两国民心相通，是外交的一个很重要，也是最高的目标，因为民心相通才能够实现各方面的联通，包括基础设施、经贸关系等。

t: Super digital platforms and new trends in new-imperialist monopoly
zh: 超级数字平台与新帝国主义垄断新趋势
paras: Responding to Xi Jinping's call to study contemporary capitalism and its changes, Xu Zhixiang asks what "super digital platforms" are, how they reshape monopoly under "new imperialism", what the essence and consequences of this change are, and how China should respond. The article argues that these platforms (Apple, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Facebook) are a new organisational form of finance capital, and that they drive imperialist monopoly towards new forms, means, scope and functions.

The article has four parts. It first defines super digital platforms and their three-dimensional operating system of "algorithm control + data concentration + cross-domain integration". It then defines new imperialism as the post-Cold War stage of monopoly capitalism and sets out four new trends. The third part analyses their essence and effects, and the last proposes responses for China.

Xu argues that monopoly shifts in four ways: from local, fragmentary monopoly to global aggregated monopoly; from a mix of production and capital concentration to mainly capital concentration, driven by speculation; from monopoly bounded by time and space to "beyond time and space" monopoly, including the "platformisation of everyday life"; and from economic to "extra-economic" monopoly, resting on control of discourse and on Western cultural and ideological hegemony. In essence, the author holds, this is a collusion between "technofeudalism" and "digital imperialism". It reshapes global accumulation by dispossession through creative destruction, deepened inequality and a "全时域+全方位" (all-time, all-round) system of exploitation. By Marx's logic of underconsumption it is said to end in a "super digital platform crisis" of relative overproduction.

Xu holds that the capitalist system is the root of these problems and that China's public-ownership-based system allows it to curb the harms of capital logic. The proposals are: classify platforms by ownership, function and degree of competition; strengthen public ownership of platforms and place a state-led "digital central enterprise" at the core of a national big-data platform; enact laws such as a Digital Labour Law and revise the Anti-Monopoly Law; accelerate indigenous innovation in core digital technologies; and build a community with a shared future for mankind in the digital field, through the Belt and Road Initiative and joint global governance. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist political economist combines Lenin's theory of imperialism with debates on platform capitalism and technofeudalism to derive concrete policy proposals.
quoteEn: The new trends in new-imperialist monopoly driven by super digital platforms merely change the outward features of traditional imperialist monopoly through the platform as intermediary; in essence they are a collusion between technofeudalism and digital imperialism, dominated by the logic of capital in the context of digital technology.
quoteZh: 超级数字平台推动新帝国主义垄断产生的新趋势，只是将超级数字平台作为中介而改变了传统帝国主义垄断的表现特征，实质上是数字技术发展背景下由资本逻辑主导的技术封建主义与数字帝国主义的合谋

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2012–13, calling for shared governance and common development among states. Here the author extends it to a "digital" community in cyberspace.
China's international infrastructure and economic cooperation programme launched in 2013. The author proposes using it to build a "Digital Silk Road".
In the article, the post-Cold War stage of monopoly capitalism, marked by non-military control through transnational corporations, finance capital and technology rather than colonial conquest.
Adapted from Zarach and Stucke's "super platforms": large internet platform firms that use network effects to control a whole ecosystem. The author treats them as a form of finance capital.
A term in recent critical debate for a system in which investment aims at extracting rents and plunder rather than developing productive forces. The author pairs it with digital imperialism.
The control by advanced countries of data, digital infrastructure and digital culture to dominate less developed countries, as the article uses the term.

t: New trends in the Philippine left movement in the twenty-first century
zh: 21世纪菲律宾左翼运动的新态势
paras: Hei Ran surveys the Philippine left from its origins to the present and asks what is new about it in the twenty-first century. The article argues that the left has gained theoretical and practical ground since 2000 but has also become fragmented, more flexible in tactics and broader in aims, and that its prospects remain uncertain.

The article is organised in four parts. It first traces the movement's history: late-colonial labour organising under US rule, the founding of the Communist Party of the Philippines in 1930, repression in 1948, the 1968 split led by Jose Maria Sison, and the splits that followed the 1986 People Power uprising and the 1990s rectification campaign. It then profiles the main parties, grouping them as communist (the CPP, the Revolutionary Workers' Party of Mindanao) and social-democratic (the Philippine Democratic Socialist Party, the Workers' and Peasants' mass-power party Partido Lakas ng Masa). It then analyses three new features and ends with prospects.

On theory, Hei reports that after the 2008 financial crisis these parties sharpened their critique of capitalism and put forward socialist visions: public ownership of strategic sectors, an ecological basis for socialism and the communal ethic of Bayanihan. On the three new features, Hei argues, first, that fragmentation comes from ideological splits, the failure of the 2005 Laban ng Masa alliance and the dominance of political dynasties. Second, tactics have shifted from a single reliance on armed struggle to a dual track of armed struggle and legal participation, shown in peace talks under Duterte and Arroyo. Third, goals have widened from class struggle and land reform to labour rights, gender equality, environment and health.

Hei concludes that the outlook is not optimistic. The Communist Party of the Philippines faces subjectivism, sectarianism and a leadership vacuum after the deaths of Sison and the Tiamzons. The social democrats suffer from weak cohesion, cadre loss and poor 2022 election results. Hei holds that only left unity can shake dynastic dominance and move towards socialism, while leaving the future an open question. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of Philippine left parties, their factional genealogy and recent programmes, with citations to party documents.
quoteEn: Since the start of the twenty-first century, the ideological and strategic divisions among Philippine left parties and organisations have kept widening, and with political dynasties dominating party politics, the left and its party system have gradually become markedly fragmented.
quoteZh: 进入21世纪以来，菲律宾左翼政党及组织在意识形态和战略路线上的分歧持续扩大，加之家族政治势力在菲律宾政党政治生态中占据主导地位，左翼政治和政党体系逐渐呈现出明显的碎片化倾向。

glossary.explanation: A Party-building practice of ideological correction and criticism within communist parties, originating in the Chinese Communist Party. The article applies it to two CPP campaigns, in 1966 and the early 1990s.

t: Efforts to unite the international Maoist movement and the latest developments
zh: 国际毛主义运动联合化探索及最新动态
paras: Yu Weihai and Shu Huiqian ask how Maoist parties around the world have tried to unite since the 1980s, and what the founding of a new international body in December 2022 means. They argue that the International Communist League, formed on the 129th anniversary of Mao Zedong's birth, is the latest result of these efforts and an important event for the international Maoist movement. In their assessment, it has real significance but also serious flaws.

The article first surveys Maoist parties since the 1980s. It sorts them into those waging armed struggle (the Philippines, India, Turkey, Peru), those not yet doing so, and those that moved to parliamentary politics (Nepal). It then traces earlier international bodies: the Revolutionary Internationalist Movement (1984–2006), the International Conference of Marxist-Leninist Parties and Organizations (International Newsletter, 1998–2017) and the International Coordination of Revolutionary Parties and Organizations (ICOR, founded 2010). It next sets out the League's theory and practice, and ends with an evaluation.

The authors report the League's own case. It holds that imperialism is in a general crisis driven by three contradictions: imperialist powers against oppressed nations, bourgeoisie against proletariat, and rivalry among imperialist states. It also holds that a new wave of proletarian revolution is rising, that Marxism-Leninism-Maoism is the guide to action, and that people's war is the path forward. In their evaluation, the authors credit the League with anti-imperialist and anti-hegemonic activity, with strengthening unity through debate and joint statements, and with offering an alternative to the parliamentary road taken by many Western communist parties. They also identify three problems. In their view the League wrongly denies that socialist countries exist today, including China. They also see sectarian tendencies: the League has recruited no new members, and the large Indian and Philippine parties have stayed out. Finally, they call its claim that people's war is the only road idealised and empty, citing objections from the Communist Party of India (Maoist) and the Communist Party of the Philippines.

The authors conclude that Maoist unity remains difficult. They see the League's weaknesses as long-standing ailments of the movement whose negative effects deserve vigilance. The article supplies a chronology of Maoist organisations, joint statements and debates, with figures on party strength. Read the original if you study the international communist movement, Maoist parties outside China, or how Chinese scholars assess them.
quoteEn: The founding of the International Communist League is an important event in the Maoist movement and the latest result of decades of efforts to unite international Maoist forces, so its founding and its subsequent theoretical and practical explorations carry significant international meaning.
quoteZh: 国际共产主义者同盟的成立，是毛主义运动中的重要事件，也是近几十年来国际毛主义力量联合化努力的最新成果，因此其成立本身及成立之后的理论与实践探索具有重要的国际意义。

glossary.explanation: Mao Zedong's strategy of protracted armed struggle led by a communist party, based on rural base areas and mass mobilisation. Maoist parties abroad treat it as the main path of revolution.
A doctrine adopted by many foreign Maoist parties, notably Peru's Shining Path, which treats Maoism as the third stage of Marxism. It differs from the official Chinese term 'Mao Zedong Thought'.

t: New features of the left–right contest in Latin America and their impact on the political ecology of parties
zh: 拉美左右翼博弈的新特点及其对政党政治生态的影响
source: Problems of Contemporary World Socialism (Dangdai shijie shehui zhuyi wenti), 2024 no. 4
paras: Yuan Dongzhen asks how the long-running competition between left and right parties in Latin America has changed in recent years, and what this means for party politics. The article argues that the clear alternation cycles of earlier decades have blurred. Left and right are now evenly matched, and neither holds a lasting advantage.

The article first traces the shift from the left-wing "pink tide" (from about 2000 to 2014) to a right-wing rebound and then to a mixed picture after 2018. It reviews the 18 elections of the 2021–2024 "super election cycle" year by year, noting that the left won 11, the right 6 and a centrist party 1. It then examines how the contest spills across borders, what economic and social changes lie behind it, and what consequences follow for the region's political ecology.

Yuan makes three main moves. The first is that the contest has become regional. The author cites links between right-wing forces and Spain's Vox, the Madrid Forum and the Conservative Political Action Conference, and left-wing networks such as the Puebla Group and the São Paulo Forum. The author also cites diplomatic ruptures over Peru's Castillo and the Ecuadorian police raid on Mexico's embassy, personal insults between leaders, and divided regional responses to Venezuela's 2024 election. The second is that the main causes are economic and social. Yuan points to a second "lost decade" in 2015–2024 with average growth of 0.9 per cent, rising poverty, voters with an anti-establishment mood, and a more independent, impoverished middle class. In this account, voters switch between left and right out of dissatisfaction rather than ideology. The third is that the effects are damaging. Winners often have weak mandates, with low first-round vote shares and few legislative seats, so governments are weak. Left–right divisions have also harmed regional bodies such as UNASUR and Mercosur.

Yuan concludes that these changes are tied to the economic and social cycle and will not alter the "normal state" of Latin American party politics. The left's appeal rests on deep inequality, and the right's elitist influence stays entrenched because few countries have undergone profound social change. The author expects left–right competition and alternation in office to continue. Read the original if you want a detailed, election-by-election account of Latin America's left–right balance since 2021, written from a Chinese academic perspective, together with the author's explanation of it.
quoteEn: The new features of the development and governance of left and right, and the new pattern of their contest, are to a large extent a consequence of Latin America's long economic stagnation and its expression in the political sphere.
quoteZh: 左右翼发展和执政的新特点以及博弈的新态势，很大程度上是拉美经济长期低迷的后果，是这一后果在政治领域的体现。

t: Evolution, current state and future of Spain's left-wing political forces since the financial crisis
zh: 金融危机以来西班牙左翼政治力量的演变、现状与未来
source: Scientific Socialism (《科学社会主义》), 2024 no. 6
paras: How have Spain's left-wing political forces developed since the 2008 financial crisis, and where are they heading? Jia and Wang argue that the left has moved from a dominant Socialist Party (PSOE), through a brief rivalry with the new party Podemos, back to a pattern of one strong party and many weak ones, now operating through coalition government. They hold that its prospects remain unpromising.

Using general elections as the main thread, the article divides the period into four phases: PSOE struggling in government (2008–2011), Podemos's rise (2011–2016), a PSOE–Podemos stand-off and the first left coalition (2016–2023), and PSOE's narrow re-election with the Sumar movement (2023 onwards). It then identifies five features of the period and closes by assessing the left's outlook.

The authors characterise the pattern as "one strong, many weak", with "two strong" appearing only briefly around 2016. They attribute Podemos's peak to the crisis, fertile populist ground and disillusion with traditional parties, and expect these conditions not to recur. They argue that Spain's trajectory tracks the radicalisation of the European left (Syriza, the Five Star Movement, Portugal's Left Bloc), and that Spain lags slightly behind. They also say right-wing parties (the Popular Party, Ciudadanos, Vox) have taken much of the space opened by populism. Coalition government brings left cooperation but also the loss of PSOE's dominance and friction between partners. Traditional parties are recasting their identity: PSOE's "we are left" slogan and the Communist Party's return to Leninism in 2017. Podemos, in their account, must balance its online grassroots model with functional party organisation.

Looking ahead, the authors point to three problems. The Sánchez government's concessions to Catalan and Basque parties have provoked mass protests and economic risk. The left cannot offer a real alternative to neoliberalism: PSOE is constrained by the EU, the right and regional forces, while the radical left criticises more than it constructs. Internal division, fragmentation, an ageing membership and the distance between the labour movement and the socialist movement also persist. They conclude that the left must strengthen itself internally if it is to help revolutionary conditions mature as capitalism's general crisis nears. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of Spanish left politics, with election data and a periodisation since 2008.
quoteEn: The development curve of Spain's left-wing political forces has consistently matched the radicalisation of the European left.
quoteZh: 西班牙左翼政治力量的发展曲线始终暗合着欧洲左翼政治力量的激进化进程。

t: The split and transformation of Europe's radical left parties: the case of Germany
zh: 欧洲激进左翼政党的分裂与蜕变：以德国为例
source: World Social Sciences (Shijie shehui kexue), 2024 no. 6
paras: Wu Huiping asks what the January 2024 split of Germany's Left Party (Die Linke) reveals about the European radical left. Sahra Wagenknecht left the party and founded the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW). Wu argues that the split is a case of radical-left parties adjusting under political pressure, and that BSW's programme marks a sharp turn away from the Left Party's democratic socialism towards what the article calls left conservatism.

The article first traces the Left Party's origins in the PDS (the successor to East Germany's ruling party) and in the WASG, a split from the Social Democrats (SPD). It then describes its factional divisions between conservative and pragmatic-reformist camps. It sets out its democratic socialist programme, the 2011 Erfurt Programme and its policy demands, followed by BSW's programme, the effects of the split on the Left Party, and similar parties in France, Italy and Slovakia. A closing section considers the radical left's prospects.

Wu's central claim is that both parties are left-populist, but they differ sharply. The Left Party criticises capitalism and is liberal on migration. BSW avoids capitalism critique and is anti-establishment rather than anti-system. It keeps radical left positions on welfare, taxation and peace but takes restrictive, culturally conservative positions on migration. Drawing on Niedermayer's theory of party competition, Wu explains BSW's success by a shift to the right in society and by the Left Party's failure to answer new challenges. According to the article, BSW drew most of its 2024 votes from the SPD and the Left Party, and the Left Party lost its parliamentary group and its position in eastern Germany. Wu sees comparable mixes of left economics and nationalism in La France Insoumise, the Five Star Movement and Slovakia's Smer.

Wu concludes that this is a pragmatic response to real political pressures rather than a general 'conservative turn'. The radical left can recover only by working with other left parties, as in France's New Popular Front and the Dutch left alliance. Wu notes that the Left Party's pacifist foreign policy obstructs this. Wu also calls on the radical left to seize the opening created by capitalist crisis and put forward practical alternatives on ownership, distribution, growth and democracy. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-academic account of the Left Party–BSW split, with poll and voter-flow data and comparisons across Europe.
quoteEn: This trend is more a pragmatic shift driven by real politics, and cannot yet be broadly defined as a "conservative turn".
quoteZh: 这一动向更多是一种现实政治驱动下的实用主义转向，还无法被笼统界定为“保守主义转向”。

glossary.explanation: A current of socialism that seeks socialist values through parliamentary democracy and gradual reform rather than revolution. The article treats it as the Left Party's guiding ideology and as distinct from Marxism-Leninism.
The label the article, citing other scholars, gives to a mix of left-wing economic and welfare policies with culturally conservative and nationalist stances, especially on migration.
The Left Party's programme, adopted at its Erfurt congress in October 2011 and still in force. It sets out a 'democratic socialism of the 21st century' and a critique of capitalism.

t: Deng Xiaoping's summing-up of the historical experience of the international communist movement and its contemporary lessons
zh: 邓小平对国际共产主义运动的历史经验总结及当代启示
source: Journal of Yangzhou University (Humanities and Social Sciences Edition), 2025 no. 1
paras: How did Deng Xiaoping draw lessons from the rise and setbacks of the international communist movement, and what do they offer today? Yuan Xiuli argues that Deng affirmed the movement's achievements while learning from the Soviet collapse, the Eastern European upheavals and the split in the socialist camp. In Yuan's reading, these lessons remain valuable for China and world socialism at a time of what Xi Jinping calls changes unseen in a century.

The article first sets out five strands of Deng's summing-up: upholding scientific socialism, seeking truth from facts, combining self-reliance with opening up, handling relations between socialist states and between parties correctly, and bringing out the superiority of socialism. A final section draws three present-day lessons. Yuan relies mainly on Deng's remarks from 1956 to 1989, framed by statements from Xi Jinping.

Yuan's central claim is that Deng opposed both "Left" and Right deviations. He rejected wholesale Westernization and bourgeois liberalization, but also dogmatic attempts to leap ahead to communism. Deng also criticised copying the Soviet model, Soviet "big-power" and "big-party" chauvinism, and China's own past habit of judging other parties by Chinese experience. Yuan presents the reform-era principles as drawn from these lessons: equality and independence between parties, with no "father party", and self-reliance that does not exclude learning from abroad. Poverty, Deng held, is not socialism, so socialism must prove itself by developing the productive forces and improving living standards.

Yuan draws three lessons. History should be summed up scientifically, looking forward and avoiding fruitless polemics. Whether the Party's leadership is upheld decides the fate of the movement, which Yuan links to full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. And the Party should show historical initiative in the face of great changes. Yuan concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics, upheld in line with Deng's insights, is the mainstay of twenty-first-century world socialism. Read the original if you want a compact, official-line account of how Deng's remarks on communist movement history are used to support present Party-building and foreign-policy positions.
quoteEn: Deng Xiaoping held that history must not be avoided, and that one must value the analysis of history, the summing-up of historical experience and the revealing of historical laws.
quoteZh: 邓小平认为，不能回避历史，要重视对历史的分析、对历史经验的总结、对历史规律的揭示

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism, associated with Deng Xiaoping's reform era and developed in later Party theory.
A principle associated with Mao Zedong and restored as the Party's ideological line at the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). It requires policy to proceed from actual conditions.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan of Xi Jinping's leadership since 2012 for stricter discipline and Party-building.
Deng's term for a party that treats other communist parties as subordinates and issues orders to them, applied to the Soviet party.

glossary.pinyin: bǎi nián wèi yǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.explanation: A phrase used by Xi Jinping to describe a period of profound shifts in the global order.

t: Deng Xiaoping's summing-up of the historical experience of the international communist movement and its contemporary implications
zh: 邓小平对国际共产主义运动的历史经验总结及当代启示
source: Journal of Yangzhou University (Humanities and Social Sciences Edition), 2025 no. 1
paras: Yuan Xiuli asks what lessons Deng Xiaoping drew from the rise and setbacks of the international communist movement, including the split in the socialist camp, the Soviet collapse and the upheavals in Eastern Europe, and what those lessons offer today. The article argues that Deng's assessment, which affirmed the movement's achievements while absorbing its failures, remains of real value for contemporary China and for world socialism. It frames this against Xi Jinping's description of a world undergoing 'changes unseen in a century'.

The article is built around five sets of lessons attributed to Deng, drawn from his speeches and talks between 1956 and 1989. These are: holding to scientific socialism; seeking truth from facts; combining self-reliance with opening up; handling relations between socialist states and between parties correctly; and bringing out the superiority of socialism. A final section sets out three present-day implications, each tied to statements by Xi Jinping.

Yuan's central claim is that Deng fought on two fronts, opposing both 'Left' errors (trying to enter communism too early) and Rightist tendencies such as wholesale Westernisation and bourgeois liberalisation. On inter-party relations, Yuan reports Deng's principles of equality and independence, his rejection of any 'father party', and his admission that the Chinese Communist Party itself made the error of pointing fingers during the polemics of the 1960s. Deng is also presented as tracing Soviet decline to rigid thinking and closure, so that reform and opening up is read as a decision built on lessons from both Soviet and Chinese experience. On superiority, Yuan cites Deng's position that poverty is not socialism: socialism must develop the productive forces and improve living standards, and Party leadership is itself part of its superiority.

Yuan draws three implications. History should be summed up scientifically, with an eye to the future. Whether Party leadership is maintained decides the fate of a communist movement. And the Party should take historical initiative amid the 'changes unseen in a century'. The article concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics, advancing under Xi Jinping, has become the mainstay of world socialism in the twenty-first century. Read the original if you want a source-based account of how Deng's remarks on the communist movement are used in current Party theory and in the framing of China's role in world socialism.
quoteEn: In summing up the rise and fall, success and failure of history, the Communist Party of China adheres to seeking truth from facts, proceeds from reality in everything, upholds scientific socialism, and brings out the superiority of socialism.
quoteZh: 中国共产党总结历史的兴衰成败，坚持实事求是，坚持一切从实际出发，坚持科学社会主义，发挥社会主义的优越性。

glossary.literal: great changes not seen in a hundred years
glossary.explanation: A formula used by Xi Jinping since about 2017 to describe a shifting global order, including the relative rise of emerging economies and growing geopolitical competition.

A principle of the Party's ideological line, associated with Mao Zedong and restored by Deng Xiaoping at the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978). It means basing policy on actual conditions rather than on doctrine or foreign models.
The policy launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, which shifted the Party's focus to economic construction and introduced market-oriented reforms and openness to foreign investment and technology.
The official name for the Party's path of socialist development since Deng Xiaoping, stressing adaptation of Marxism to China's conditions.
Deng's term for a party that treats other parties as subordinates and issues orders to them, used here to criticise Soviet 'big-party chauvinism'.
A term used in 1980s Party discourse for liberal political ideas seen as undermining socialism and Party leadership. Deng repeatedly opposed it.

t: South Asian communist parties' exploration of the socialist road amid changes unseen in a century
zh: 百年变局背景下南亚共产党对社会主义道路的探索
source: Issues in Contemporary World Socialism (Dangdai shijie shehuizhuyi wenti), 2024 no. 4
paras: Hei Ran asks how communist parties in South Asia have responded to what Chinese official discourse calls the changes unseen in a century, with the East rising and the West declining and the international system in transition. The article argues that these parties hold to Marxism, produce new theoretical positions and seek socialist paths suited to their national conditions. In Hei's view they have made progress but still face serious obstacles.

The article surveys parties in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka, including several Maoist and Marxist-Leninist groups. It has four parts: new theoretical views, struggle and governing practice, main problems, and prospects. The first part covers the parties' readings of the international situation, their critiques of capitalism and their definitions of socialism. The second covers shifts in strategy, governing experience and inter-party exchanges.

Hei reports that the parties see a multipolar world in which capitalism's contradictions sharpen, citing US-led "unipolarity", NATO expansion and a "new Cold War" against China. They trace economic crises, such as Sri Lanka's external debt of US$52 billion, to capitalism and neoliberalism. Their socialist models are labelled "socialism with Indian characteristics", "socialism with Nepali characteristics" and "socialism with modern features". Hei also credits the rise of China and socialism with Chinese characteristics with strengthening confidence in socialism. On governing practice, Hei cites the Left Democratic Front in Kerala, whose leader Pinarayi Vijayan reported falling unemployment, and Prachanda's government in Nepal. The obstacles Hei lists are weak party-building, sectarian divisions, the Hindu-nationalist BJP, religious forces and interference by India and the United States, notably through the Millennium Challenge Compact.

Hei concludes that the parties will strengthen party-building, build left unity (the Progressive Left Alliance in Pakistan, the Socialist Front in Nepal), counter right-wing and religious pressure and resist outside interference. The article presents the movement as developing in a winding, long-term and varied way, while world socialism remains at a low ebb overall. Read the original if you want a country-by-country account of South Asian communist parties' positions and strategies, as presented in a Chinese academic journal.
quoteEn: As an important force in the international communist movement, South Asian communist parties are actively exploring socialist paths suited to their national conditions, delivering an ever stronger shock to the South Asian capitalist system.
quoteZh: 南亚共产党作为国际共产主义运动的重要力量，积极探索符合本国国情的社会主义发展道路，对南亚资本主义体系造成愈加强烈的冲击。

glossary.pinyin: bǎi nián wèi yǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.literal: great changes not seen in a hundred years
glossary.explanation: A phrase used by Xi Jinping and in Chinese official discourse since about 2017 to describe a shifting global balance of power and a transforming international order.

glossary.en: the East rising and the West declining
glossary.explanation: A Chinese formulation for the perceived shift of global economic and political weight from the West towards Asia, especially China.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's theory and system of socialism since the reform era.

t: The new "networked" pattern of relations among communist parties abroad in the 21st century
zh: 21世纪国外共产党政党关系的“网络化”新态势
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehui zhuyi), 2025 no. 1
paras: Yu Weihai and Li Yuwei ask how relations among communist parties outside China have changed since the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and argue that the best description is "networking" (wangluohua). In their view, existing Chinese scholarship treats these relations only as a matter of unity versus division. They hold that 21st-century relations are better captured as a network, and they link this to Xi Jinping's call in 2017 for a new type of party relations.

The article first reviews domestic literature, then sets out five manifestations of networking: differentiated party types, dense exchanges, varied forms of connection, loose internationalism and routinised disputes. It then identifies four features of the network: parallel yet interwoven paths, unity alongside conflict, a flat and grid-like structure, and internationalism set against sectarianism. It closes with three reflections for the Chinese Communist Party.

The authors report, citing incomplete statistics, more than 400 communist parties, which differ in guiding ideology (Marxism-Leninism, Maoism, Hoxhaism, Trotskyism and others). These parties meet through annual international meetings, regional forums, joint statements and online platforms, but have no central leadership, common programme or binding charter. They cite the 2022 international meeting, which produced two conflicting resolutions on Ukraine, and the 2023 dissolution of the Initiative of Communist and Workers' Parties in Europe, as evidence of persistent dispute. The authors argue that the Soviet-centred "centre–periphery" model has given way to a decentred, flat network. In their reading this network reduces the risk of fragmentation but is held back by sectarian parties that claim Marxist orthodoxy and attack others' national explorations.

Yu and Li conclude that the international communist movement has not disappeared but has taken a new form, which requires a new discourse and disciplinary system in scientific socialism. They judge networking a sign of immature international unity and consider that only "limited unity" is feasible now. They urge the Chinese Communist Party to adopt an outlook centred on itself, to apply the new type of party relations through channels such as the Dialogue with World Political Parties and the World Socialism Forum, and to promote cohesion among communist parties. Read the original if you study contemporary communist parties, the typology of their ideologies, or how Chinese scholars frame the international communist movement and the Party's role in it.
quoteEn: To some extent it can be said that the "networking" of communist parties abroad today is in essence an expression of the immaturity of Marxist parties' exploration of international unity.
quoteZh: 一定程度上可以说，当今国外共产党“网络化”实质是马克思主义政党探索国际联合不成熟的表现。

glossary.explanation: A concept Xi Jinping put forward in 2017 at the CPC Dialogue with World Political Parties. It calls for relations among parties based on seeking common ground while setting aside differences, mutual respect, and mutual learning.

glossary.en: the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
glossary.explanation: The standard Chinese term for the fall of the ruling communist parties in the USSR and Eastern Europe around 1989–1991.

The worldwide movement of communist parties and organisations, from the First International and the Comintern to the present. In Chinese scholarship it is a field of study within scientific socialism.

keywords: International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties

t: Twenty-first-century Marxism in the perspective of the international communist movement
zh: 国际共产主义运动视域中的21世纪马克思主义
paras: Tao Wenzhao takes up a formula from the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), which called Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era "contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism". The article asks what "twenty-first-century Marxism" means and why the label fits this body of thought. Tao answers that the label marks an epoch-making theoretical innovation, grounded in the history of Marxism and of the international communist movement, and that China is its natural centre.

The article is organised in five parts. It analyses in turn the time dimension ("twenty-first century"), the geographical dimension ("world"), the historical tasks that the concept implies, China's responsibility for fulfilling them, and the theoretical standing of the concept within the lineage of Marxism. Tao compares earlier theoretical landmarks, such as Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought, with the way each was named and assessed in Party documents.

Tao argues first that a theory's "era" is not mere calendar time: it is defined by changes in the epoch's themes, revolutionary subjects, contradictions and tasks. Twenty-first-century Marxism should therefore address new themes and contradictions of the century, and Tao notes that the era still needs a precise substantive characterisation. Second, the unstated geographical default is the world, because Marxism is inherently global. Tao points to irreversible globalisation and to a changing contest between the two systems, which the author describes as "the East rising, the West declining" as a trend, while the United States remains stronger than China in the present. Third, Tao holds that the concept must solve problems left open: revolution in developed countries, socialist construction, and coexistence and competition with capitalism. Because the world socialist movement's centre has shifted to China, Tao argues, China's Marxism is the principal form of twenty-first-century Marxism, and some foreign Marxist currents are described as largely confined to the study.

Tao concludes that Xi Jinping Thought, by advancing Marxist theory in many fields and by proposing a community with a shared future for mankind, forms the mainstream of world Marxism in this century. Tao distinguishes "twenty-first-century Marxism" (a proper name for this thought) from "Marxism of the twenty-first century" (the plural Marxisms existing in the period), and says other countries' explorations also have value. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese scholar of the international communist movement justifies the claim that Chinese Marxism leads the world Marxist tradition in this century.
quoteEn: Twenty-first-century Marxism essentially means a Marxism that addresses the new themes of the twenty-first century, resolves its new contradictions, draws on its new forces and fulfils its new mission.
quoteZh: 21世纪马克思主义实质上是指针对21世纪新主题、解决21世纪新矛盾、运用21世纪新力量、完成21世纪新使命的马克思主义。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017. It is presented officially as the latest stage in adapting Marxism to China.
The official name for China's path and system since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership, a socialist market economy and national conditions.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's foreign-policy and global-governance concept, stressing common interests and shared responsibility among nations.

t: The problem of poverty in American society in the 1960s
zh: 20世纪60年代美国社会中的贫困问题
source: China Social Sciences Today (Chinese Social Sciences Net), January 2025
paras: This short newspaper commentary asks why poverty persisted in the United States in the 1960s, despite its postwar economic strength. Li Yun argues that behind the apparent prosperity lay a serious social crisis, and that federal anti-poverty policy could not remove poverty because its institutional roots in inequality were left untouched.

The article proceeds in three parts: poverty as a chronic ailment of American society, the failure to eradicate it fundamentally, and the continuing widening of the wealth gap into the 1970s and later. It draws on Michael Harrington's The Other America, the sociologist Diana Pearce, Lyndon Johnson's reforms and Robert Putnam's Our Kids.

Li identifies Black poverty and the 'feminization of poverty' among single-mother households as the two most visible cases, citing figures on female-headed households among poor families (23% in 1959, 28.5% in 1965). Johnson's 'war on poverty' and 'Great Society', including the 1964 Economic Opportunity Act, education laws, medical aid and aid for families with dependent children, are said to have cut the poverty rate from 22% to 13%. Li nonetheless calls such reforms 'scratching an itch through the boot', leaving many Black Americans in worsening poverty amid racial conflict and urban unrest.

Li concludes that widening inequality, class stratification and the decline of the white blue-collar class have undermined the American Dream and public belief in 'equality of opportunity'. The article contrasts the founding ideals of the Declaration of Independence with this reality. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese academic commentary characterises American poverty and inequality.
quoteEn: Poverty is a chronic ailment plaguing American society; easing the plight of disadvantaged groups through a few reform measures can only be scratching an itch through the boot and cannot eradicate it at root.
quoteZh: 贫困问题是困扰美国社会的一个痼疾，通过一些改革措施来缓解弱势群体的生活窘境也只能是隔靴搔痒，无法从根本上予以消除

t: Three major issues in building Marxist parties from the perspective of the historical course of the international communist movement
zh: 国际共产主义运动历史进程视域下马克思主义政党建设的三个重大问题
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (当代世界与社会主义), 2024 no. 2
paras: Why has the international communist movement alternated between triumphant advances and severe setbacks? Lin Jianhua answers that the decisive factor is the Party, and that the quality of Marxist party-building can be measured by three things: scientific theory, outstanding leaders and iron discipline. The article, published in 2024, treats these as the three major issues running through more than 170 years of the movement since the Communist League (1847) and the Communist Manifesto (1848).

The article is organised in three sections, one for each issue. It draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Stalin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and moves through the Communist League, the First, Second and Third Internationals, the October Revolution, the dissolution of the Soviet Communist Party and the history of the Communist Party of China. Each section ends by linking the historical lessons to the Party's present situation.

On theory, Lin argues that Marxism guides the Party and must develop with its era. Each theoretical breakthrough answered the questions of its time, and the Party prospers when it upholds Marxism's guiding role. In this reading, the Chinese Party's growth and the Soviet Party's dissolution show the contrast. On leaders, Lin grounds the argument in historical materialism: the people make history, but outstanding leaders give direction and cohesion, and upholding their authority is a vital principle. Lin cites the Paris Commune's failure, attributed by Marx and Engels to a lack of centralisation and authority, and the praise given to successive leaders. On discipline, Lin holds that unity of thought underpins organisational unity. Lin attributes the Soviet Party's collapse to abandoning centralised leadership and allowing Party organisations to become autonomous.

Lin concludes that Marxist parties succeed when guided by scientific theory, steered by outstanding leaders and forged by iron discipline. Since the 18th Party Congress (2012), Lin writes, Xi Jinping has been the Party's core and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era its guide. The article presents the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds as the logical outcome of this history, together with full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and the Party's self-reform as the Chinese answer to the problem of historical cycles of rise and decline. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how Chinese scholars frame Party theory, leadership authority and discipline within the history of the communist movement.
quoteEn: The history of the international communist movement has repeatedly shown that the most fundamental measure of the quality and level of party-building is whether the Party has scientific theory, outstanding leaders and iron discipline.
quoteZh: 国际共产主义运动史一再表明，衡量党的建设的质量和水平，最根本的就在于看其是否拥有科学的理论、杰出的领袖和铁的纪律。

glossary.explanation: A formula from the 6th Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021) affirming Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Party Central Committee and the whole Party, and the guiding role of Xi Jinping Thought.
A Party requirement to uphold the authority of General Secretary Xi Jinping as the core and the centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The slogan for the Party's drive since 2012 to tighten discipline, combat corruption and strengthen internal supervision.
Official term for the Party's continuous internal self-correction, presented as the second answer, after popular supervision of government, to the problem of the historical cycle of rise and decline.

t: The idea of self-reform in the perspective of the history of the international communist movement
zh: 国际共运史视域中的自我革命观
paras: Chai and An ask what the 170-year history of the international communist movement shows about the link between a Marxist party's own transformation and the success of social revolution. Taking Xi Jinping's statement that the Party must be bold in carrying out self-reform as their starting point, they argue that Marxist parties have led social revolution through self-reform, and that winning socialism and holding power over the long term require keeping the founding mission and applying full and rigorous self-governance of the Party to the end.

The article moves chronologically through four stages. It begins with Marx and Engels, the Communist League and the Communist Manifesto. It then turns to Lenin's ideas on party building, to the Soviet and East European experience, and finally to the Communist Party of China from its founding to the present. It also surveys the Communist Parties of Vietnam, Cuba, Laos, Russia, Brazil and South Africa, and the Workers' Party of Korea.

The authors note that Marx and Engels never used the term "self-reform" (自我革命). They argue, however, that the "two ruptures" in the Manifesto, with traditional property relations and traditional ideas, imply that communists must remould themselves while transforming the world. In their reading, Lenin supplied the substance: theoretical guidance, a vanguard that stays advanced, pure and tied to the masses, democratic centralism with criticism and self-criticism, vigilance against bureaucracy, and strict discipline. The Soviet case is treated as the negative lesson. Stalin's extreme centralisation and personality cult are said to have cut the party off from the people. Gorbachev's "democratisation" and pluralism then replaced self-reform and led to the party's dissolution in 1991. On the Chinese side, the authors trace Mao Zedong's rectification campaigns, Deng Xiaoping's "the Party must govern itself" and the post-2012 answer to the "historical cycle" problem, which they call self-reform as the second answer after supervision by the people.

The authors conclude that a strong Marxist party is the decisive condition for the proletarian cause. They argue that the Chinese Party's self-reform offers a reference for other communist parties, several of which they say have drawn on it. They call for treating full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as a permanent task for solving the problems unique to a large party. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-theoretical account of how the history of the communist movement is used to justify self-reform, including its reading of the Soviet collapse and of other parties' experience.
quoteEn: The history of the international communist movement proves that the most fundamental and critical condition for the proletarian cause to flourish is a strong Marxist party, and that self-reform is the key to the party leading social revolution to victory.
quoteZh: 国际共运历史证明，无产阶级事业能够兴旺发达，最根本、最关键的就在于有一个强大的马克思主义政党，自我革命是党领导社会革命取得胜利的关键。

glossary.explanation: A concept stressed by Xi Jinping since 2016–17 for the Party's ability to correct its own faults and purge corruption. The article reads it back into the classical Marxist tradition.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party-discipline and anti-corruption drive and Party-building programme pursued since the 18th Party Congress (2012).
The Leninist organisational principle combining internal discussion and elections with binding decisions and subordination of minority to majority and lower to higher bodies.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party

t: Grand theft capital: the increasing exploitation and robbery of the US working class
zh: 资本大劫掠：美国工人阶级面临日益严重的剥削和洗劫
orig: Monthly Review, vol. 75, no. 1, 2023 (original title "Grand Theft Capital: The Increasing Exploitation and Robbery of the U.S. Working Class")
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2024 no. 3
paras: This is an abridged Chinese translation of an article by the American scholars Fred Magdoff and John Bellamy Foster, first published in Monthly Review in 2023. The authors ask why the US working class has grown steadily worse off over roughly half a century. They argue that the cause is a class war waged by capital against labour, which began as a response to a structural crisis of monopoly-finance capitalism and has intensified both ordinary exploitation and outright appropriation of workers' income.

The article opens with capitalism's long history of plundering land, resources and human life, then sets out the postwar 'golden age' and its end. It moves through the neoliberal turn, the assault on trade unions, and the conditions of US workers in the first two decades of the twenty-first century. It closes with estimates of income redistributed upward and a brief note on renewed labour organising.

Following Baran and Sweezy's Monopoly Capital, the authors treat stagnation as the normal condition of monopoly capitalism and the postwar boom as the exception that needs explaining. In their account, capital met stagnation by raising interest rates, financialising the economy, concentrating firms, cutting taxes for the rich, offshoring production and weakening unions. They describe wage theft, misclassification of workers as contractors, non-compete clauses, understaffing, global labour arbitrage and a regressive tax system. They cite figures showing that real pay for production and non-supervisory workers rose only 15 per cent in forty years while productivity rose 75 per cent. A RAND study they cite puts the income 'lost' by the bottom 90 per cent between 1975 and 2018 at more than 47 trillion dollars.

The authors conclude that the real class struggle is the one capital has waged against labour, and they quote Warren Buffett's remark that his class is winning it. They suggest that higher taxes on the rich and lower military spending could fund jobs and social programmes. Citing Bernie Sanders, they note that workers are now reorganising, and they hold that only a mass uprising from below, like that of the 1930s, can build the power needed for a fairer society. Read the original if you want a Marxist account of US inequality, financialisation and union decline, with a dense set of statistics, in a version that Chinese journals chose to translate.
quoteEn: But the real class struggle, which has lasted more than half a century, is the struggle launched by capital against labour.
quoteZh: 但持续了半个多世纪的真正的阶级斗争是资本对劳工发起的斗争。

glossary.explanation: The stage of capitalism dominated by a few large firms, analysed by Paul Baran and Paul Sweezy in Monopoly Capital (1966). The authors build on this theory to argue that stagnation is its normal state.
The authors' term for the shift since the 1970s toward deregulation, tax cuts for the rich, attacks on unions and a closer fusion of state and capital.
The growing weight of debt, speculation and financial profit in the economy. The authors treat it as a response to stagnation, not a cure for it.

The practice of shifting production to low-wage countries so as to profit from the gap between wage differences and productivity differences. The authors link it to the exploitation of workers in the Global South.

t: The US "Summit for Democracy" and new challenges to China's ideological security
zh: 美国“民主峰会”与我国意识形态安全的新挑战
paras: Wang Jianfeng asks what the Biden administration's global "Summit for Democracy" is for and what it means for China. The article argues that the summits, three of which had been held by March 2024, are a tool of ideological war against China and other states, and that they create a series of new external challenges for China's ideological security. Wang presents them as part of a wider "new Cold War" strategy aimed at preserving declining US hegemony.

The article has four parts. It first explains the background to the summits: the role of "democracy" in sustaining US global leadership, and the need to restore America's "beacon of democracy" image after political polarisation and the Capitol riot. It then analyses the summits' "normative" and "functional" aspects, and identifies three inherent flaws. It ends with the pressure on China's ideological security and proposed responses at macro, meso and micro levels.

Wang argues that the summits are mainly about values promotion, with practical functions subordinate to that aim. The article describes the "generalisation of democracy": technology controls, supply-chain restructuring and the Ukraine crisis are framed as democracy-versus-autocracy issues so that allies share costs. It also describes funding schemes under the Presidential Initiative for Democratic Renewal, which Wang says target trade unionists, labour groups and NGOs as potential agents of "colour revolutions". The three flaws are a single "American-style" model of democracy, vague and interest-driven criteria for invitations (Wang cites Freedom House ratings to show inconsistencies), and a false democracy–autocracy narrative that ignores the internal causes of democratic decline.

On China, Wang says the summits challenge its ideological security through a contest over core values, set against the "common values of all humanity", and through a contest over development models, aimed at Chinese modernization. Wang calls for a holistic ideological security outlook under the overall national security concept, stronger international communication combining official and civil channels, and tighter online supervision and vigilance against foreign NGOs. The article also warns against being drawn into a full-scale ideological competition as the Soviet Union was. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist-institution scholar frames US democracy promotion as ideological confrontation and what countermeasures are proposed.
quoteEn: The "Summit for Democracy" is a product of the US viewing strategic competition with China through a Cold War mindset, and an indispensable ideological link in the Biden administration's opening of an all-domain "new Cold War" against China.
quoteZh: “民主峰会”是美国以冷战思维审视对华战略竞争的产物，它是拜登政府开启对华全领域“新冷战”在意识形态领域不可或缺的重要一环。

glossary.explanation: A component of China's political security concept, referring to protecting the dominance of Marxism and socialist values against perceived external and internal ideological challenges.
A framework put forward by Xi Jinping in 2014 that treats security as covering many fields, including politics, economy, culture, society and cyberspace.
The official term for China's own path of modernization, presented as distinct from Western models.
A formula promoted by Xi Jinping since 2015 naming peace, development, equity, justice, democracy and freedom as shared values, offered as an alternative to "universal values" of the West.
Term used in Chinese official discourse for Western-backed mass movements that overthrow governments, such as those in post-Soviet states.

t: The basic meaning, major impact and multidimensional evaluation of the Bolshevization of the Communist International
zh: 共产国际布尔什维克化的基本内涵、重大影响与多维评价
paras: Gong Yutao asks how the Comintern's slogan of "Bolshevization" should be understood and assessed. Writing in Contemporary World and Socialism (2024), Gong argues that it was a reflection of a major strategic turn by the Communist International, that it became a movement affecting every section, and that its positive effects were the mainstream, although its negative effects must be seriously reflected upon.

The article has three parts. The first traces how the Fifth Comintern Congress (1924) launched the slogan and how the Fifth Enlarged Plenum of the Executive Committee (1925) systematised it. The second examines the impact on Western communist parties (Germany, France, Italy, Britain) and then on the Communist Party of China, from the early 1920s through the Zunyi Meeting and the 1942 Rectification Movement. The third offers an evaluation of the slogan's origins, its positive effects and its negative effects.

Gong shows that the 1924 congress defined Bolshevization as transplanting the internationally valid elements of Russian Bolshevism, not copying Russian experience mechanically. The 1925 plenum added eight requirements, including combating right and ultra-left deviations, theoretical training in Marxism-Leninism, winning the masses and allies, factory cells, discipline, and loyalty to the Comintern's leadership. Gong's account of Germany describes Comintern pressure that removed Arkadi Maslow's leadership, and of Italy describes Gramsci replacing Amadeo Bordiga with Comintern backing. For the Chinese party, Gong notes that Bolshevization became central after the Sixth Congress (1928) and brought leftism and dogmatism. After Zunyi, Mao Zedong's calls and the sinification of Marxism gave it a Chinese form.

In evaluation, Gong holds that the slogan met the Comintern's needs as a "revolutionary international" and a "unified world party", and that it helped young parties mature and strengthened unity. Gong also criticises an inflated reading of right-wing danger, hostility towards social democrats, weakened independence of sections, the sanctification of Russian experience, and the replacement of leaders (50 parties' main leaders in the late 1920s and early 1930s, according to the article). These problems are said to be products of their circumstances and should be neither ignored nor exaggerated. Read the original if you study the Comintern, the history of the Chinese Communist Party's organisational development, or how Chinese scholars currently evaluate this history.
quoteEn: Overall, the positive effects of the Comintern's Bolshevization were the mainstream, and they can be seen even more clearly from the Comintern's 24-year history and from the overall history of the building and struggles of the communist parties of various countries.
quoteZh: 总体而言，共产国际的布尔什维克化的积极效应是主流，从共产国际24年的历史及各国共产党整体的建设史、斗争史更能看到布尔什维克化的积极效应。

glossary.explanation: A Comintern slogan and campaign launched in 1924 to remodel member parties on the organisational and ideological lines of the Russian Bolshevik party. It stressed centralism, discipline and loyalty to the Comintern.
The international organisation of communist parties founded in Moscow in 1919 and dissolved in 1943. Its member parties were called sections.
The Chinese Communist Party's term for adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions, a theme formulated by Mao Zedong in the late 1930s.

A January 1935 Party leadership meeting during the Long March, regarded in Party history as the turning point at which Mao Zedong's leadership emerged and the Party became less dependent on Comintern direction.
An ideological and organisational campaign in the Chinese Communist Party, centred on 1942–45 in Yan'an, aimed at unifying the Party around Mao Zedong's line and combating dogmatism.

t: New explorations of the Communist Party of Belgium on the road to socialism in the 21st century
zh: 21世纪比利时共产党对社会主义道路的新探索
paras: Guo Taiying asks how the Communist Party of Belgium (founded 1921) has sought a path to socialism suited to national conditions since 2000, and what its experience shows about communist parties in Western capitalist states. The author argues that the party has revised its theory and adjusted its practice, but that results have been limited and its prospects are not promising.

The article has three parts. It first divides the party's history into three stages: early exploration from 1921 to 1945, a period of zigzag and drift in the Cold War from the 1950s to the 1980s, and adjustment and transition from the 1990s onwards. It then examines new theoretical positions, and finally the party's political practice in elections, mass work and inter-party relations. Guo draws on party congress decisions and statements, including the 36th Congress of 2018.

On theory, Guo reports that the party describes capitalism as in systemic crisis (economic, technological, ecological and military) and demands that Belgium leave NATO and the EU, which it calls an imperialist bloc serving monopoly capital. The party remains committed to Marxism-Leninism but reinterprets core concepts: it replaces "dictatorship of the proletariat" with "workers' power" and "class struggle" with "class solidarity". It envisions a gradual, democratic, multi-party, federal and self-managed socialism, rejects Belgian-style federalism as a drift towards confederalism, and treats religion dialectically. In practice, Guo shows, the party stays on the peaceful parliamentary road. It runs in electoral alliances with the Workers' Party of Belgium, supports strikes and trade unions, and joins the International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties and the World Anti-Imperialist Platform. It also issues statements on Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Palestine.

Guo concludes that the party's search for goals fitting the times, its self-transformation, its parliamentary struggle, its mass line and its inter-party contacts have somewhat improved its position. The party has held no parliamentary seats since 1985, and the author judges its achievements unremarkable. Its future depends on seizing opportunities and strengthening itself. Read the original if you study European communist parties, the revision of core Marxist-Leninist concepts in Western Europe, or the Chinese scholarly reading of foreign communist parties.
quoteEn: The Communist Party of Belgium's exploration of theoretical and practical paths to socialism undoubtedly carries some practical lessons.
quoteZh: 比利时共产党探索社会主义的理论和实践路径，无疑具有一定的现实启示。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist concept for working-class political power in the transition from capitalism to socialism. The article reports that the Belgian party now prefers the term "workers' power" because it sees "dictatorship" as negative and outdated.

A principle developed in the Chinese Communist Party that stresses close ties with the masses and leading their movements. The article applies it to the Belgian party's work in strikes and labour movements.

glossary.zh: 世界共产党和工人党国际会议
glossary.pinyin: shìjiè gòngchǎndǎng hé gōngréndǎng guójì huìyì
glossary.en: International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties
glossary.explanation: An annual international forum of communist and workers' parties on a shared Marxist basis. The article says the Belgian party attends every year.

t: African left-wing ruling parties' joint self-strengthening in a multidimensional perspective
st: The case of the "six sister parties" of Southern Africa
zh: 多维视阈下的非洲左翼执政党联合自强
zhSub: 以南部非洲六姊妹党为例
paras: Against the backdrop of a wave of de-Westernising transformation in Africa, Deng Yanting asks how six left-wing ruling parties in Southern Africa have built a joint, transnational political bloc and what it means for African development. The six are the Revolutionary Party of Tanzania (CCM), the ANC (South Africa), the MPLA (Angola), FRELIMO (Mozambique), SWAPO (Namibia) and ZANU-PF (Zimbabwe), known as the "six sister parties". Deng argues that their joint self-strengthening grew out of shared history, now underpins Africa's autonomous development, and still faces internal and external risks.

The article has three parts. The first traces the bloc through three stages: revolutionary friendship during the liberation struggles, collective resistance to neoliberalism after the Cold War, and collective reflection on governance problems since the early 2000s. The second part sets out the bloc's present significance for regional integration, for China–Africa ties and for a revival of socialism in Africa. The third part examines internal differences among the parties and pressure from the United States and the West.

Deng's central claim is that Nyerere's Pan-Africanist idea of "Ujamaa", shared socialist convictions and armed struggle against colonialism, racism and imperialism created a bond that later shaped resistance to "Washington Consensus" reforms. Deng cites Zambia's United National Independence Party, which lost power after the 1991 turn to multiparty politics, as a warning. The six parties kept their ideology, party organisation and public ownership, and Deng credits this with making Southern Africa the continent's most stable sub-region. Deng presents the Southern African Development Community as party-based integration, and describes China's support, from the Tanzania–Zambia Railway to the Julius Nyerere Leadership School, as strengthening the bloc. Deng also names risks: South Africa's heavier governing burden and the ANC's loss of its parliamentary majority in 2024, Angola's oil-driven governance strains, and Western "cognitive warfare", opposition backing and selective economic incentives and sanctions.

Deng concludes that ideological and institutional advantages, together with the parties' self-reform centred on their peoples, will let them overcome these constraints. In Deng's view the bloc will keep acting as a model for African unity and a base for Chinese modernization to support African revival and the Global South. Read the original if you study the Chinese academic view of African left-wing parties, party-to-party ties between China and Africa, or Southern African politics from a socialist perspective.
quoteEn: The revolutionary friendship among the six sister parties is in essence a political consensus formed through the organic fusion and joint advance of the six countries' national liberation movements.
quoteZh: 六姊妹党间的革命友谊本质上是六国民族解放运动在有机融合与一体推进中凝聚的政治共识

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's own path of modernization, promoted by the Communist Party since 2021 as an alternative to Western models.
A term for developing countries, used in Chinese official discourse to describe a group of states whose collective rise is said to be reshaping world order.
Julius Nyerere's Tanzanian version of African socialism, built on communal village life and self-reliance, set out in the 1967 Arusha Declaration.

t: Challenges and strategic adjustments of the Communist Party of the Netherlands in pursuing socialism
zh: 荷兰共产党追求社会主义过程中面临的挑战及策略调整
paras: Wang Yanlong asks how the Communist Party of the Netherlands (CPN) shaped its political position, defended socialist values and balanced socialism with democratic ideas across the twentieth century. The article argues that the party's history shows a political organisation adapting to changing international and domestic conditions. Wang holds that the party survived as long as it adjusted its policies, organisation and ideas, and that its legacy outlived its dissolution.

The article follows the party chronologically in four stages. It begins with the CPN's emergence from the left wing of the Social Democratic Workers' Party and its early aims. It then treats the Second World War, when the party moved underground and led resistance. A third section covers the Cold War, from postwar peak through de-Stalinisation and the Prague Spring to decline and merger. The last section examines the party's legacy in GroenLinks (the Green Left) and in Dutch politics, followed by a brief conclusion.

Wang's central claim is that the party repeatedly redefined its socialism under external pressure. In its early years it stressed class struggle, the dictatorship of the proletariat and the Comintern line. Under Nazi occupation it joined socialism to anti-fascism and democracy, set up underground networks, helped hide Jews, and organised the February 1941 Amsterdam strike. After the Hungarian events of 1956 and especially the Prague Spring of 1968, Wang says, the party questioned the Soviet model, turned to a more democratic and plural socialism, and allied with trade unions, students, feminists and peace and environmental movements. Wang attributes the party's decline in the 1980s to the collapse of Soviet-bloc socialism, a shrinking working class, a rising middle class and internal splits between reformers and traditionalists. The article cites a fall in membership from 150,000 to 6,000 and a vote of 0.6 per cent in 1986.

Wang concludes that parties must respond to their environment and also renew themselves in organisation and ideas. The article credits the CPN, dissolved in 1991, with lasting influence through GroenLinks, which Wang says carried on its commitments to social justice, environmental protection and intra-party democracy. Wang also links the party to Dutch welfare, housing, education and employment policy and to popular participation. Read the original if you want a detailed, sympathetic Chinese account of a small Western European communist party and its Cold War transformation.
quoteEn: The history of the CPN shows that a political party must not only respond to changes in its external environment but also keep renewing and adjusting itself from within.
quoteZh: 荷共的历史表明，政党不仅需要对外部环境变化作出反应，还需要在内部进行不断的自我更新和调适。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist-Leninist concept for working-class political rule during the transition from capitalism to socialism. Wang says the CPN endorsed it in its early years.
The Communist International, founded in Moscow in 1919 to coordinate communist parties worldwide. The CPN joined in 1919 and, in Wang's account, followed its line until the Second World War.
The 1968 reform movement in Czechoslovakia, ended by a Soviet-led military intervention. Wang treats it as the decisive event in the CPN's turn away from the Soviet model.

t: Lenin's merits and historical contributions are indelible
zh: 列宁的功勋和历史贡献是不可磨灭的！
paras: Marking the centenary of Lenin's death in 2024, Cheng Enfu argues that Lenin's achievements and historical contributions are indelible and that Leninism remains relevant in the twenty-first century. The short commentary first appeared in Guizhou Daily under the title "Commemorating the 100th anniversary of Lenin's death".

Cheng moves from Lenin's analysis of imperialism, through the October Revolution and Soviet construction, to the Communist International. He then turns to the present world situation and to the relation between "war and revolution" and "peace and development".

Cheng recalls Lenin's account of imperialism as monopoly, parasitic and moribund capitalism, and his law of uneven economic and political development, which Cheng links to the First World War. Cheng credits Lenin with leading the revolution in backward Russia and, afterwards, with building socialism in one country amid capitalist encirclement. Citing Deng Xiaoping's remarks of 1984 and 1990, Cheng holds that "peace and development" does not negate Lenin's "war and revolution" but is dialectically united with it. In Cheng's account, today's "new imperialism" is an international-monopoly stage of capitalism and a hegemonic system, yet the twenty-first century is an era of workers defending peace, of rapid socialist development and of building a community with a shared future for mankind.

Cheng concludes that Leninism guided revolution and construction in Soviet Russia and internationally, and ranks as international Marxist theory alongside Marxism. Cheng calls on all Marxist-Leninists to re-examine the value of Lenin's Communist International amid "changes unseen in a century". Read the original if you want a brief example of how a leading Chinese Marxist economist commemorates Lenin and links him to Deng Xiaoping's thesis on the era.
quoteEn: Leninism not only guided the proletarian revolution and construction in Soviet Russia to victory, but also guided the international proletarian revolution and construction; it is an international Marxist theory standing alongside Marxism.
quoteZh: 列宁主义不仅指导苏俄无产阶级革命和建设取得了胜利，而且指导国际无产阶级革命和建设，是与马克思主义并列的国际马克思主义理论。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2012–13. It calls for countries to cooperate on shared global interests and development.

glossary.pinyin: bǎi nián wèi yǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.literal: great changes not seen in a hundred years
glossary.explanation: An official phrase, used by Xi Jinping since about 2017, for a perceived shift in the global balance of power and order.

t: The Party's self-reform in the perspective of the history of the international communist movement
zh: 国际共运史视域中的自我革命观
paras: Writing in 2024, Chai Shangjin and An Yaqin ask what the 170-plus years of the international communist movement show about why Marxist parties succeed or fail in power. Their thesis is that Marxist parties have led social revolution through self-reform, and that a ruling party can secure a complete victory for socialism and long-term rule only by keeping to its founding mission and carrying full and rigorous self-governance of the Party through to the end.

The article moves chronologically through four stages. It begins with Marx and Engels and the founding of the proletarian party, from the Communist League to the Communist Manifesto. It then turns to Lenin's thinking on party-building after the Bolsheviks took power. Next it sets the Soviet Union under Stalin and Gorbachev, and the communist parties of Eastern Europe, against those of Vietnam, North Korea, Cuba and Laos. It ends with the Communist Party of China, from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping, and with the influence of its experience on other parties.

The authors contend that Marx and Engels never used the term "self-reform" (自我革命) but supplied its principles: the Manifesto's "two ruptures" with traditional property relations and ideas imply that communists must remould themselves while changing the world. They present Lenin as systematising these principles into four requirements: theoretical guidance, the vanguard's advanced character and purity, democratic centralism with criticism and self-criticism, and strict organisation and discipline. In their account, Stalin's over-centralisation, suppression of dissent and personality cult cut the Soviet party off from the people, and Gorbachev's "democratisation" and ideological pluralism replaced self-reform and led to the party's dissolution in 1991.

The authors conclude that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Chinese party has given a "second answer", self-reform, to the question of escaping the historical cycle of rise and fall, alongside Mao's answer of supervision by the people. They claim this experience offers a model that parties in Vietnam, Cuba, Laos, Russia, Brazil and South Africa have drawn on. They call for treating full and rigorous self-governance of the Party as a permanent strategic task, since the "unique difficulties of a large party" require a long process. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-theoretical account of how the history of the international communist movement is used to justify the doctrine of self-reform.
quoteEn: The history of the international communist movement proves that the proletarian cause can flourish above all because there is a strong Marxist party, and that self-reform is the key to the party leading social revolution to victory.
quoteZh: 国际共运历史证明，无产阶级事业能够兴旺发达，最根本、最关键的就在于有一个强大的马克思主义政党，自我革命是党领导社会革命取得胜利的关键。

glossary.explanation: A concept stressed by Xi Jinping meaning that the Party rids itself of problems that harm its advanced character and purity, through its own efforts. Official English texts render it "the Party's self-reform".

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: The policy, prominent since the 18th Party Congress (2012), of tightening Party discipline, anti-corruption work and organisational standards.

The organisational principle of communist parties combining internal discussion and election with binding obedience to majority and higher-level decisions. The authors credit Lenin with first using the term.
A Party slogan about the founding aspiration of seeking the people's happiness and national rejuvenation; here it paraphrases the phrase the authors use for keeping to the Party's original purpose.

keywords: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
