The 2014 revision of the Trade Union Law removed the right to strike from the union's functions, and more than 600 worker-founded unions were dissolved. Kang argues that workers therefore turned to strikes and demonstrations rather than bargaining. Independent unions and left organisations, notably the banned Communist Party and the Socialist Movement of Kazakhstan, are credited with raising demands such as nationalisation and workers' control, not only wages. The author also warns that, with about two-thirds of workers outside official unions, strikes risk disorder and exploitation by outside forces, and cites the "colour revolution" label applied to January 2022.

Kang draws three lessons: coordinate action across sectors and regions, link the workers' movement with the socialist movement, and prevent strikes from being turned into "colour revolutions". Four obstacles are listed: the lack of a legal communist party, unions that cannot meet workers' demands (where the author notes John Foster's suggestion of working inside official unions), the difficulty of organising against transnational firms, and legal and coercive repression. Kang sees little sign that the 2022 constitutional reform will change labour relations. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of post-Soviet labour struggles in Central Asia, with data on privatisation, union law and the January 2022 events.
quoteEn: Worker-founded unions are lacking and most workers are unwilling to join the official unions, so in labour disputes workers tend to pursue their demands through strikes and demonstrations rather than through bargaining and signing labour agreements.
quoteZh: 工人自建工会缺乏，而大部分工人又不愿意加入官方工会，因此当发生劳资纠纷时，工人更倾向于通过罢工、示威等行动来实现自己的诉求，而非进行劳资谈判、签订劳资协议。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Chinese and Russian official and academic discourse for popular uprisings that are portrayed as engineered by foreign powers to change a government. Here it is applied to the January 2022 events in Kazakhstan.

t: New viewpoints and significance of the 22nd International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties
zh: 第22次共产党和工人党国际会议的新观点和价值意蕴
paras: This article examines the 22nd International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties, hosted by the Communist Party of Cuba in Havana on 27–29 October 2022. According to the author, 145 delegates from 78 parties in 60 countries attended. Luo argues that the meeting gave communist parties a platform for exchange and strengthened the international standing of world socialism. The author also stresses that it exposed unresolved disagreements over the Russia–Ukraine conflict.

The article first sets the context: an intensifying imperialist offensive led by the United States, and the Covid-19 pandemic. In this context Luo credits socialist-led states and non-ruling communist parties with advancing the socialist movement. It then reports the meeting's 'new viewpoints' under five heads: the condition of the working class during the pandemic, the nature and causes of the Russia–Ukraine conflict, calls for international solidarity, support for Cuba and other peoples' struggles, and a joint Action Plan. A closing section assesses the meeting's value and shortcomings.

Much of the argument consists of positions taken by individual parties. On the pandemic, parties from Greece, Spain, Brazil and Mexico, among others, are reported as holding that capitalism's profit-first logic and its drive to extract surplus value worsened workers' conditions. On the Russia–Ukraine conflict, the author sets out two camps: parties that call it an inter-imperialist war, and parties that deny Russia is imperialist and describe the war as a response to NATO expansion. Two opposing resolutions were adopted, each signed by about 20 parties with no overlap. Luo also describes the shift of communist cooperation from 'one road, one centre' to a model of equality, independence, voluntary participation and plural levels.

Luo concludes that the meeting's value lies in mutual learning, in raising the international voice of socialist forces and in drawing parties together. The author lists three weaknesses: differences of theory and stance still divide the parties, the means of reaching the stated goals remain vague, and the meeting's function needs strengthening, since some delegates doubt its role. Luo calls for further efforts to narrow differences and build broader consensus against imperialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how parties in the international communist movement positioned themselves on the pandemic, the Ukraine war and solidarity with Cuba.
quoteEn: The meeting was rich in content and produced broad consensus, but there are also aspects that remain to be improved.
quoteZh: 此次会议内容丰富，形成了广泛共识，但也存在有待改善和提升之处。

glossary.zh: 共产党和工人党国际会议
glossary.en: International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties
glossary.explanation: An annual or regular gathering of communist and workers' parties from many countries, held in a different host country each time. The 22nd meeting took place in Havana in 2022.

keywords: International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties

t: A scientific demonstration of the decisive significance of the communist ideal
zh: 共产主义理想决定性意义的科学论证
paras: Hou Huiqin takes up the claim that the communist ideal is only a "result" of historical events, a distant "other shore" and not a real force, so that it plays no decisive role in history. Hou argues that this claim rests on a crude reading of historical materialism, and that the ideal's decisive role can be established scientifically, in theory and in practice. Citing Xi Jinping, Hou treats wavering ideals and convictions as the most dangerous kind of wavering for a Marxist party.

The article has three parts. The first sets out the basic theory: the dialectic of matter and consciousness, the two senses of "determining" and the two senses of "reaction". The second argues that Marxism created a scientific form of belief, after surveying earlier religious and traditional Chinese forms. The third examines the features of communist belief, its link to Chinese modernization, and the standards and mechanisms for testing Party members' convictions.

Drawing on Engels, Hou separates economics as determining "in the last instance" from the actual course of history, where politics, culture and ideas can be decisive. Hou argues that Western "economic determinism" is aimed at the communist ideal. Hou distinguishes a spontaneous agency, such as capitalist production, from agency guided by a scientific worldview, which can accelerate history. In Hou's account, Marx's critique of German ideology, of the modern state and of commodity fetishism resolved the two keys to scientific belief: the knowability of the thing-in-itself and the unity of relative and absolute truth. This, Hou says, grounds a belief based on the unity of working-class and human interests.

Hou describes communist belief as real, because it runs through the transition process, as staged, like a relay, and as lofty, because it ends humanity's "prehistory". Hou criticises Popper and Hayek for rejecting conscious historical creation, and presents Chinese modernization as conscious modernization under Party leadership, as against Western spontaneous modernization. In peacetime, Hou proposes loyalty to the Party as the test of conviction, applied through the "key minority" of leading cadres, learning and supervision systems, and the Party's self-reform, with a stated target of "two-faced" officials. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Chinese Marxist philosopher links the epistemology of belief to Party discipline and ideological work.
quoteEn: This draws an important theoretical boundary: the determining role of the economy is only the standpoint from which to grasp historical necessity, and is not the actual historical process itself.
quoteZh: 这里划出了一个重大的理论边界，即经济的决定作用只是认识历史客观必然性的立脚点，并不是现实的历史过程本身。

glossary.explanation: The official term, prominent since the 20th Party Congress (2022), for China's own path of modernization led by the Party, which official texts contrast with Western modernization.
An official formula for the Party's efforts to correct itself and keep its vitality, presented as the counterpart of its leadership of social revolution.
Official term for leading cadres, especially top officials at provincial and ministerial level, who are the main target of Party discipline and ideological education.
A term used in Party discourse for officials who profess loyalty in public but act otherwise in private.

t: The Communist Party of China's major contributions to the international communist movement since the 18th Party Congress
zh: 论十八大以来中国共产党对国际共产主义运动的重大贡献
source: Scientific Socialism (科学社会主义), 2023 no. 2
paras: Zhuo Mingliang asks how the international communist movement should be assessed three decades after the collapse of the Soviet Union and the upheavals in Eastern Europe, and what the Communist Party of China (CPC) has contributed since the 18th Party Congress (2012). The article argues that the movement's condition should be judged not by the number of ruling communist parties but by the real influence and guiding power of existing socialist states. On that basis it describes a situation of an "overall ebb" alongside a "local high tide", the latter being the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era.

The article has three parts. The first sets out five ways in which the CPC has raised its standing in the movement. The second surveys the roughly 950 communist organisations in over 130 countries, classified by relation to state power, membership size, guiding ideology, attitude towards China and choice of revolutionary road. The third turns to what the CPC should do to promote the movement in the twenty-first century, drawing on lessons from the Soviet period and on statements by foreign communist figures.

In the first part, Zhuo credits the CPC with advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, including Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It also credits the Party with building a community with a shared future for mankind, opposing hegemonism, hosting party-to-party exchanges, and winning favourable assessments from foreign communist parties, which the author illustrates with statements from several of them. The survey stresses diversity and division: parties follow Marxism-Leninism, Maoism, Trotskyism and other lines, and differ sharply on whether China is socialist. Zhuo reads the overall trend as combining independent national paths with growing calls for international unity.

Zhuo concludes that the CPC, as the world's largest ruling party, should supply a "CPC answer" for the movement's revival. The author calls for avoiding the great-party chauvinism attributed to the Soviet Communist Party, and for leading by example rather than by command. Concrete proposals include a "twenty-first-century internationalism", deeper ties with international communist and left organisations, wider forms of party cooperation, an international coordinating body of Marxist parties and a "community with a shared future for communist parties worldwide". Read the original if you want a Party-affiliated account of how Chinese scholars map the world's communist parties and envisage the CPC's role among them.
quoteEn: The situation of the international communist movement should be judged not by the number of countries ruled by communist parties, but by the real international influence of existing socialist states and their power to lead humanity's future development.
quoteZh: 判断国际共产主义运动是处于何种形势不应是共产党执政国家数量的多少，而是由现有社会主义国家所产生的实际国际影响力和对人类未来发展的引领力来衡量的

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The CPC's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017. Party documents describe it as Marxism of the twenty-first century.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2012–13, calling for shared responsibility and cooperation among states. Party texts present it as China's contribution to global governance.
The official name for China's current path since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership and public ownership with market mechanisms.
The author's term for the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics, set against an "overall ebb" of the international communist movement.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Party-building thought in "Left-Wing" Communism: An Infantile Disorder and its contemporary implications
zh: 《共产主义运动中的“左派”幼稚病》中的党建思想及其当代启示
source: Journal of Ningbo University (Humanities Edition), 2023 no. 3
paras: Wang Youchen and Zhao Feng ask what Lenin's 1920 pamphlet "Left-Wing" Communism: An Infantile Disorder contributes to the theory of proletarian party building, and what it offers the Communist Party of China today. They argue that, beyond guiding the new communist parties of its time, the work sets out general principles on discipline, theory, leadership and tactics that can inform the new great project of Party building in the new era.

The article has three parts. It first sets the historical background: after the October Revolution, ultra-left sectarianism and adventurism appeared in the European and American workers' movements, including refusal to join parliaments and slogans such as "down with the leaders" and "abolish the party". It then reconstructs four strands of Lenin's Party-building thought. It closes with four lessons for the contemporary Chinese Communist Party.

In the authors' reading, Lenin's four strands are: iron discipline and theoretical construction; a struggle on two fronts against "Left" and Right opportunism; the authority of leaders; and correct strategy and tactics, including reasoned compromise. The authors stress that Lenin's discipline rests on democracy and combines voluntary and compulsory elements. They also stress that leadership authority is exercised by a stable collective, not an individual, and that Lenin distinguishes revolutionary compromise from the compromise of traitors. From this the authors draw four implications. Discipline-building should be systematic, linked to ideological education, the mass line and the Party's political line. The Party should guard against "Left" deviation first while watching for Right deviation in opposing it. The Two Upholds should be realised in both knowledge and action, avoiding personality cults and blind adulation. Finally, the Party should promote inner-Party harmony by allowing principled yet flexible compromise on inner-Party contradictions, which the authors treat as non-antagonistic.

The authors conclude that the Chinese Party's approach to Party building stands in a continuous line with Lenin's pamphlet. Learning from it, they say, can widen and deepen Party building and support theoretical innovation and practical breakthroughs. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Party-theory scholarship in 2023 draws on a Leninist text to support current positions on discipline, the Two Upholds and inner-Party harmony.
quoteEn: The Party's political line in the new period should be made the "yardstick" of Party discipline building, strengthening the guidance of political strategy and tactics over it and firming up the value orientation that discipline building serves that political line.
quoteZh: 要把新时期党的政治路线作为党的纪律建设的“标尺”，强化党的纪律建设的政治战略和政治策略引领，坚定党的纪律建设为新时期党的政治路线服务的价值导向。

glossary.explanation: A Party formula, formalised around 2018 to 2019, requiring Party members to firmly uphold Xi Jinping's core position in the Central Committee and the whole Party, and the Central Committee's authority and centralised, unified leadership.
A Party principle, associated with Mao Zedong, that the Party must draw on the masses' views and return to them, and keep close ties with the people.

A concept first put forward at the Sixth Plenum of the 16th Central Committee (2006). It stresses unity, and resolving inner-Party contradictions without escalating them, as a basis for social harmony.

t: The major contributions of the Communist Party of China to the international communist movement since the 18th Party Congress
zh: 论十八大以来中国共产党对国际共产主义运动的重大贡献
source: Scientific Socialism (科学社会主义), 2023 no. 2
paras: Zhuo Mingliang and Tan Guoqing ask what the Communist Party of China (CPC) has contributed to the international communist movement since the 18th Party Congress (2012), and what it should do next. They argue that the movement is currently marked by a 'general ebb' alongside a 'local high tide'. In their account, the 'local high tide' is the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics, which they call the movement's main 'growth point' since the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe.

The article has three parts. The first lists five contributions of the CPC in the new era. The second surveys the roughly 950 communist organisations in over 130 countries, sorted by relation to state power, membership, guiding ideology, attitude towards China and choice of revolutionary path. The third sets out how the CPC should advance the movement in the twenty-first century, from historical review to concrete mechanisms. The authors draw on statements by foreign communist figures, including Mick Kelly, Michael Hooper, Mincho Minchev and Mauro Alboresi.

The authors' five contributions are: advancing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as its result; promoting a community with a shared future for mankind and opposing hegemony; offering 'Chinese solutions' to global problems; building a 'Chinese platform' for exchanges among communist parties; and winning more positive appraisals from foreign communist parties. The survey stresses diversity: some parties praise China's path, others, such as the German Marxist-Leninist Party and the Revolutionary Communist Party USA, doubt its socialist character. The authors say that parties seek both independent development and international unity, and that the failure of parliamentary roads to socialism means the feasibility of violent revolution should not be ignored.

Zhuo and Tan call on the CPC, which they describe as the world's largest ruling party, to supply a 'CPC answer, plan and contribution'. They urge it to learn from Soviet great-party chauvinism and to lead by 'exemplary demonstration' rather than coercion. Their proposals are a 'twenty-first-century internationalism', deeper ties with international communist and left organisations, wider forms of party cooperation, an international coordinating body of Marxist parties, and a 'community with a shared future for communist parties of the world'. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how the CPC sees its role in the global communist movement, with a classification of the world's communist parties.
quoteEn: The situation of the international communist movement should be judged not by the number of countries ruled by communist parties but by the actual international influence of existing socialist states and their capacity to lead humanity's future; fundamentally it is determined by quality.
quoteZh: 判断国际共产主义运动是处于何种形势不应是共产党执政国家数量的多少，而是由现有社会主义国家所产生的实际国际影响力和对人类未来发展的引领力来衡量的，根本上是由质量来决定的。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the CPC's model of socialism since reform and opening up. The article treats it as the main source of vitality in the international communist movement.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The CPC's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017. The article presents it as twenty-first-century Marxism.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept put forward by Xi Jinping around 2012–13. It calls for shared development, security and governance among countries.

t: The major contributions of the 20th Party Congress to world socialism
zh: 党的二十大对世界社会主义的重大贡献
paras: Writing after the 20th Party Congress (2022), Wu Degang asks what the Congress contributes to world socialism. Taking his cue from Xi Jinping's report, he argues that scientific socialism has taken on new vitality in twenty-first-century China and that the Congress has made major contributions on four fronts: theory, practice, the revival of world socialism, and global problem-solving.

The article is organised in four numbered sections. It first traces the successive theoretical achievements of the Party, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. It then reviews the record of the past decade and Chinese modernization, places socialism with Chinese characteristics within five centuries of world socialist history, and ends with the Party's international outlook and its proposals for a community with a shared future for mankind.

Wu's central claim is that Xi Jinping Thought, by answering questions that the classic Marxist writers, earlier socialist states and developed Western countries did not resolve, marks a new milestone in scientific socialism and adapts Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. The author cites a rise in GDP from 54 trillion to 114 trillion yuan, a world economic share of 18.5 per cent, and the removal of all 832 poor counties from the poverty list. In Wu's account, these results refute the claims of the 'obsolescence of Marxism', the 'end of socialism' and the 'collapse of China'. He also argues that China halted the ebb of world socialism after the Soviet collapse and that Chinese modernization widens the options of developing countries that want both growth and independence.

Wu concludes that socialism with Chinese characteristics is becoming the banner of twenty-first-century scientific socialism and a mainstay in reviving world socialism. He presents the Belt and Road Initiative, a new type of international relations and a community with a shared future for mankind as Chinese contributions to global challenges. The text is an affirmative interpretation of the Congress and offers little critical engagement. Read the original if you want to see how a senior Party historian frames the 20th Party Congress as a contribution to world socialism and to Chinese claims of international leadership.
quoteEn: Socialism with Chinese characteristics is a "new version" of scientific socialism, one that originates in scientific socialism and has written into it the content of the new era.
quoteZh: 中国特色社会主义是源于科学社会主义、又写出了新时代内容的科学社会主义“新版本”。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018. It is presented as the latest stage in adapting Marxism to China.
The Party's official term for China's own path to modernization, set out prominently at the 20th Party Congress in 2022. It is presented as an alternative to Western models.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept in Xi Jinping's foreign policy since about 2013. It calls for shared development, security and governance among nations.
An international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative proposed by Xi Jinping in 2013.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: On socialism with Chinese characteristics and the revitalisation of world socialism
zh: 论中国特色社会主义与世界社会主义的振兴态势
source: Journal of Ideological and Theoretical Education (思想理论教育导刊), 2023 no. 1
paras: Zhang Zhiyuan and Li Juanjuan ask how socialism with Chinese characteristics relates to the current revival of world socialism after its low ebb. Writing in the first issue of 2023 of a Chinese journal on ideological and theoretical education, they argue that socialism with Chinese characteristics is the most consequential component of twenty-first-century world socialism. In their account it supplies the central force, the new prospects and the historical direction of that revival.

The article opens with the path from Thomas More's Utopia (1516) to the Communist Manifesto (1848) and then proceeds in three parts. The first treats Chinese achievements of the past decade as a pillar of world socialism: the people as principal force, the building of a moderately prosperous society in all respects, and the drive towards a modern socialist country. The second turns to Chinese modernization, a new form of human civilisation and a community with a shared future for mankind. The third reviews the historical course from the lessons of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe to the present.

Their central claim is that China's experience offers other countries a model. They hold that poverty eradication, achieved by the socialist economic system, shows the superiority of the system. Chinese modernization, they say, gives developing countries a new option that is neither a closed, rigid old path nor a path of abandoning socialism. They also present the new form of civilisation and the community with a shared future as Chinese answers to Western-centred models and to global governance deficits. Historically, they contrast the Soviet and East European reforms of the late 1980s, which they associate with abandoning Party leadership and Marxist guidance and ending in collapse, with China's reforms. They credit the latter with holding the banner of scientific socialism, and with reaching the stage where capitalism, hit by the financial crisis, populism and de-globalisation, faces a rising socialism.

The authors conclude that the centre of world socialism has shifted to China in the twenty-first century. They state that socialism with Chinese characteristics in some sense represents the future of world socialism and is becoming its mainstay and banner. They add that the Party has the responsibility, confidence and capacity to contribute more to scientific socialism. Read the original if you want a representative example of how Chinese Party-school scholars frame China's role in the international socialist movement.
quoteEn: In the twenty-first century, the centre of world socialism has shifted to China.
quoteZh: 在21世纪，世界社会主义的中心转移到中国。

glossary.explanation: The official Party formulation of China's path to modernization, promoted especially since the 20th Party Congress (2022). It is presented as having both features common to all modernizations and distinctive Chinese ones.

glossary.en: a new form of human civilisation
glossary.explanation: A phrase used in official documents, notably the Party's 2021 historical resolution, to describe the civilisation said to be created by Chinese modernization. It is presented as an alternative to Western models.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept associated with Xi Jinping since 2013. It calls for countries to share interests and responsibilities in global governance.

t: The historical experience of the Communist Party of China in maintaining its vanguard character over a century: a perspective from the international communist movement
zh: 百年中国共产党永葆先进性的历史经验——基于国际共产主义运动的视角
paras: Writing for the Party's centenary in 2021, Lü Weizhou asks why the Communist Party of China has grown from a small force into a ruling party and what lessons the international communist movement offers on keeping a party "advanced". The article holds that maintaining "advanced character" (xianjinxing) is the essential attribute of a Marxist party and the fundamental reason for the Party's success. It also treats this as a permanent task bearing on a party's survival.

The article has two main parts. The first draws on Marx, Engels and Lenin, and on the Soviet and East European experience, to identify four foundations of a vanguard party: guidance by scientific Marxist theory, communist ideals and convictions, the support of the people, and democratic centralism as the organisational principle. The second part traces how the Chinese party has realised each of these over its hundred years. A short conclusion looks ahead to the "two centenary goals" and the building of a modern socialist country.

Lü reads the collapse of the Soviet Communist Party and of the East European parties as a negative test of each foundation. In this account, the Soviet party abandoned Marxism by adopting "humane, democratic socialism", lost its ideals, developed bureaucratic privilege that cut it off from the people, and weakened democratic centralism through past repression and later through Gorbachev's "unconditional democracy". The Chinese party, by contrast, is presented as having kept each foundation. The author names the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context (from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era), a spiritual lineage of ideals and sacrifice, the mass line, and democratic centralism, citing the Zunyi Conference and the Zhang Guotao split as successes and the Cultural Revolution as a failure.

Lü concludes that vanguard status is neither achieved once and for all nor permanent. Under long-term rule, factors that weaken the Party are always present, so the Party must treat maintaining its vanguard character as a major strategic task, keep drawing on historical experience and improve its governing capacity. Read the original if you want a Party-theory account that sets the Chinese party's history against the Soviet collapse and the wider communist movement.
quoteEn: That a party was advanced in the past does not mean it is advanced now, and being advanced now does not mean it will be advanced forever.
quoteZh: 一个政党过去先进不等于现在先进，现在先进不等于永远先进。

glossary.explanation: A standard Party-building concept for the quality that qualifies a Marxist party to lead, covering its theory, ideals, ties to the people and organisation. Chinese Party discourse treats it as something to be continually maintained.

glossary.en: adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context
glossary.explanation: The idea, put forward by Mao Zedong in 1938, that Marxism must be applied to China's specific conditions and take on Chinese features. It is now used to describe successive Party theoretical innovations.

The Party's working method of drawing on the people's views and returning to them as policy, developed in the revolutionary period and written into the Party constitution in 1956. It is presented as the basis of the Party's tie to the people.

The Leninist organisational principle that combines discussion within the Party with binding unity once a decision is made. Chinese texts describe it as the Party's basic organisational and leadership system.
The goals of building a moderately prosperous society by the Party's centenary in 2021 and a modern socialist country by the People's Republic's centenary in 2049.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017. It is presented as the latest stage in adapting Marxism to China.

t: New readings of Gramsci's thought in Chinese and foreign scholarship from a historical perspective, and their implications
zh: 历史性研究视角下国内外理论界对葛兰西思想的新解读与启示
paras: Marking the 85th anniversary of Antonio Gramsci's death, this review surveys roughly the last ten years of Chinese and foreign research on Gramsci's thought. Pan Xihua argues that understanding Gramsci requires returning to his own historical setting, and that research adopting such a historical perspective has produced new readings of long-contested questions. The article is a literature review that also draws lessons for socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The article has three parts. The first lists new historically oriented publications: new Chinese editions of the Prison Notebooks (2014, 2016), the forthcoming direct translation from Italian by Tian Shigang, Chinese monographs on Gramsci's historicism and cultural hegemony, and works from Italy, Mexico, France and the Anglophone world on the reception of Gramsci. The second part examines three clusters of new interpretation: Gramsci's historical standing, the relation of his philosophy of praxis to Marxism, and fresh uses of his cultural hegemony in analysing historical events. The third part draws implications for China.

On historical standing, Pan reports that Chinese scholars now largely agree Gramsci is a founder of Western Marxism, while foreign scholars such as Eric Hobsbawm stress his priority in developing Marxist political theory. Pan notes that evaluations bear the mark of their era, citing a Russian scholar who says Gramsci's emphasis on consent was alien to Soviet ideology. On the philosophy of praxis, Pan describes one Chinese view equating it with Marxism, used partly to evade prison censorship, and another stressing its originality. Pan reports that most scholars, including Yohann Douet and Michael Löwy, see it as an innovative development of Marxism rather than an identity with it. Pan also highlights a newer trend abroad of applying cultural hegemony to the history of the communist movement, such as Aleksandr Maisuryan's account of how dissidents eroded the Soviet Communist Party's hegemony before the Soviet collapse. Pan says this trend has not yet drawn attention in China.

Pan draws three implications. Studying the "five histories" (of the Party, new China, reform and opening up, socialism and the Chinese nation) should strengthen confidence in socialism with Chinese characteristics. Marxism should continue to be localised and innovated, as Gramsci did against dogmatic "orthodox Marxism". Because ideological hegemony must be built and maintained continuously, the Party must hold leadership and discourse power in ideological work in the new-media era, where Pan sees historical nihilism and Western ideological infiltration as threats. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language bibliographic map of recent Gramsci scholarship and an example of how Chinese Party scholars draw political lessons from him.
quoteEn: To understand Gramsci, one must return to Gramsci.
quoteZh: 理解葛兰西，就必须回到葛兰西。

glossary.explanation: Gramsci's concept of rule exercised through consent and the shaping of values rather than force alone. The Chinese term also serves in Party discourse about ideological leadership.
Gramsci's term in the Prison Notebooks for Marxism, partly a code word to avoid prison censors. Chinese scholars debate whether it is identical to Marxism or an original development.
The tradition associated with Lukács, Korsch and Gramsci, which emphasises philosophy, culture and consciousness.
The official name for China's current path and theoretical system, used since the 1980s.
Party education slogan for the study of the history of the Party, of new China, of reform and opening up, of socialism and of the Chinese nation.
In official Chinese usage, a label for views seen as denying or distorting the Party's history and revolutionary tradition.

t: An analysis of Marx's early communist thought
st: A reading based on the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844
zh: 马克思早期共产主义思想探析
zhSub: 基于《1844年经济学哲学手稿》的解读
source: Journal of Liaoning Normal University (Social Sciences Edition), 2022 no. 6
paras: Xie Xiaojuan and Li Shuting ask what Marx's first systematic account of communism, in the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, contains and why it matters. They argue that the Manuscripts set out a communism grounded in the sublation of private property and the human being's return to itself. In their view this work prepared Marx's later "new worldview". They also claim that revisiting it helps strengthen belief in communism and the shared ideal of socialism with Chinese characteristics, in support of the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation.

The article has three parts. The first treats the critical premises of Marx's thinking: his critiques of crude communism, of political communism, and of Hegel's idealist view of nature. The second sets out the basic content of communism in the Manuscripts. The third examines the route to its realisation. The authors close by linking the Manuscripts to The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto.

In the authors' reading, Marx judged earlier communisms to be incomplete. Crude communism, they say, merely redistributes property mechanically, never reaches the level of private property, and negates human individuality. The two political forms recognised alienation but remained "unfinished". Against these and against Hegel's abstract treatment of labour, Marx defined communism as the positive sublation of private property and alienated labour. The authors present this as three unities: the real appropriation of human essence, the return of the human being to a social existence, and the fusion of humanism and naturalism.

On the path to communism, the authors argue, Marx held that it must draw on all the wealth created under private property. It also rests on large-scale industry and the natural sciences, and it requires the full liberation of human needs, senses and individuality. They conclude that the Manuscripts, despite Feuerbach's influence, already go beyond his outlook and contain the seeds of historical materialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic overview of the 1844 Manuscripts' account of communism and how it is linked to Marx's later works.
quoteEn: Communism is the sublation of all alienation throughout society.
quoteZh: 共产主义是对全部社会中一切异化的扬弃

glossary.explanation: The Chinese rendering of Hegel's Aufhebung: a process that negates something while retaining and raising its positive content. Marxist texts use it for how communism relates to private property.
A slogan popularised by Xi Jinping from 2012, meaning the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. It is used in official discourse as a shared national goal.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's theory and system of socialism since the reform era. It is presented as Marxism adapted to China's conditions.

t: The fundamental cause of the collapse of the Soviet Party and state: lessons and implications (Part 1)
st: Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
zh: 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示(上)
zhSub: 写在苏维埃社会主义共和国联盟成立100周年之际
paras: Writing in 2022, a century after the founding of the USSR and 31 years after its collapse, Li Shenming asks what was the decisive cause of the loss of the Soviet Party and state. The article argues that, although many factors contributed, the fundamental cause was the ideological and political degeneration of the leadership group from Khrushchev to Gorbachev. This is the first instalment of a two-part study.

Li opens by invoking Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping on the Soviet case, and by citing Russian reflections after 1991. The first half then has two parts. One sets out eight areas in which the leadership is said to have degenerated: belief, theory, politics, the economy, organisation, work style, foreign policy and outlook on life. The other briefly assesses twelve rival explanations from among the more than fifty Li says exist.

The central move is a Maoist distinction between principal and secondary contradictions, together with the claim that a correct ideological and political line decides everything. Li traces a continuous descent. Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin and his theories of a 'party of the whole people' and 'state of the whole people' are said to have prepared Gorbachev's 'humane, democratic socialism', privatisation, abolition of the Party's leading role, nepotistic personnel policy and concessions to the West. The article draws on memoirs, Russian commentators and US figures such as David Kotz and Jack Matlock. It rejects as one-sided explanations including the 'original sin' of the October Revolution, the rigidity of the Stalin model, nationalities policy, the arms race, external pressure, one-party rule, 'blame Gorbachev alone' and the 'convergence of factors' view. Li holds that popular abandonment of the Party was a result of the leadership's degeneration, not its cause.

Li concludes that research on the cause is never purely academic, because historical nihilism uses attacks on Soviet history to attack the Chinese Communist Party and Mao. He insists on a clear political standpoint and warns that a wrong conclusion could shake the foundations of the Party and the People's Republic. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned Chinese account of the Soviet collapse, with its critique of competing explanations, and are ready to read it as an argument for Party leadership and ideological discipline today.
quoteEn: The fundamental cause of the collapse of the Soviet Party and the disintegration of the USSR was, in the final analysis, the ideological and political degeneration of the leadership group from Khrushchev to Gorbachev.
quoteZh: 苏共亡党、苏联解体的根本原因，说到底，就是从赫鲁晓夫到戈尔巴乔夫领导集团在思想上政治上的蜕变。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Party discourse for the wholesale negation of the history of the Party, socialism or revolutionary leaders. Xi Jinping has made it a prominent target of ideological work.

glossary.zh: 人道的、民主的社会主义
glossary.pinyin: réndào de, mínzhǔ de shèhuì zhǔyì
glossary.explanation: Gorbachev's formula for the Soviet Party's aims from 1988–90. The author treats it as a form of social democracy that served to introduce capitalism.
A thesis put forward at the 22nd Soviet Party Congress (1961) that the Party no longer represented one class. The author treats it as a revisionist abandonment of Marxism-Leninism.

t: Fundamental causes, lessons and implications of the collapse of the Soviet Party and state (Part 2)
st: Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
zh: 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示(中)
zhSub: 写在苏维埃社会主义共和国联盟成立100周年之际
paras: This is the middle instalment of a three-part essay marking the centenary of the USSR's founding (published in World Socialism Studies, 2022 no. 10). Li Shenming asks what lessons the fall of the Soviet Communist Party and state holds. The author's answer is that the decisive lesson concerns the Party's own building, especially problems inside its leadership group, and that these lessons bear directly on China.

Part 2 sets out nine lessons. They cover the link between a big party's self-construction and the fate of nation and people; leaders' convictions and theoretical grounding; ideological and political clarity; embedding fundamental institutions in the constitution; communist ideals; two kinds of reform; ideological work; Party leadership of the army; and Western "peaceful evolution". Li draws on the records of Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev, post-Soviet Russian commentators, and the writings and statements of Allen Dulles and other Western figures.

Li argues that after Lenin and Stalin the CPSU lost a strong leadership core. A privileged bureaucratic stratum grew, and the leadership abandoned Marxism for "abstract humanism", class conciliation and Western values. Gorbachev's "reform" is described as a reform of a fundamentally non-socialist kind that aimed at capitalisation, in contrast to the Marxist view of reform as socialism's self-improvement. Li presents abolition of Article 6 of the Soviet constitution, "depoliticisation" of the army and a flood of historical nihilism, including slanders against war heroes such as Matrosov, as steps that dismantled the Party's legal and military base.

In Li's account, the Western strategy of "peaceful evolution" worked through exchanges, foundations, prizes, NGOs and the cultivation of a "fifth column" inside the leadership. Li names Gorbachev, Yakovlev, Shevardnadze and Yeltsin, citing Russian memoirists and statements by Western leaders. Li calls the infiltration of the leading group an "undisputed fact". Li then links each lesson to China, criticising "constitutional democracy", stressing ideological leadership, absolute Party command of the army and a reform that never changes direction. The essay ends with "to be continued". Read the original if you want to see how a leading CASS scholar reads the Soviet collapse and ties it to current Chinese Party-building and ideological policy.
quoteEn: It was not "constitutional democracy" that could save the Soviet Union; it was precisely "constitutional democracy" that brought the Soviet Union down.
quoteZh: 不是“宪政民主”能够拯救苏联，而恰恰是“宪政民主”搞垮了苏联。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese political discourse for alleged Western strategies of changing socialist systems from within by ideological, cultural and economic means rather than force. It is associated in Chinese writing with John Foster Dulles in the 1950s.
Borrowed from the Spanish Civil War, it refers here to people inside a state or party who are said to work for hostile outside powers. The author applies it to senior Soviet leaders.
In Chinese Party discourse, the negation or denigration of the Party's revolutionary history, leaders and heroes. The author applies it both to late-Soviet and to Chinese cases.

A Western-style model of constitutional government with multiparty competition and separation of powers. Chinese official writing treats advocacy of it as a challenge to Party leadership, and the author does so here.

t: Fundamental causes, lessons and implications of the collapse of the Soviet Communist Party and state (Part 2)
st: Written on the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
zh: 苏联亡党亡国的根本原因、教训与启示(下)
zhSub: 写在苏维埃社会主义共和国联盟成立100周年之际
paras: This is the second and final part of Li Shenming's study of why the Communist Party of the Soviet Union lost power and the USSR dissolved, published in World Socialism Studies in late 2022 to mark the Soviet Union's centenary. Having treated causes and lessons in the first part, Li turns here to what he calls the important implications for the Communist Party of China. His thesis is that China can avoid the Soviet fate only if it keeps Marxist leaders at the head of the Party, preserves public ownership, wins the ideological struggle and stays close to the people.

The article sets out ten imperatives, each drawn against the Soviet record: leadership and succession; the Party's self-reform; the economy and common prosperity; ideological work; the Party's purpose and style; Party control of the army; foreign policy; cadre selection and education; Marxist theoretical study; and a correct view of the era. Li draws on Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, and on episodes from the Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev periods.

Li argues that a Party leader's firm Marxism is often decisive, and he presents the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds as essential safeguards, calling for guarding against 'two-faced' people and 'ambitious schemers'. On the economy, he holds that without public ownership there is no socialism, and that Soviet collapse followed the plundering of the public-ownership base by a degenerate leadership. He also criticises one-sided reform practices in China, including neglect of class analysis, downplaying of collective farming and income polarisation. On ideology, Li contends that class struggle persists within limits, denounces historical nihilism and calls for stronger leadership in universities and research bodies. He defends Party command of the army against 'nationalisation of the army', and reads the present as still an age of imperialism, requiring courage to struggle.

Li concludes that the Soviet experience warns the Party to treasure its hard-won leadership core, to reform itself so as to escape the 'historical cycle' of rise and fall, and to keep faith with the people. He makes concrete proposals: five political standards and public notice periods for promoting senior cadres, institutionalised Marxist study tied to appraisal, and further volumes of Mao's Selected Works and full collections of Xi Jinping's writings. He expects world socialism to enter an active period in the coming decades. Read the original if you want a detailed example of how a leading Party theorist draws practical political and ideological conclusions from the Soviet collapse for China today.
quoteEn: Without public ownership there is no socialism.
quoteZh: 没有公有制就没有社会主义。

glossary.explanation: A formulation from the Party's 2021 resolution on history, affirming Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Central Committee and the whole Party, and the guiding status of Xi Jinping Thought.
A political requirement that Party members uphold Xi Jinping's core position and the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee.
Xi Jinping-era term for the Party's efforts to discipline itself and fight corruption, presented as the answer to the 'historical cycle' of dynastic rise and decline.
A goal of shared wealth for all, promoted under Xi Jinping as a defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
In official Chinese usage, a label for views seen as denigrating the history of the Party, socialism or its leaders.

t: New changes and characteristics of contemporary capitalism
zh: 当代资本主义的新变化及特点
paras: Writing in a journal issue of early 2023, against a background of the pandemic, the Ukraine crisis and what the article calls the 'four deficits' in global governance, Tan Youzhi asks how contemporary capitalism has changed since 1945 and especially since the turn of the century. The article takes up Xi Jinping's call to strengthen research on contemporary capitalism. Tan's thesis is that capitalism has gained new vitality and is still adjusting, but that its historical fate of being replaced by socialism is unchanged, and that the replacement will be long.

The article has two parts. The first, on 'new changes', reads these changes through historical materialism and names two main drivers: successive scientific and technological revolutions, and the course of globalization. Tan reviews three past technological revolutions (steam, electricity and internal combustion, atomic energy and computing) and a fourth now under way around the digital economy and intelligent manufacturing. The second part sets out two characteristics of contemporary capitalism.

On the changes, Tan argues that each technological revolution has renewed capitalism, and that the fourth has helped Western economies recover from the 2008 financial crisis and eased class conflict for the time being. Globalization, by contrast, has met a counter-current of unilateralism, populism, protectionism and 'decoupling', which pandemic disruption to supply chains has intensified. On the characteristics, Tan reads Marx's 'two inevitables' together with his 'two never wills' of 1859 (the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy). The first concerns the specific law of capitalist development and the objective certainty of socialism's succession. The second concerns the general law and the long and arduous character of that succession. Welfare policy and state intervention, Tan holds, cannot remove the contradiction between socialized production and private appropriation, so inequality, crises and instability persist.

Tan concludes that capitalism still has a capacity to expand, so it will not collapse soon, and calls for combining the necessity of its demise with the long duration of the process. The author also calls for combining capitalism's decay with its continuing possibilities, and the stages of history with its direction, so as to avoid blind optimism. The article describes a 'strong capitalism, weak socialism' pattern alongside a trend of 'the West declining, the East rising'. It also says the United States shifts crises onto others through rule-setting, sanctions and intervention. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese scholarship in 2023 applied the 'two inevitables' and 'two never wills' to contemporary capitalism, technology and globalization.
quoteEn: Marx's idea of the 'two never wills' is a reasonable extension and a natural implication of his idea of the 'two inevitables'.
quoteZh: 马克思的“两个决不会”思想是其“两个必然”思想的合理延伸与应有之义

glossary.explanation: The thesis, drawn from the Communist Manifesto, that the fall of the bourgeoisie and the victory of the proletariat are equally inevitable. Chinese Party theory summarises it as capitalism's inevitable demise and socialism's inevitable victory.

Marx's 1859 formulation that no social formation perishes before its productive forces are fully developed. New, higher relations of production never appear before their material conditions have matured in the old society. Chinese writers often use it to stress the length of the transition to socialism.

t: New trends in the development of world socialism amid great changes
zh: 大变局下世界社会主义发展新趋势
paras: Chen Mingfan asks where the world socialist movement is heading in what the article calls a once-in-a-century transformation of the world. The thesis is that the movement, now emerging from a trough that followed the Soviet and East European upheavals, is gradually moving towards revival. Chen attributes this to two irreversible forces: the decline of capitalism and the development of China under the Communist Party.

The article has three parts. The first reviews how socialism rose through successive world upheavals, from the British industrial revolution and the French Revolution to the Paris Commune, the First World War and the October Revolution, the postwar expansion of socialism, and the setback of 1989–91. The second traces the movement's division into currents: communist parties, parties in capitalist and developing countries, democratic socialism, and 'national socialism' in the developing world. The third turns to China's role and the prospects for revival.

Chen argues that after Engels's death the movement split into a revolutionary line, scientific socialism, and a reformist line, democratic socialism. The latter, in Chen's account, has in essence abandoned socialism and become reformed capitalism, acting as the 'doctor at the sickbed' of capitalism. Chen presents the Communist Party of China as the mainstay of the movement, with Vietnam, Cuba, Laos and the DPRK also holding to the socialist course. Chen then credits Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, Chinese modernization, whole-process people's democracy and a community with a shared future for mankind with offering models and theoretical tools to socialists abroad, citing favourable comments from foreign communists and commentators.

Chen cites Lenin's conditions for a revolutionary situation to caution that the Western crisis alone is not enough. Rulers still control strong state machinery, proletarian parties remain immature and mass discontent has not yet become rational political demand, so the movement faces a long period of tempering. Chen says the Party bears a 'two rejuvenations' task: national rejuvenation and leading socialism's revival. Chen expects China's goal of becoming a leading modern socialist power by mid-century to have an immeasurable effect on the movement. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of the world socialist movement's history and prospects that casts China as its leading force.
quoteEn: The decline of capitalism results from the laws of historical development and therefore cannot be stopped; however many 'salvation plans' the bourgeois rulers' advisers put forward is of no avail, and however many lies they fabricate will only expose them the more.
quoteZh: 资本主义的衰落是历史发展规律使然，因而是无法阻挡的，不管资产阶级统治者的智囊提出多少“救世方案”也无济于事，编造多少谎言也只会欲盖弥彰。

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official guiding ideology of the Communist Party of China, written into the Party constitution in 2017. Official texts describe it as the latest stage of adapting Marxism to China.
The official name for China's development path, presented in the 20th Party Congress report (2022) as distinct from Western modernization.
An official term for China's democratic model, used since 2019. It is presented as involving the people at every stage of governance, not only at elections.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's foreign policy concept, which stresses shared interests, cooperation and opposition to hegemonism.
In Chinese Party discourse, the reformist social-democratic current descended from the Second International. It is usually treated critically as a departure from scientific socialism.

t: Assessment of political developments in Vietnam in 2021
zh: 2021年越南政治发展动态评析
paras: Pan Jin'e reviews Vietnamese politics in 2021, a year that combined the 13th National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam, the five-yearly National Assembly and local elections, and a severe Covid-19 wave. The article argues that the political cycle ran smoothly overall and showed the Party's ability to set the country's course. It also contends that the year exposed unresolved problems: leadership succession, factional balance, weak governance in the pandemic and poor coordination between Party and state organs.

The article is organised in four parts. It first covers the Party congress of January–February 2021 and its personnel outcomes. It then sets out the congress's medium- and long-term development strategy. A third part describes the elections and the work of the National Assembly and the Fatherland Front. A closing assessment draws conclusions. Throughout, Pan frames Vietnamese politics through the formula of Party leadership, state management and the people as masters of the country.

Pan reads the congress's personnel arrangements as breaking established norms: Nguyen Phu Trong's third term as General Secretary, age exemptions granted through a 'special circumstances' rule, and a Politburo of 18 members with fewer southern members. Pan interprets this as a bid for stability and a sign that no agreed successor exists, and possibly a transitional arrangement. On strategy, the article lists Vietnam's 'two centenary' goals, with high-income developed status by 2045, plus twelve directions, six key tasks and three strategic breakthroughs. Pan notes that the congress report put little emphasis on theoretical work. In the assessment, Pan reports that Vietnam went from a model of pandemic control in 2020 to a major outbreak, that growth in 2021 was 2.58 per cent against a target of 6–6.5 per cent, that local authorities did not carry out central orders, and that strikes followed in 2022. Pan links these failures partly to a weakening of Party authority as 'rule of law' reforms advanced.

Pan concludes that Vietnam's politics ran steadily but met real difficulties, and that meeting the two centenary goals will require more effort from political actors at all levels. The author argues that democratisation should avoid the flaws of Western political models, which the article describes as being in decline. It should instead preserve the strengths of Communist Party-led democracy and the capacity to concentrate resources on major tasks. Read the original if you want a China-based specialist's detailed, mixed assessment of the 13th Congress, Vietnamese elite politics and the pandemic's political consequences.
quoteEn: The theme of the report to the 13th Party Congress, and its 'three-step' plan for achieving the 'two centenary' goals by the middle of this century, embody the will of the Communist Party of Vietnam.
quoteZh: 越共十三大报告的主题以及到本世纪中叶实现“两个一百年”目标的“三步走”计划，是越南共产党意志的体现。

glossary.explanation: Vietnam's united front organisation, grouping the Communist Party, mass organisations, religious and ethnic groups. The article describes it as promoting national unity and social supervision under Party leadership.
A provision in the Party's election rules, amended in 2014, that lets candidates beyond the age limit stay in office if the Politburo nominates them and the Central Committee approves.

Vietnam's goals set by its 13th Congress: developed-country status by the 100th anniversary of the state's founding in 2045, with a goal for 2030 tied to the Party's centenary. The article notes they echo the Chinese term.

glossary.zh: 党领导、国家管理、人民当家作主
glossary.pinyin: dǎng lǐngdǎo, guójiā guǎnlǐ, rénmín dāngjiā zuòzhǔ
glossary.en: Party leadership, state management and the people as masters of the country
glossary.literal: Party leads, state manages, people are masters
glossary.explanation: The formula the article uses to describe Vietnam's political system and the aim of its political renewal since doi moi in the 1980s.

t: The Communist Party of Cuba and the Communist Party of China amid changes unseen in a century
st: An interview with Balaguer Cabrera, a founder of the Communist Party of Cuba
zh: 百年未有之大变局下的古巴共产党与中国共产党
zhSub: 访古巴共产党创始人之一巴拉格尔·卡夫雷拉
paras: This is an interview by Lou Yu, a reporter for World Socialism Studies, with José Ramón Balaguer Cabrera, born in 1932, a founder of the Communist Party of Cuba and a Central Committee member since 1975. He has also served as head of the Party's International Relations Department, Cuban health minister and ambassador to the Soviet Union. Asked about relations between the two parties and about the Communist Party of China (CPC), Balaguer presents them as a model of friendship between Marxist parties and praises the CPC's leadership, achievements and contribution to world socialism.

The interview has three parts. The first covers the history and present of Cuba–China party ties; the second the CPC's achievements and experience; the third the CPC's contribution to Marxism and world socialism, including the Belt and Road Initiative and a community with a shared future for mankind. Balaguer speaks of the world being in a period of 'changes unseen in a century'.

On bilateral ties, Balaguer traces mutual trust to the first Chinese labourers arriving in Havana in 1847 and to Chinese participation in Cuba's independence war. He recalls Fidel Castro's 1960 decision to recognise the People's Republic and later gestures, including Jiang Zemin's 1993 visit during Cuba's 'Special Period'. On the CPC, he holds that its main strength is its leadership: long-term planning, analysis of the principal contradiction at each stage, collective wisdom, and willingness to correct errors. He cites the end of absolute poverty in 2020 and nearly 800 million people lifted from poverty in forty years. He says the CPC's adaptation of Marxism to Chinese conditions and traditional culture, and its steadfastness after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, showed that socialism had not died.

Balaguer concludes that China has become a world centre of Marxist research. He argues that capitalism's problems are structural and that the only solution is a transition to socialism, which he expects to prevail in the medium to long term. He describes the CPC as building a more equal, multilateral international order, opposing sanctions and Cold War thinking, and calls for reform of international organisations. Read the original if you want a Cuban Party veteran's first-hand view of Cuba–China party relations and of how he sees the CPC's role in world socialism.
quoteEn: Today, China, as a socialist country, has become the centre of Marxist theoretical research in the whole world.
quoteZh: 如今，作为社会主义国家的中国已经成为全世界马克思主义理论研究的中心。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since the early 2010s as China's vision for international relations based on cooperation, equality and shared development.
An international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative launched by China in 2013, linking China with countries across Eurasia, Africa and Latin America.

glossary.pinyin: bǎi nián wèi yǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.literal: great changes not seen in a hundred years
glossary.explanation: An official formula, used by Xi Jinping from 2017–18, describing the current period of major shifts in the global order and balance of power.

t: Re-examining the causes of the break-up of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia
zh: 南斯拉夫联邦解体原因再探析
paras: Thirty years after the collapse of the Yugoslav federation, Ma Xipu asks why a state that built a distinctive self-managing, non-aligned socialism disappeared. The article argues that the break-up cannot be explained by one factor. In Ma's account it resulted from a flawed founding of the Yugoslav state, a series of internal failures in the economy, nationalities policy and the ruling League of Communists, and the direct and indirect intervention of outside powers.

The article is organised in three parts. The first traces the state from the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (1918) through the royal dictatorship, the 1939 Croatian autonomy agreement, the 1941 invasion, the postwar six-republic federation, the declarations of independence of 1991 and the short-lived Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of Serbia and Montenegro. The second part examines internal causes under three headings. The third turns to external causes, including the fall of the Soviet bloc and Western policy.

Ma holds that the first Yugoslavia was an ill-constructed, partly artificial creation of the Versailles order, with unresolved Serb–Croat tensions over centralism and federalism. Among internal causes, he cites the economic crisis of the 1980s (inflation of more than 2,000 per cent, mass bankruptcies, heavy foreign debt) and nationalities policy errors. These included recognising Bosnian Muslims as a nation, applying 'equal opportunity' and rotation mechanically, weakening Serbia by enlarging the powers of Kosovo and Vojvodina, and treating the national question as solved. He also argues that the League's 'guiding role' formula, the 'federalisation' of the Party, consensus replacing democratic centralism, the purges of Djilas and Ranković, and a rotating collective presidency removed the unifying centre. On external causes, Ma accepts that internal factors are primary but says outside powers bear heavy responsibility. He cites declassified material said to show that West Germany sought Yugoslavia's dissolution from 1976–77, and he describes the 1999 NATO action and Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence as the continuation of this aim.

Ma concludes that Yugoslavia should receive fair historical judgement and respect. He also stresses that the national question is long-term and complex and that a central government must work to narrow regional gaps. He ends with hope for the revival of the region's peoples, Serbia above all. Read the original if you want a Chinese historian's integrated account of Yugoslavia's dissolution that gives particular weight to nationalism, Party organisation and Western intervention.
quoteEn: The key factor in the success or failure of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, and in the rise and fall of Yugoslavia, lay in the League of Communists itself.
quoteZh: 南共联盟的成败和南斯拉夫兴亡的关键因素在南共联盟本身。

glossary.explanation: The Yugoslav formula that replaced the Soviet-style 'leading role' of the Party. As Ma describes it, it meant the Party would coordinate rather than command state and self-management bodies.
The Leninist organisational principle of free discussion followed by binding, unified action. Ma says it was replaced in Yugoslavia by consensus between the Party's federal and republican levels.

t: New trends in the development of left-wing parties amid Europe's political transformation
zh: 欧洲政治转型背景下左翼政党发展新动向
paras: Postwar European party politics rested on a relatively stable contest between left and right mainstream parties. Wu Yunxi argues that since the 2010s, a series of crises has fragmented party systems and blurred the boundaries between old and new, mainstream and non-mainstream parties. The article's thesis is that Europe's left has entered a new phase of adjustment, marked by sharply divergent electoral results, flexible governing alliances and serious difficulties in office.

The article treats the left as three families: social democratic parties, green parties and radical left parties, each with its own group in the European Parliament. It then proceeds in three steps: electoral performance across Western, Northern, Southern and Central-Eastern Europe, the forms of governing cooperation, and the challenges the left faces once in government. It draws on many national cases, including Germany, the Nordic states, Portugal, Spain, France, Britain, Greece and Finland, and on recent election figures.

Wu's central claim is that social democracy is split between recovering parties (Germany, the Nordic countries, Portugal) and parties in steep decline (France, the Netherlands, Greece, much of Central and Eastern Europe). Greens have gained from climate politics, and new radical left parties such as Syriza and Podemos surged and then fell back, while old communist parties remain weak. Fragmentation, rightward drift and populism mean that single-party majorities are rare. Social democrats now depend on minority governments, multi-party coalitions and cross-camp deals, as in Portugal, Spain, Finland and Germany's three-party coalition. Wu identifies three challenges in office: policy differences and rivalry with partners, instability when partners withdraw, and limited resources and room for error amid economic weakness, polarisation and the pandemic.

Wu concludes that social democracy suffers a deeper crisis of representation, policy effectiveness and social base than the centre-right, and that in some countries short-term weakness has become long-term decline. Greens and radical left parties, in this reading, have not yet shown they can replace it, and Syriza's brief tenure exposed the practical limits of new parties' programmes. The Portuguese Socialist Party is singled out as a useful model, having united the left, balanced growth, public spending, employment and deficit reduction, and won repeated re-election. Read the original if you want a dense, data-rich survey of European left parties' elections, coalitions and governing problems as of 2022.
quoteEn: Compared with centre-right parties, social democracy suffers a more serious crisis of mainstream-party representativeness, problems with the effectiveness of its policy instruments, and structural contradictions in its social base.
quoteZh: 社会民主党的主流政党代表性危机、政策工具实效性问题和社会基础结构性矛盾更加严重

t: The forward trajectory of Lenin's view of socialist society after the October Revolution
zh: 十月革命后列宁社会主义社会观的前进轨迹
paras: Yu Min asks how Lenin's view of what socialist society is developed after the October Revolution, once the Bolsheviks had taken power and were exploring paths of socialist construction. The article argues that this view moved along two traceable lines. One kept the communist society described by Marx and Engels as its direction of travel. The other explained what socialism is by reference to the practice and wishes of the masses.

The article is organised in three parts. The first follows the first line through four Lenin texts: the Declaration of the Rights of the Working and Exploited People (1918), the draft Programme of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) (1919), The Tasks of the Youth Leagues (1920) and the 1922 article marking the tenth anniversary of Pravda. The second part gathers Lenin's remarks from 1918 and 1922 that identify socialism with specific popular practices. The third assesses the historical role and present-day value of the two lines.

In Yu's reading, Lenin's definition of communism as common ownership of land and factories and common labour, his call on the young to build communist society, and his confidence in world revolution all show continuity with Marx and Engels. For the second line, Yu cites Lenin's statements that accounting and control, the wish of everyone to improve their lives, the fair distribution of grain, and whatever the masses judge "better than the old system" are socialism. Yu notes that Marx and Engels' basic theory contains no such formulations. Lenin made them, Yu argues, because he judged these practices to be what the people were actually doing and wanted. The two lines form an organic unity: the great goal stays fixed while tasks change with each period.

Yu credits this unity with three historical effects. It gave the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) political steadiness during the New Economic Policy. It spread communist spirit, as in the "communist subbotniks". It affirmed the masses' own experience and so raised their enthusiasm. For the present, Yu argues that Lenin's view helps Chinese Communists, especially cadres, keep to the Party's founding mission and take a people-centred approach to development, and cites Xi Jinping's 2017 remarks on not forgetting the road travelled. Read the original if you want a close reading of how Lenin's post-1917 texts are used to link a communist goal with popular practice, and how that reading is applied to current Party-building themes in China.
quoteEn: These views of his show that he was adept at explaining what socialism is on the basis of the content of the masses' social practice and their wishes.
quoteZh: 他的这些观点证明，他善于以人民群众的社会实践的内容和心愿为依据说明什么是社会主义。

t: Overseas perceptions of the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind
zh: 海外人士关于人类命运共同体理念的认知图景
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai lilun dongtai), 2022 no. 3
paras: This literature-style survey, published in 2022, asks how scholars, politicians and commentators outside China understand Xi Jinping's concept of a community with a shared future for mankind. The authors want to know what overseas observers focus on, what main views have formed and what characterises them. They conclude that overseas views, while wide-ranging and often favourable, remain shallow in height, depth and breadth, and that China should respond actively.

The review is organised around four themes: the grounds on which the concept was put forward (theoretical and practical), its basic meaning, its value and significance, and its practical paths. It cites many named figures from Europe, North America, Russia, Asia, Africa and Latin America, including academics, think-tank reports, Party leaders and former officials. It also devotes a section to views the authors regard as misunderstandings.

On origins, the authors report that overseas commentators trace the concept to traditional Chinese 'all under heaven' thinking, to Marx's internationalism, to earlier Chinese Party leaders' diplomatic thought and to international law. Practical grounds are seen either as China's need for a favourable environment and greater influence, or as a response to deepening interdependence, global problems and an outdated hegemonic order. Meanings are read as a vision of the future, a wisdom for global governance, a new model of international relations, or a foreign policy. Overseas figures see the concept as going beyond Western zero-sum thinking. They propose paths through the Belt and Road Initiative, through particular fields (politics, security, economy, culture, ecology) and through regional or sectoral communities such as health or cyberspace. The authors attribute critical readings, for example that the concept implies Chinese domination or a deliberately vague definition, to a long-standing Western habit of binary, zero-sum thinking.

The authors identify three weaknesses: overseas observers often view the concept through 'tinted glasses', treat it insufficiently in depth, and neglect its relation to capitalism and socialism. Little attention goes to cultural, ecological and micro-level aspects, or to who bears which responsibilities. They propose targeted rebuttal of mistaken views, a stronger cultural construction of the concept as a new civilisational outlook beyond capitalist alienation, and its translation into practice. Read the original if you want a catalogue of named overseas commentators and their positions on the concept, as framed by Chinese scholars.
quoteEn: Only by continually turning into a material force that changes the world can the concept of a community with a shared future for mankind convince and win recognition from more people, and exert greater attraction on the international stage.
quoteZh: 人类命运共同体理念只有不断转变成为改变世界的物质力量，才能被更多人信服和认可，也才能在国际舞台上产生更多、更大的吸引力。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.literal: community of common destiny for humankind
glossary.explanation: A concept associated with Xi Jinping since 2012–13 that presents states as having interlinked interests and calls for cooperative, win-win international relations. It is now a central theme of Chinese foreign-policy discourse.
A Chinese initiative launched in 2013 for infrastructure, trade and investment links across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: The German Greens' return to federal government and the likely direction of their China policy
zh: 德国绿党重返联邦政府及其对华政策走向
source: Foreign Theoretical Trends (Guowai Lilun Dongtai), 2022 no. 3
paras: After the 2021 Bundestag election the German Greens won 14.8 per cent of the vote and 118 seats, and joined the Social Democrats (SPD) and the liberal FDP in a "traffic light coalition" that gave them five cabinet posts, including the foreign ministry. Xuan and Zhao ask what kind of party the Greens are, why they succeeded, why the coalition formed, and what stance they will take towards China. Working within a parliamentary-politics framework, they argue that the Greens' left-wing image should not be taken as a sign of friendlier relations with Beijing, and that campaign hardness will not automatically carry into government.

The article first traces the Greens since 1980 in three stages: grassroots opposition, "junior partner" in the 1998–2005 red-green government, and opposition from 2005 with internal reflection and adjustment. It then examines the causes of their rise, the formation of the traffic light coalition, and the Greens' China positions in their manifesto and leaders' statements. A closing section draws three cautions for assessing their influence on China policy.

The authors argue that the Greens moved from a marginal, fundamentalist left towards a pragmatic centre. They attribute the 2021 result to external conditions, namely Western fatigue with political polarisation and a hollowing-out of the German political centre, as voters left the Union parties, the Left Party and the SPD. They add internal preparation: an optimistic climate-focused message, a reconciled pragmatist leadership and a cooperative stance towards business.
