quoteEn: Engels's works made Marx feel both the importance and the urgency of this research, and directly brought about his "turn to political economy".
quoteZh: 恩格斯的论著既让他感到这种研究的重要性和紧迫性，更直接促成了他的“政治经济学转向”。
keywords: The Condition of the Working Class in England

t: The philosophical awareness and answer to the "riddle of man"
st: Marx's fourfold determination of the human being in the 1844 Manuscripts
zh: “人之谜”的哲学自觉与解答
paras: Wang Huxue asks how Marx understood "man", which the author treats as the core concept of Marxist philosophy. Writing in a period when the Party stresses putting the people first, Wang argues that a scientific grasp of the human being bears directly on how Marxism itself is understood, since Marxism is the science of real human beings and their historical development. The article's thesis is that the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 give a fourfold determination of the human being, which shows Marx's philosophical awareness of, and answer to, the "riddle of man".

The article, a newspaper-length piece, is organised around the four determinations in turn: the human being as a natural being, as a species-being, as an objective being, and as a social being. Each section is built mainly from close reading of passages in the Manuscripts, with occasional contrasts to Feuerbach, Hegel and Fichte.

Wang argues that as a natural being the human is both passive, dependent on nature and driven by passion, and active, so that nature becomes the human's "inorganic body". Species-being rests on free, conscious life-activity, realised in labour; Wang holds that Marx keeps Feuerbach's term but sublates it, giving it a new content that overcomes Feuerbach's abstract, mute generality. As an objective being, the human confirms essential powers through objects. Wang reads this process of objectification as carrying the possibility of alienation, which becomes actual when labour is estranged under private property. Finally, the social determination, which Wang describes as a transition toward the later formula that the human essence is the ensemble of social relations, makes society the ontological basis of the human. Individual and society, in this reading, mutually determine and generate each other, and even solitary activity such as science is social.

Wang concludes that the human being is a social being who, through free and conscious objective labour, merges into nature and also steps out of it to realise the self. The author presents this fourfold account as showing the fullness and depth of Marx's view of the human and as the philosophical basis for today's emphasis on the people. Read the original if you want a concise, text-based Chinese exposition of the 1844 Manuscripts' conception of the human being and its link to current Party discourse on the people.
quoteEn: The human being is a social being who, through free and conscious objective labour, merges into nature, steps out of it, and realises the self.
quoteZh: 人就是通过自由自觉的对象性劳动融入自然又走出自然、实现自我的社会存在物。

glossary.explanation: A slogan in Xi Jinping-era Party discourse stating that the interests of the people take priority in governance. Here the article cites it as evidence of continuity with Marx's focus on human beings.

t: Why Marxism could take root in China
zh: 马克思主义为什么能在中国落地生根
paras: Why did Marxism, born in the West, take root in China when it did not become the mainstream of thought in the other countries that formed communist parties after the First World War? Luo Pinghan, in a short historical commentary in Guangming Daily, answers that several factors combined. These were the failure of earlier attempts to save the nation by learning from the West, the impact of the October Revolution, the work of pioneering propagandists, and a Chinese cultural tradition that Luo says made Marxism feel familiar.

The article follows a chronological path in three parts. It begins with the decline of China after 1840 and the successive failures of the Self-Strengthening Movement, the Reform Movement of 1898 and the 1911 Revolution. It then turns to the early, scattered introduction of Marxism and the changed attitude after 1917. Finally it covers the spread of Marxism after the May Fourth Movement and the founding of early communist groups in 1920. Luo draws heavily on testimony from Mao Zedong, Liu Shaoqi, Qu Qiubai, Lin Boqu and Wu Yuzhang.

Luo argues that the October Revolution turned Marxism from a theoretical idea into a working social system, which set it apart from other socialist doctrines. Its appeal grew further after the Paris Peace Conference of 1919 ended Chinese hopes in the capitalist West, while Soviet Russia declared it was renouncing tsarist-era unequal treaties. Pioneers such as Li Dazhao and Chen Duxiu then spread the doctrine, and study societies turned into the early Party organisations. Luo adds a cultural explanation, citing Ai Siqi and Wu Yuzhang: ancient Chinese ideals of a "world of great harmony" meant that Marxism awakened a longing already present in the tradition.

Luo concludes that China's particular circumstances and cultural tradition produced wide resonance with Marxism and the first generation of Chinese Marxists. In his account, successive generations of firm believers then led Marxism to put down roots and, with the Communist Party as its bearer, produce what he calls an unprecedented development miracle. The text closes with a quotation from Xi Jinping on the Party's emergence. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed narrative of how Marxism reached China, with first-hand quotations from early Chinese revolutionaries.
quoteEn: The October Revolution turned Marxism from a theoretical conception into the construction of a real social system, and opened a wholly new path of development for human society.
quoteZh: 十月革命把马克思主义从一种理论设想变成了现实社会制度构建，开创了人类社会崭新的发展道路。

t: The Communist Party of China, born of its time, and its world-shaking historic undertaking
zh: 应运而生的中国共产党与开天辟地的历史伟业
paras: Published in Guangming Daily on 30 June 2020, shortly before the Party's centenary year, this article asks why the founding of the Communist Party of China in 1921 is called an event that 'opened up a new heaven and earth' (kaitian pidi). Mu Zhaoyong argues that the founding was historically necessary and that its significance can be grasped only by placing it within modern Chinese history and the goal of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.

The article has two main parts. The first explains why the Party 'arose in response to the call of the times'. The second explains why its founding was epoch-making, first through the Party's own qualities and then through three transformations that the author says followed. The text draws heavily on Xi Jinping's statements about the Party's origins.

In the first part, Mu says the Party's birth reflected the 'historical logic' of social development, the 'practical logic' of revolutionary struggle and the 'theoretical logic' of ideas. The Opium War of 1840 turned China into a semi-colonial, semi-feudal society, and over some eighty years of anti-imperialist and anti-feudal struggle the tasks of the revolution went unfinished. The October Revolution brought Marxism-Leninism to China, and a growing proletariat provided a new social force. The May Fourth Movement then supplied the final conditions: intellectuals such as Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu, Mao Zedong and Zhou Enlai became Marxists, early Party organisations formed, and the Communist International sent representatives. In the second part, Mu lists what the Party had from its start: Marxism as its guide, communism as its ultimate goal, close ties with the masses, and strict organisation and discipline. On this basis the author says the Party changed the direction of the Chinese nation's development, the fate of the Chinese people, and the pattern of world development.

Mu concludes that the Party moved the nation from decline towards rejuvenation through the new-democratic revolution, socialist transformation, reform and opening up, and the new era after the 18th Party Congress (2012). In the author's account, China's rise has also widened the paths to modernization open to developing countries and supports the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a concise example of the official Party narrative of the CPC's founding and its significance, as presented in the national press ahead of the centenary.
quoteEn: The founding of the Communist Party of China is an 'epoch-making event' also because the historic undertaking it opened up was itself world-shaking.
quoteZh: 中国共产党的成立之所以是“开天辟地的大事变”，还在于由此而开创的历史伟业是开天辟地的。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party slogan describing the goal of restoring China to national strength and prosperity after the 'century of humiliation'. It is closely tied to the Chinese Dream.

glossary.literal: opening up heaven and splitting earth
glossary.explanation: An idiom drawn from creation myth, used in Party histories to describe the founding of the CPC as an unprecedented turning point.
The policy of economic reform and engagement with the outside world launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since the early 2010s, which calls for joint global governance and shared development.
Mao Zedong's term for the stage of Chinese revolution from the May Fourth Movement to 1949, led by the proletariat and aimed against imperialism and feudalism.

t: Engels after he met Marx
zh: 遇见马克思以后的恩格斯
paras: Published in Guangming Daily in June 2020, to mark the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, this short commentary asks what defined Engels's life after his decisive meeting with Marx in Paris in 1844. Luo's answer is that defending, promoting and revering Marx became the portrait of Engels's life from then on. The author presents the meeting as a "chemical reaction", even a "nuclear fission", in the field of social revolution.

The piece is organised under three headings: Engels's firm political consciousness, his sense of responsibility in spreading and developing Marxism, and his personal integrity in respecting Marx. It draws on Engels's early writings, letters between the two men, and episodes from 1844 to the years after Marx's death.

Luo argues that Engels, from a devout Prussian family, gave up a comfortable bourgeois life for the proletarian cause. He is said to have fought Marx's detractors in print and accepted twenty years of commercial work, his "Egyptian captivity", so that Marx could finish Capital. Luo then lists Engels's efforts to spread Marx's work: reviews of the Critique of Political Economy, nine reviews of Capital, and over a decade spent editing Volumes 2 and 3 of Capital. Engels's own works, notably Anti-Dühring, are presented as enriching Marxism. Luo adds that Engels stressed that he merely harvested the glory Marx had sown, and cites the two men's mutual praise and trust as evidence of their friendship.

Luo closes by saying that the trials and successes of the cause the two founded show the "power of truth" in Marxism. Continuing along the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics is described as the best way for Chinese communists of the new era to honour them. Read the original if you want a brief, celebratory portrait of the Marx–Engels relationship as it was presented in the Chinese Party press for the 2020 anniversary.
quoteEn: Defending Marx, promoting Marx and revering Marx: this is the portrait of Engels's life after he met Marx.
quoteZh: 维护马克思、宣传马克思、敬重马克思，是恩格斯遇见马克思之后的人生写照。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path of socialist development since reform and opening up. It is the standard reference point in Party commentary.

t: Lenin's in-depth study of Marxist texts
zh: 列宁对马克思主义文献的深入研究
paras: This short piece, first published in Guangming Daily on 29 June 2020, asks how Lenin related to the textual legacy of Marx and Engels. Zhao argues that Lenin was both a close student of the classic texts and the person who decisively launched the first large-scale collection, editing and systematic publication of that legacy. In Zhao's account, this work gave the international workers' movement and world socialism a theoretical weapon and ideological guide.

The article follows Lenin's engagement in three stages. It begins with his early study and first translation and publishing work, then turns to his overall grasp of Marx's writings as shown in his 1914 encyclopaedia entry on Marx. It ends with his role after the October Revolution in building the institutional and material basis for editing the Marx–Engels legacy.

Zhao first shows, from Lenin's writings of 1893–94, that he already used Capital, the Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy and even the little-known manuscript of The German Ideology against the Narodniks. In 1907 Lenin also revised the Russian edition of Marx's letters to Kugelmann and wrote a preface to the Sorge correspondence. Zhao then reads the bibliography appended to Lenin's entry "Karl Marx" as evidence of systematic knowledge, noting that Lenin repeatedly observed that many of Marx's articles had not been collected, republished or translated into Russian. After 1917, Zhao says, Lenin backed the Marx–Engels Institute under David Ryazanov, set out seven questions that served as a work programme, and approved an extra 75,000 gold roubles for buying libraries in Vienna.

Zhao concludes that study of the texts equipped Lenin to lead the October Revolution, and that the new Soviet state in turn allowed him to promote the systematic collection and compilation of Marx and Engels's works. This, in Zhao's view, laid a deep ideological and theoretical foundation for the world socialist movement. Read the original if you want a concise account, drawn from Lenin's prefaces, notes and letters, of how he treated Marxist textual scholarship and the founding of the Marx–Engels Institute.
quoteEn: Even before the October Revolution, Lenin had keenly perceived that the writings and articles of Marx and Engels were incompletely collected, insufficiently published and insufficiently studied.
quoteZh: 早在十月革命前，列宁就已经敏锐地觉察到马克思恩格斯著作文章搜集不全、出版不够、研究不足的现状

t: The narrative features of Engels's theory of nature's revenge
zh: 恩格斯“自然报复论”的叙事特征
paras: Marking the 200th anniversary of Engels's birth, Li and Zhang revisit his theory of nature's revenge, which they treat as central to his dialectics of nature. They argue that Engels used the theme as a thread to develop materialist dialectics, folding background, rhetoric and intent into the text. In their reading, this prepared the way for the idea of the "two reconciliations": between humanity and nature, and within humanity itself.

The piece is a short newspaper commentary in five parts: how the theory took shape, the context in which it was written, Engels's intentions, his rhetorical strategies, and the theory's relevance to reality. It traces the idea from Engels's early writings on industrial pollution through On Authority, The Part Played by Labour in the Transition from Ape to Man, Anti-Dühring and Dialectics of Nature.

The authors argue that Engels wrote against several targets: naturalism and anthropocentrism, vulgar materialism and social Darwinism, and metaphysical views of nature and idealist dialectics. They identify three rhetorical devices: personification, analogy and model abstraction from cases such as deforestation in Mesopotamia, Italy and Spain. On their account, Engels traced nature's revenge to limits on human knowledge, to capitalist production driven by profit and surplus value, and to consumer desires stimulated by capital. Only a communist society that truly resolves the conflicts between humans and nature, and among humans, could end it.

The authors conclude that the theory offers a dialectical basis for seeing humans and nature as a community of life, with practical transformation as its aim. They link it to the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) and call for guidance from Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization, a change in the traditional development model, and respect for ecological red lines. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese reading of Engels's ecological thought and its tie to official ecological civilization policy.
quoteEn: Engels held that flaws in human understanding, together with the defects of production, consumption and distribution under capitalism, would inevitably give rise to nature's revenge, and in an ever more serious form.
quoteZh: 恩格斯认为人类的认识缺陷、资本主义制度下的社会生产和消费分配弊端必然会导致自然报复的产生,并会越来越严重

glossary.explanation: A official Chinese policy concept, prominent since the 2010s, that makes environmental protection part of national development and Party strategy.

glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization
glossary.explanation: The part of Xi Jinping's thought dealing with the environment and the relationship between humans and nature. It is officially presented as the guide for ecological work.
Officially defined limits for protecting key ecological areas and resources, which development activity must not cross.

t: Engels's construction of the system of Marxist philosophy
zh: 恩格斯对马克思主义哲学体系的建构
paras: This short commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in June 2020, asks what Engels contributed to building Marxist philosophy into a system. Yang argues that Engels contributed in both form and content. In form, he helped criticise the rigid closed systems of older philosophy and turn philosophy into an open structure and dynamic thought. In content, he unified ontology, dialectics and the conception of history.

The article is organised around four themes: Engels's reading of the fundamental question of philosophy, the ontological foundations of Marxism, dialectics as worldview and method, and the interaction among historical factors. It draws on Engels's works, including his editing of volumes two and three of Capital, Anti-Dühring, Ludwig Feuerbach and the End of Classical German Philosophy, Dialectics of Nature and The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State.

Yang holds that through these works Engels produced the first complete systematisation of Marxist philosophy. He did so by separating the relation of thinking and being from other forms of philosophical struggle and making it the criterion for judging philosophical positions. On this basis he is said to have grounded the unity of the world in its materiality and examined matter, motion, time and space. Dialectics runs through all of this as the main thread, and Yang lists its laws and categories. Finally, Engels stressed the relative independence of political, legal, philosophical and religious factors, and their reaction on the economic base, to correct misreadings of historical materialism.

Yang concludes that these achievements make Engels's self-description as the 'second violinist' fully deserved. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language overview of how Engels is credited with systematising Marxist philosophy.
quoteEn: Engels's indelible contribution to constructing the system of Marxist philosophy makes his self-description as the "second violinist" fully deserved.
quoteZh: 恩格斯对马克思主义哲学体系的建构所作出的不可磨灭的功绩，使其“第二小提琴手”的自我认同实至名归。

t: The Yan'an Spirit: a nutrient for Party members and cadres to nourish the original aspiration and temper the soul
zh: 延安精神：党员干部滋养初心、淬炼灵魂的营养剂
paras: Taking its cue from Xi Jinping's remarks during an inspection tour of Shaanxi, this commentary (first published in Guangming Daily, 13 May 2020) asks how the Yan'an Spirit can serve Party members and cadres today. Tan argues that this revolutionary spirit, formed in the Yan'an period, has value that transcends its time. In the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics it can, in the author's phrase, work as a "nutrient" that nourishes the original aspiration and tempers the soul of Party members.

The piece is divided into four numbered sections. The first presents the Yan'an period as a systematic refresher of the Party's original aspiration and mission, built on seeking truth from facts, practical work and strict discipline. The second sets out the lasting value of the Yan'an Spirit: its view of the masses, its commitment to putting the people first, and its Marxist stance and method. The third traces how Xi Jinping has drawn on it since the 18th Party Congress (2012) for innovation, self-reliance and a sense of responsibility. The fourth proposes using it as a mirror for self-examination.

Tan's central move is to treat the Yan'an Spirit as a set of concrete practices that Party members can compare themselves against. Drawing on statements by Mao Zedong and Chen Yun, the author presents the Party-people relationship as one of roots and soil, the mass line as "from the masses, to the masses", and "whole-hearted service to the people" as the core principle of the Party's purpose. The Great Production Movement and the "three-thirds" system of government are cited as examples. The author then names three tests for today's cadres: whether their political direction is firm and correct, whether their service to the people is wholehearted, and whether they have eliminated formalism and bureaucracy. The Yan'an rectification campaign is offered as the historical model for the last test.

Tan concludes that keeping the original aspiration and mission is a lifelong task, not a passing campaign. The Yan'an Spirit should be used again and again as a mirror to correct one's appearance and remove selfish thoughts. The author links the fight against formalism and bureaucracy to the eight-point regulations and the campaign against the "four undesirable work styles" since 2012. Tan holds that this struggle must be protracted and combine concentrated campaigns with sustained effort. Read the original if you want a compact example of how Party-affiliated writers in 2020 drew on Yan'an history to frame cadre education and Party discipline.
quoteEn: The Yan'an Spirit is a mirror for Party members and cadres; by looking into it constantly we can straighten our attire, brush off the dust, rid ourselves of selfish thoughts, and become qualified Communists.
quoteZh: 延安精神就是党员干部的一面镜子，不断照这面镜子，能够使我们正衣冠，去灰尘，去私心杂念，做一名合格的共产党员。

glossary.explanation: A term for the values the Communist Party attributes to its years based at Yan'an (1935–1948). It typically covers seeking truth from facts, self-reliance, hard struggle and serving the people.
A slogan of Xi Jinping-era Party building. It refers to the Party's founding purpose of seeking happiness for the Chinese people and rejuvenation for the nation.
A Party principle, associated with Mao Zedong, of gathering views from the masses and returning them as policy. It is summed up as "from the masses, to the masses".

glossary.literal: Yan'an campaign to straighten work styles
glossary.explanation: An ideological education and criticism campaign in the early 1940s. It targeted dogmatism, sectarianism and formalism within the Party.

Rules on officials' work style, such as curbing extravagance and bureaucratic habits. The Party leadership issued them in December 2012 as the starting point of a campaign against the "four undesirable work styles".

t: Study and solve problems by proceeding from reality: the meaning and present-day lessons of "Oppose Book Worship"
zh: 坚持一切从实际出发来研究和解决问题——《反对本本主义》的深刻内涵与现实启示
paras: Marking the 90th anniversary of Mao Zedong's "Oppose Book Worship" (1930), this commentary, first published in Guangming Daily in May 2020, argues that the essay remains a foundational text for the Party's ideological line of seeking truth from facts. Yang Mingwei holds that rereading it helps Party members proceed from reality in their thinking, work methods and leadership methods.

The piece first recounts the essay's history: written in May 1930 as "Investigation Work" against dogmatism in the Red Army, lost, recovered in 1961, and added to the 1991 second edition of the Selected Works of Mao Zedong. It then summarises the essay's main formulations, such as "no investigation, no right to speak". Yang goes on to describe present-day forms of dogmatism and ends with four lessons for current work, all supported by quotations from Xi Jinping.

Yang argues that the essay treats investigation as both a worldview and a method, and contains the early forms of seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence. Yang identifies several persistent tendencies that depart from the Party's ideological line: separating theory from China's conditions, rote-learning classic texts, passive formalism that follows documents literally, and talking about Marxism without acting on it. Yang also criticises copying Western "dogmas" and cases.

The four lessons are to be practical doers, to avoid copying Western theory and capitalist experience blindly, to combine upholding Marxism with developing it through new theoretical creation, and to keep strategic resolve on the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Yang concludes that rereading the essay helps oppose all forms of subjectivism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the 1930 text is used in official commentary on the Party's ideological line today.
quoteEn: Seeking truth from facts is a fundamental tenet of Marxism and a basic requirement for Chinese Communists in understanding and changing the world. It is our Party's basic way of thinking, working and leading, and must be upheld over the long term.
quoteZh: 实事求是，是马克思主义的根本观点，是中国共产党人认识世界、改造世界的根本要求，是我们党的基本思想方法、工作方法、领导方法，必须长期坚持。

glossary.explanation: A principle central to Mao Zedong Thought, later made the core of the Party's ideological line, stressing that policy should rest on actual conditions rather than on doctrine.
Mao Zedong's term for dogmatism: treating written texts, including Marxist ones, as binding regardless of real conditions.
The Party's guiding approach to knowing and handling problems, summed up as proceeding from reality and seeking truth from facts.
A Party method of work that stresses going among the people, learning from them and relying on them.

t: The global fight against COVID-19 shows the world significance of the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind
zh: 全球抗疫彰显人类命运共同体理念的世界意义
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in May 2020, Pang Lisheng takes up the COVID-19 pandemic as a test case for the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind. The article argues that the global response shows how closely human destinies are bound together, and that this gives the idea fresh practical and historical significance.

The short commentary has three parts. The first treats the pandemic as a sign of mutual dependence in the present era. The second considers how the global anti-epidemic effort brings out the idea's meaning, including China's role. The third presents the idea as a guide to the progress of human civilisation.

Pang draws on Marx's theory of world history. In this reading, the present is a world-historical age in which isolated, self-sufficient conditions have given way to deep mutual dependence. The same age brings global problems: humanity's unrestrained exploitation of nature, and global risks arising from the worldwide expansion of capital. Pang argues that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind answers these conditions and is rooted in them. The article also describes China as a responsible major country that has shown capability and commitment in its own epidemic control and in international cooperation.

Pang says the idea draws on traditional Chinese civilisation and on Marxism, and that it is moving from theory to practice through the Belt and Road Initiative, regional bilateral communities and new multilateral platforms. Citing Engels, Pang calls on humanity to reflect on the disaster and strengthen the idea, working toward a world of lasting peace, universal security, common prosperity, openness and cleanliness. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese commentary in 2020 linked the pandemic to the community-of-shared-future concept.
quoteEn: The condition of humanity in the age of world history, marked by interdependence, universal connection and a shared fate, is the real foundation of the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind.
quoteZh: 世界历史时代人类相互依存、普遍联系、休戚与共的存在状况，是人类命运共同体理念的真实根基。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and theoretical concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–2013. It calls for cooperation among states on shared global challenges and is presented as an alternative to zero-sum rivalry.
A Chinese initiative launched in 2013 to build infrastructure and economic links across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Populism in Central and Eastern Europe: current state, basic ideas and impact
zh: 中东欧民粹主义：现状、基本理念及影响
paras: Writing in 2020, Zhang Li asks why populist parties in Central and Eastern Europe have grown so steadily in national and European Parliament elections, and what they stand for. The article argues that these parties rest on two basic ideas, nationalism and "illiberalism", and that their continued strength reflects an impasse in further European Union integration and a deepening East–West split.

The article opens with the electoral record of populist parties across the region, citing Freedom House figures that put their average vote share at 9.2% in 2000 and 31.6% in 2017. It then follows developments in the four Visegrád states (Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovakia), noting Orbán's Fidesz, Kaczyński's Law and Justice, Babiš's ANO 2011 and Fico's Smer, and briefly mentions Bulgaria, Serbia and the Baltic states. A section on basic ideas is followed by one on impact and prospects.

Zhang contends that populism is at root a rejection of liberal ideology and liberal elite politics. In the author's account, the neoliberal economic model adopted after 1989, then the 2008 financial crisis, austerity and the 2015 refugee crisis, fed popular discontent that leaders such as Orbán and Kaczyński turned into support for an "illiberal" political model, with Hungary and Poland as the clearest cases. Zhang adds that a narrow, historically rooted nationalism, expressed through "restorative nationalism" in Hungary and Poland, turned identity into the main party dispute and set nationalists against pro-European liberals.

As for impact, Zhang argues that populism has become the glue binding sovereigntists and nationalists, so it may dominate these countries' politics for some time, and that it has damaged the liberal-democratic consensus the EU promoted after 1989. The region's governments favour intergovernmental cooperation over ceding sovereignty, reject refugee quotas and "multi-speed Europe", and resent EU criticism and sanctions. Zhang concludes that populism has become mainstream in the region and that more such parties may take power; if they join forces with Western European populists, European politics could change at a larger scale. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language overview of Central and Eastern European populism, with election data and a Chinese scholarly reading of its causes and its effect on EU integration.
quoteEn: Nationalism and \"illiberalism\" have become the basic ideas of populism in Central and Eastern Europe.
quoteZh: 民族主义和“非自由主义”成为中东欧地区民粹主义的基本理念。

t: Giving full play to the people's congress system as the fundamental political institution
zh: 充分发挥人民代表大会制度的根本政治制度作用
paras: This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 29 May 2020, argues that the people's congress system must be used to the full as China's fundamental political institution. Cheng Tongshun describes it as the institutional arrangement that unites Party leadership, the people being masters of the country, and law-based governance. In Cheng's view, this system lets the people hold the nation's future in their own hands.

The piece is organised around three roles of the system. It is presented as an essential support for upholding the Party's overall leadership, as the fundamental route to the people being masters of the country, and as the institutional basis and practical vehicle for comprehensively advancing law-based governance. Cheng places this in the context of the new era and the goals of building a moderately prosperous society and national rejuvenation.

On Party leadership, Cheng argues that the Party's leading position was chosen by history and the people and is written into the Constitution. The system is the channel through which Party positions become state will through legal procedures, and Party-recommended candidates become state officials. On popular sovereignty, Cheng stresses that people's congresses are not parallel to other state organs: administrative, supervisory, judicial and procuratorial organs are created by, answerable to and supervised by them, while the congresses themselves answer to the people. On law-based governance, Cheng calls for stronger legislation, constitutional supervision, constitutionality review and oversight of law enforcement through the congresses.

Cheng concludes that Party leadership, the people being masters of the country and law-based governance converge in the people's congress system, which Cheng identifies as the source of the scientific character and vitality of Chinese-style democracy. The article calls for political resolve and for firmly following the path of political development of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line account of how the people's congress system is justified in Party discourse around 2020.
quoteEn: The most notable feature of the people's congress system is that the relationship between the people's congresses and other state organs is not a parallel one.
quoteZh: 人民代表大会制度最显著的特点就是人民代表大会与其他国家机关的关系不是平行的。

glossary.explanation: China's basic political system, in which the National People's Congress and local people's congresses are the organs of state power. Other state organs are formed by and answerable to them.

glossary.en: the people being masters of the country
glossary.literal: the people act as masters of the household
glossary.explanation: A Party formulation for popular sovereignty, described as the essence of socialist democracy. It is exercised mainly through the people's congresses.

glossary.literal: governing the country according to law
glossary.explanation: The official principle of ruling the country by law. In Party usage it operates under Party leadership.
The official name for China's path, theory and system of socialism since reform and opening up.

glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and standing, often linked to the Chinese Dream and the two centenary goals.

keywords: people as masters of the country

t: People's democracy is a whole-process democracy
zh: 人民民主是一种全过程的民主
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in 2020, Xin argues that people's democracy in China is a "whole-process democracy". In the article's account, major legislative decisions follow procedure, pass through democratic deliberation and are made scientifically and democratically. Xin presents this as the broadest, most genuine and most effective form of democracy for protecting the people's fundamental interests.

The commentary is built around three claims. Whole-process democracy means that no link in the democratic chain may be missing. It means that each democratic institution has a complete process of its own. And it is genuine and continually improving. Xin draws on Xi Jinping's statements and on examples such as the people's congresses, consultative bodies, regional ethnic autonomy and grassroots self-governance.

Xin holds that democracy covers elections, decision-making, management and oversight, and criticises systems that stress only voting. Xin cites measures such as reserved delegate quotas for ordinary people, hearings on draft laws, staff congresses in enterprises and open government affairs. Xin also traces the Party's democratic experiments from Soviet-area democracy and the wartime "three-thirds system" to the people's congress system and grassroots self-governance. According to Xin, a century of Party leadership has built a "democratic rationality" that avoids the "one-off democracy" and "street politics" the article attributes to some other countries.

Xin concludes that whole-process democracy is substantive rather than formalistic, "not a decoration", and keeps developing through institutionalisation and standardisation. Read the original if you want a concise official-line statement of the "whole-process democracy" idea as it was formulated in 2020, with its main institutional examples.
quoteEn: Whole-process democracy does not practise democratic formalism, put on a "democracy show" or stage political theatre, and does not seek superficial glamour and affectation.
quoteZh: 全过程的民主不搞民主形式主义，不搞“民主秀”，不搞政治戏剧，不追求表面的华丽和做作

glossary.explanation: A concept in Chinese official discourse, associated with Xi Jinping from 2019, holding that democracy should cover elections, decision-making, management and oversight rather than voting alone. Officials present it as an alternative to electoral democracy in Western systems.

China's fundamental political institution, a system of congresses from local level up to the National People's Congress. Official texts describe it as the organ through which the people exercise state power.
The system under which areas with concentrated ethnic minority populations exercise autonomy within the unitary state. Official sources describe it as a basic political system.

t: The methodological horizon of a reality-oriented philosophy of culture
zh: 文化哲学面向现实的方法论视域
paras: Hu Changshuan takes up two basic questions in the philosophy of culture: how the field should be understood and how it should be studied. Writing in Guangming Daily in 2020, Hu starts from the Marxist premise that worldview determines methodology, so that a given understanding of the philosophy of culture and the method used to study it are inseparable. The article argues that the field should be grasped through a dialectical combination of several conceptions, and that its method should be grounded in five principles, which together keep it oriented towards reality.

The article opens by linking the philosophy of culture to cultural confidence, which it describes as the deepest form of confidence underlying confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It then has two parts. The first sets out three common conceptions of the field, taking its cue from the founder Ernst Cassirer's warning against both naturalism and metaphysics. The second draws five methodological requirements from the Marxist classics and from Hegel, Jaspers, Husserl-style phenomenology and Benedetto Croce.

In Hu's account, the three conceptions are a naturalistic one, which treats culture as an external object of empirical science and in essence belongs to cultural studies; a metaphysical one, which takes culture as the essence of the world and of humanity and in essence belongs to philosophy; and an anthropological one, which sees the human being as a symbolic animal and the philosophy of culture as a philosophy of the human. Hu urges treating these as complementary dimensions rather than rivals. The five methods are: philosophy as the history of philosophy; metaphysical thinking that goes beyond empirical cultural facts; critical logic that finds the new world in criticism of the old, including reflection on scientism; a return to things themselves, which starts from everyday cultural phenomena and facts; and a realist stance, following Marx's remark that problems are the slogans of the age.

Hu concludes that the philosophy of culture is a philosophy with real-world concerns. It has to move beyond both positive science and metaphysics, supplying a cultural interpretation of the theory of the human being and so advancing human liberation and the true appropriation of human essence. The stress on starting from present-day life is meant to give the field practical relevance and to support cultural confidence. Read the original if you want a short, Marxist-inflected methodological outline of Chinese philosophy of culture, with its reading of Cassirer and its list of five research principles.
quoteEn: The philosophy of culture arose from the outset in facing reality, and it must necessarily proceed from reality, holding to a realist stance rooted in human beings' present life, so as to strengthen its relevance and significance.
quoteZh: 文化哲学从一开始就是在面向现实中产生的，也必然要从现实出发，坚持一种立足人类当下生活的现实立场，以增强其现实针对性和意义。

glossary.explanation: A Party slogan, prominent since the 2010s, for confidence in China's own cultural traditions and in socialist culture. It is presented as a foundation for the other forms of confidence in the path, theory and system.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era. It combines state leadership with market mechanisms.
A branch of philosophy that studies culture and its relation to human existence. In the article it is traced to Ernst Cassirer.

t: Principles for building a philosophical academic system with Chinese characteristics
zh: 构建中国特色哲学学术体系的原则
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in May 2020, Wang Xinyan asks what principle should govern the construction of a philosophical academic system with Chinese characteristics, Chinese style and Chinese manner. Taking up Xi Jinping's statement that Marxist guidance is what distinguishes contemporary Chinese philosophy and social science from others, Wang argues that the work must adhere to the adaptation of Marxist philosophy to the Chinese context.

The short piece has three parts. The first derives the principle from two requirements: Marxist guidance and a footing in Chinese reality. The second reviews the twentieth-century search for a modern Chinese philosophy after the May Fourth period. The third sets out three reasons why the adaptation of Marxist philosophy is the basic principle for the new era.

Wang holds that a philosophical system is an ideological system carrying values, so it needs a theoretical standpoint, and Marxist philosophy supplies one. Chinese reality, understood as history (especially fine traditional culture), present conditions and the world's great changes, is both the object and the resource. In Wang's account, cultural conservatism (Xiong Shili, Feng Youlan, He Lin, Jin Yuelin) and liberalism (Hu Shi's pragmatism) failed to handle the relation among Marxist, Chinese and Western philosophy. Only Marxists succeeded, producing what Li Da called a system of 'one body, two wings'. Adaptation is then said to secure continuity and national character, originality and timeliness, and systematic, professional coherence across all fields of philosophy.

Wang concludes that adaptation does not mean Chinese philosophy should study only that topic. Every field should follow its requirements, each in its own way. Read the original if you want a brief, official-line statement of how a Party-aligned philosopher frames the history and guiding principle of Chinese philosophy.
quoteEn: Only by adhering to the adaptation of Marxist philosophy to the Chinese context can a philosophical academic system with Chinese characteristics be built that is original and attuned to its times.
quoteZh: 只有坚持马克思主义哲学中国化，才能构建具有原创性、时代性的中国特色哲学学术体系。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义哲学中国化
glossary.en: adaptation of Marxist philosophy to the Chinese context
glossary.explanation: The official idea that Marxist philosophy should be combined with China's realities and cultural heritage. It is a philosophical branch of the broader programme of adapting Marxism to China.
Li Da's image of Chinese philosophy: Sinicized Marxist philosophy as the body, with the study of Chinese traditional philosophy and of Western philosophy as two wings.

t: The course and theoretical exploration of Vietnam's economic renovation
zh: 越南经济革新的历程及理论探索
paras: Pan Jin'e asks how Vietnam's economic renovation (doi moi), launched in 1986, produced both practical results and a distinctive theory. Writing in 2020, Pan argues that the theoretical product is the "socialist-oriented market economy", and that practice succeeded because ideas were first liberated and theory then guided reform.

The article has two main parts. The first traces the practice of renovation from the Sixth Party Congress (1986), moving from agricultural contracting to state-enterprise equitisation and then to finance and services. It divides this into three phases: building internal capacity (1986–2006), international integration (2006–2019), and a technology-driven phase expected to start with the 13th Congress in 2021. The second part follows how the Vietnamese Communist Party's congress documents changed its concepts, from the Sixth to the Twelfth Congress. A closing section lists current problems and compares Vietnam with China.

Pan's central reasoning is that the Party moved step by step from rejecting the market to treating it as a tool of socialism. After the early-1980s crisis under a Soviet-style planned economy, Vietnam defined itself as in the initial stage of a transition period to socialism. It then accepted a commodity economy (1986), multiple sectors (1989), and the market as a human civilisational achievement not identical with capitalism (the Ninth Congress, 2001, and a 2008 resolution). Pan notes that the Tenth and Eleventh Congresses dropped public ownership of the main means of production as a basic feature of socialism, which Pan says still divides Vietnamese theorists. Pan reads this as a shift from "public ownership" to "socialisation", alongside a falling state-enterprise share of GDP (about 20 percent, with a target of about 10) and a more plural distribution system.

Pan reports major gains: per-capita GDP rose from under US$100 in 1986 to US$2,800 in 2019, and poverty fell to 1.45 percent. Pan also identifies risks, including uneven development, weak infrastructure, pollution, slow digitalisation (76 percent of firms have not started), and heavy dependence on foreign capital and trade, with trade agreements such as the CPTPP possibly weakening state control. On China, Pan observes that Vietnam locates itself in a transition period while China speaks of the primary stage of socialism, so goals and policies differ, and the two countries can learn from each other. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's concise account of how Vietnamese Party congresses redefined ownership, the market and socialism.
quoteEn: The Sixth Congress of the Vietnamese Communist Party already recognised multiple economic sectors, but stressed the dominant position of the state economy, so as to guide the other sectors towards socialism.
quoteZh: 越共六大已承认多种经济成分，但强调国营经济的支配地位，以引导其他经济成分朝着社会主义方向发展。

glossary.explanation: The official Chinese Communist Party assessment that China is at an early, long-lasting stage of socialist development. It underpins China's policy mix of public and private ownership.
The Vietnamese reform programme launched at the Sixth Party Congress in 1986. It moved Vietnam from central planning towards a market-oriented economy under Communist Party leadership.

glossary.zh: 社会主义定向的市场经济
glossary.pinyin: shèhuì zhǔyì dìngxiàng de shìchǎng jīngjì
glossary.explanation: The Vietnamese Communist Party's official formula for its economic model, adopted in 2001. It describes a market economy managed by the state and led by the Party, said to be directed towards socialism.
A Marxist-Leninist notion of the period between capitalism and socialism. The Vietnamese Party uses it to describe its present stage.

t: New opportunities for the international communist movement amid changes unseen in a century
st: Report on the development of the international communist movement, 2019–2020
zh: 百年未有之大变局背景下国际共产主义运动的新机遇
zhSub: 2019～2020年国际共产主义运动发展报告
authors: Research group on the 2019–2020 report on the development of the international communist movement
paras: This annual report, produced by a CASS research group, surveys the international communist movement in 2019 and early 2020 against the background of what it calls changes unseen in a century. It argues that the period brought new features: major anniversaries prompted renewed reflection on international unity, socialist states pursued reform and planning, non-ruling parties had mixed results, and the COVID-19 pandemic strengthened the case for socialism and for a community with a shared future for mankind.

The report has four parts. It first covers commemorations of the Comintern's centenary and the debate over its lessons. It then reviews China's anniversaries (the May Fourth Movement and the founding of the People's Republic) and developments in Vietnam, Cuba, Laos and North Korea. Next it assesses communist parties outside socialist states, in South Asia, the former Soviet and Eastern European region, Western Europe, Japan, the Americas and Oceania. It ends with the 2020 anniversaries of Engels and Lenin and the pandemic.

On the Comintern, the report describes broad agreement that it helped found parties and supported anti-colonial and anti-fascist struggles, alongside criticism of over-centralisation, policy towards social democrats and "leftist" errors. Parties disagree on how to unite: the Communist Party of Greece stresses ideological and strategic unity, while the Turkish and US parties favour exchange of experience and respect for autonomy. The authors read these disagreements, over how to treat and develop Marxism and how to view socialist reform, as the main obstacle to unity. They treat Belgium's Workers' Party of Belgium as a notable success, crediting its explicit aim of a classless society, while seeing most Western parties as stagnant and the Japanese Communist Party as drifting away from its former stance on China, Vietnam and Cuba.

On the pandemic, the report holds that China's containment and the low reported case numbers in Vietnam, Laos and North Korea (as of 30 April) show the superiority of the socialist system. It contends that Western governments' responses exposed capitalism's flaws and double standards. It also expects capitalist forces to intensify pressure on communist parties and sees long coexistence of the two systems as unavoidable, so it urges promotion of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially aligned Chinese survey of party-by-party developments, election figures and Comintern debates in 2019–2020.
quoteEn: These disagreements centre on how to treat Marxism, how to uphold and develop Marxism, and how to view socialist reform.
quoteZh: 这些分歧重点涉及如何对待马克思主义，如何坚持和发展马克思主义，以及如何看待社会主义改革等问题。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2013, presenting countries as interdependent and calling for cooperation across different systems.

glossary.pinyin: bǎi nián wèiyǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.literal: great changes not seen in a hundred years
glossary.explanation: A phrase in Chinese official discourse, widely used since about 2017–2018, describing a shifting global balance of power and rapid technological and geopolitical change.

t: Changing trends and impacts of Latin American social democracy since the 21st century
zh: 21世纪以来拉美社会民主主义的变化趋势与影响
paras: Yuan Dongzhen asks how Latin American social democratic parties have changed since 2000 and what those changes mean for the region. The article, published in Contemporary World in 2020, argues that many of these parties have revised their guiding ideology, ideological identity, theory and policy platforms. In Yuan's account, three tendencies have strengthened: "de-Marxification", "popularisation" and a drift towards democratic socialism.

The article first describes how social democracy grew into a mainstream political force in the region after the Second World War. It lists the parties involved, including Chile's Socialist Party, Argentina's Radical Civic Union and Mexico's Party of the Democratic Revolution. It then sets out eight traditional principles, among them pluralist ideology, a "third way", moderate reform, multi-class alliances and legal electoral struggle. Next it examines four areas of change, using mainly Chile, Venezuela and Nicaragua as cases. It then gives four causes and three consequences.

Yuan contends that parties such as Chile's Socialist Party, Nicaragua's Sandinista Front and Venezuela's Movement towards Socialism dropped Marxism-Leninism as their sole guide. They also redefined themselves from working-class parties to broad parties of "all working people", and shifted from overthrowing capitalism to defending the existing democratic order. On policy, they moved to moderate and patch neoliberalism, coordinating economic and social policy. Yuan attributes this to adaptation to European social democracy, an escape from the dead ends of traditional policy, the search for wider electoral support, and pressure from the new left governments that rose after 1999.

Yuan concludes that these changes will deepen ideological confusion among left parties, whose communist, left-nationalist and social democratic strands are drifting further apart. The author also expects them to push regional politics towards moderation and reform, since both left and right governments have failed to solve development problems, and to make party competition among centre-left forces more complex. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of how Latin American social democratic parties have changed ideologically, with party-by-party examples.
quoteEn: The changes in Latin American social democratic theory and policy are meant to adapt to the global trend in social democracy and to Latin America's new political and social environment, and especially to escape the predicament of traditional social democratic policy practice in the region.
quoteZh: 拉美社会民主主义理论和政策主张的变化，既是为了适应世界社会民主主义的发展趋势，也是为了适应拉美新的政治社会生态，特别是试图摆脱拉美传统社会民主主义政策实践的困境。

glossary.explanation: The author's label for parties abandoning Marxism as their guiding ideology or sole theoretical basis.
Here it means parties playing down their working-class identity to present themselves as broad, catch-all parties representing many social groups.
In Chinese discourse the term usually denotes the post-war Socialist International current, which accepts parliamentary democracy and gradual reform and rejects revolutionary transformation.
A path said to lie between capitalism and communism, which the article lists among the traditional positions of Latin American social democratic parties.

t: Understanding the way of major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics in the new era through three "unwaverings"
zh: 从三个“坚定不移”悟新时代中国特色大国外交之道
paras: This short commentary, published in Contemporary World in 2020, takes up the three "unwaverings" in China's foreign policy statements: Xi Jinping's 2020 New Year message and the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) both pledged to unwaveringly follow the path of peaceful development, to safeguard world peace and promote common development, and to safeguard national sovereignty, security and development interests. Ji argues that together they reveal the way of major-country diplomacy with Chinese characteristics in the new era.

The piece sets the three commitments against what it calls changes unseen in a century and the entry of socialism with Chinese characteristics into a new era. It treats each commitment in turn, then shows how they relate to one another.

On peaceful development, Ji says it is a strategic choice rooted in Chinese cultural tradition, in the historical experience of national humiliation and recovery, and in the fact that a stable external environment enabled China's rapid growth. On world peace and common development, the author links the commitment to the Party's original mission and to building a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative, citing the China–US phase-one trade agreement as an example. On sovereignty, security and development interests, Ji holds that these are the guarantee and precondition of the other two. The author warns that China will not yield on core interests and names Taiwan, Hong Kong, Tibet and Xinjiang separatism as issues on which outside forces are, in this account, working against national rejuvenation.

Ji concludes that the three commitments run through the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind and show China's resolve to build a new type of international relations. The author calls them a golden key to understanding Xi Jinping's diplomatic thought. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in early 2020 framed the logic linking peaceful development with firm defence of core interests.
quoteEn: China's pursuit of peace and development is by no means peace for the sake of peace or development for the sake of development, and it by no means implies retreating without principles or bottom lines.
quoteZh: 中国追求和平与发展绝不是为了和平而和平，为了发展而发展，绝不意味着没有原则、没有底线地退让。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–13 as the guiding idea of China's foreign policy, stressing interdependence and shared interests among states.
A Chinese infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative launched in 2013, linking China with countries across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era; the 19th Party Congress (2017) declared it had entered a new era.
The official name for the body of ideas on foreign affairs associated with Xi Jinping, treated as part of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: European political fragmentation and the direction of China–EU relations
zh: 欧洲政治碎片化与中欧关系走向
paras: Writing in 2020, after Brexit and as COVID-19 spread across Europe, Zheng Chunrong argues that political fragmentation has become a "new normal" in Europe. The article asks how this fragmentation, driven by declining mainstream parties and rising populist ones, will affect the EU and its relations with China. Zheng's answer is that China–EU relations will show a simultaneous increase in the need for cooperation and in competition.

The article begins with the evidence of fragmentation: the 2019 European Parliament elections, and national cases from 2017 onwards in the Netherlands, France, Germany and the Czech Republic. It then sets out three consequences for the EU and its member states. The final sections turn to China–EU relations and offer four proposals for guiding them.

Zheng contends that fragmentation pushes European politics to the right. In the author's account, mainstream parties adopt populist positions, especially on migration, and populism becomes mainstream and normalised, as in Austria and Hungary. Coalition-building also becomes harder at every level, with Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden and the German state of Thuringia given as examples. The EU's capacity for collective action weakens, and the EU and its members turn to more protectionist policies in trade, investment and industry. Zheng argues that Europe's concern over its declining strength strengthens its push for strategic autonomy. The EU therefore needs China more, given shared support for multilateralism and for climate and Iran-deal commitments. At the same time, it fears China more, and the 2019 EU strategic outlook calls China a "systemic rival".

Zheng proposes four courses of action. They are to deepen cooperation, with a new strategic plan centred on digitalisation and greening; to uphold multilateralism and free trade, including progress on the investment agreement; to raise cooperation to a higher level in high technology and reject "decoupling"; and to build a new type of international relations on the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence. Europe, the author says, should not blame others for its own problems or follow the United States on "systemic competition". Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of how European populism and party fragmentation are read in Beijing-oriented policy discussion of China–EU ties around 2020.
quoteEn: European political fragmentation will increase the complexity and uncertainty of China–EU bilateral relations.
quoteZh: 欧洲政治碎片化将使中欧双边关系复杂性、不确定性增加。

glossary.explanation: A label for China in the EU's March 2019 strategic outlook on EU–China relations. Zheng reads it as stressing the contrast between the EU's social market economy and a state-led Chinese model.

Principles of mutual respect for sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence. They have been a long-standing basis of Chinese foreign policy since the 1950s.
A Chinese foreign-policy formula that stresses mutual respect, fairness and justice, and win-win cooperation as an alternative to power politics.

t: Carrying forward the great revolutionary spirit
st: Studying and implementing General Secretary Xi Jinping's important speech during his inspection of the Xiangshan revolutionary memorial site in Beijing
zh: 弘扬伟大革命精神
zhSub: 深入学习贯彻习近平总书记视察北京香山革命纪念地重要讲话精神
paras: Du Feijin's article, published in Qiushi in 2020, is a study-and-implementation piece on Xi Jinping's speech of 12 September 2019 at the Xiangshan revolutionary memorial site in Beijing. It asks what the Communist Party's 181 days at Xiangshan in 1949 should teach today. Du argues that three elements of the 'great revolutionary spirit' formed there must be inherited and carried forward: seeing the revolution through to the end, a revolutionary commitment to serve the people, and a modest, prudent and hardworking style.

The article opens by recalling what the Central Committee did at Xiangshan between March and September 1949: the order to advance across the country, Mao Zedong's 'On the People's Democratic Dictatorship', and preparations for the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference and its Common Programme. Three sections follow, each opening with a passage from Xi's speech and then drawing on historical episodes. A final section turns to the tasks of the 'new era'.

On the first element, Du presents the Party's determination to see the revolution through as rooted in Marxism's idea of a radical break with old property relations and in the lessons of struggle. He contrasts Chen Duxiu's right-opportunism, which he says surrendered proletarian leadership, with the Party's firm struggle during the War of Resistance against Japan. On the second, Du describes the Common Programme as the result of broad consultation with non-communist parties. He cites Mao's conversation with Liu Yazi, in which Mao credited popular support for the Yangtze crossing, and argues that the Party's interests coincide with the people's. On the third, he cites the 'going to the capital to sit the exam' remarks, the six rules adopted at the Second Plenum of the 7th Central Committee (1949), and anecdotes of Mao's frugality. He presents the Party's capacity for self-reform as its defining strength.

Du concludes with proposals for the present. The Party should strengthen the four-sphere confidence and prepare for 'great struggle', stay close to the masses and tackle problems such as access to healthcare, schooling, jobs and housing, and keep an honest, pragmatic style. This includes the Two Upholds, full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, the eight-point rules, and sustained anti-corruption work. He ties these tasks to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want an example of how Party media in 2020 drew on the Xiangshan period to frame ideals of political discipline, mass line and self-reform.
quoteEn: The greatness of our Party lies not in never making mistakes, but in never shying away from treatment, daring to face problems, being bold in self-reform, and having a very strong capacity for self-repair.
quoteZh: 我们党的伟大不在于从不犯错误，而在于从不讳疾忌医，敢于直面问题，勇于自我革命，具有极强的自我修复能力。

glossary.explanation: A formula calling for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It was popularised in Party discourse in the early 2010s.
A Party requirement to uphold Xi Jinping's core position on the Central Committee and the Party's centralised, unified leadership. It was formalised around 2018–2019.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: The slogan for the Party's campaign on discipline, anti-corruption and internal supervision since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The central national goal in Party discourse, associated with the Chinese Dream and with the 'two centenary goals'.
Rules adopted by the Politburo in December 2012 to curb formalism, extravagance and bureaucratic habits among officials.
A term for the Party correcting its own faults and purging internal problems without outside pressure. Official English usage is 'the Party's self-reform'.

t: The Party's enduring cause and the establishment of a system for staying true to the original aspiration and keeping the mission in mind
zh: 从党的千秋伟业看不忘初心、牢记使命制度的建立
paras: Writing in Qiushi in 2020, Sun Yeli takes up a question posed by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019): how can the Communist Party of China keep its "original aspiration and founding mission" (chuxin and shiming) over the long term? Sun's answer is that this can be secured only by institutions. The Plenum's Decision put the creation of such a system first among its measures for upholding and improving socialism with Chinese characteristics, and Sun presents it as a precondition for the Party's lasting cause.

The article opens with a historical argument and then sets out four requirements for building the system. It begins with Huang Yanpei's 1945 remarks to Mao Zedong on the "historical cycle" of dynastic rise and fall. It then follows the Party's record of rectification campaigns and discipline-building, from the Yan'an period to the education campaigns after the 18th Party Congress (2012). The four requirements concern theoretical armament, the Party's self-reform, political life within the Party, and institutional innovation.

Sun's central claim is that rules are more dependable than exhortation. Dynasties declined, in this account, because ruling groups lost their founding spirit once in power, and the Party escapes this pattern through discipline, Party regulations and long-term mechanisms. Citing Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, Sun argues that firm conviction comes from firm theory, so that theoretical innovation must be matched by theoretical study. The Party must therefore arm itself with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. Sun also argues that the Party should rely on criticism and self-criticism and on the 2016 guidelines for intra-Party political life to purge corruption and the "thief in the heart". Finally, Sun argues that institutions must be practical, systematic and enforceable, neither too sweeping nor too fragmentary.

Sun concludes that if the Party sums up historical experience, meets present needs and builds a lasting mechanism, it can open new prospects in the great social revolution and strengthen itself through the Party's self-reform. In Sun's account, this will lead the people to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. The article is an official-line exposition of the Plenum's Decision. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory writer links the 2019 Decision on institutions to Chinese dynastic history, Mao-era rectification and the discipline of the Party.
quoteEn: Firm ideals and convictions, and remaining true to the original aspiration and keeping the mission in mind, depend on study and education, and even more on discipline and institutions.
quoteZh: 坚定理想信念，不忘初心、牢记使命，靠学习、靠教育，更要靠纪律、靠制度。

glossary.literal: never forget the original heart, firmly remember the mission
glossary.explanation: A Party slogan, prominent from 2019 in a campaign of themed education. It refers to the Party's founding goals of seeking the people's well-being and national rejuvenation.
The pattern of sudden rise and sudden fall of regimes that Huang Yanpei described to Mao Zedong in Yan'an in 1945. Party writers cite it as the danger the Party must escape.
A term used under Xi Jinping for the Party's efforts to purify, improve and renew itself through discipline, criticism and anti-corruption work.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology associated with Xi Jinping, written into the Party Constitution at the 19th Party Congress in 2017.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The official goal of restoring China's national strength and standing, closely tied to the Chinese Dream.

t: Firm confidence in our values: recognising the essence of the "universal values" thesis
zh: 坚定价值观自信——认清“普世价值论”的实质
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2020, Ren Xiaoshan takes up the thesis of "universal values", which the author defines as the claim that bourgeois ideas of freedom, democracy and human rights apply to every society and era, beyond class, nation and history. Ren argues that the thesis is in essence bourgeois ideology, a reflection of capitalist private-property relations. The author holds that, although its spread in China has weakened, it still runs underneath and is part of a Western strategy of Westernising and dividing China, so that the struggle against it concerns paths and systems as well as ideas.

The short commentary has three parts. The first argues that "universal values" are not in fact universal. The second sets out how the thesis threatens China's chosen path and political system. The third presents measures of response: strengthening the Four-sphere Confidence, struggling openly against the thesis, and promoting the core socialist values.

In the first part Ren concedes that bourgeois ideals of freedom, equality and fraternity once enlightened minds and advanced human society. The author argues, however, that once they are "politicised" and made into instruments of class rule and of intervention abroad, their hypocrisy shows. Ren cites Western double standards, withdrawals from treaties and the "colour revolutions" in West Asia and North Africa as examples. The author also rejects two conflations: that China's core socialist values simply accept "universal values", and that "universal values" equal humanity's common values. Democracy, for instance, means people's democracy under Communist Party leadership, not parliaments, separation of powers or party elections.

In the second part Ren claims that Western promotion aims at ideological confusion, especially among young people, at splitting social consensus, and at undermining the Party's governing position by advocating privatisation, multiparty competition and pluralism in guiding ideology. In response Ren calls for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture, citing China's handling of the COVID-19 epidemic as evidence of institutional advantage. Ren also urges building a discourse system for the core socialist values, and clarifying their boundary with "universal values". Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary in 2020 framed the critique of "universal values" and linked it to ideological security.
quoteEn: The struggle against the "universal values" thesis is a contest of values and of thought and culture, and even more a contest over paths and systems.
quoteZh: 与“普世价值论”的斗争，既是价值观念之争、思想文化之争，更是道路之争、制度之争。

glossary.explanation: The view that values such as freedom, democracy and human rights apply to all societies. In Party discourse it is criticised as a Western ideological current.
A set of 24 characters in twelve values, promoted since the 18th Party Congress (2012), at national, social and individual levels. They include freedom, equality, justice and democracy.
Official slogan calling for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
Term for popular uprisings that toppled governments in several countries. Official Chinese discourse describes them as Western-backed subversion.
Official concept, associated with Xi Jinping, of shared human values such as peace, development, fairness, justice, democracy and freedom. Officials distinguish it from "universal values".

t: The contemporary value of the spirit of striving for first-class performance in the Soviet Areas period
zh: 苏区时期争创一流精神的当代价值
paras: Zhong Xiaoming asks what the revolutionary spirit of "striving for first-class performance" (zhengchuang yiliu), which emerged in the Soviet Areas of the 1930s, can offer today. Published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020, the short piece argues that this spirit reflects the Communists' high standards, their basic attitude to revolution and their lofty values, and that it remains relevant in the new era.

The article has two parts. The first sets out the spirit's content in the Soviet Areas period, said to have been promoted by Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai and other leaders. The second draws out its present-day value in four requirements.

In the first part Zhong identifies three strands: forging ahead while serving the people wholeheartedly, illustrated by a 1933 Red China report on cadres helping distressed villagers; daring to take the lead and set examples, illustrated by a 1932 work competition in Xingguo county; and seeking truth from facts in order to create "first-class work". For the last, Zhong cites Mao's 1934 praise of Xingguo and northeastern Jiangxi comrades for linking mass livelihood to revolutionary war. Zhong contends that where this attitude was applied well, the revolution succeeded, and that where it was not, it suffered heavy losses.

For today, Zhong calls for a down-to-earth work style, supported by Xi Jinping's remarks on practical action and on study, and for diligent learning aimed at solving real problems. Zhong also calls for selfless dedication, to counter people who are materially comfortable but spiritually empty, and for conscious practice of the core socialist values. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-history themes are used to promote cadre conduct and values education in 2020.
quoteEn: Creating first-class work is the goal of seeking truth and being pragmatic, and seeking truth and being pragmatic is a necessary condition for creating first-class work.
quoteZh: 创造第一等工作是求真务实的奋斗目标，求真务实是创造第一等工作的必要条件

glossary.explanation: Revolutionary base areas, such as the Central Soviet Area in Jiangxi, where the Communist Party set up Soviet governments in the late 1920s and 1930s.
A set of 24 characters in twelve values at national, social and individual levels, promoted by the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

glossary.literal: strive to create the first rank
glossary.explanation: A slogan of striving for excellence in work, here traced by the author to the Soviet Areas period.
A Party watchword for a practical, evidence-based work style, closely linked to investigation and research.

t: "Washington should abandon its pretence of sanctity and its double standards on human rights"
st: World opinion criticises violent law enforcement in the United States
zh: “华盛顿应该抛弃在人权问题上假装圣洁的双重标准”
zhSub: 世界舆论批评美国暴力执法
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2020, no. 12), Di Yingna and Zhou Luming take up the death of George Floyd, an African American man killed by US police, and the protests that followed across the United States. The article contends that the case shocked the world and drew strong criticism from international bodies, governments, media and public figures. Its main claim is that this reaction exposes systemic racism in the US and a double standard in Washington's human rights diplomacy.

The piece is a compilation of reported statements organised under four quoted headings: the case as revealing the nature of the US state, racism as the "virus" behind police violence, Washington's double standards, and the call to reflect on America's failures. It draws on the UN Secretary-General and the UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, the African Union, the EU, and officials from Ghana, Russia, Cuba, Iran, South Africa and Jordan. It also quotes media in Japan, Germany, Britain, Australia and the US, as well as US figures such as Nancy Pelosi, Jimmy Carter, Barack Obama and George W. Bush.

The authors argue first that the killing is not an isolated incident. They cite figures from the US National Academy of Sciences, the Trial Project and the NAACP on police killings, incarceration rates and racial disparities. On this basis they describe African Americans as facing institutional oppression in both law enforcement and the justice system. Second, they present foreign critics, including the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, as saying that the US lectures other countries on human rights while excessive force was used against protesters and journalists at home. The article cites a Singapore social media post contrasting US reactions to unrest in Hong Kong and in Minnesota, a Russian foreign ministry spokesperson, and US diplomats who said they looked like "hypocrites".

The article ends by combining foreign analysis of a deeper US crisis, citing the pandemic, unemployment, economic decline and polls showing most Americans think the country is out of control, with statements from US ex-presidents acknowledging persistent racial injustice. The authors do not add a separate policy proposal. Their implied conclusion is that the US lacks the standing to judge other countries on human rights. Read the original if you want a dense catalogue of the international and domestic quotations that Chinese official media used to frame the Floyd protests in mid-2020.
quoteEn: From this it is not hard to see that African Americans face institutional oppression in the United States on two levels: violent law enforcement and judicial injustice.
quoteZh: 由此不难看出，非洲裔群体面临着美国暴力执法与司法不公两个层面的体制性压迫。

t: "An epic struggle that moved heaven and earth": studying Xi Jinping's important statements on the history of New China
zh: “一部感天动地的奋斗史诗” ——学习习近平总书记关于新中国史的重要论述
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020, Li Zhenghua offers a study guide to Xi Jinping's statements on the history of New China, the period since the founding of the People's Republic in 1949. The article takes up why this history should be studied and how.
