Li's thesis is that Xi's statements give a full account of the importance, achievements and logic of that history, and set out the Marxist method for studying it. Li presents the study as bearing on strengthening the Four Consciousnesses, the Four-sphere Confidence and the Two Upholds.

The article has three parts. The first gives three reasons why studying the history of New China is \"very necessary\": to understand the Party and the nation correctly and locate the country's historical position, to grasp historical laws, and to take responsibility for the future. The second part sets out Xi's assessment of the epic of New China's development. The third part sets out the methodological requirements for studying it.

For Li, Xi stresses the founding of New China as a great leap and a new epoch. Xi also divides the history into stages and describes the move from \"standing up\" to \"becoming prosperous\" to \"becoming strong\". He treats reform and opening up as a \"key move\" and \"the only way forward\", and presents socialism with Chinese characteristics and Party leadership as historically necessary. On method, Li stresses that research must be guided by Marxism, with historical materialism and seeking truth from facts. It must distinguish the \"mainstream\" from the \"tributary\" of history, and see history as continuous. The periods before and after reform and opening up must not be set against each other. Li adds that figures must be judged within their own historical conditions. Li presents the treatment of the two periods as above all a political question, and reads Xi's position as a rebuttal of historical nihilism, which Li says denies Marxism's guiding role and Party leadership.

Li concludes that Xi's statements combine an accurate grasp of the history with an analysis of how New China's history connects to the history of reform and opening up, of the Party and of socialism. In Li's view they give the fundamental guidance for studying the subject. Read the original if you want a compact, officially aligned digest of how Party commentary in 2020 framed the study of New China's history and its fight against historical nihilism.
quoteEn: Correctly handling the relationship between socialist practice and exploration before and after reform and opening up is not merely a historical question but, above all, a political one.
quoteZh: 正确处理改革开放前后的社会主义实践探索的关系，不只是一个历史问题，更主要的是一个政治问题。

glossary.explanation: The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched at the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee in 1978. Official narratives treat it as the dividing line between two periods of the People's Republic.
In official Chinese usage, a label for views that deny the Party's historical record, the Party's leadership or the necessity of socialism in China. The article treats it as a political threat.
Confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics, a formula promoted under Xi Jinping.
The Party requirement to uphold General Secretary Xi Jinping's core position and the authority and centralized, unified leadership of the Central Committee.
A Party slogan calling on members to maintain political awareness, to think in terms of the overall situation, to follow the core and to keep in line with the Central Committee.
The official name for China's path of socialist development since reform and opening up.

t: Achieving the people's complete spiritual initiative
zh: 实现人民精神完全主动
paras: Taking up a line from Xi Jinping's report to the 19th Party Congress (2017) that, with the founding of the Communist Party in 1921, the Chinese people moved 'from passivity to initiative' in spirit, Li Xiangjun and Luo Zhongyou ask how this shift came about and what it demands today. They argue that the Party has led the Chinese people from spiritual passivity to initiative, and that achieving the people's 'complete' spiritual initiative is now a major mission of the Party in the new era.

The article, published in 2020, has three parts. It first analyses why the people were spiritually passive in old China, then describes how the Party enabled the change, and finally sets out why complete spiritual initiative matters for the present. It draws on Marxist theory, on Lu Xun's images of a 'silent China', on Xi Jinping's statements, and on a Harvard Kennedy School survey cited for popular satisfaction with the central government.

Li and Luo name three causes of passivity: feudal ethics and the patriarchal clan system, which weakened independent consciousness; semi-colonial, semi-feudal conditions, which destroyed national self-respect and cultural confidence; and the lack of an advanced organisation to mobilise the masses as the makers of history. In their account the Party reversed this through the guidance of Marxism, the ideal of communism and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the development of socialist culture, and a governing philosophy that puts the people's all-round development and主体 status first. The authors also reject a US official's claim that Marxism-Leninism treats individuals as mere instruments of the state, calling it ignorant prejudice, and cite the Harvard survey's figure of over 93 per cent satisfaction as evidence of popular support.

For the new era, the authors present complete spiritual initiative as an inexhaustible driving force for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, a component of the good life, and a requirement of China's active role in global governance. They tie it to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, the initiative of a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. Read the original if you want to see how a 2020 Party-journal article frames popular morale, cultural confidence and national rejuvenation as a historical shift in the people's 'spirit'.
quoteEn: The formation of the people's spirit of initiative is closely tied both to whether needs for social respect and self-realisation are met, and to the overall condition of society, such as national cohesion and national identity.
quoteZh: 人民群众主动精神的形成，既与社会尊重需求、自我实现需求的满足状态密切相关，也与国家凝聚力、民族认同力等社会整体状况密切相关。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal, closely associated with Xi Jinping's 'Chinese Dream', of restoring China's strength and international standing after the 'century of humiliation'.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official body of ideas associated with Xi Jinping, written into the Party constitution in 2017 as its guiding ideology.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012, calling for joint international development and governance.
A Chinese initiative launched in 2013 to build trade, infrastructure and investment links across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.
The article's key notion: a state of mind in which the people are self-aware, confident and self-driven rather than subordinated to others, linked to the idea of 'seizing the initiative' in history.

t: Racial discrimination highlights the crisis of American political values
zh: 种族歧视凸显美国政治价值观危机
paras: Writing after the death of George Floyd and the protests that followed in 2020, Di and Gao argue that the episode exposes the hypocrisy of the values the United States presents as its core: democracy, freedom, equality and human rights. In their account, the country styles itself a model and uses "human rights" to pressure other states, while racial discrimination, wealth polarisation and social division are plain at home. The article is a commentary in a Party-theory journal.

The text is organised around four headings: visible democratic defects, a slide into an "illiberal era", inequality that permeates society, and long-accumulated systemic human rights problems. Almost all of the evidence consists of quotations from others: Barack Obama, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, US academics and commentators, the American press, UN officials, the Russian foreign ministry, the African National Congress, the African Union's member states and writers from Africa, Turkey, Cuba and Iran. The authors also cite Joseph Stiglitz and US polling and press-freedom data.

The authors' central move is to present the protests as a verdict on the American system rather than on a single police act. On democracy, they cite reports that the Economist Intelligence Unit downgraded the US to a "flawed democracy" and that a multinational poll found most respondents thought the US harmed global democracy. On freedom, they point to force used against peaceful demonstrators and more than 300 reported violations of press freedom. On inequality, they follow Stiglitz in tracing racial injustice to economic inequality, and cite figures on Black unemployment, income, home ownership and poverty, and a rate of police killing three times that of whites.

The authors conclude that "American-style human rights" suffer a fundamental crisis marked by ideological double standards. They stress that the UN Human Rights Council held an urgent debate on racism in June 2020, that a resolution was passed condemning Floyd's death, and that US civil-liberties groups and African states sought UN scrutiny of the US. The text closes with a quotation that it is time for America to reflect on its failures. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party media in 2020 assembled foreign voices to criticise US claims on human rights and democracy.
quoteEn: Inequality has deeply permeated every aspect of American society and become the deepest internal structural contradiction affecting its development.
quoteZh: 不平等问题已经深深渗透到美国社会的方方面面，成为影响美国社会发展最深层次的内在结构性矛盾。

t: China's solutions advance the improvement of global governance
zh: “中国方案”推动全球治理水平提升
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020, Liu Naiya takes up the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019), which called for an all-round diplomatic layout, an open system built on win-win cooperation, active participation in reforming global governance, and the building of a community with a shared future for mankind. Liu reads this as both a summary of more than 70 years of New China's diplomacy and a guide for present practice. The article's thesis is that China's independent, peaceful foreign policy and its "China solutions" are raising the level of global governance.

The piece has three main sections. The first traces the continuity of China's independent foreign policy and its commitment to peaceful development, from the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence to the present. The second presents China's approach to global governance, centred on sustainable development, the Belt and Road Initiative and new international institutions. The third treats the community with a shared future for mankind as the central question of current international relations, citing a series of Xi Jinping speeches from 2017 to 2019 and taking China–Africa relations as its case.

Liu argues that China's own development, including the poverty-reduction goal to be met in 2020, ten years ahead of the UN 2030 Agenda, is a contribution to world peace and development. In this account China offers public goods through the Belt and Road Initiative and the new development philosophy, and has founded bodies such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, BRICS and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, each backed by funding. Liu contrasts this with Western-led governance, which the article says shows growing shortcomings in ideas, institutions and capacity. On Africa, Liu cites China's reported contribution of over 25 per cent to the continent's economic growth, the Forum on China–Africa Cooperation, the Addis Ababa–Djibouti railway, and a Chinese record of following through on agreements, which the article sets against Western rhetoric without delivery.

Liu concludes that China's cooperation with Africa, grounded in shared colonial history and shared development aims, can serve as a model for building a community with a shared future elsewhere. The article also suggests that China's self-reliant development path is worth other developing countries' study. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese commentary in 2020 linked the Fourth Plenum's foreign-policy guidance to global governance, the Belt and Road Initiative and China–Africa ties.
quoteEn: China uses a development-oriented approach to solve problems of development, keeps the inclusiveness of development always in mind, does not forget the development needs of the broad range of developing countries, and pursues the sustainable development of the world economy; this is both the goal that global governance is meant to reach and the means by which that goal is achieved.
quoteZh: 中国用发展的思路解决发展中的问题，时刻牢记发展的包容性，不忘广大发展中国家的发展需求，实现世界经济的可持续发展，这既是全球治理所要达成的目标，也是这一目标借以实现的手段。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since 2013, holding that countries' interests are interlinked and should be pursued through cooperation. It is now a standard slogan of Chinese diplomacy.
An infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative launched by Xi Jinping in 2013, linking China with countries across Asia, Africa and Europe.
A framework put forward in 2015 stressing innovative, coordinated, green, open and shared development as the guide to China's economic policy.

glossary.en: the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence
glossary.explanation: Principles of mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence. Zhou Enlai advanced them in the 1950s, and they remain a basis of China's foreign policy.

t: Building consensus for realising the Chinese Dream of the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
zh: 为实现中华民族伟大复兴中国梦凝聚共识
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2020, no. 8), Jiang Zelin asks how the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) can contribute to the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation. The article argues that ideological and political guidance and the building of broad consensus are the central link in the CPPCC's work in the new era. Jiang contends that this consensus must be built under the leadership of the Communist Party of China.

The piece has three parts. The first explains why consensus is needed for the Chinese Dream, drawing on China's history, the people's role as makers of history, and the tasks of completing a moderately prosperous society. The second treats consensus-building as a core CPPCC function, discussed through its political consultation, democratic oversight and participation in the deliberation and administration of state affairs, and through its two themes of unity and democracy. The third lists several problems to be handled, including Party leadership, unity of consistency and diversity, and the CPPCC's concentration of expertise.

Jiang presents the Chinese Dream as a dream of national rejuvenation and of the people's well-being. The author links it to the shift from "standing up" to "becoming rich" to "becoming strong", and to the principal contradiction identified at the 19th Party Congress (2017). The CPPCC is described as a united front body, a consultative institution and a channel of socialist consultative democracy. In this account, it turns the Party's decisions into the shared will of all sectors through democratic procedures. Jiang's key image, borrowed from Xi Jinping, is to seek the "greatest common denominator" and draw the "biggest concentric circle", with a firm political bottom line at its centre and wide tolerance at its radius. Patriotism and socialism are named as the greatest political consensus among CPPCC participants, and Jiang says this extends to compatriots in Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan and to overseas Chinese.

Jiang concludes that the CPPCC should strengthen Party leadership, including Party groups within it, and should expand the breadth and depth of consensus. It should do so by drawing on its members' expertise, its standing consultative mechanisms and the representation of non-public-sector figures, religious and ethnic representatives, and other groups. Jiang describes this as the CPPCC's distinctive contribution to national governance and to the Chinese Dream. Read the original if you want an official-line account of how the CPPCC's consultative role is framed in the language of consensus and the united front.
quoteEn: Holding fast to the political bottom line as the centre of the circle, the CPPCC consolidates consistency, respects diversity and lengthens the radius of inclusiveness, thereby achieving the unity of consistency and diversity.
quoteZh: 人民政协在固守政治底线这个圆心基础上,巩固一致性，尊重多样性，拉长包容性半径，做到一致性和多样性统一。

glossary.explanation: A slogan popularised by Xi Jinping from 2012, centred on national rejuvenation, national prosperity and the people's well-being.

A national and local advisory and consultative body that brings together the Communist Party, other parties, mass organisations and representatives of various sectors. Officially it is a united front organisation and a channel of consultative democracy.
The Communist Party's strategy and set of institutions for building alliances with non-Party groups and social forces. Official texts call it one of the Party's key instruments.

A term for deliberation among Party, non-Party and social representatives before decisions are taken. Official discourse presents it as a distinctive feature of Chinese democracy alongside electoral democracy.

t: The contemporary value and practical significance of the popularisation of Marxism
zh: 马克思主义大众化的时代价值与现实意义
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2020, no. 7), Wang Weiguang asks why Marxism must be popularised among the masses (大众化, dazhonghua) and what this means today. Starting from Lenin's formula that the maximum of Marxism equals the maximum of popularisation, Wang argues that popularisation is an essential requirement of Marxism and follows from its "people-ness" (人民性), its character as a theory of, from and by the people.

The article is organised in three parts, each tied to one feature of Marxism: it is a theory for the people, a theory that comes from the people, and a theory that relies on the people. A final section draws out the consequence that popularisation leads to the adaptation of Marxism to China and to the times. Wang draws on Marx, Engels, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Xi Jinping, and on the sequence of Chinese theoretical achievements from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

Wang argues first that Marxism's "people" is not an abstract, supra-class human being but the working class and the broad masses. In Wang's account, bourgeois theories that preach universal values hide their class character, whereas Marxism openly admits its class nature, which therefore coincides with its people-ness and guarantees its truth. Second, Marxism arises from the practice of the people: Wang traces Marxism, Leninism and the successive theories of the Chinese Communist Party to workers' movements and revolutionary and reform practice. Third, theory becomes a material force once it grips the masses, so that Marxism can fulfil its task of changing the world only by educating, mobilising and relying on the people.

Wang concludes that popularisation, the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, is one unified process. Marxism must be accepted by the people in each nation and era, so it has to take on Chinese style and respond to the main social contradiction of each period, which Wang traces from the Eighth Party Congress through the post-1978 period to the new era. Wang calls popularisation an important means by which the Party opens new prospects for its cause. Read the original if you want a concise statement of the official Party-theory case linking Marxism's people-ness, its popularisation and its adaptation to China and to the times.
quoteEn: The process of popularising Marxism is both a process in which Marxism grips the masses and merges with the people's practice, and a process in which the people's practice nurtures Marxism and keeps driving its innovative development.
quoteZh: 马克思主义大众化的过程既是马克思主义掌握人民群众、与人民实践相结合的过程，又是人民群众实践孕育马克思主义并不断推进马克思主义创新发展的过程。

glossary.explanation: The process by which Marxism is accepted, mastered and applied by the broad masses. In Chinese Party theory it is usually paired with 'adaptation to the Chinese context' and 'adaptation to the times'.
A term in Chinese Party theory for a theory's orientation towards serving the people. Wang treats it as the defining feature of Marxism, identical with its class character.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official name of Xi Jinping's body of ideas, written into the Party constitution in 2017. Wang places it as the latest result of adapting Marxism to China.

t: New changes in the Communist Party of Cuba since Raúl Castro took office
zh: 劳尔·卡斯特罗主政以来古巴共产党的新变化
paras: Yang Jianmin asks what has changed in the Communist Party of Cuba (PCC) and in Cuban socialism during Raúl Castro's twelve years in power, from taking over from the ailing Fidel Castro in 2006 to leaving the state presidency in April 2018 while remaining the Party's First Secretary. The article argues that the Party has responded to social demands by shifting its priorities to economic development, exploring a new socialist model, strengthening Party leadership and pursuing an all-round foreign policy.

The article is organised in four parts. It covers the shift in the Party's and state's priorities and the "updating of the model"; the defence of the Party's leading position and reforms in Party organisation and leadership succession; the new diplomacy towards the United States, the European Union, China, Russia and Latin America; and Cuba's support for the Latin American left and its place in the world socialist movement. Yang draws mainly on Raúl Castro's speeches and the documents of the Sixth (2011) and Seventh (2016) Party Congresses and the 2012 National Conference.

Yang argues that Raúl moved the Party from treating revolution and social welfare as the main task to treating economic growth as the precondition for sustaining socialism. Egalitarianism was criticised as a distortion of social justice, and Cuba now accepts a market role within the framework of state planning, social ownership of the basic means of production, and a diversified non-state sector. Yang stresses, however, that Cuba remains cautious about private business and bars the concentration of property and wealth in private hands. Alongside this, the Party reaffirmed the one-party system, held congresses regularly again, set age and term limits for senior leaders, criticised bureaucracy, and founded a college for training cadres. Succession was handled carefully, ending with Díaz-Canel taking over the state posts and a constitutional revision under way. Abroad, Yang describes the normalisation with the United States from 2014, reversed under Trump, as well as closer ties with the EU and continued reliance on Venezuela, China and Russia.

Yang concludes that Cuban socialism matters greatly for the Western Hemisphere and for world socialism, and that the success of the "updating" is therefore important. As the only country building socialism in a Western cultural setting, Cuba, in Yang's view, may develop a model different from the Eastern one, despite ageing and low investment. Yang holds that this exploration can solve Cuba's long-standing economic problems and enrich the experience of the world socialist movement. Read the original if you want a Chinese specialist's overview of Raúl Castro's reforms and the PCC's changing positions, drawn from Cuban primary sources.
quoteEn: On the whole, Cuba's understanding of the market is still developing, and this process is far from over.
quoteZh: 总体上讲,古巴对市场的认识还在不断发展,而且这个过程还远未结束。

glossary.explanation: The official Cuban term (actualización del modelo) for the economic and social reforms launched under Raúl Castro, formalised in the 2011 Guidelines. It presents the changes as renewing, not abandoning, socialism.

The practice or idea of equalising incomes regardless of work contribution. In Chinese and Cuban reform discourse it is criticised as distinct from socialist equality and as producing "eating from the same big pot".
The political arrangement in which the Communist Party is the only legal party. Raúl Castro defended it in 2012 as a strategic safeguard of national unity and sovereignty.

t: A classic for understanding the origin and withering away of the state
st: A reader's guide to The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State
zh: 理解国家起源与消亡的经典著作
zhSub: 《家庭、私有制和国家的起源》导读
paras: This is a reader's guide, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020, to Engels's The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State. Ming Yi presents the book as Engels's application of historical materialism to the state, one that explained how the family, private property and classes gave rise to the state and so greatly enriched Marxist political theory.

The guide has three parts. It first sets out the book's background: it was written in March–May 1884 from Marx's notes on Lewis Henry Morgan's Ancient Society, and it was aimed at bourgeois theories of the state and at reformist currents in the workers' movement such as 'state socialism', 'socialism of the lectern' and the Fabians. It then summarises the nine chapters and their main doctrines. Finally it discusses the book's theoretical and historical significance and its relevance to China in the new era.

On the book's content, Ming reports five points. The first is the theory of the two kinds of production, the production of the means of subsistence and the production of human beings themselves. The second is the historical sequence of family forms. The third is the origin of private property and classes through three great divisions of labour. The fourth is a theory of the state that treats it as a historical category arising from irreconcilable class contradictions. In this account the state divides its subjects by territory, holds a public power backed by force, and levies taxes. Its essence is class rule, expressed in slave, feudal and bourgeois forms. The fifth is the state's eventual withering away, which Ming says is conditional on highly developed productive forces and the abolition of private property and classes.

Ming concludes that the work gives a scientific basis for analysing the state, democracy and rights. The author describes capitalist democracy as an indirect and concealed form of bourgeois rule. China's system, by contrast, is described as people's democratic dictatorship resting on public ownership. For the present day, Ming draws three lessons: family-building and gender equality, the long historical process of abolishing private property, and the need to strengthen rather than weaken state functions while socialism and capitalism still compete. Ming adds that class struggle still exists in China to some extent. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented introduction to Engels's text and to how it is applied to contemporary Chinese state theory.)
quoteEn: The state is the upholder of the ruling class's political order.
quoteZh: 国家是统治阶级政治秩序的维护者。

glossary.explanation: A constitutional description of China's state system, led by the working class and based on the worker–peasant alliance. It combines democracy for the people with coercion against those regarded as hostile to the system.

t: How is common progress of the world possible? The world-historical significance of the thought of a community with a shared future for mankind
zh: 世界共同进步何以可能？——人类命运共同体思想的世界历史意义
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2020, no. 4), Di Yingna asks what the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind contributes to the world's common progress. The author argues that its significance cannot be gauged from international relations or diplomacy alone, and should be assessed from the wider standpoint of how we understand the laws governing human social history. In this reading, the idea is a theoretical response, developed since the 18th Party Congress (2012), to the question of what is wrong with the world and what should be done.

The article is built around three shifts, each presented as a new contribution to understanding human development. The first concerns modernization, moving from a single model to plural paths. The second concerns the way of thinking about social development, moving from zero-sum games to win-win cooperation. The third concerns relations between civilizations, moving from one flower blooming alone to a hundred flowers in bloom. Di draws on Marx's Communist Manifesto and on remarks by Xi Jinping.

On modernization, Di contends that some Western scholars treat Western priority in time as moral priority, so that only one modernization is possible. The author calls this a hegemony of discourse that denies non-Western countries the chance to find their own path. China's experience of independent exploration is presented as showing that every nation has the right to choose its own road. On thinking, Di holds that a Cold War mentality and the logic of the strong preying on the weak produce the belief that a strong country must seek hegemony, and that the postwar order served a few developed states. China's peaceful development and the Belt and Road Initiative are said to break this logic, and concerns about a Chinese threat are described as a misreading. On civilization, Di identifies capitalist cultural hegemony, which asserts barriers, hierarchy and inevitable clash between civilizations, as the central obstacle. The author argues that exchange and mutual learning are the alternative.

Di concludes that the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind widens understanding of the paths to modernity, offers a cooperative way of thinking and promotes equal exchange among civilizations. These are described as the code for harmonious development and common progress. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Party journal presents this concept as a contribution to historical materialism and to debates on modernization, global order and civilizational dialogue.
quoteEn: The paths by which humanity moves towards modernization are plural rather than single, open rather than exclusive; the key is to find a development path suited to each country's national conditions.
quoteZh: 人类走向现代化的途径是多元的而非单一的、是开放的而非排他的，关键是要找到适合本国国情的发展道路。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and theoretical concept associated with Xi Jinping since around 2012–13. It calls for cooperative, win-win international relations and respect for different development paths.
A Chinese initiative launched in 2013 to build infrastructure and economic links across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.
Marx's theory that material production and its contradictions shape the course of social history. Chinese texts treat it as the scientific basis for understanding historical laws.
The 2012 Congress of the Communist Party of China, at which Xi Jinping became General Secretary.

t: Grasping the broad trends of the world and of China: a reader's guide to Marx and Engels on China
zh: 把握世界和中国的发展大势——《马克思恩格斯论中国》导读
paras: This is a reader's guide to the collection Marx and Engels on China, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2020. Wang Yi asks what Marx and Engels's scattered writings on China contribute to understanding modern Chinese history and China today. The author argues that their judgements remain practically important for grasping the Marxist standpoint, understanding the choices made by the Chinese people, and unwaveringly upholding the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The guide has three parts. The first sets out the historical conditions that drew Marx and Engels to China: its forced incorporation into the capitalist world market after the Opium Wars, the needs of proletarian revolutionary theory after the defeats in Europe, and Marx's work as a correspondent for the New York Daily Tribune. The second summarises five groups of their arguments. The third draws lessons for present-day China.

In the second part, Wang presents Marx's analysis of China's economy as a combination of small-scale farming and household industry, which supported centralised autocracy and long-lasting stability until Western guns broke it open. Wang also reports Marx's exposure of the opium trade, his account of British, French and Russian aggression, and the Engels passage calling resistance a people's war to defend the nation. The guide ends this section with their predictions: the old system would collapse, China would influence world civilisation, and the Chinese people would eventually take the socialist road, which Marx and Engels imagined as a "Chinese republic".

The third part applies these lessons to three areas. Wang says that China must be read within world history amid "changes unseen in a century", grasping both what has changed and what has not, notably the primary stage of socialism. It treats deepening reform as the answer to the lesson of backward productive forces and relations of production, and it links reform to modernising state governance. It calls for building a community with a shared future for mankind, opposing hegemonism, and staying alert to interference from some Western forces. Read the original if you want to see how a Party journal draws on Marx and Engels's writings on China to support current policy themes.
quoteEn: The views of Marx and Engels on China are not only of important guiding value for correctly understanding modern Chinese history; today, as socialism with Chinese characteristics enters a new era, they still have important practical significance.
quoteZh: 马克思、恩格斯的中国观不仅对我们正确认识近代中国历史具有重要的指导价值，在中国特色社会主义进入新时代的今天，依然有着重要的现实意义。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era, combining Party leadership, a socialist market economy and other features presented as adapted to Chinese conditions.

The official judgement that China is still in an early, long-lasting stage of socialist development, with underdeveloped productive forces. It was formalised in the 1980s and reaffirmed in later Party congress reports.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013. It calls for cooperation, shared security and mutual benefit among states.

glossary.pinyin: bǎi nián wèiyǒu zhī dà biànjú
glossary.explanation: A phrase used in Chinese official discourse for the current period of shifts in the global order, including the relative rise of emerging economies.

glossary.zh: 国家治理体系和治理能力现代化
glossary.pinyin: guójiā zhìlǐ tǐxì hé zhìlǐ nénglì xiàndàihuà
glossary.literal: modernisation of the national governance system and governance capacity
glossary.explanation: A goal set out at the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013) as the overall aim of comprehensively deepening reform.

t: Several relationships to handle well in building a community with a shared future for mankind
zh: 构建人类命运共同体要处理好几对关系
paras: Writing in 2020, Tao Wenzhao takes up the question of how to build a community with a shared future for mankind at a time the article calls a period of changes unseen in a century. Tao argues that the project requires dialectical handling of three pairs of relationships: ideas and plans, seeking common ground while reserving differences, and harmony and change. Tao presents the ability to combine independence with opening up and to take part in global governance as one of the distinctive strengths of the Chinese system.

The article is a short commentary in Red Flag Manuscripts, organised under three headings, one for each pair. Each section first treats the two poles separately and then explains why they must be held together. Tao draws on Party Congress documents, the 2018 constitutional amendment, speeches by Xi Jinping and classical Chinese sayings, and refers to the Belt and Road Initiative as an example of practice.

In the first pair, Tao distinguishes the community as a Chinese idea, which answers what kind of world should be built and which is said to go beyond the law of the jungle, zero-sum games and the clash of civilizations. As a Chinese plan it has concrete goals (lasting peace, universal security, common prosperity, openness and inclusiveness, a clean and beautiful world) and the principle of consultation, joint contribution and shared benefits. In the second pair, shared interests and values are the goal, while diversity is the starting point, so tolerance is essential. Tao states that China will not export its model or interfere in others' internal affairs, and says conflicts should be resolved through dialogue. In the third pair, harmony is the basic method: China is described as a participant in and beneficiary of the existing international order, which it seeks to reform rather than overturn. Change is nonetheless unavoidable, including reform of global governance and of bodies such as the IMF and World Bank.

Tao concludes that the community is a historical process that cannot be achieved at one stroke or without setbacks. It calls for firm commitment to change, careful control of its pace, shared benefits and gradual, sustained effort. Read the original if you want a compact, official-leaning exposition of how Chinese Party writers framed the community with a shared future for mankind in terms of idea, difference and reform of global governance.
quoteEn: If differences cannot be tolerated, how can common ground be sought?
quoteZh: 不能存异，何以求同？

t: Sensing the truth-power of Marxism: revisiting the Communist Manifesto
zh: 感悟马克思主义的真理力量——重温《共产党宣言》
paras: Opening the new "Classics Guide" column of Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2020, Yan Lianfu rereads the Communist Manifesto as a text whose principles, in the author's view, have not become outdated. Yan argues that the Manifesto's scientific character, truth and predictive power are confirmed by the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The piece follows Xi Jinping's call for Communists to treat reading the classics as a habit and a spiritual pursuit.

The article has four parts. It first explains why the Manifesto arose, then sets out the truths it expounds, then assesses its theoretical and historical significance, and finally draws lessons for the present. The historical section cites four conditions: industrial capitalism and the rise of the proletariat, the growth of the workers' movement, Marx and Engels's own intellectual development, and the founding of the Communist League, which commissioned the programme in 1847 and published it in February 1848.

Yan holds that the Manifesto set out the scientific world view of Marxism. It covers historical materialism, class struggle, communism, all-round human development and world history. It also shows the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation, the inevitability of capitalism's fall and the proletariat's historic mission. Yan highlights four features: the vanguard character of the proletarian party, the critical stance towards reactionary, conservative and utopian socialisms, and the "uninterrupted" revolutionary character of the movement. The article says the text turned the proletariat from a class "in itself" into a class "for itself", and treats the October Revolution and the Chinese Communist Party's path as its historical outgrowths.

Yan draws four lessons for the new era. The Party should strengthen its own building and carry out the Party's self-reform. It should hold to the basic principles of scientific socialism while giving them Chinese features, and reject the "end of history" thesis and a single-line view of history modelled on the West. The Manifesto's theory of world history is said to supply the premises for a community with a shared future for mankind. Finally, Marxism must keep pace with the times through adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, with Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era as its latest achievement. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-school scholar presents the Manifesto as a guide to current Party-building and ideological work.
quoteEn: The replacement of capitalism by communism is the inevitable result of historical development, but this historical necessity will not fulfil itself automatically; it can be truly accomplished only through continuous struggle and continuous revolution.
quoteZh: 共产主义取代资本主义是历史发展的必然结果，但这种历史必然性不会自动完成，而是需要不断斗争、不断革命才能真正完成。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept associated with Xi Jinping since the early 2010s, describing a vision of international relations based on shared interests and cooperation. Chinese writers often link it to Marxist ideas of world history.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng

glossary.explanation: The official name for Xi Jinping's body of ideas, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018. It is presented as the latest stage of Marxism adapted to China.

glossary.explanation: The official formula for combining Marxism's basic tenets with China's concrete conditions and its historical era. The article uses the shorter earlier form "Sinicisation of Marxism" (Marxism Zhongguohua).

t: The answer of our times to "what to uphold and consolidate, what to improve and develop"
zh: “坚持和巩固什么、完善和发展什么”的时代回答
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in early 2020, Yan Xiaofeng reads the Decision adopted by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) on upholding and improving the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and modernizing the national governance system. Yan argues that the Decision answers a major political question: what to uphold and consolidate and what to improve and develop. In Yan's account, this answer extends the basic question of what kind of socialism to build and how to build it, and is a major innovation in combining the basic principles of scientific socialism with Chinese practice.

The article has three parts. The first places the question within the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics and links the Fourth Plenum to the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee (2013). The second sets out the "deep roots, notable strengths and systematic layout" of the institutional and governance system. The third lists three innovations that the Decision represents for the new era.

Yan holds that institutions are the foundation of the state and governance is their effective application, so the new era's central task is to make the system more mature and settled. On the system's roots, Yan describes it as guided by Marxism, grounded in China, rooted in Chinese culture and supported by the people. On its layout, Yan notes the 13 areas the Decision lists and explains that the system should be more complete, more stable and more effective. Yan then draws three conclusions. The Decision strengthens the long-term institutional foundation of socialism with Chinese characteristics, sets the institutional axis for building a modern socialist country, and shows the strength of the system in the contest between two ideologies and two social systems. Yan cites the Soviet and East European experience of the 1980s and 1990s as a lesson, attributing the collapse to the lack of a developed system and effective governance.

Yan concludes that upholding and improving the system and modernizing governance is the fundamental remedy for growing external pressure and risks, and a "sea-calming needle" for the long struggle until the second centenary goal. Yan sets the Decision's targets for 2021, 2035 and 2049 as a milestone on the new journey. Read the original if you want a representative Party-theorist reading of the Fourth Plenum Decision and the way it is tied to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.
quoteEn: The Decision lays the institutional and governance platform for comprehensive modernization, establishes its pivotal mechanism, runs through every field of it, and is a milestone on the new journey of building a modern socialist country in all respects.
quoteZh: 《决定》奠定了全面现代化的制度和治理平台，确立了全面现代化的枢纽机制, 贯通于全面现代化各个领域，是全面建设社会主义现代化国家新征程的一个里程碑。

glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path of socialist development since reform and opening up.

t: The fundamental system of upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere
zh: 坚持马克思主义在意识形态领域指导地位的根本制度
paras: This commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao) in 2020, reads a single formulation in the Decision adopted by the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019) on upholding and improving the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics and modernizing national governance. Dong Xuewen focuses on the Decision's naming of "upholding Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere" as a "fundamental system" (genben zhidu), listed first among the requirements for developing advanced socialist culture. The author argues that this is a creative step, without precedent in Marxist intellectual history or earlier Party documents.

After a short assessment of the Decision as a whole, Dong organises the piece in three parts. The first explains why the formulation is new and what "fundamental system" means. The second argues that the move advances the Chinese-adapted Marxist theory of culture. The third places the system within the Decision's framework of governance modernization and applies it to literature and art.

Dong's central claim is that joining "guiding position" to "fundamental system" turns what had been a call at the level of theory into an institutional and practical rule tied to national governance. The author distinguishes the Decision's "important", "basic" and "fundamental" systems, and defines the last as the most important procedure or norm that everyone must follow. Such a system, Dong says, is rigid, allows no bargaining or selective compliance, and guides all other systems. The author links it to ideological security and to keeping leadership, administrative and discourse power firmly in Party hands. Dong cites the harm of historical nihilism as evidence that if the ideological line is breached, other defences are hard to hold. Tying the system to "modernization", Dong adds, shows that the view that Marxism is "outdated" is arbitrary and wrong. In literature and art, Marxist guidance is presented as the first standard for judging works and criticism.

Dong concludes that the system is the top priority of cultural institution-building and must be implemented thoroughly. The author calls for correcting tendencies to ignore or dilute Marxism's guiding position, refuting challenges to it and exposing "two-faced" conduct. Marxism, in Dong's words, must not become a stage mask or cosmetic but a pointer and a weapon. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party-affiliated scholar interpreted the ideological provisions of the 2019 Plenum Decision and their application to cultural work.
quoteEn: The establishment of the \"fundamental system\" raises theoretical formulations and declarations of principle to the level of fundamental institutional arrangements.
quoteZh: “根本制度”的确立，就是把理论表述和理念宣示提升到了根本性的制度安排层面。

glossary.explanation: In the 2019 Decision, institutions are ranked as important, basic and fundamental systems. A fundamental system is the highest tier, meant to guide all others.
The field of ideas, culture, media and theory that the Party treats as an arena of political struggle and leadership.
A label used in Party discourse for views seen as denying or distorting the Party's and socialism's history. Critics of such views regard them as an ideological threat.
The official name for China's current socialist path, theory and system since the reform era.

t: The Gutian Congress Resolution and the foundation of the Party's system of centralised and unified leadership
zh: 《古田会议决议》与党的集中统一领导制度的奠基
paras: Marking the 90th anniversary of the Gutian Congress, Wang Junwei asks how the resolution adopted by the Ninth Party Congress of the Red Fourth Army on 29 December 1929 helped establish the Communist Party's system of centralised and unified leadership. Wang argues that the Gutian Congress Resolution laid the foundation of that system by fixing the Party's absolute leadership over the army, and that it still holds lessons for upholding and improving the Party's leadership system, as stressed at the Fourth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2019).

The article has three parts. The first reconstructs the dispute inside the Red Fourth Army in 1929 over "who leads and whom to obey", including the Seventh and Eighth Party Congresses of the army, Mao Zedong's loss of the Front Committee secretaryship, and the Central Committee's "September letter". The second sets out what the eight-part resolution decided, especially its first section on correcting erroneous ideas within the Party. The third turns to the detailed rules and disciplines attached to those principles and to how they were carried out.

Wang's central claim is that the resolution combined principle with concrete rules. Drawing on Mao's 1929 letter to Lin Biao, Wang lists the errors it targeted: weak Party leadership, a purely military viewpoint, small-group mentality, ultra-democracy, disregard for organisation and slack discipline. In response the resolution defined the Red Army as an armed body carrying out political tasks, placed Party branches at company level, introduced political commissars who countersign orders, and set the relations between military and political organs under the Front Committee. It also prescribed conditions for admitting members, rules for meetings, methods of Party education and propaganda, and the principle that a decision, once made, must be firmly carried out. Wang adds that the congress itself was possible only because the army's Party organisations deferred to the Central Committee's authority.

Wang concludes that the resolution established the principle that the Party commands the gun, which Wang calls the "soul" of the people's army, and made it theoretical, institutional and standardised. Wang takes Mao's remark in January 1930 that the congress had "laid a foundation" as the essence of its historical standing, and presents it as a model of institution-building for implementing the Fourth Plenum today. Read the original if you want a detailed, officially oriented account of the Gutian Congress and its concrete rules on Party organisation, education and propaganda.
quoteEn: The Gutian Congress Resolution not only answered and settled a series of major questions of principle in building the Party and the army, but also turned those principles into concrete, detailed and standardised institutional safeguards.
quoteZh: 《古田会议决议》不仅回答并解决了建党建军的一系列重大原则性问题，而且把这些原则具体化、细节化、规范化为制度保障。

glossary.explanation: The Ninth Party Congress of the Red Fourth Army, held in Gutian village, Fujian, on 28–29 December 1929. Mao Zedong drafted its resolution, which is treated in Party history as founding the principle of Party control over the army.
A standard Party formula for the Central Committee's overall authority over all work. Official discourse presents it as the basic principle of the Party's leadership system.
A term used in the Gutian resolution for the tendency to submit every matter to lower-level discussion and to resist central direction. The resolution criticised it as a deviation.
A system in which Party-appointed officers sit alongside military commanders and countersign orders. It serves to ensure Party control of the armed forces.
The Party's front-line committee in the Red Fourth Army, the army's highest Party organ. Mao Zedong served as its secretary.

t: The international communist movement in 2018: change, adjustment and revival
zh: 2018年国际共产主义运动：变革、调整与复兴
paras: Writing in 2019, Pan Jin'e surveys the international communist movement in 2018, a year that coincided with the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto. The article argues that the movement was marked by change, adjustment and revival: socialist countries advanced reform steadily, communist parties elsewhere made strategic adjustments, and capitalist countries sank into institutional difficulties.

The article opens with the worldwide commemorations of Marx, from socialist states (China, Vietnam, Cuba, Laos) to conferences and exhibitions in Russia, Japan, Germany, France, Italy, Portugal, Belgium and elsewhere. It then moves through three parts: reform in Vietnam, Cuba, North Korea and Laos; the activities of communist parties in other countries; and the crisis of capitalist states, including anti-globalisation, populism and the decline of European social democracy.

On socialist countries, Pan reports Vietnam's central committee plenums on cadre building, the combining of the posts of general secretary and state president under Nguyen Phu Trong, and an anti-corruption drive reaching senior figures. Pan also describes Cuba's leadership succession and constitutional revision, North Korea's shift to concentrating on socialist economic construction and diplomacy, and Laos's Party-building measures. On other parties, Pan highlights the merger of two Nepalese communist parties, electoral gains and losses elsewhere, and repression of some parties. For capitalist countries, Pan treats the US–China trade conflict as rooted in rivalry between two political-economic models and in US internal problems, and reads "new Cold War" thinking as hegemonism. Mass protests such as the Yellow Vests are described as fragmented, decentralised movements in which communist parties had little guiding influence.

Pan concludes that the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics over forty years confirm Marxism's scientific character and have helped world socialism begin to recover. Even so, the basic pattern of strong capitalism and weak socialism has not changed, and the struggle between the two systems now appears in trade and development-model disputes. The article leaves open how communist parties can lead spontaneous social movements, how socialist countries can reform without losing direction, how the movement's forces can cooperate, and what role China should play. Read the original if you want a dated, China-based overview of 2018 events across communist parties and socialist states, with the specific party congresses, plenums and electoral results it lists.
quoteEn: The basic pattern of "strong capitalism, weak socialism" has not changed.
quoteZh: “资强社弱”的基本格局未能改变。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership and public ownership with market mechanisms. The article treats its forty years of practice as evidence of Marxism's vitality.

The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership and public ownership with market mechanisms. The article treats its forty years of practice as evidence of Marxism's vitality.

glossary.en: combining of the posts of general secretary and state president
glossary.literal: Party and government on one shoulder
glossary.explanation: The practice of one person holding both the top Party post and the top state post. In Vietnam it was long debated, and the article reports its realisation in 2018.

t: Tracing the sources of the shift in Russian public opinion on Stalin and the Soviet Union
zh: 俄罗斯民众对斯大林及苏联评价转变探源
source: Journal of Anhui Normal University (Humanities and Social Sciences Edition), 2019 no. 6
paras: Li Ruiqin asks why nostalgia for the Soviet Union and Stalin has grown in Russia the longer capitalism has lasted. The article starts from three events of 2018–2019: a Levada Centre poll in which 70 per cent of Russians credited Stalin with a positive role, the highest since 1991; the highest regret over the Soviet collapse in ten years; and a new Stalin statue in Novosibirsk. Li's answer is that the shift reflects dissatisfaction with present realities and a practical comparison of two social systems, not simple nostalgia.

The article is built around four sections. The first compares Russia's economic standing with that of the USSR. The second examines poverty and inequality. The third sets Russia's difficulty with Western sanctions against the Soviet post-war recovery. The fourth reviews Levada survey data, the return of Stalin monuments and what Li reads as a revival of socialism. Evidence comes mostly from Russian polls, press reports and statements by Russian economists, historians and Communist Party figures.

Li argues first that the USSR held second place in the world economy in 1990, while Russia in 2018 ranked twelfth. Li notes that Putin has repeatedly promised a top-five place without delivering. Second, the article draws on figures and commentary on poverty (about 20.3 million poor, mostly working people) and wealth concentration, including the economist Ruslan Grinberg's remark that the richest 3 per cent hold 89 per cent of financial assets. Li presents this as the result of rejecting "Soviet justice" and as evidence that capital's logic now governs. Third, Li holds that Stalin's leadership in the Great Patriotic War and the rapid post-war rebuilding explain why Russians credit him. Li also treats demonisation of Stalin as aimed at socialism and Marxism, and says rising approval of Stalin alongside falling trust in Putin signals discontent.

Li concludes that the criterion for judging a development path is the sense of gain among the broad population. In this reading, Russians prefer the Soviet record because of the practical results of the two paths, not because of ideology. Li admits Stalin's grave errors, including the excesses of the purges, but presents rising approval as historical necessity and as evidence of a revival of Marxist scientific socialism, which Li sees as confirming Deng Xiaoping's prediction. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist interpretation of post-Soviet Russian opinion polls, with many Russian-language sources and economic data cited in support.)
quoteEn: The socialist and capitalist paths of development do not arise from an ideological opposition between them, but from the sharply opposed practical results of the two paths.
quoteZh: 社会主义与资本主义发展道路并不起因于二者意识形态意义上的对立,而是因为两种道路截然相反的实践结果。

t: Recent developments and characteristics of communist parties abroad
zh: 当今国外共产党的发展变化及其特点
paras: How should one describe the state of communist parties outside China today? Yu Haiqing, writing in 2019, argues that no simple linear rise or decline fits. Using two reference points, the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe around 1989–91 and the 2008 international financial crisis, Yu describes a landscape in which recovery and decline, achievement and difficulty, cooperation and splits, setbacks and hope exist side by side.

The article is organised around four paired assessments: organisational strength, parliamentary performance, left-wing unity and cooperation, and exploration of paths to socialism. It draws on membership figures and election results for parties in Asia, Africa, Latin America, the former Soviet and Eastern European region and developed capitalist countries. It also covers the ruling parties of Vietnam, Cuba, Laos and the DPRK.

On organisation, Yu cites a fall from about 180 parties and over 40 million members to around 120 parties and 6 million after the Soviet and East European upheavals, and a partial recovery to about 130 parties and over 13 million members. Over 8 million of these belong to the four ruling parties, and only some twenty parties have more than 10,000 members. Gains in South Africa, Brazil and Russia contrast with sharp falls in the French, Italian and Spanish parties. Electoral breakthroughs, such as in Belgium, Portugal and Kazakhstan, are in Yu's view scattered and often short-lived, and in alliances communist parties are mostly subordinate. Cooperation has grown through international meetings and the Party of the European Left, yet disputes persist, including a rival grouping set up by the Greek and other parties. Yu sees no case of a successful peaceful, democratic transition to socialism. The author adds that armed struggle has lost influence, and that some parties, such as the Spanish and French, are adjusting strategy.

Yu concludes that new practices and bright spots may become sources of growth, but uneven and unstable development means serious challenges and a need for theoretical rethinking and strategic adjustment. The author also notes a growing tendency to "look east" towards China, with parties studying its experience, supporting a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative, though they still need to integrate Marxism with their own national conditions. Read the original if you want a compact, data-rich account of foreign communist parties' membership, elections and alliances as seen from the Academy of Marxism in 2019.
quoteEn: Only by adhering to a holistic perspective and the comparative method can one assess more scientifically and accurately the current development trends and future configuration of communist parties abroad.
quoteZh: 只有坚持整体视角和比较方法, 才能更加科学、准确地研判当前国外共产党的发展态势与格局走向。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–13, calling for shared development and global governance. It is presented officially as China's vision for international relations.
A Chinese international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative launched in 2013, linking China with countries across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

glossary.en: the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
glossary.literal: drastic change in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
glossary.explanation: The Chinese standard term for the collapse of ruling communist parties and socialist states in the USSR and Eastern Europe around 1989–91.

t: Keep the original aspiration and mission firmly in mind and advance the Party's self-reform
zh: 牢记初心使命，推进自我革命
paras: This is a speech by Xi Jinping, General Secretary of the Communist Party of China, delivered on 24 June 2019 at the 15th collective study session of the Political Bureau of the 19th Central Committee. It was published in Qiushi, 2019 no. 15. The session was held during the Party-wide campaign of education on 'staying true to the original aspiration and keeping the mission firmly in mind'. Xi's central claim is that a long-ruling Party can keep its vanguard character, purity and popular support only if it holds to its founding aspiration and mission and keeps up the spirit of self-reform.

Xi first frames the question of how a Party of a hundred years can retain its vitality and rule for the long term. He then grounds the Party's aspiration in Marxist theory and reviews its history through revolution, socialist construction, and reform and opening up. Next he assesses the situation since the 18th Party Congress (2012), sets out concrete tasks in the Party's political, ideological, organisational and conduct-and-discipline building, and gives guidance on four relationships. He ends with a call for leading cadres to set an example and with two passages from Mao Zedong.

Xi argues that the Party's success rests on its steady pursuit of happiness for the Chinese people and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. He holds that forgetting this aim would change the Party's nature and cost it the people. He warns against complacency in the new era and says only the Party itself can defeat it. He says problems such as impurity in politics, thinking, organisation and conduct remain unresolved, and that the 'four tests' and 'four dangers' remain severe. He sums up self-reform as 'four selves': self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation. He proposes four balances: strong central leadership with solving internal problems; keeping fundamentals with innovation; strict supervision with care for cadres; and organisational drive with individual initiative. He says self-reform must not weaken the Party's leadership and must accept supervision by the people.

Xi concludes that leading cadres, especially senior ones, must take the lead in studying Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and in criticism and self-criticism. He says Political Bureau members should set the example for the whole Party. Citing Mao's 1949 warning that the road after revolution is longer, he presents the campaign as a lasting task for all members. Read the original if you want a primary-source statement of how the Party leadership framed self-reform and long-term rule at the start of the 2019 education campaign.
quoteEn: Staying true to the original aspiration and keeping the mission in mind ultimately means solving the various problems within the Party that run counter to them, and the key is to have the awareness to face problems squarely and the courage to turn the blade inward.
quoteZh: 不忘初心、牢记使命，说到底是要解决党内存在的违背初心和使命的各种问题，关键是要有正视问题的自觉和刀刃向内的勇气。

glossary.en: staying true to the original aspiration and keeping the mission firmly in mind
glossary.literal: do not forget the original heart, keep the mission firmly in mind
glossary.explanation: A slogan used for a Party-wide education campaign launched in 2019. It calls on members to recall the Party's founding aim of serving the people and achieving national rejuvenation.

A phrase Xi Jinping uses for the Party's internal self-correction, covering discipline, criticism and self-criticism, and anti-corruption work. Official English usually renders it 'the Party's self-reform'.

Xi's summary of the content of self-reform: self-purification, self-improvement, self-renewal and self-elevation. He set it out at the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection plenary session in early 2019.

glossary.pinyin: sì dà kǎoyàn, sì zhǒng wēixiǎn
glossary.explanation: Official shorthand for challenges facing the Party. The tests are ruling, reform and opening up, the market economy and the external environment. The dangers are lack of drive, lack of ability, detachment from the people and corruption.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A long-standing official goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing. It is closely tied to the Party's declared mission.

t: Reflections on creating "We Are Walking on the Great Road"
zh: 《我们走在大路上》创作感言
paras: Wang Junwei, writing in Qiushi in 2019, reflects on making the documentary series "We Are Walking on the Great Road", produced for the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic of China as a panoramic account of the country's journey. The author argues that, with so much material and limited running time, the series needed one unifying theme, and that this theme is the Chinese path.

The piece describes how the production team chose this theme and then organised the episodes around it. It first explains the three-part treatment of the theme, then walks through how the episodes map onto three periods: socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

Wang says the team took Xi Jinping's remark that socialism with Chinese characteristics "did not fall from the sky" as the key to the series. The path is presented as having emerged from China's national conditions and long history, from persistent struggle, and from reliance on the people and shared development. For each period Wang names the episodes and the events they feature, for example land reform and major construction projects in the early decades, rural and urban reform in the reform era, and poverty alleviation and ecological themes since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

Wang concludes that the series aims to evoke shared memory, tell the story of new China well and strengthen public confidence and pride in the Chinese path. Read the original if you want a short insider account of how an official documentary was structured and which narrative of the 70 years it was built to convey.
quoteEn: Our film must go further in answering the "why" behind the success.
quoteZh: 我们的片子必须进一步深入回答成功背后的“所以然”。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era, combining Party leadership, public ownership and a socialist market economy.
The Communist Party congress of 2012 that began Xi Jinping's leadership; official texts treat it as the start of the "new era".

t: The important place and significance of the new era in the history of the Party and of New China
zh: 新时代在党史、新中国史上的重要地位和意义
paras: Writing in 2019, the seventieth anniversary of the People's Republic, Qu Qingshan asks what the "new era" declared at the 19th Party Congress (2017) means within the history of the Party and of New China. Qu treats the two histories as largely overlapping, with Party history as the core of national history. The article's thesis is that the new era is at once an extension of the period of reform and opening up and the start of a new historical stage.

The article is organised under three headings: the new era as an important component of Party and New China history, as an epoch-making new coordinate, and as a new milestone. Qu divides the history from 1921 into four periods, each with a keyword: revolution (1921–1949), construction (1949–1978), reform (1978–2012) and rejuvenation (from 2012 to the middle of the century).

Qu first argues that the Party has carried two historical tasks since its founding: national independence and people's liberation, completed in 1949, and national prosperity and people's happiness, still unfinished. The four periods are then summarised as saving the nation, building it, enriching it and strengthening it, each laying the foundation for the next. Second, Qu grounds the new era in three objective factors: great changes in the world not seen in a century, China's stage of development, and a shift in the principal contradiction to one between the people's growing need for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development. Third, Qu calls the new era the meeting point of the "two centenary goals" and describes the two-step plan to 2035 and mid-century, which brings forward the target of basically realising modernization by 15 years.

Qu concludes that the new era will become a milestone alongside the founding of the Party, of the People's Republic, and of reform and opening up. Achieving this requires unwavering adherence to socialism with Chinese characteristics under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, continued Party building through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and heightened vigilance against major risks. Read the original if you want an official Party-history framing of the periodisation from 1921 to the present and of how the new era is positioned within it.
quoteEn: The new era is both the result of the quantitative accumulation of achievements in the new period of reform and opening up and socialist modernization, and a qualitative leap beyond that period.
quoteZh: 新时代既是改革开放和社会主义现代化建设新时期各项成就在量的积累上的结果，也是对改革开放和社会主义现代化建设新时期在质的方面的跃升。

glossary.explanation: The label proclaimed at the 19th Party Congress (2017) for the stage of socialism with Chinese characteristics beginning with the 18th Party Congress in 2012.
The official name for the Party's model of socialism, developed since the start of reform and opening up in 1978.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's guiding ideology associated with Xi Jinping, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
Official goals of building a moderately prosperous society by the Party's centenary (2021) and a modern socialist country by the People's Republic's centenary (2049).

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The slogan for the Party's discipline and anti-corruption drive since 2012.

The Party's formulation of society's central problem, which defines its tasks. The 19th Party Congress redefined it as one between the people's need for a better life and unbalanced, inadequate development.

t: Without a core, the Communist Party cannot win victory
zh: 没有核心，共产党就不能取得胜利
paras: Pang Xianzhi, in a short commentary in Qiushi (2019), takes up the Central Committee's opinion on strengthening the Party's political building. Pang argues that the most fundamental task is to strengthen the "Four Consciousnesses", above all consciousness of the core, and that a communist party cannot succeed without a correct and strong leadership core.

The piece first treats whether a core is needed at all, drawing on the Party's history from the Zunyi Meeting through Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. It then turns to why Xi Jinping is the core of the Central Committee and of the whole Party, listing seven qualities, and closes with a short assessment of his selection.

Pang contends that proletarian and bourgeois parties differ in nature, and that before Mao became the core the Party's cause suffered repeated setbacks partly for lack of a mature, stable core. Pang credits Mao and Deng's core positions with the new China and with reform and opening up. For Xi, the seven qualities are: fidelity to and development of Marxism, expressed in Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; a people-centred stance, including poverty alleviation; long-term vision; a global outlook, including the Belt and Road Initiative; attention to Party building and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party; decisiveness rooted in grassroots experience; and a grasp of Party and national history. Pang also claims Chinese leaders are chosen through layers of testing by the Party and the people, unlike American leaders chosen by money and rhetoric.

Pang concludes that choosing Xi as General Secretary and core was correct and reflects the will of the whole Party and people. Pang adds that capable leaders are rare, especially in a severe and complex domestic and international situation, and must be cherished, supported and loved. Read the original if you want a brief example of how the Party's core-leadership principle was justified in official-journal commentary in 2019.
quoteEn: The Communist Party must have a correct and strong leadership core.
quoteZh: 共产党必须有一个正确的坚强的领导核心。

glossary.explanation: A Party slogan from 2016 calling on members to maintain political awareness, awareness of the overall situation, awareness of the core, and awareness of alignment with the central leadership.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017 and 2018.
A Chinese international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative launched in 2013.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party's drive since 2012 to tighten discipline and fight corruption within its ranks.
A Party term for the paramount leader around whom the collective leadership is said to unite; applied to Mao, Deng and, since 2016, Xi.

t: "Spark of Fire Can Start a Prairie Fire": a red classic written in blood and life
zh: 《星火燎原》：用鲜血和生命写就的红色经典
paras: Published in Qiushi in 2019, this commentary introduces Xingxiao liaoyuan (literally "a single spark can start a prairie fire"), a multi-volume collection of memoirs of the Chinese revolutionary wars. The authors present it as a "red classic" and argue that it should be studied not for historical colour but to draw on its living political and moral energy today.

The article first describes the origins of the work: a 1956 Central Military Commission call for writings marking thirty years of the People's Liberation Army, contributions from marshals and ordinary soldiers alike, and publication in eight volumes between 1958 and 1963. It then notes the Central Military Commission's Political Work Department's selected edition for the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic (2019), drawn from the 2009 complete edition.

The core of the piece is a series of lessons the authors say the book teaches, each tied to named chapters. These are loyalty to the Party, firm ideals and convictions, fighting ability, innovation, fine work style and discipline, and close ties between army and people. The authors link these to present tasks: political army-building, the Two Upholds, the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, rule of the military by law, and anti-corruption work.

The authors conclude that Party, national and military history is an inexhaustible spiritual treasure, and they call on readers to take up the torch from the older generation. They add that the selected edition comes with multimedia products such as audio, short videos and AR for younger readers. Read the original if you want an example of how Party media promote a revolutionary memoir as a tool of political and military education.
quoteEn: Studying and using the red classic Spark of Fire Can Start a Prairie Fire well is by no means to pick dazzling flowers from history, but to "draw the ground fire that surges like flowing lava".
quoteZh: 学好用好《星火燎原》这一红色经典,决不是为了到历史中采摘耀眼的花朵,而是为了“获取熔岩一般运行奔腾的地火”。

glossary.explanation: A Party formulation calling on members to uphold Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Party Central Committee and the whole Party, and to uphold the Central Committee's authority and centralised, unified leadership.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, associated especially with Xi Jinping's leadership and the idea of the Chinese Dream.
The principle that the armed forces are built on Party leadership and political loyalty, stressed as a foundation of army-building in the Xi era.
