Party bodies that supervise members' compliance with Party rules and investigate violations. The Central Commission was founded in 1949 with Zhu De as secretary.
A Party campaign of ideological education and criticism aimed at correcting members' work-style and attitudes; the practice dates from the Yan'an period.

t: Report on the development of the international communist movement (2018–2019)
st: The "Yellow Book" of the international communist movement
zh: 国际共产主义运动发展报告（2018~2019）
source: Social Sciences Academic Press release, 4 June 2019 (posted on marxism.cass.cn, 19 June 2019)
paras: This is a press-release-style digest of the annual "Yellow Book" on the international communist movement, published on 1 June 2019 by the Academy of Marxism of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and Social Sciences Academic Press. The report argues that in 2018 the movement was stirred by interactions between history and reality, theory and practice, and China and the world. It expects the same trends to continue in 2019.

The digest follows seven headline findings. They cover US–China technological rivalry and the prospect of a "new Cold War"; the movement's progress in 2018 in ruling and non-ruling parties; socialism with Chinese characteristics as a force in the revival of world socialism; commemorations of the Communist Manifesto and Marx's 200th birthday; flaws in global governance; cadre-building in the Communist Party of Vietnam; and self-reliance in North Korea.

The report argues that high technology and artificial intelligence are changing how parties operate and sharpening the contest between capitalism and socialism. It describes Western containment of China as widening from trade into science, education, culture and ideology. It still expects most countries to pursue dual-track diplomacy, so the old Cold War pattern would not return. It says global governance, dominated by developed countries, is flawed by unequal voting power, weak binding force, unfair outcomes and a lack of effective solutions. It cites US wealth concentration (the top 1 per cent holding 38.6 per cent in 2016) and rising Gini coefficients in the EU. It attributes these problems to the capitalist system itself. On Vietnam, it holds that the quality of strategic-level cadres decides socialism's fate. It points to the Seventh Plenum of the 12th Central Committee, which adopted cadre resolutions ahead of the 13th Congress expected in 2021. On North Korea, it predicts that self-reliance will be the basic principle of reform and opening, though it says the eventual path remains uncertain.

The report anticipates that the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, the centenary of the May Fourth Movement and the centenary of the Third International will prompt parties to review historical lessons and strengthen cooperation. It cites foreign communists and scholars who praise China's achievements, and Western communists who call the Manifesto an "X-ray" of contemporary capitalism. It also says Vietnam's cadre-building offers lessons for China. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese state-affiliated researchers assessed world socialism, US–China rivalry and the ruling parties of Vietnam and North Korea at the end of the 2010s.
quoteEn: The Yellow Book holds that Western \"new Cold War\" thinking continues to spread, and that the containment and encirclement of China will extend from trade and economics to science and technology, education, culture and ideology.
quoteZh: 黄皮书认为，西方“新冷战”思维继续蔓延，对中国进行的遏制和围堵将从经济贸易领域扩展到科技、教育、文化和意识形态。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since reform and opening up, combining Marxist principles with China's conditions.
The series name of annual reports published by the Social Sciences Academic Press, in which CASS researchers review a field and make forecasts.

t: What the Russian reversal in assessments of Stalin suggests
zh: 俄罗斯人对斯大林评价反转的启示
paras: Writing in Global Times on 9 May 2019, Russia's Victory Day, Wu Enyuan asks why Russian opinion of Stalin has turned so positive and what China should learn from it. Wu argues that the shift is not sudden but inevitable, and that its lesson is a warning against historical nihilism.

The short commentary begins with the 2019 survey by the Levada Centre, which Wu says found more than 70 per cent of Russians viewing Stalin's historical role positively and under 19 per cent negatively. Wu describes the quota-sample method (1,638 respondents in 137 localities) to show that it was not a casual poll. The article then sets out three causes and closes with implications.

Wu names three causes. First, the aftermath of the Soviet collapse, with a sluggish economy, inequality and confrontation with the West, leads people to link Stalin with stability and international standing. Second, official attitudes have changed: Putin named the Soviet collapse as the event he would most want to change and rejected the 'demonization' of Stalin, and the 2017 state history textbook credits Stalin-era industrialization and victory over fascism while noting breaches of legality. Third, the government draws on Soviet methods, such as a possible revived military-political directorate, a pioneer-style youth organisation and a strong defence industry.

Wu concludes that official bodies, mainstream media and the public in Russia now broadly acknowledge Stalin's positive role, overturning the verdict dominant since the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party and especially under Gorbachev. Wu holds that deliberately distorting history and wholly negating a major figure, that is, historical nihilism, confuses thinking and can break up a party and a state, and calls this a warning for China. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese academics used the Russian Stalin debate to argue against historical nihilism.
quoteEn: Deliberately distorting history, wholly negating an important historical figure and practising historical nihilism ultimately throws thinking into disorder, and a great party and a great country then fall apart.
quoteZh: 刻意歪曲历史，全面否定一个重要的历史人物，搞历史虚无主义，最终就是把思想搞乱了，偌大一个党、一个国家就分崩离析了。

glossary.explanation: In Chinese Party discourse, a label for views that are said to distort or wholly negate the Party's or socialism's history. It is often invoked in discussions of the Soviet collapse.

t: Overseas scholars on the experience of 70 years of development in New China
zh: 海外学者论新中国70年发展经验
paras: Writing in 2019, on the eve of the 70th anniversary of the People's Republic, Sun surveys how foreign academics explain the question "why China can". The article is a review of overseas scholarship rather than an original study. Sun notes that the positions, methods and conclusions of these works are varied and complex, but argues that they broadly affirm China's achievements and that a "China experience" as seen from abroad can be distilled from them.

The review covers economists, sociologists and China specialists in the United States, Britain, Australia, India, Germany, France and Egypt, as well as the former German chancellor Helmut Schmidt. Examples include Ross Garnaut, Thomas Rawski, Andrew Walder, Thomas Heberer, Dwight Perkins, Barry Naughton, Martin Jacques and Elizabeth Perry. It is organised in three parts: development grounded in national conditions and traditional culture; economic construction as the centre, backed by political construction; and the leading role of the Communist Party of China and a people-centred orientation.

In the first part, Sun reports scholars who credit China's success to policies fitted to its own conditions, including decentralisation, a gradual shift from collective to household farming, and a "socialist market economy". They describe the Soviet failure as dogmatic Marxism, and trace China's core values to Confucian roots. In the second part, scholars stress the state's role in guiding the market, the growth of non-state firms and township enterprises, political stability, and the combination of domestic reform with opening up. The third part presents overseas views that Party leadership gave policy continuity through field investigation and "adaptive mobilization", anti-corruption work and the mass line. These scholars also point to the people's congress system, rural land reform and poverty reduction, and environmental policy as evidence of people-centred development.

Sun concludes that overseas scholars, whatever their stance, identify a distinctive set of factors behind China's development: starting from national conditions, economic construction under political guidance, and Party leadership tied to popular welfare. The article presents these as outside confirmation of China's own account of its path. Read the original if you want a catalogue of foreign scholars and works that are cited in support of the official narrative of 70 years of development, or a starting list of sources to check.
quoteEn: Overseas scholars hold that the achievements of New China's 70 years of development are inseparable from China's sustained advance of socialist construction and reform.
quoteZh: 海外学者认为，新中国70年的发展成就与中国持续推进社会主义建设和改革是密不可分的。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's economic system since the early 1990s. It combines market mechanisms with public ownership and state guidance.
A Party method of governance, associated with Mao Zedong, in which leaders gather views from the people and turn them into policy, summed up as "from the masses, to the masses".

t: The ebb of Western-style democracy and the collapse of its "myths"
zh: 西式民主的退潮与“神话”的破灭
paras: Writing in People's Forum in 2018, Zhang Shuhua asks why Western-style democracy, promoted as a universal value after the Cold War, has produced disorder abroad and decay at home. The article argues that over three decades it has passed from being sacralised and generalised to being alienated and polarised. Zhang concludes that the myths surrounding democracy must be dispelled so that countries can find political paths suited to their own conditions and protect their political and ideological security.

The piece opens by tying the issue to the Party's faith in Marxism and to the fortunes of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It then tells the post-Cold War story in three stages: the birth of the myth after the Soviet and East European upheavals, the expansion of democratisation, and the bursting of the "democracy bubbles". It next sets out six "logical myths" and the hegemonic character of Western democracy, and ends with proposals for a different approach. Examples include Gorbachev's reforms, the "colour revolutions" and the "Arab Spring".

In Zhang's account, Western democracy was monopolised and magnified as the West rose. After 1945 it became an ideological weapon against the socialist camp, and after the Cold War a tool of power. The six myths are its internationalisation, sacralisation, instrumentalisation, labelling and fragmentation, vulgarisation, and absolutisation. Zhang says it has been reduced to competitive elections on Schumpeter's elitist model and used to intervene in other states, and that it is shaped by class in the West itself. Fukuyama and Huntington are cited as scholars who treat it as an end point or the best option. Zhang likens treating it as a universal model to nineteenth-century "white supremacy" claims.

Zhang calls for a correct view of democracy as growing, diverse, concrete and historical. Democracy should respect national character and sovereignty, since no two countries share identical systems. It should be understood as historical and specific, with no single blueprint, and it must fit the level of productive forces. It should also proceed in stages, with attention to "degree" and timing. Zhang says the lessons of the past three decades support this. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Party-affiliated scholar framed the critique of Western democracy and "universal values" in 2018.
quoteEn: In short, democracy is growing, diverse, concrete, real and historical.
quoteZh: 总而言之，民主是成长的、多样的、具体的、现实的以及历史的。

glossary.explanation: The idea that freedom, democracy and human rights are valid for all societies. Chinese official and academic discourse often criticises it as a vehicle of Western ideological influence.
Term for the mass protest movements that changed governments in post-Soviet states in the early 2000s. Chinese writers often present them as externally promoted regime change.
The Communist Party's official name for China's path since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership, a socialist system and a market economy.

t: American-style capitalism faces a struggle over its path
zh: 美式资本主义面临道路之争
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2018, Chen Chenchen asks how far the "disruptive" policies of US President Donald Trump can really change the United States and the world. The author argues that warnings are necessary but that exaggerating Trump's impact, or "deifying" him, is unwise. In Chen's view, Trump's administration is in essence caught in a struggle over the path of American-style capitalism: financialization against industrialization.

The short commentary first considers Trump's political success, then the economic background of the past three decades. It turns to the internal contradictions of his programme and ends with the balance of power between industrial and financial capital.

Chen credits Trump with skilful populism that taps the grievances of people "forgotten by the elites" in the Rust Belt, the countryside and Appalachia. The author notes that his "America First" logic dates back some thirty years. Over that period, according to Chen, the US economy became financialized and hollowed out, and the recovery since 2008 rested on deeper financialization rather than industry. Chen holds that Trump's promises of industrial revival, jobs and fair trade lack well-considered policies, and that frequent personnel changes and erratic implementation add to the difficulty. Industrial capital's correction of finance has dim prospects, since financial capital gained the upper hand twice, at the start of the twentieth century and in the 1980s, and even the 2008 crisis did not reverse this.

Chen concludes that the contest between re-financialization and re-industrialization holds little suspense, because de-industrialization is deeply entrenched. The administration's reshoring incentives and employment measures are described as beggar-thy-neighbour protectionism that runs against economic globalization and is bound to meet great difficulty. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese Party journal in 2018 framed Trump's economic nationalism in terms of the conflict between industrial and financial capital.
quoteEn: In essence, what the Trump administration faces is a struggle over the path of American-style capitalism: a contest between financialization and industrialization, between re-financialization and re-industrialization.
quoteZh: 特朗普政府本质上面对的，是美式资本主义的道路之争，是金融化与工业化之争，是再金融化与再工业化之争。

t: Mounting worries over US economic growth
zh: 美国经济增长隐忧频现
paras: Writing in 2018, Liu Ying asks whether the Trump administration's claim of a "perfect" US economy holds up. The article argues that the boasts rest on selective figures and that the economy faces growing difficulties from slowing growth, rising debt and policy-induced risks.

The commentary first lists the administration's measures: tax cuts, continued interest-rate rises, deregulation of coal and finance (including changes to the Dodd-Frank Act) and trade wars against China and several allies. It then tests Trump's second-quarter claims against year-on-year GDP data and historical peaks. Three headings structure the rest: difficulty of growth, burden of debt and worry over risk.

Liu says the 4.1% figure (later revised to 4.2%) is a quarter-on-quarter rate. On the usual year-on-year basis, the author puts growth at about 2.87%, below the peaks under Obama and several earlier presidents. Citing the Congressional Budget Office, the article expects growth to fall to 2.4% in 2019 and 1.7% in 2020, and sees weakening consumption, investment and exports. It points to a budget deficit that rose from 1.1% of GDP in 2007 to 3.5% in 2017, debt above 20 trillion dollars, and debt-service costs projected to reach 800 billion dollars by 2027. Liu adds that tax cuts and rate rises in an upswing, with unemployment at 3.8%, risk inflation and a stronger dollar. In the author's view, a stronger dollar hurts exports and widens the trade deficit.

Liu concludes that if Washington persists with trade protection and reversing globalization, rapid growth will be hard to sustain and financial risks will build up. The article quotes former Fed chairman Paul Volcker, who said he saw a "mess" in every direction, and calls the aim of making America strong again an empty phrase. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Chinese Party journal assessed Trump-era economic policy during the 2018 trade war.
quoteEn: But this is not the real American economy.
quoteZh: 但这并非真实的美国经济。

t: Protectionism, an old prescription, cannot cure America's present ills
zh: 保护主义旧药方难医美国当前病症
paras: Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2018, as the United States was imposing tariffs and launching trade investigations against other countries, Tian Wenlin asks why Washington is returning to protectionism and whether it can work. Tian argues that protectionism did help build American industry in the past, but that the Trump administration is now applying it under entirely different conditions. In the article's account, the policy will not bring back manufacturing and will instead hasten the erosion of US global hegemony.

The article has three parts. The first reviews the history of American protectionism, from British colonial restrictions on manufacturing to the statements of Washington, Hamilton, Jefferson, Lincoln and McKinley. The second describes the financialisation of the contemporary US economy and its effects on the real economy. The third compares US decision-making with the strategic misjudgements of Germany, Japan, the Soviet Union and the post-Cold War United States.

Tian's central move is a historical contrast. In the nineteenth century a tariff wall of about 30 per cent shielded a young industrial economy, whereas today manufacturing is said to account for roughly 12 per cent of GDP and finance for the core of the economy. Drawing on Marxist arguments about the falling rate of profit, the author claims that financialisation works against production in three ways. Speculative logic overrides productive logic, the real economy is crowded out by high asset prices and rents, and banking risk grows. Tian adds that the US lacks young industrial workers and a complete supply chain, so earlier re-industrialisation efforts under Obama had little effect. The article then argues that US hegemony rests on military, technological, financial (dollar) and cultural pillars. The last three depend on close ties with the outside world, such as other countries buying American technology and holding dollars earned from exports. In Tian's reading, the trade war and the pressure on the Chinese firm ZTE therefore undermine the material basis of the dollar and the profitable position of US high-tech firms in global supply chains.

Tian concludes that the Trump administration defines national interest in terms of the 1960s and 1970s and of lower- and middle-income white Americans. On this basis, "America First" is described as isolationist and at odds with the globalisation the US had long promoted. The author holds that US–China trade benefits the United States far more than China and that the administration is accelerating the collapse of American hegemony rather than making the country great again. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Party journal in 2018 framed the US–China trade war through historical analogy and the theory of financialisation.
quoteEn: The Trump administration's reckless approach is not making America strong again, but accelerating the destruction of America's global hegemonic position.
quoteZh: 特朗普政府的蛮干做法，不是在“使美国重新强大”，而是在加速摧毁美国的全球霸权地位。

t: Understanding the Communist Manifesto through "five constancies"
zh: 从“五个始终如一”领悟《共产党宣言》
paras: Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto, Han Qingxiang asks how the Chinese Communists' original aspiration and mission can be traced to the Manifesto and how it should be commemorated. The piece is a short commentary published in Guangming Daily on 2 April 2018, in a series Han hosted. Han argues that the best commemoration is to study how the Communist Party of China and contemporary Chinese Marxism have upheld and developed the Manifesto, and that this is visible in five "constancies".

In the host's introduction, Han presents "staying true to the original aspiration and keeping the mission firmly in mind" as the guiding principle, understood as a dialectic of upholding and developing. Han then takes five headings in turn: the people's standpoint, the basic principles of historical materialism, materialist dialectics, the historical mission, and a scientific attitude towards Marxism. Under each, Han first sets out what the Manifesto says and then lists how successive Chinese leaders, from Mao Zedong to Xi Jinping, are said to have continued it.

Han's central move is to read the Manifesto together with its seven prefaces and Engels's draft texts as one whole, then to show a line of continuity. The Manifesto is described as written for the proletariat. Its core is historical materialism, together with the unstated principle of the basic contradictions of society. Han also finds in it five dialectical pairs, including the historical and the value-based standard, and criticism and construction. The Party is said to apply the same principles today to reform, to the principal contradiction in society, and to the Party's thorough self-reform. On attitude, Han stresses that Marx and Engels in their 1872 preface held the general principles correct but their application dependent on historical conditions. Han reads this as a warning against both dogmatism and narrow empiricism.

Han concludes that Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era are all innovations in adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions. These innovations, Han says, both uphold the basic principles and integrate them with China's concrete realities. The Party's mission is presented as the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the Party-school mainstream in 2018 linked the Manifesto to the lineage of Chinese Marxist theory.
quoteEn: The effective way to commemorate the Communist Manifesto (hereafter the Manifesto) is to study how the Communist Party of China and contemporary Chinese Marxism have upheld and developed it.
quoteZh: 纪念《共产党宣言》(以下简称《宣言》)的有效方式,就是要研究中国共产党、当代中国马克思主义对《宣言》的坚持和发展。

glossary.en: staying true to the original aspiration and keeping the mission firmly in mind
glossary.literal: do not forget the original heart, firmly remember the mission
glossary.explanation: A slogan prominent in Party discourse under Xi Jinping, stressing fidelity to the Party's founding purpose of serving the people.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official name of Xi Jinping's body of ideas, written into the Party constitution in 2017.
Hu Jintao's guiding concept, centred on people-oriented, comprehensive and sustainable development.
Jiang Zemin's theory that the Party represents advanced productive forces, advanced culture and the fundamental interests of the vast majority.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's official long-term national goal, presented as the historical mission of the Party in the new era.

keywords: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context

t: The contemporary meaning of Marx's thought on world history
zh: 马克思世界历史思想的时代内涵
paras: This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in July 2018, asks what Marx's thought on world history means for the present. Yan Xiaofeng argues that the thought, which he calls the realistic basis and theoretical cornerstone of scientific socialism, has been confirmed in the new century. In his account it has also acquired new content in the new era, above all through the building of a community with a shared future for mankind.

The piece takes its cue from Xi Jinping's speech marking the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth, which called on Party members to study and apply Marx's ideas on world history. Yan draws mainly on The German Ideology and the Communist Manifesto, which was then 170 years old. The text has three parts: how the capitalist mode of production changed the course of world history, the contradictions and the prospect of human liberation that this process produced, and the present-day meaning of the thought.

On the first point, Yan describes how industrial revolution, steam transport and the world market tied nations together. In his reading, capital's drive to transcend every spatial limit dissolved feudal relations and made production, consumption and intellectual life worldwide. He stresses that this process was unequal. Because market power is uneven, the spread of culture is largely one-directional, and the bourgeoisie subordinates the East to the West and produces cultural conflict. Yan also notes that it produced a social form bound together by things, in which, in Marx's words, the increase in the world of things goes hand in hand with a devaluation of the human world. The same process, however, created the universal exchange and many-sided capacities that are preconditions for an association in which the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all.

Yan concludes that multipolarity, economic globalization, informatization and cultural diversity have made humanity's interdependence deeper than ever. He presents the building of a community with a shared future for mankind as a major development of Marx's thought by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. He cites Xi's concepts of development, security, cooperation, civilization and global governance as its basic path. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese Party scholarship links Marx's world-history theory to the official idea of a community with a shared future for mankind.
quoteEn: Building a community with a shared future for mankind is a major development of Marxist thought on world history by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.
quoteZh: 构建人类命运共同体,是习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想对马克思主义关于世界历史思想的重大发展。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and global-governance concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–2013. It calls for common development, shared security and cooperation among states.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official body of Party theory associated with Xi Jinping, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
The official name for China's path since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership and public ownership with market mechanisms.
The term for the socialism founded by Marx and Engels, set against utopian socialism and based on the analysis of capitalist development.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Sensing the power of truth of Marxism through the Communist Manifesto
zh: 从《共产党宣言》感悟马克思主义的真理力量
paras: Published in Economic Daily on 24 May 2018, shortly after the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth, this commentary asks what rereading the Communist Manifesto, issued 170 years earlier, can teach about the truth of Marxism. Fu and Li argue that the Manifesto shows Marxism to be a scientific, revolutionary, practical and open body of theory that remains vital. An editor's note frames the piece with Xi Jinping's call to study the classics closely and to keep opening new horizons for contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism.

The article is organised under four headings: the Manifesto's scientific insight into the laws of social development; Marxism's capacity to keep pace with the times; its practical character; and the continuing adaptation of Marxism to China. It draws on the Manifesto's own formulations, on its prefaces, and on several statements by Xi Jinping from the anniversary speech.

The authors' central claim is that Marxism's scientific and revolutionary character derives from dialectical and historical materialism. In their reading, the Manifesto acknowledges the productive forces created by the bourgeoisie while showing that capitalist relations of production increasingly obstruct them, and it sets out the tendency of human society towards communism. They stress that Marx and Engels revised the Manifesto through successive prefaces, for example the 1872 German preface, which holds the basic principles to be correct but their application dependent on historical conditions. They add that the Manifesto criticised the mechanical transplanting of French theory into Germany. Marxism, they say, is therefore not an "absolute truth" but an open system that absorbs human knowledge. They also point to its practical orientation: its class-struggle thesis, its sharp critique of rival socialist currents, and its stance that the proletarian movement serves the great majority.

The authors conclude that the Communist Party of China is the faithful heir of the Manifesto's spirit and that Marxism's scientific character has been fully tested in China. Facing what they call unprecedented tasks and risks in reform, development and stability, they call on the Party to treat advancing Marxism as a sacred duty. They urge it to raise its ability to solve China's practical problems with Marxist principles, to apply the Manifesto's principles to the great struggle, great project, great cause and great dream, to pursue the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and to write new chapters of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a short example of how the Manifesto was presented in the official press during the 2018 Marx bicentenary.
quoteEn: Marxism has never been a theory that stands still or clings to old ways, and it never regards itself as "absolute truth".
quoteZh: 马克思主义从来都不是一种固步自封、因循守旧的理论，绝不会将自身视为“绝对真理”。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal, prominent since Xi Jinping's leadership began in 2012, of restoring China's national strength and international standing.
The official name for China's current path and system, introduced under Deng Xiaoping in the early 1980s, combining Party leadership with market-oriented reform.

glossary.zh: 当代中国马克思主义、21世纪马克思主义
glossary.en: contemporary Chinese Marxism and twenty-first-century Marxism
glossary.explanation: Official formulation describing the Party's current theory as a continuing development of Marxism, associated with Xi Jinping's statements on Marxism's development.

t: The revolutionary spirit of the Communist Manifesto will never be outdated
zh: 《共产党宣言》的革命精神永不过时
paras: Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto, this newspaper commentary (Guangming Daily, 2 April 2018) asks whether the work still has value for China as it pursues socialist modernization and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Chen Xueming answers that it does, because the Party remains a revolutionary party and the Manifesto's revolutionary spirit is still needed.

Chen first affirms that the Manifesto is a revolutionary work that once played an epoch-making role, and that Marxism guided China's revolution and national liberation. The real issue, in Chen's framing, is whether it is still needed after 1949 and especially after the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978), when the focus shifted to economic development. The piece is short and addresses mainly the opening of this problem.

Chen takes issue with the view of some people that the Party is now purely a "party of construction" and that its work has nothing to do with "revolution". Chen argues that the word "revolution" must first be rehabilitated, since it has come to be treated by some as pejorative. According to the Manifesto, Chen says, revolution arises of necessity, regardless of personal wishes, and is the fundamental driving force of history. Chen holds that the claimed shift from revolution to construction is meant to show that economic work no longer needs revolutionary spirit, reducing it to a technical operation.

Chen concludes that economic construction is something every ruling party does, but a party that abandons the social values and spiritual drive that define its political nature risks not only losing power but disintegrating. Revolutionary spirit therefore remains necessary for the Party's construction work. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar defended the continuing relevance of revolution and the Manifesto in the reform era.
quoteEn: Whether we look back on the past or ahead to the future, revolution is forever the basic driving force of human historical progress.
quoteZh: 无论是回顾过去,还是展望未来,革命永远是人类历史前进的基本动力。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: the great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central Party goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing, prominent in official discourse especially since 2012.

glossary.pinyin: Dǎng de shíyī jiè sān zhōng quánhuì
glossary.en: the Third Plenum of the 11th Central Committee (1978)
glossary.explanation: The 1978 meeting that shifted the Party's work focus to economic development and launched reform and opening up.

t: Holding to the original aspiration by rereading the Communist Manifesto
zh: 在重温《共产党宣言》中坚守初心
paras: Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto, this commentary from PLA Daily (25 April 2018) asks what Chinese Communists should take from rereading it in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li Yin argues that rereading the Manifesto means holding to the Party's "original aspiration" (chuxin) and mission. The author presents the text both as a guiding document for the international communist movement and as the Chinese Communists' "primer".

The piece is organised in three parts, each beginning with the phrase "rereading the Manifesto" and each tied to one aspect of the original aspiration. These are realising the lofty ideal of communism, upholding and developing Marxism, and strengthening the building of a Marxist Party. Li links each to Xi Jinping's statements and to episodes in the Party's history, from its founding in 1921 to the present.

On the first aspect, Li argues that the Manifesto is the source of the communist ideal written into the Party's programme at its founding. The author holds that socialism with Chinese characteristics unites the Party's maximum and basic programmes, and that Party members must therefore be firm believers in the common ideal. On the second, Li describes the Manifesto as the first comprehensive statement of scientific socialism. The author traces its adaptation through Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, and names individualism, historical nihilism and "universal values" as current challenges. On the third, Li presents the Manifesto as the foundation of proletarian party-building. The author credits full and rigorous self-governance of the Party since the 18th Party Congress (2012) with strengthening the Party, and cites the "four tests" and "four dangers" as long-term pressures.

Li concludes that, without Marxism, the Party's cause would lose its soul and direction. The author calls on Party members to study Xi Jinping Thought, to carry out the strategy of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and to ensure the Party remains the "backbone" of the Chinese people and nation. Read the original if you want a short example of how the Party press framed the Manifesto's anniversary in 2018 in terms of Party loyalty, ideology and discipline.
quoteEn: If we depart from or abandon Marxism, or fail to enrich and develop it, our cause will lose its soul, lose its direction and lose its distinctive character.
quoteZh: 背离或放弃马克思主义，不丰富和发展马克思主义，我们的事业就会失去灵魂、迷失方向、丢掉特色。

glossary.explanation: A term used prominently in Party discourse, often paired with "mission" (使命), for the founding ideals Communists are expected to keep. It was heavily emphasised under Xi Jinping, notably at the 19th Party Congress (2017).

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly governing the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the campaign to tighten Party discipline and fight corruption, pursued since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's guiding ideology associated with Xi Jinping, written into the Party constitution in 2017.

glossary.pinyin: sì dà kǎoyàn hé sì zhǒng wēixiǎn
glossary.explanation: Official shorthand for the long-term challenges facing the Party. The tests are governing, reform and opening up, the market economy and the external environment. The dangers are lack of drive, inadequate ability, detachment from the people, and inaction and corruption.

t: The Communist Manifesto in China: dissemination, influence and lessons
zh: 《共产党宣言》在中国的传播、影响与启示
paras: Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto, Ji Zhengju (writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2018) asks how the text reached China, what it did there and how it should be treated today. The author holds that the Manifesto's spread and influence in China are the most persuasive proof of its reach, vitality and truth, and that its history in China mirrors the Sinicization of Marxism.

The article has three parts. The first traces the arrival of the Manifesto in China through three channels, Japan, France and Russia, and follows the making of the first full Chinese translation and later versions. The second sets out the Manifesto's influence on the founding of the Communist Party of China and on its leaders. The third draws two lessons for the present.

In the first part, Ji notes that the Manifesto had little echo in China for fifty years after 1848, which the author attributes to the Qing policy of closure and cultural control. Fragments then appeared through missionaries and Chinese students in Japan, with erratic renderings of names and terms. Chen Wangdao's complete translation, from Japanese and with a English text supplied by Chen Duxiu, was published in August 1920, and five more Chinese versions appeared before 1949. Ji argues that increasingly complete and accurate translations track a deepening understanding of Marxism. In the second part, Ji claims the Manifesto directly promoted the Party's founding and its First Congress documents, and cites Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Liu Shaoqi on its formative effect on them.

Ji's lessons are, first, to hold to the ideal of struggling for humanity's future, which Marx and Engels grounded in historical materialism and the theory of surplus value rather than utopian fantasy. Second, the Manifesto should be treated as a developing theory: Ji points to the seven prefaces, such as the 1872 and 1888 revisions, as evidence of the founders' rigorous, evolving scientific attitude. Read the original if you want a brief, Party-oriented account of the Manifesto's Chinese translation history and its place in the narratives of early Party leaders."
quoteEn: The process by which the Communist Manifesto entered China and spread widely is a microcosm of the Sinicization of Marxism.
quoteZh: 《共产党宣言》传入中国并广泛传播的过程，就是马克思主义中国化的一个缩影。

glossary.explanation: The Party's term for adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions and combining it with Chinese practice. It is associated with Mao Zedong's writings of the late 1930s and later became an official formula.
Marx and Engels' theory that material production and class relations drive historical development.

t: Why the Nepali left alliance won the 2017 elections, and what it means for the future
zh: 尼泊尔左翼联盟2017年大选获胜的原因、影响及其前景
paras: Writing in 2018, Yuan Qun asks why the left alliance of the Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist-Leninist) and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre) won a sweeping victory in Nepal's first elections under the new constitution, completed in December 2017. The article argues that the win, which brought the UML chairman Khadka Prasad Oli to the premiership in February 2018, was the first time Nepali communists had succeeded through unity. Yuan sets out the causes, consequences and prospects of the victory.

The article opens with the electoral system and the results. In the local, provincial and federal contests the alliance took first and second place, and Yuan reports that it won 63.27 per cent of seats and more than two thirds of the National Assembly. The analysis then has three parts: four causes of the victory, three consequences, and three challenges ahead.

On causes, Yuan stresses that the two parties set aside years of rivalry, drawing on the lessons of unstable coalitions and on electoral calculation. The article also credits a joint manifesto promising stability, development and a Nepali-style socialism with multiparty competition, and a nationalist stance against Indian interference, notably during the 2015 blockade. It adds that the Nepali Congress was weakened by factional infighting and failed coalition-building. The consequences, in Yuan's account, are a new round of consolidation in Nepal's communist movement through a planned merger, an example of unity for the international communist movement, and faster progress for the Belt and Road Initiative in Nepal and South Asia.

Yuan identifies three challenges. The first and most important is the parties' theoretical divergence: the UML's "people's multiparty democracy" against the Maoist Centre's "21st-century democracy" and its refusal to renounce violence entirely. The others are the demands of the Madhesi people of the Terai plain, and relations with an India that Yuan expects to pressure the alliance. Yuan concludes that finding an acceptable ideological line within Marxism will decide the legitimacy and durability of the alliance and the new party. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of Nepal's 2017 election, with detailed results and background on Nepali party politics and Madhesi and India issues.
quoteEn: How the two sides can seek common ground while reserving differences, find an ideological line acceptable to both within the framework of Marxism, and give a theoretical account of Nepal's future socialist path will determine the legitimacy and durability of the left alliance and the soon-to-be-founded Communist Party of Nepal.
quoteZh: 如何求同存异，在马克思主义的框架内找到双方都能接受的思想路线，并对未来尼泊尔的社会主义发展道路作出理论阐释，将决定左翼联盟以及即将成立的尼泊尔共产党的合法性和持久性。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese foreign-economic initiative launched in 2013 to promote infrastructure, trade and connectivity across Asia, Europe and Africa.

t: Green capitalism runs into difficulties
zh: 绿色资本主义发展遭遇困境
paras: Zhuang Guiyang asks whether capitalism can be made environmentally sustainable through "green" growth. Writing in 2018, the author argues that capitalism without moral guidance cannot resolve its basic contradiction with ecological limits, and that green capitalism has therefore run into difficulties. The short commentary treats the US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement as the clearest recent illustration.

The article first sets out the case made by supporters of green capitalism, citing Paul Hawken's 2000 book and figures on record renewable-energy investment. It then turns to critics such as Richard Smith, to the US withdrawal announced in 2017, to wavering among developed countries at the Bonn climate talks, and finally to the rise of city networks and sub-national alliances in climate action.

Zhuang reports the supporters' view that green growth is a natural extension of capitalism's self-evolution, since scarcity and efficiency incentives are compatible with it. Against this, the author sides with critics who hold that the profit motive and the expansionary logic of capital conflict with saving the planet. In this reading, carbon taxes cannot fully remove market externalities, and technology cannot rescue the system. The author describes Trump's withdrawal, justified by 'America First' and by the aim of reviving oil and coal, as proof of the limits of self-regulation under capitalism. The article also claims that developed countries evade their obligations, citing the unmet US$100 billion annual climate-finance pledge and calls to end 'differentiated responsibilities'.

Zhuang notes that, after Copenhagen (2009), cities, firms and other non-state actors filled part of the gap. Examples include the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy, the 'America's Pledge' style coalitions of US states and the 'We Are Still In' pavilion at Bonn. Because these initiatives are bottom-up, the author holds they cannot replace states under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, and the outlook remains uncertain. The article calls for a development paradigm that goes beyond industrial civilisation. Read the original if you want a concise 2018 Chinese critique of green capitalism that links Paris Agreement politics to the contradictions of capitalism.
quoteEn: The current capitalist system, lacking moral guidance, has spun out of control, and no amount of green patching will help.
quoteZh: 当前缺乏道德指引的资本主义制度已经失去控制,再多的绿色修补也无济于事。

t: Why Western left-wing currents of thought have stalled
zh: 西方左翼思潮为何陷入停滞
paras: Writing in People's Forum in 2018, Chen Jiangsheng asks why Western left-wing currents of thought, which revived after the 2008 financial crisis, have recently stopped advancing. The article argues that since about 2016 uncertainty and stagnation have become the dominant picture. In Chen's view this follows from the unclear course of Western economies and societies, from a rethinking of the left's earlier rapid rise, and from the lack of a sound guiding ideology.

The article first explains how the 2008 crisis gave the left new momentum, then surveys four countries. It closes with a three-part explanation of the stagnation. Chen sets the revival against what the article calls the failure of neoliberalism and of American hegemony, and cites works by Chris Harman, Andrew Kliman and Thomas Piketty as examples of critique that won the left new followers.

Chen identifies three sources of the earlier growth: criticism of capitalism, the link with anti-globalisation sentiment, and an impact on national politics, such as the shift in France and a more reflective mood in the West. The country survey is then used as evidence of stalling. In the United States, Sanders's defeat and Trump's election are read as a left-wing ebb, though the 2017 left forum and protests suggest it is temporary. Britain's Brexit vote is described as 'left-wing people doing right-wing work', leaving the left without a clear position. The failed coalition talks in Germany show left and right unable to reconcile. Macron's win in France is judged only a limited gain for the left.

Chen uses the Marxist principle that social being determines social consciousness to explain the stagnation. Western economies are adrift internally and face competition from new theories and paths from the East. The left also grew too fast on discontent with the crisis, and people began to doubt its remedies. Finally, it is not guided by Marxism, so its critique of capitalism is incomplete and cannot solve basic problems within the old framework. Chen concludes that it will rise and fall in waves with popular discontent rather than transform Western society. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese journal in 2018 interpreted the post-crisis Western left through the lens of historical materialism.
quoteEn: Western left-wing currents lack a useful guiding ideology, which leaves their development unsustainable.
quoteZh: 西方左翼思潮缺乏管用的指导思想,带来了其发展缺乏可持续性。

t: A study of the Chinese translations of the Communist Manifesto
zh: 《共产党宣言》汉译考
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 17 July 2018
paras: Chen Hongjuan takes up a bibliographical question: how many distinct complete Chinese translations of the Communist Manifesto exist, and by what criteria should they be counted? The author notes that scholars have counted ten, twelve or even twenty-three translations. Chen argues that, by a consistent standard, there are six verifiable complete translations before 1949 and three "translation systems" after it. The author presents this clarification as a precondition for tracing how Marxist theory spread and developed in China.

The short article, published in a newspaper in 2018, is divided into two parts: complete translations before the founding of the People's Republic in 1949, and those after it. For the earlier period it lists the translations by Chen Wangdao (1920), Hua Gang (1930), Cheng Fangwu and Xu Bing (1938), Bo Gu (1943) and Chen Shoushi (1943), the last being the only one by a non-Communist. It then examines disputed cases: the 1948 Qiao Guanhua edition, Cheng Fangwu's 1953 and 1978 versions, the 1954 and 1958 texts, and the four versions issued by the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau.

Chen's central move is to separate a new translation from a revision or reprint. Qiao Guanhua's 1948 edition counts as a new translation because he worked from an English text rather than the German one used before. He also made over a hundred changes, such as replacing "propertied class" with "bourgeoisie", and he resolved the terminological inconsistencies caused by the 1938 split between two translators. By contrast, Cheng's 1953 edition is classed as an interim proofreading of his own work, and the 1954 and 1958 texts as reprints and revisions of the 1949 Moscow centenary edition. Chen groups the Bureau's 1964, 1978, 1995 and 2009 versions as one "translation system", citing the changes in annotation counts and the shifts in theoretical understanding behind each revision. The author borrows this approach from Gong Yuzhi's treatment of editions of Mao Zedong's Selected Works.

Chen concludes that the verifiable complete translations are the six pre-1949 ones plus, afterwards, the 1949 Moscow centenary text, Cheng Fangwu's 1978 translation and the Bureau's translation system. In the author's view, the translation history of the Manifesto is also the history of Marxist truth spreading in China and of Chinese Communists' persistent pursuit of truth and self-reform. Read the original if you want a compact guide to how Chinese scholars classify Manifesto translations and why the counts differ.
quoteEn: The translation history of the Manifesto is also the history of the spread of Marxist truth in China.
quoteZh: 《宣言》的翻译史也是马克思主义真理在中国传播的历史

glossary.explanation: The Party's central organ for translating and editing the works of Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin into Chinese. It produced the official Chinese editions of the Manifesto.
A category the author uses to group successive revisions by one translator or body as a single lineage. It lets each revision be recognised without counting it as a wholly new translation.

t: The Communist Manifesto and the development of the Japanese Communist Party
st: An interview with Fuwa Tetsuzo, head of the Japanese Communist Party's Social Science Research Institute
zh: 《共产党宣言》与日本共产党的发展
zhSub: 访日本共产党社会科学研究所所长不破哲三
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 27 September 2018
paras: This is an interview conducted by Shi Shaobo and Xie Zongrui for Chinese Social Sciences Today on the 170th anniversary of The Communist Manifesto. The interviewee is Fuwa Tetsuzo, a theorist of the Japanese Communist Party (JCP), nearly ninety years old, who heads its Social Science Research Institute. The interviewers ask what the Manifesto has meant, historically and today, for Japanese communists.

The conversation has five parts. Fuwa traces how the Manifesto reached Japan, from the 1904 translation by Sakai Toshihiko and Kotoku Shusui to the 1906 full text and its circulation under repression. He then turns to the Manifesto's place in the JCP's theory, three passages on abolishing private property and on violent revolution, the Party's study activities, and the 2004 Party Programme as a counterpart to a 'JCP manifesto'. He ends with the Manifesto's significance for the future.

Fuwa's central claim is that Marx must be read within Marx's own intellectual history. He reads the Manifesto's 'abolition of private property' as the socialisation of the means of production, not the abolition of personal property in the means of life. On violence, he argues that the Manifesto's line reflected Europe before universal suffrage. He points to Marx's 1872 Amsterdam speech and his 1878 notes, which in Fuwa's account allow for a peaceful, parliamentary route in some countries and point towards a 'majority revolution'. Fixing the Manifesto's stage-bound line into dogma, he says, contradicts Marxism's development. The JCP therefore studies all the classics, with 21 Capital seminars a year at the Central Committee, and avoids dogmatism.

Fuwa describes the 2004 Programme, which revised the 1961 version and which he says settles accounts with the errors inherited from the Stalin era, as the Party's equivalent of a manifesto. For the future, he stresses the Manifesto's formula of a society where the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all. He reads 'freedom' in Marx as, above all, free time for everyone, which would make human development rather than profit the driving force of society and open the 'real history' of humanity. Read the original if you want a JCP leader's account, published in a Chinese outlet, of how Japanese communists read the Manifesto on property, revolution and the future society.
quoteEn: Our reading and discussion of the Marxist classics will not be dogmatic, still less will we cut the foot to fit the shoe.
quoteZh: 我们对马克思主义经典的解读和研讨不会教条，更不会削足适履。

t: The Communist Manifesto shines in the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics
zh: 《共产党宣言》在中国特色社会主义新时代绽放光芒
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 26 April 2018
paras: Marking the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto and the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth in 2018, this newspaper commentary asks what the Manifesto means for China in what it calls the new era of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Tao argues that the text is not only a founding document of Marxism and scientific socialism but also the source of the Chinese Communists' faith, the intellectual root of Chinese socialism and a vision for humanity's future. The piece first appeared in the China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao) in April 2018.

The commentary is organised under three headings: the Manifesto as the source of Chinese Communists' faith, as the intellectual root of socialism with Chinese characteristics, and as a vision of human social development. Tao draws on the Manifesto's passages on the proletarian movement as one of the great majority, on world history and on the association of free individuals. The piece also cites recollections by Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping, the story of Chen Wangdao's translation, and statements by Xi Jinping and the 19th Party Congress (2017).

Tao's central claim is that the Party's "original aspiration and founding mission" and its people-centred approach to development trace back to the Manifesto's statement that the proletarian movement serves the vast majority. Citing Marx and Engels's 1872 preface, Tao says the Manifesto's general principles remain correct while their application depends on historical conditions. Tao therefore calls for grasping what changes and what does not in the Manifesto and for combining its principles with Chinese realities. On this reading, socialism with Chinese characteristics is scientific socialism in a Chinese form, and upholding it amounts to upholding Marxism. Tao also reads the Manifesto's account of world history and proletarian internationalism as the root of the 19th Party Congress's call for a community with a shared future for mankind, which Tao presents as an inheritance and development of Marx and Engels's theory.

Tao concludes that Marxism is the Communists' "true scripture" and that China must uphold it rather than any other doctrine, a necessity Tao ties to both its scientific character and China's modern history. Tao calls for firm political resolve and deeper understanding of the laws of socialist construction, of Communist Party rule and of human social development, so as to carry forward the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party-affiliated commentary in 2018 linked the Manifesto to Party faith, the Chinese Dream and the idea of a shared-future community.
quoteEn: It can be said that socialism with Chinese characteristics is scientific socialism and not some other -ism; it is scientific socialism in a Chinese form.
quoteZh: 可以说，中国特色社会主义是科学社会主义而不是其他主义，是中国化的科学社会主义。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path of socialist development since reform and opening up, presented by the Party as Marxism applied to Chinese conditions.

glossary.literal: do not forget the original heart, keep the mission firmly in mind
glossary.explanation: A slogan emphasised at the 19th Party Congress (2017) calling on Party members to remember their founding purpose of serving the people and pursuing communism.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept of international relations, written into Party documents at the 19th Party Congress, stressing shared interests and cooperation among states.
Xi Jinping's slogan, from 2012, for national rejuvenation and the prosperity of the Chinese people.

t: The Communist Manifesto shows renewed appeal in the new era
zh: 新时代《共产党宣言》再显魅力
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 17 July 2018
paras: This short newspaper commentary, published in 2018, takes the strong sales of the Communist Manifesto as a sign of the Party's condition. Wang argues that since the 18th Party Congress (2012) the Party has resolved the question of how to treat the Marxist classics and communist ideals and convictions, and that the book's popularity shows the truth-power of the Manifesto in the new era.

Wang opens with publishing figures. A new single-volume edition compiled by the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau appeared in December 2014 and, by March 2018, had gone through ten printings totalling 640,000 copies. A further edition in a special collection marking Marx's 200th birthday reached 392,000 copies by May, and a hardback commemorative edition added 20,000. Wang reports that over three and a half years the People's Publishing House editions alone passed one million copies.

The commentary then cites Xi Jinping's emphasis on studying Marxist theory as the Party's "essential skill", his 2016 speech on the Party's founding ideals, and the Politburo study session of 23 April 2018 devoted to the Manifesto. It also recalls Engels's remark that the Manifesto's circulation in a country indicates the state of its workers' movement and of large-scale industry. Wang reads the Manifesto's popularity as evidence that full and rigorous self-governance of the Party has been effective, that Party unity and relations with the public have improved, and that the people endorse the Party's governance.

Wang concludes that ideals and convictions have grown firmer, that enthusiasm for the classics is rising among Party members, students and society, and that the achievements under Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era have increased the number of people abroad who take Marxism seriously. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Party-aligned commentary in 2018 linked book sales to the Party's self-governance and ideological confidence.
quoteEn: In the new era, the Manifesto has once again displayed the charm of truth.
quoteZh: 《宣言》在新时代再次显示出了真理的魅力。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012), covering the anti-corruption campaign, discipline enforcement and ideological education within the Party.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The official guiding ideology of the Party, written into the Party constitution at the 19th Party Congress in 2017.

t: The historical roots of American trade bullying
zh: 美国贸易霸凌主义的历史溯源
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in July 2018, during the US-China trade war, Dong asks why the United States acts so unilaterally in trade. Some analyses blame one leader's personal style. Dong instead looks to US trade history and argues that trade has long served as a tool of American economic and political hegemony, a pattern the author calls trade bullying (maoyi baling zhuyi).

The commentary opens with Charles Kindleberger's 1973 "hegemonic stability theory", which Dong says merely legitimises hegemony. It then moves through several periods: protectionism from 1776 to the First World War, the Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930, Cold War embargoes and investment screening, and postwar relations with Japan and Europe. It ends with the present value-chain economy and a 2018 economists' letter.

Dong argues that the US has used protectionism at every stage of its development and has paired it with multilateral free-trade institutions after 1945. The article cites the 1930 tariff, which raised average duties to 59%, and a two-thirds fall in world trade from 1929 to 1934. It describes export controls on the Soviet Union and the 1975 Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States as strategic tools, now aimed at China's high-tech industries. Dong says the US both nurtured and suppressed its allies, citing its deficit with Japan and trade disputes with Europe. Its stated rules and order, in Dong's view, amount to double standards.

Dong concludes that bullying will provoke retaliation and may hurt the US itself. In today's value chains, the article says, tariffs fall on foreign-added content, which it puts at 35–40% of China's exports to the US. Dong compares the 1,028 economists who warned Congress in 1930 with the more than 1,100 who wrote to Trump in May 2018, both ignored. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese official commentary framed the 2018 trade war historically.
quoteEn: It is not hard to see that trade has always been used by the United States as a tool for advancing economic and political hegemony.
quoteZh: 不难看出,贸易一直被美国用作推进经济霸权和政治霸权的工具。

t: The contemporary crisis of capitalism and the rise and fall of Western identity politics
zh: 资本主义当代危机与西方身份政治学兴衰
paras: Zhang Liang asks why Western identity politics, which presented itself as an alternative to capitalism, declined quickly after the 2008 financial crisis, just when neoliberalism seemed discredited. The author argues that its theoretical flaws were exposed by the crisis, and that it declined because it was drawn into the ideology it set out to criticise.

This newspaper commentary traces the origins of identity politics in the 1970s and 1980s, when traditional workers' movements waned and new social movements took over the Western left. It covers postwar immigration, the strain on the welfare state, the neoliberal turn, and the collapse of the socialist bloc. It also covers the influence of postmodernism, and three stages of development, from deconstructing binary identities to reasserting suppressed identities and, finally, to using difference as resistance.

Zhang gives three reasons for the decline. First, identity politics adopted the neoliberal image of the person as a consumer, so that its critique became complicit in market ideology. Second, its alternative to capitalism stayed at the level of ideological imagination, without changing the mode of production, and so amounted to patching up the system. Third, the bourgeoisie took over identity issues, especially race, to deflect attention in times of crisis. In Zhang's reading, the root error was treating Marxism and postmodernism as equals.

Zhang concludes that theoretical innovation must be guided by Marxism. The author calls for restoring the working class's foundational and leading role, arguing that marginalised groups belong to the working class and can unite only on the basis of class identity. Zhang also calls for a historical-materialist view that takes the development of the productive forces as the basic measure of social progress, and links this to common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Marxist commentator assesses Western identity politics.
quoteEn: In the end, the alternative to capitalism proposed by Western identity politics is nothing more than a strategy of repair within the capitalist system.
quoteZh: 西方身份政治学的资本主义替代方案说到底不过是资本主义体系内的修补策略。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese policy goal of broadly shared wealth for all the people, stressed in Party documents and especially since the 2010s under Xi Jinping.

t: The historical position of the new era in the development of world socialism and its major significance
zh: 新时代在世界社会主义发展中的历史方位及其重大意义
paras: Writing in 2018, Wang Tingyou asks where the "new era" of socialism with Chinese characteristics, declared at the 19th Party Congress (2017), stands within the history of world socialism, and what follows from that position. The article argues that Chinese socialism is an important component of world socialism and now acts as its mainstay, and that grasping this relationship is a precondition for understanding Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era.

The article has three parts. The first discusses the idea of a "historical position" and traces how Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping each defined the stage their movement had reached, culminating in Xi Jinping's 2013 survey of Chinese socialism from the standpoint of world socialism. The second part reviews the mutual relationship between China and world socialism: Soviet and international support for China, then China's contribution, the Soviet and East European collapse, the neoliberal turn in the West, and the Chinese reform record. The third part sets out three ways the new era matters for world socialism.

Wang contends that the new era is the product of the historical, theoretical and practical logic of Chinese socialism. In the author's account, the Soviet and East European collapse pushed world socialism into a trough, with socialist states falling from 15 to 5, while China held its position and kept advancing reform and opening up. Wang sets this against what the article calls the most serious crisis of Western capitalism since the Second World War, citing the 2008 financial crisis, Occupy Wall Street and the "yellow vests". The three significances are: that China's development displays the superiority of the socialist system and the viability of Marxism; that Xi Jinping Thought offers experience on Party governance, socialist construction and social development to other countries and parties; and that Chinese success encourages Marxist parties elsewhere, who the author says remain marginal. Wang cites Gennady Zyuganov's 2017 remarks that China, Cuba and Vietnam inspire socialist forces.

Wang concludes that, with the example, experience, material strength and ideological guidance of new-era Chinese socialism, scientific socialism and world socialism will develop greatly, shifting the balance of forces between socialism and capitalism and bringing about a renewal of world socialism. The article also presents China as a builder of peace and a contributor to a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar placed the new era within the history of world socialism in 2018, and how official discourse linked Xi Jinping Thought to the global socialist movement.
quoteEn: Socialism with Chinese characteristics is an important component of world socialism and plays an ever greater role in advancing world socialism and the cause of human progress.
quoteZh: 中国特色社会主义是世界社会主义的重要组成部分，在促进世界社会主义和人类进步事业中发挥着越来越重大的作用。

glossary.explanation: The 19th Party Congress (2017) declared that socialism with Chinese characteristics had entered a new era, marked by a changed principal contradiction in Chinese society. It frames the period since the 18th Party Congress (2012) as a new historical stage.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017 and the state constitution in 2018. It is presented as the latest stage of adapting Marxism to China.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path, system and theory since reform and opening up, associated with Deng Xiaoping.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept promoted by Xi Jinping as the guiding idea of China's foreign policy, stressing shared interests and cooperation among states.
The policy launched at the end of 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, introducing market-oriented economic reform and opening China to foreign trade and investment.

t: The Communist Manifesto and the development of the French Communist Party
st: An interview with Jean-Numa Ducange, young theorist of the French Communist Party
zh: 《共产党宣言》与法国共产党的发展
zhSub: 访法国共产党青年理论家让-驽马·迪康热博士
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 31 May 2018
paras: This is an interview, published in 2018 to mark the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth and the 170th anniversary of the Communist Manifesto. Yu Weihai interviews Jean-Numa Ducange, who is described as a young theorist close to the French Communist Party, a special representative of the Gabriel Péri Foundation and a member of the team translating Marx and Engels into French (GEME). The question is how the Manifesto has been spread in France and what it still means for the French Communist Party (PCF) and the French left.

The interview is organised around five questions. They cover the history of the Manifesto's translation and circulation in France, the ideas of the text that the PCF still draws on, how the party and the wider left study Marx, the influence of Marxism on French politics, and Ducange's personal reading of the text. Yu also asks whether the PCF could produce a manifesto of its own.

Ducange traces French editions from a lost 1848 version to Laura Lafargue's 1885 translation, which appeared in Jules Guesde's newspaper. He says the PCF, founded in 1920, was the first party to publish the Manifesto in France, and that the text circulated widely while the party was a major force between 1935 and 1980. Marxism and the PCF declined from the 1980s, but he reports a renewed interest in Marx in the early 2000s, read with less political partisanship. He argues that the Manifesto has little direct ideological influence on today's PCF, which he calls relatively short of Marxist ideology. Even so, its treatment of the nation, capitalist expansion and alliances still bears on current debates over sovereignty, Europe and left alliances. He adds that Marx's writings on France, such as The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, must be read alongside it. He also notes the Manifesto's Eurocentric limits.

Ducange says the Manifesto remains a foundational text for the PCF and still gives hope for the future. He credits the PCF with popularising Marxism among hundreds of thousands, even millions, of French people, despite misreadings. He regrets that the party has no equivalent founding text. He proposes a new manifesto for the twenty-first century, to be discussed with the 'radical left' and pursued only through an internationalist approach. He describes Chinese experience as very valuable and calls for China–France cooperation across differences in social system. Read the original if you want a French Communist-affiliated historian's view of the Manifesto's reception in France and of the PCF's current position, as presented to a Chinese audience.
quoteEn: It is necessary to put forward a new kind of manifesto. It need not be exhaustive (in fact Marx and Engels did not ask for an exhaustive description either), but it can fully show the new balance of world forces, explain the changes and needs of the world, and think through Marxism in the twenty-first century.
quoteZh: 有必要再提出一种新的宣言，它不一定是详尽的（事实上，马克思和恩格斯也没有要求详尽的描述），但它可以充分展示新的世界力量对比，来解释世界的变化和需要，思考21世纪的马克思主义。

t: The Communist Party of Australia's active exploration of the socialist movement
zh: 澳共对社会主义运动的积极探索
paras: This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2018, reports on the 13th National Congress of the Communist Party of Australia (CPA), held in Sydney in December 2017. Yang argues that the congress's resolutions show a distinctive Party analysis of capitalism in crisis and a realistic programme for advancing the socialist movement at home.

The article opens with a brief history: the CPA's founding in 1920, its dissolution after the Soviet and East European upheavals, and the 1996 renaming of the Socialist Party of Australia, which split from the earlier CPA in 1971, as the Communist Party of Australia. It then summarises the congress's assessment of capitalism and the practical guidelines adopted under the theme "Taking the Party to the People". Bob Briton was re-elected general secretary, and the programme and constitution were amended.

On the first point, Yang reports the CPA's view that the 2008 financial crisis stemmed from monopoly corporations shifting capital into the virtual economy, leaving the real economy starved. According to the CPA, Western states are now cutting workers' welfare and exporting their contradictions through imperialist aggression. It cites Roy Morgan Research figures putting real Australian unemployment in 2017 above 9.5%, against an official rate of about 5.5%. The guidelines stress the Party's leading role, grassroots branch-building, work among workers whose composition has changed, and a two-stage path in the 2005 programme: an anti-imperialist, anti-monopoly democratic stage, then a socialist revolution. They also stress Party unity, a broad united front including trade unions and Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australians, and international solidarity, including with Cuba and the Polish communists.

Yang concludes that the CPA's understanding of the crisis is distinctive and its action plan realistic. The author adds that the Party's particular exploration offers a new perspective for understanding the world socialist movement. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language account of the CPA's 2017 congress and how a Chinese commentator presents it.
quoteEn: On the whole, the CPA has its own distinctive understanding of the deep crisis of today's Western capitalist countries, and the domestic action plans it proposes are realistic.
quoteZh: 总体而言，澳共对当前西方资本主义国家深处危机的认识有着自己独到的理解，所提出的相关国内工作行动方案具有现实性。

t: Scientific socialism has strong vitality
zh: 科学社会主义具有强大生机活力
paras: Writing in the People's Daily on 8 June 2018, Wu Enyuan takes up Xi Jinping's speech at the commemoration of the 200th anniversary of Marx's birth. The commentary asks what the history of scientific socialism shows about its vitality. Wu argues that studying Xi's remarks helps readers see that vitality and grasp the significance of socialism with Chinese characteristics entering a new era.

The piece is a short historical survey that runs from the Communist Manifesto of 1848 to the present. It passes through the October Revolution, the Great Depression of 1929–1932, the upheavals in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union around 1990, and the years after the 2008 financial crisis.

Wu's core argument is that each stage of the Chinese Communist Party's history confirms the strength of scientific socialism. Wu says the Party combined the basic principles of Marxism with China's concrete conditions, which produced three leaps for the Chinese nation: from being weak to standing up, then to becoming prosperous, then to becoming strong. Each leap is said to prove that only socialism could save China, that only socialism with Chinese characteristics could develop China, and that only upholding and developing it can achieve the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Wu credits Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era with a major contribution to scientific socialism. Wu also presents Western talk of "the end of history", of a "China collapse" and of a "China threat" as attempts to contain China.

Wu concludes that looking back, comparing other paths and looking ahead all reveal the truth of Marxism and the vitality of scientific socialism. This, Wu says, should strengthen the Four-sphere Confidence. Read the original if you want a compact example of how a Party-affiliated scholar told the history of socialism in 2018 for a general newspaper audience.
quoteEn: The success of the theory and practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics has made scientific socialism radiate vigorous vitality on Chinese soil.
quoteZh: 中国特色社会主义理论和实践的成功,使科学社会主义在中国大地上焕发出勃勃生机。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's theory and path of socialist development since reform and opening up.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018.
Official slogan calling for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
