quoteEn: Cuba's socialist revolution and construction, and its reform and opening up, will certainly continue along the programme and policies set by the Sixth and Seventh Party Congresses; Cuba's political and social situation will not see major turmoil, and the updating of the Cuban model will go on.
quoteZh: 古巴的社会主义革命和建设，古巴的改革开放一定会沿着古共六大和古共七大制定的纲领和政策走下去，古巴的政治和社会局势不会出现大的动荡，古巴更新模式会继续进行下去。

glossary.explanation: The official description of China's economic system since the early 1990s, combining market mechanisms with public ownership and Party leadership.

t: The centenary of the October Revolution should be commemorated with great ceremony
zh: 应隆重纪念十月革命100周年
paras: Writing in 2017, Wu Enyuan argues that the hundredth anniversary of the Russian October Revolution should be marked solemnly. In Wu's view the revolution turned Marxism from theory into practice and proved its scientific character. Reviewing a century of socialist development, the author says, strengthens the ideal that socialism and communism will inevitably prevail and supports the values of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The short commentary has two parts. The first sets out the revolution's historical significance. The second lists three themes that commemoration should convey to the public: adapting Marxism to national conditions, opposing historical nihilism, and educating young people in core socialist values.

On significance, Wu claims the revolution showed that economically backward countries can take the socialist road, pointed to humanity's direction of development, and spurred national liberation movements. Wu credits socialist systems with planning, full employment and social security. The author presents the founding of socialist China as both a fruit of the October Revolution and an extension of its world-historical meaning. On historical nihilism, Wu rejects the view that the revolution's "original sin" caused the Soviet collapse. Citing Putin and Xi Jinping, the author blames Gorbachev's abandonment of the Party's leadership and his negation of Soviet history.

Wu concludes that commemoration means "remaining true to the original aspiration", drawing lessons and strengthening confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author calls for stronger value education among youth, citing post-Soviet Russia's loss of values as a warning. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Russian-history specialist framed the 2017 centenary for a general audience.
quoteEn: Gorbachev and other Soviet leaders betrayed the basic principles that the October Revolution had indicated.
quoteZh: 戈尔巴乔夫等苏联领导人背弃了十月革命指示的基本原则。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Chinese Party discourse for interpretations that negate the Party's or socialism's history, often applied to critical accounts of the Soviet and Maoist past.
The official name for China's current system and theory, associated with Deng Xiaoping's reform-era line.

glossary.zh: 道路自信、理论自信和制度自信
glossary.pinyin: dàolù zìxìn, lǐlùn zìxìn hé zhìdù zìxìn
glossary.en: confidence in the path, theory and system
glossary.literal: path confidence, theory confidence and system confidence
glossary.explanation: Official slogan, promoted by Xi Jinping's leadership, calling for confidence in China's socialist road, theoretical system and institutions; later extended to a fourth, culture.

t: The predicament of Western capitalism's normalised economic stagnation
st: An interview with Professor He Zili of the School of Economics, Nankai University
zh: 西方资本主义经济陷入停滞常态化的困境
zhSub: 访南开大学经济学院何自力教授
paras: This is an interview, published in 2017, with He Zili, a professor in the School of Economics at Nankai University. The interviewer, who is not named, asks why Western capitalism, once seen as unbeatable and symbolised by Fukuyama's "end of history", has fallen into lasting stagnation since the 1970s and especially after the 2008 crisis. He argues that this stagnation is no passing cyclical downturn but a normalised condition rooted in capitalism's internal contradictions and institutions.

The interview has four parts: the stages of capitalist development and the features of stagnation; the institutional roots of stagnation; its effects on the world; and how China should respond. On periodisation, He sets the familiar sequence of free-competition, monopoly, state-monopoly and global monopoly capitalism against his own scheme of mercantile, industrial and service capitalism. In that scheme, industrial capitalism has moved since the early 1970s into "de-industrialisation", with industrial capital losing ground to financial and service capital.

On the first question, He lists eight consequences of de-industrialisation and heavy reliance on services: collapsing welfare systems, a financial sector detached from the real economy, loss of industrial competitiveness, mounting government debt, persistent economic decline, high unemployment, a hollowed-out middle class, and a paralysed political system. On causes, he names private ownership with wage labour, a political system in which interest groups capture legislatures, and neoliberalism as the dominant ideology. In his account, private interest and social interest cannot be reconciled while private ownership endures, for example when capital replaces workers with machines. He also argues that stagnation is bringing political and social turbulence, a rightward political shift he compares with the 1930s, a retreat from economic globalisation, and a US that defends its declining hegemony through protectionism, interest-rate moves and interventions abroad.

He concludes that stagnation follows from capitalism's inner contradictions and the law of surplus value, and that it will persist unless neoliberal dogma and the underlying arrangements change. China, as the second-largest economy, cannot stand aside. He points to the "innovative, open, interconnected and inclusive" world economy that China proposed at the 2016 G20 Hangzhou summit, and to a community with a shared future for mankind, as remedies for sluggish recovery and weakening globalisation. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist economist's account of post-2008 Western stagnation and the policy line it supports, along with its statistics on unemployment and its view of US policy.
quoteEn: Western capitalism's lasting stagnation is produced by its inner contradictions and its political and economic institutions; as long as these contradictions and institutional arrangements remain unchanged, being unable to escape stagnation is capitalism's inevitable fate.
quoteZh: 西方资本主义经济陷入持续停滞，是资本主义内在矛盾和政治经济制度造成的，只要资本主义内在矛盾和制度安排不改变，资本主义经济陷入停滞不能自拔就是其必然的宿命。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2013. It calls for cooperation, common development and a more inclusive international order.

t: China as the locomotive towards a just world
zh: 中国是通向公正世界的火车头
paras: This is a Chinese-language interview with Gennady Zyuganov, chairman of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation, conducted by a reporter from Cankao Xiaoxi and reprinted in Marxist Digest in 2017. Asked how Russia sees China's present and future after almost four decades of reform and opening up, Zyuganov argues that the development of socialist China serves the interests of the whole world and that China is 'the locomotive towards a just world'.

The interview has four parts: the reasons for China's success and its long-term planning; the progress of the 'two centenary goals' and the Chinese Dream; China's contribution to culture, science and technology; and the internal and external challenges China faces, including the place of Russia–China cooperation. Zyuganov repeatedly compares China with post-Soviet Russia, using figures on industrial output, research spending and trade.

Zyuganov attributes China's rise to the fact that it kept a socialist orientation and combined it with a sound cadre policy and market instruments, all aimed at the people's welfare. He contrasts this with Russia in the 1990s, when, in his image, the authorities removed the ship's rudder before pushing it into the market. He contends that the Chinese Dream, unlike an individualist 'American Dream' that he says leads to expansion, carries responsibility for the world's progress, and that the Belt and Road Initiative shows how peaceful prosperity attracts neighbours. Among internal challenges he lists the exhausted export-oriented, cheap-labour model and corruption, citing the lesson of the Soviet Communist Party's collapse. He sees the leading role of the Communist Party of China as the guarantee of the chosen course. Externally, he describes US and NATO attempts at encirclement, protectionism and tariff barriers, which he says fail against China's firm but peaceful foreign policy.

Zyuganov concludes that achieving the two centenary goals would make China a global superpower and a centre of attraction for progressive forces and poor peoples, provided it holds high the banner of social justice and friendship among peoples. He hopes a renewed socialist Russia will go hand in hand with China, and urges closer economic and security ties, since Russia accounts for only 2% of China's trade by his figures. Read the original if you want a Russian communist leader's view of China's development, as published for a Chinese readership in 2017.
quoteEn: China is the locomotive towards a just world.
quoteZh: 中国是通向公正世界的火车头。

glossary.explanation: Official targets to build a moderately prosperous society by 2021, the centenary of the Communist Party's founding, and a modern socialist country by 2049, the centenary of the People's Republic.
A slogan popularised by Xi Jinping from 2012, meaning national rejuvenation, prosperity and the people's happiness.
A Chinese initiative launched in 2013 to build infrastructure and trade links across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

keywords: Communist Party of the Russian Federation

t: Global Times: how Russia views the 1917 revolutions a hundred years on
zh: 《环球时报》：100年后的今天俄罗斯如何看1917年革命
source: Marxism Digest (Makesizhuyi Wenzhai), 2017 no. 3; originally in Global Times
paras: This is a 2017 Global Times (Huanqiu Shibao) news report, reprinted in Marxism Digest, on how Russian society and the Russian state approached the centenary of the February and October Revolutions of 1917. The report's main finding is a deep division: some Russians see the revolutions as the start of the country's best era, others as an obstacle to its development. It presents President Putin as seeking a frank assessment while refusing to carry old divisions into the present.

The report draws on Western agencies and newspapers (AFP, The New York Times, Art News), Russian media, opinion polls, interviews with Moscow residents and comments from Russian and Chinese specialists. It first describes the official commemorations: about 500 conferences, round tables, exhibitions and festivals, and a committee set up in December 2016. It then turns to public opinion and party positions. Finally it traces how the Russian state has marked 7 November since Soviet times and sets out Putin's own statements.

On the commemorations, the report says officials stressed remembrance and understanding rather than celebration, and asked that the events not be politicised. Museums were described as avoiding controversy. Western outlets read this caution as unease, while a Kremlin cultural envoy is quoted as saying that state celebrations would deepen divisions. On opinion, the report cites polls in which roughly equal shares call the revolution a major event, a driver of progress or a catastrophe, and in which 40 per cent view Lenin positively against 20 per cent negatively. Russian interviewees range from admirers of Lenin to critics of the civil war, and some young people say they are indifferent. The Communist Party and the Liberal Democratic Party are shown as taking opposing stances. Wu Enyuan of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences describes Putin's view as two-sided: he respects Soviet achievements but criticises the shooting of the Romanov family and the Soviet federal structure.

The report concludes that the revolutions and the Soviet era remain tied to the military strength, industrial base and social security system on which Russia still relies. It adds that more young people are drawn to a Soviet Union they never knew. It quotes the Russian analyst Stepan Surakshev as saying that rising inequality and inefficient administration make the lessons of 1917 relevant today. Read the original if you want a compact, Chinese-media overview of Russian opinion, party positions and official policy on the 1917 centenary, with Chinese scholarly comment.
quoteEn: "For more than twenty years, two sharply opposed views of the October Revolution have kept clashing in the public eye and in academia."
quoteZh: “这二十多年来，关于十月革命的两种泾渭分明的看法，一直在公众视野里、学术界碰撞着。”

t: New features of the crisis of contemporary capitalism
zh: 当代资本主义危机呈现新特征
paras: This short commentary, originally published in the People's Daily in 2017, asks what is new about the crisis of capitalism in the developed countries since the 2008 international financial crisis. Ding Xiaoqin argues that weak growth, widening inequality, political polarisation, populism and right-wing extremism show deepening internal contradictions. In the author's view, attempts to blame globalisation or foreign intervention cannot reverse the overall trend.

The article is organised around three features: difficult economic recovery and ineffective policy, a widening wealth gap with sharper political polarisation, and declining soft power and international influence. It draws mainly on the United States, with references to the eurozone, Britain, Germany and Japan, and gives statistics on public debt and income shares.

Ding argues that bailouts, stimulus and quantitative easing only postponed collapse while raising government debt. The article cites US debt rising from 61.8% of GDP in 2006 to 106.1% in 2016, and Japan's exceeding 250%. Policy swings between neoliberalism and Keynesianism without improving conditions for ordinary workers. Ding says that after the war, capitalist states eased class conflict through higher wages and welfare. With growth slowing, capitalists now fight over their share of output, so real incomes stagnate. The article also holds that the crisis exposed the myth of the US economic system and eroded its soft power, which force and financial hegemony cannot restore.

Ding concludes that crisis-shifting cannot alter capitalism's essential traits and basic flaws. The author predicts further inequality, a shrinking middle class, lasting policy deadlock, government credit held hostage by monopoly capital and continuing polarisation. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Marxist economist framed post-2008 Western capitalism in 2017.
quoteEn: Although some developed countries strive to shift the crisis and rescue their economies, they cannot change capitalism's essential characteristics and fundamental defects, and can hardly stop the cycle and worsening of capitalist crisis.
quoteZh: 虽然一些发达国家竭力转嫁危机、拯救本国经济，却无法改变资本主义的本质特征及其根本缺陷，难以阻挡资本主义危机的循环和恶化。

t: Differing assessments of the October Revolution inside Russia
st: Right-wing, left-wing and government views on the eve of the centenary
zh: 俄罗斯国内关于十月革命的不同评价
paras: Writing on the eve of the revolution's 100th anniversary in 2017, Chen Hong asks how the October Revolution is judged in Russia today. The author argues that assessments remain divided and fall into three camps: a negative right-wing view, an affirmative left-wing view, and a government position that tries to reconcile the two. Chen draws on seminars held in Russia in early 2017, including a Moscow University conference and a Moscow Economic Forum panel the author attended.

The article is organised into three sections. The first covers right-wing writers, both monarchist and liberal, and traces their arguments to Western liberal and Menshevik positions and to post-Soviet historiography. The second covers left-wing scholars, taking the "post-Soviet critical Marxists" as their main representatives. These include Slavin and Buzgalin, who edited the volume The Culmination of the Great Revolution, and Vayikov. The third section follows the Russian government's stance from Yeltsin to Putin and the 2016 commission planning the centenary.

Chen reports that the right treats 1917 as a conspiracy or coup, citing the "German gold" and spy stories. The right prefers the February Revolution and holds that October pushed Russia off its natural path, toward either a constitutional monarchy or a normal capitalism. Chen presents the critical Marxists as rebutting this with historical materialism: in their account the revolution was a social revolution driven by popular discontent, and Soviet tragedies do not discredit its ideals. Chen says the author agrees with the left's basic view, but notes internal disputes over the revolution's nature. Vayikov sees it as a continuation of a bourgeois revolution, while Slavin, Buzgalin and others stress socialist and cultural elements. On the government, Chen describes a move from wholesale denial under Yeltsin to "harmless" treatment under Putin. This includes commemorating February and October together and appealing to national unity. Chen judges this stance contradictory and concludes that it in effect makes the "red" yield to the "white".

Chen concludes that the October Revolution can be understood correctly only through the concrete historical facts and the popular mood of its time, and that this also allows right-wing claims to be refuted with evidence. The author calls for summing up the revolution's experience and for continuing to uphold and develop socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language survey of Russian debates around the 2017 centenary, with named Russian scholars and sources, and a view of how a Chinese Marxist scholar assesses them.
quoteEn: Every historical event has its roots, and only by considering the concrete historical facts and where popular sentiment stood in the concrete situation of the time can we gain a correct understanding of the October Revolution.
quoteZh: 任何一个历史事件的发生都有其根源，我们只有结合当时具体的历史事实和具体历史形势下的人心向背才会对十月革命有着正确认知

glossary.explanation: The official label for China's current system and path, developed since the reform era and central to Party ideology. Here the author links it to the legacy of the October Revolution.

t: Financialization has intensified the contradictions and crises of capitalist society
zh: 金融化加剧了资本主义社会的矛盾与危机
source: World Economics and Politics (Shijie jingji yu zhengzhi), 2016 no. 7
paras: Luan Wenlian asks how the financialization of capitalism since the 1970s–80s has changed the contradictions of capitalist society, and argues that it has sharpened them and made crises more frequent. In the author's account, financialization is the newest form of capital's rule and the logical outcome of monopoly capitalism, in which accumulation of money wealth through the financial system rises above, and increasingly detaches from, production.

The article first sets out a three-stage periodisation of capitalism: free competition (Marx and Engels), monopoly capitalism (Lenin), and the present stage dominated by fictitious financial capital. It then examines four areas of intensified contradiction: the basic contradiction between productive forces and relations of production; the separation of finance from the real economy; the exploitation of working people; and the dominance of financial capital within capitalist contradictions. A concluding section draws out four features of contemporary crises. Luan draws on Foster, Epstein, Keynes and Chinese and US statistics.

Luan argues that technological and financial innovation are seized by financial capital and turned into means of reproducing capitalist relations. The basic contradiction acquires a new form: the socialisation of capital, through joint-stock companies and wider share ownership, coexists with the private ownership, use and returns of that capital. The article cites figures that the richest 10 per cent of Americans hold 89.3 per cent of stock value. It also traces the delinking of the US dollar from gold, after which dollar issuance grew sharply, and cites a rising ratio of financial to real assets and falling real wages in the United States. Financial profit, Luan holds, remains ultimately a redistribution of surplus value created in production, so the separation can never be complete. The author reads the M–M′ circuit as already containing the reality of crisis. Luan also describes the financialization of workers' incomes (pensions, housing credit, insurance) as a new form of exploitation, and argues that states serve financial capital, citing the scale of the 2008 bailout.

Luan concludes that capitalist crises are unavoidable, take new forms in which financial institutions transmit and amplify shocks, and are more frequent and shorter in cycle. The author adds that the originating powers harm the world most, since developing countries suffer in their real economies and in the value of their dollar reserves. The article judges this accumulation model, set against productive forces, value creation and the working majority, to be unsustainable. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist political-economy account of financialization that draws on Monthly Review-school and Western critical literature and on statistics about US inequality and finance.
quoteEn: True value comes from labour and from production, not from the manipulations of finance.
quoteZh: 真正的价值是来自劳动、来自生产，而不是来自金融的操弄。

glossary.explanation: The process, since the 1970s–80s, by which financial motives, markets and institutions come to dominate the economy. The author treats it as a new stage of monopoly capitalism.
The stage of capitalism analysed by Lenin, in which monopolies and finance capital dominate. The author sees financialization as its latest development.

t: On inequality in the various spheres of contemporary Western society
zh: 论当代西方社会各领域的不平等
source: Economic Research Reference (Jingji yanjiu cankao), 2016 no. 58
paras: Writing in 2016, Song Lidan asks how far inequality has deepened in Western societies since the end of the Cold War. The article argues that growing economic inequality has widened the political, cultural and developmental gaps between bourgeoisie and proletariat, and even gaps in health and life expectancy. Citing Lenin, Song holds that exploiters cannot be equal to the exploited, and that this inequality is rooted in capitalist private ownership and is an incurable chronic disease of capitalism.

The article moves through five spheres of inequality (economic, political, educational, developmental, and health and longevity) before a final section on lessons for China. Song draws mainly on Western authors and data, including Anthony Giddens, Thomas Piketty, John Westergaard, Howard Zinn, Paul Krugman, Elizabeth Warren, John Scott, Joseph Stiglitz and Ulrich Beck, together with an International Labour Organization report of 2015 and German health statistics.

Song treats economic inequality, grounded in unequal ownership of the means of production, as the determining one. Citing Piketty, Song reads the post-1945 rise in the capital/income ratio as showing that the Kuznets curve was largely a Cold War product. Political equality is called formal only: elections are described as contests among the bourgeoisie, and without economic democracy there can be no real political democracy. Education is presented as a market-driven competition for social rank, with rising student debt, the Gatsby curve and an "class ceiling" in Britain. Insecure work, limited mobility and unequal health outcomes are said to show that individual effort mostly yields a slightly better position in the labour market.

In the closing section Song draws three lessons for China. China, unlike the West, cannot draw profit from colonialism and must rely on a socialist basic economic system with distribution according to work. Song also warns that economic inequality has appeared with the growth of the non-public sector and, if it worsens, could invite unrest and endanger the goals of the "two centenaries". Finally, Song sees capitalism in a legitimacy crisis since 2008 and calls for firm adherence to the basic socialist system in order to realise the Chinese Dream of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want to see how a CASS researcher in 2016 assembled Western critical data on inequality to support an argument for China's socialist path.
quoteEn: Without economic democracy, there can be no genuine political democracy.
quoteZh: 没有经济民主，就不会有真正的政治民主。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A long-term national goal in Party discourse, associated with the Chinese Dream, referring to restoring China's strength and international standing.
A slogan popularised by Xi Jinping from 2012, identifying national rejuvenation, prosperity and the collective well-being of the Chinese people as shared aims.
Two target dates in Party strategy: building a moderately prosperous society by the Party's centenary (2021) and a modern socialist country by the centenary of the People's Republic (2049).

A socialist distribution principle under which individuals receive remuneration in proportion to the labour they contribute; it is treated in China as the main form of distribution within the basic economic system.

t: Development trends of world socialism in the twenty-first century
zh: 21 世纪世界社会主义的发展趋势
source: Jilin Party School Journal (Jilin dangxiao bao), 15 June 2016, p. 3
paras: Writing in 2016, Sun Jinsong asks where the world socialist movement is heading in the twenty-first century. The author argues that the shock and disorientation that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe have largely ended. In Sun's account, socialism is now reviving in some countries in forms different from the twentieth-century Soviet model, and socialism with Chinese characteristics will become an important driving force for the movement.

The article is organised around three trends: the relationship between humans and nature as a defining feature of socialism, globalization as socialism's historical stage, and the role of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It surveys socialist thought from early utopian socialism and classical Marxism to Soviet practice, and divides capitalist globalization into three phases. A closing periodisation sums up the argument.

Sun first contends that earlier socialism centred on conflicts within human society, whereas sustainable development now makes the human–nature relationship central. The author traces the "ecological crisis" to capitalism's profit-driven mode of production and presents "ecological civilization" as socialism's concern. Sun then describes globalization 1.0 as colonial trade, 2.0 as WTO-era transnational production that moves manufacturing to developing countries, and 3.0 as a new model of equal consultation and mutual benefit represented by the Belt and Road Initiative. Third, Sun argues that China's industrialization was driven by external pressure and national survival, was led by the Communist Party rather than a national bourgeoisie, and shows that modernization without wholesale Westernization is possible. The author cites the failures of Western-style democracy in Iraq, Libya and Egypt, and says China's peaceful rise differs from Western colonial industrialization.

Sun concludes that nineteenth-century socialism was marked by theory (Marxism), twentieth-century socialism by practice (the Soviet model), and twenty-first-century socialism by exploration, symbolised by socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author acknowledges remaining problems in China, naming Party corruption as the greatest danger, and holds that China's influence rests on its achievements rather than coercion. Read the original if you want an example of how a Central Party School scholar framed China's place in world socialism around 2016, including the "globalization 1.0, 2.0, 3.0" scheme.
quoteEn: If the hallmark of nineteenth-century socialism was theory, marked by Marxism, and that of twentieth-century socialism was practice, marked by the Soviet model, then the hallmark of twenty-first-century socialism is exploration, marked by socialism with Chinese characteristics.
quoteZh: 如果说，19世纪社会主义的特征是理论，以马克思主义为标识;20世纪社会主义的特征是实践，以苏联模式为标识;那么，21世纪社会主义的特征就是探索，是以中国特色社会主义为标识。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership and public ownership with market mechanisms. It is presented as Marxism adapted to Chinese conditions.
An official concept for development that balances economic growth with environmental protection. It was written into Party documents in the 2000s and 2010s.
A Chinese initiative launched by Xi Jinping in 2013 to build infrastructure and trade links across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

t: The Communist Party of Sweden's new explorations of the road to socialism since the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
zh: 苏东剧变以来瑞典共产党对社会主义道路的新探索
source: Journal of Liaoning University (Philosophy and Social Sciences Edition), 20 April 2017
paras: How has a small West European communist party reconsidered the road to socialism since the collapse of the Soviet bloc? Zhou and Guo examine the Communist Party of Sweden (SKP), founded in 1917, and argue that since the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe it has kept to Marxism-Leninism while adapting its strategy to Swedish conditions. In the authors' view, this makes its exploration significant even though the party remains weak.

The article first traces the party's organisational history, including its 1960s–70s split, the re-founding of a communist party in 1977, the 1989 extraordinary congress and the 1995 return to the name Communist Party of Sweden. It then follows the SKP's own documents, above all its 2013 programme and statements on its website, through four themes. These are its analysis of contemporary capitalism; its views on the Soviet collapse, the Swedish labour movement, the European Union and NATO; its goals, principles and tasks; and its vision of a future socialist society.

The authors report that the SKP sees capitalism as unchanged in its exploitative essence, with globalisation as the current form of imperialism and neoliberalism. On the Soviet collapse, the party names institutional flaws, including a highly centralised planned economy, bloc integration during the Cold War and the fusion of party and state. It still holds that this was not a failure of socialism itself and that socialism can correct its errors. The SKP condemns the EU as imperialist and undemocratic, and it opposes covert Swedish ties to NATO, defending military neutrality. The authors describe its positive programme as public ownership and a planned economy, a fairer international trade system, and a classless society that guarantees work, housing, health care and education and aims at the free and all-round development of every person. The party rests on democratic centralism and on criticism and self-criticism.

Zhou and Guo conclude that the SKP's programme preserves public ownership, planning and the universal features of socialism while reflecting Swedish conditions, such as an advanced economy and well-developed bourgeois democracy. For them, this shows that socialism has no single model. They acknowledge that the party's base is narrow, that it is unlikely to take power for a long time, and that its immediate tasks are to broaden its class and mass base through anti-monopoly and anti-imperialist struggle. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of a small European communist party's programme and its positions on the Soviet collapse, the EU and NATO.
quoteEn: This also shows that there is no single, uniform model of socialism.
quoteZh: 这也说明了社会主义不存在千篇一律的模式。

t: Sanders's "socialism" and the thesis of "American socialist exceptionalism"
zh: 从桑德斯的“社会主义”看“美国社会主义例外论”
paras: Why did Bernie Sanders, a self-declared socialist, defeat Hillary Clinton in several state primaries in the first half of 2016 in a country long labelled an exception to socialism? Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2017, no. 2), Xuan Chuanshu and Tan Yangfang argue that this is not anomalous once the historical logic behind it is examined.

The short commentary is organised in three numbered sections. It first traces the economic and political background of Sanders's rise, then assesses what his "socialism" actually is, and finally revisits the claim that the United States is an exception, drawing on the history of American labour and socialist movements.

The authors contend that the turn towards socialism was produced by the contradictions of capitalism, not by Sanders's campaign: neoliberal financialisation since the 1980s, the financial crisis and the Occupy Wall Street movement widened inequality and shifted public attitudes. They cite a 2011 Pew survey and a 2016 Boston Globe poll on young Americans' views of socialism. In their reading, Sanders is a reformist rather than a true socialist: he takes Denmark and Sweden, the New Deal and Johnson's reforms as models, relies on class cooperation and the Democratic Party, and in effect reflects the ruling class's effort to channel unrest into reformism. They also argue that Sombart's question explains only why America lacks Soviet, Latin American or European-style socialism, not why it lacks socialism altogether; they point to the 1886 Chicago strike, Eugene Debs, the Socialist Party and the Communist Party.

The authors conclude that the United States is not an exception but has socialism in different forms and along different paths. Cycles of crisis and reform, they say, have left socialist ideas and elements behind, and the revival of socialist forces shows that history has not ended. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Party journal in 2017 interpreted Sanders and the exceptionalism debate.
quoteEn: But all these peculiarities can only explain why the United States has no Soviet-style socialism, no socialism of the South American type next door, and no European-style socialism of its distant relatives; they cannot support the conclusion of "American socialist exceptionalism", that is, that "America has no socialism"!
quoteZh: 但是所有这些独特性，只能说明美国为什么没有苏联式的社会主义、没有其近邻南美地区式的社会主义、没有原本属于其远亲的欧洲式社会主义，而不能得出“美国社会主义例外论”，即“美国没有社会主义”的结论！

t: How to view populism in Europe today
zh: 如何看待当前欧洲的民粹主义
paras: Writing in Qiushi in 2017, Yao Yao asks why populism and extreme currents have risen so quickly in Europe and what this means for European integration and globalisation. The author argues that debt, refugee and terrorist crises have left Europe's lower and middle strata in a state of material and spiritual distress. In Yao's reading, populism reflects long-accumulated strategic mistakes and institutional deadlocks in European states, not only the mood of the moment.

The article has three parts. The first defines populism as an anti-elite current of thought, a movement for radical reform by ordinary people, and a strategy that elites can use to manipulate the public. It traces its causes to the 2008 financial crisis, the Spanish protests of 2011 and neoliberal globalisation. The second part sets out four deadlocks, illustrated by Spain, Greece, France, Italy and EU demographic data. The third part turns to the transatlantic relationship and the EU's internal imbalances.

Yao holds that neoliberal policy produced growth but distributed it unevenly, since capital moves more freely than labour and migration brings cultural friction. Left populism, on this account, "hates the rich" and opposes austerity and capital mobility. Right populism "hates foreigners" and opposes immigration. Both therefore oppose the existing international order and European integration. The four deadlocks are deindustrialisation and financialisation, unaffordable welfare, population decline and migration, and an electoral system in which populists block reforms. Yao cites France's labour law and Italy's 2016 constitutional referendum as examples. The author also argues that Europe is unequal in its relationship with the United States and that the EU's rights and responsibilities are unbalanced.

Yao concludes that populism is both appealing for confronting real problems and destructive for aggravating them. The author expects it to push Europe towards a retreat from integration and globalisation. Protectionism and isolationism may offer temporary shelter but would harm national and world economies in the long run. Yao calls on responsible politicians to adjust strategy, advance institutional reform and guide public opinion towards a balanced, inclusive and win-win globalisation. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2017 Chinese Party-journal commentary explained European populism and its link to globalisation.
quoteEn: Populism has both the deceptive allure of confronting problems head-on and the subversive, destructive power to intensify them.
quoteZh: 民粹主义既有直面问题的迷惑性和吸引力，也有激化问题的颠覆性和破坏力。

t: Recent corrective measures in Russia's field of history
zh: 近年来俄罗斯历史领域的系列纠偏举措
paras: Writing in 2016, Wu Enyuan introduces what the article presents as a new trend in Russian historical studies: a series of government measures to correct what Wu describes as a distortion of the national past since the Soviet collapse. The piece is an informational commentary offered "for reference", reporting Russian policy rather than arguing a theoretical case. Its thesis is that Russia's government now treats a shared reading of history as the basis of civic identity and has moved to counter Western "colour revolution" influence in culture and education.

The article begins with the background: Wu cites a 2014 presidential decree on the damage done by the crisis of the 1990s and by Western culture, and describes Western and East European efforts around the 70th anniversary of the Second World War to equate Stalin's system with Nazism. It then lists three sets of measures: a drive to produce a unified national history textbook, the December 2014 decree no. 808 on the principles of state cultural policy, and wider popularisation of history, including training for about 6,000 history teachers. The longest section sets out the "new conception of history" in four areas: the October Revolution, the Soviet role in the Second World War, the evaluation of Soviet history, and attitudes to Stalin.

In Wu's account, the textbook commission headed by Duma chairman Naryshkin, with academician Chubarian reporting to Putin, concluded that the revolutions of 1917 and the civil war can be called a "great revolution" that advanced social progress. Wu reports Putin's rejection of equating Nazism with Stalinism, his defence of the Soviet–German treaty as a way to gain time for rearmament, and his claim that Soviet forces saved East European peoples from destruction. On Soviet history, the commission reportedly settled on viewing the 1930s as one path of modernization with both positive and negative aspects. Wu contrasts this with Gorbachev's wholesale negation, which the article blames for the Soviet collapse. Wu also notes the July 2015 bust of Stalin in the Rzhev district and Culture Minister Medinsky's statement that Stalin must have a place in historical memory.

Wu concludes that these views reflect the mainstream position of the current Russian government, while acknowledging that Russian society still holds differing assessments of Stalin. The article draws no explicit lessons for China beyond offering the material as a point of reference. Read the original if you want a concise, sympathetic Chinese account of Russia's mid-2010s history policy and of how Chinese scholars of the Soviet Union reported it.
quoteEn: It was precisely because Gorbachev wholly negated Soviet history, especially the "Stalin model", that the Soviet Union disintegrated.
quoteZh: 戈尔巴乔夫正是因为全盘否定苏联历史、特别是“斯大林模式”才导致了苏联的解体。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Chinese official and scholarly writing for non-violent, Western-backed regime changes, such as those in Georgia, Ukraine and Kyrgyzstan in the 2000s. It is generally used to warn of external ideological subversion.
Here it refers to the Soviet-era drive for industrialisation and state-planned development, which the article says Russian historians now treat as a path of modernization.

t: The world-historical significance of the Chinese path
zh: 中国道路的世界历史意义
paras: This commentary, first published in the People's Daily in December 2016, asks what the path of socialism with Chinese characteristics (the "Chinese path") means beyond China itself. Wang Mingsheng argues that the path is the necessary road to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the Chinese Dream. In the author's view it also has major world-historical significance, because it breaks the Western monopoly on development models and offers experience that other countries, especially developing ones, can draw on.

The piece is organised under three headings: the path enriches the diversity of routes to modernization; it offers a new model of peaceful development; and it helps developing countries find their own roads. Wang draws on China's post-1949 and post-1978 record, a historical sketch of Western great-power rise and colonial expansion, and quotations from Xi Jinping, Deng Xiaoping and Samuel Huntington.

Wang contends that after decolonisation and the collapse of the Soviet Union, Western discourse hegemony declared liberal democracy the endpoint of history. China's growth, the author says, shows that modernization does not have to mean Westernisation. The article cites the world's second-largest economy, over 700 million people lifted out of poverty and per capita GDP above US$8,000. It describes Western rise as built on violence, colonialism and world wars, and treats the belief that a strong country must seek hegemony as a product of that history. Peaceful development, in Wang's account, is rooted in Chinese culture and is a strategic choice, not a diplomatic expedient. The article further holds that developing countries which copied Western models suffered distorted growth, social conflict and instability, whereas China, which borrowed selectively, succeeded.

Wang concludes that the Chinese path belongs to the world as well as to China. According to the article, it has restored China's international standing and discourse power, and it is an important part of humanity's civilisational achievements and its search for socialism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Chinese commentary in 2016 presented the Chinese path as an alternative to Western development models and as a reference for the Global South.
quoteEn: The Chinese path belongs not only to China but also to the world, and it has major world-historical significance.
quoteZh: 中国道路不仅是中国的，也是世界的，具有重大世界历史意义。

t: Political stability underpins Russia's great-power strength
st: Russia in 2016
zh: 政治稳定支撑俄罗斯大国力量
paras: This short newspaper commentary reviews Russia in 2016. Wang argues that, despite a sluggish economy and falling living standards, political stability and public morale let the country keep up what the author calls an 'inspiring posture of rise'. Wang presents Vladimir Putin as the key to that stability and to Russia's status as a great power.

The article moves from foreign policy to domestic politics, then the economy, and ends with relations with China. It draws on Forbes's ranking of Putin, Russia's role in Syria, the Duma elections, Russian opinion polls, the 'anti-crisis plan' and Russia's 'turn to the East'.

Wang describes Russia as gaining influence in the Middle East while the United States loses ground there, and as holding firm against the United States and NATO, whose Russia policy the author calls confused. At home, the Duma elections are said to have strengthened Putin's political system. United Russia now controls the Duma, and pro-Western and 'in-system' opposition forces have lost support. Wang reads this as rising anti-Western sentiment, nationalism and patriotism, backed by polls showing high approval for Putin. On the economy, the anti-crisis plan is credited with curbing falling output and rising inflation, with agricultural growth and grain exports as a base for stability.

Wang notes that Russia formally adopted a 'turn to the East' policy in 2016 and describes Russia–China relations as entering a new stage, with the Belt and Road Initiative as a platform for cooperation. The author reports Russian opinion that the era of American global dominance is over and that a more democratic and just world order is emerging. The piece closes with open questions and concludes that Russia is consolidating its strategic foundations and building its 'strong-state dream'. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese official newspaper presented Russia's domestic and foreign situation at the end of 2016.
quoteEn: The political strongman Putin is the key to Russia maintaining political stability and displaying the posture of a great power.
quoteZh: 政治强人普京是俄罗斯保持政坛稳定、展示强国姿态的关键。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese foreign-policy and economic initiative announced by Xi Jinping in 2013. It aims to build infrastructure, trade and investment links across Eurasia, Africa and beyond.

t: The turning point of the world order and the chronic ills of twenty-first-century America
zh: 世界秩序的转折点与21世纪美国的沉疴
paras: Writing in early 2017, Yang Guangbin and Lin Xuefei ask what Donald Trump's election and the British Brexit vote of 2016 signify. They reject the common view that economic globalization has reversed, arguing that globalization has lasted some 500 years and what has failed is the neoliberal form it took over the past three decades. Trump's response, in their view, is to treat a twenty-first-century illness with a nineteenth-century prescription: nationalist protectionism, isolationism and white supremacy. His programme is therefore, they say, more deconstructive than constructive and offers no 'third way'.

The article has four sections. The first sets out the content of 'Trumpism': opposition to the establishment, to 'political correctness' and cultural pluralism, and the 'America First' slogan. The second examines neoliberalism's 'three liberalizations' (economic, political and cultural) and their damage to the United States. The third looks back at American history from the founding to the Second World War, drawing on Friedrich List. The fourth considers the unintended results of liberalization and the prospects for a clash between 'two Americas'.

The authors divide the past century of Western thought into three roughly thirty-year phases: laissez-faire liberalism, Keynesianism and neoliberalism. They argue that financial-capital-led globalization hollowed out American manufacturing, widened inequality and turned 'liberal democracy' into 'capitalist democracy'. They contend that Trump's election expresses a conflict between traditional industrial workers and finance capital. Political liberalization, in their account, drained national strength through 'democracy promotion' and colour revolutions. Cultural pluralism, they say, challenged the 'American Creed' and produced a crisis of national identity. They link Trump's agenda to nineteenth-century protectionism, isolationism and white supremacy, including the treatment of Native Americans.

Yang and Lin conclude that liberalization produced results the United States did not intend. Economic and political damage can be repaired, they say, but the cultural 'de-Americanization' is potentially fatal. Because Trump's agenda fits no scheme of the past hundred years, they argue it must be understood against the America of a century earlier. They expect a clash between a nineteenth-century and a twenty-first-century America that may deepen social division, though they leave open how far Trump will go. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic interpretation of Trump's rise through neoliberalism, historical institutionalism and American history.
quoteEn: Treating America's serious twenty-first-century illness with a nineteenth-century prescription, Trump has not opened a 'third way' out of the present predicament; his policy positions are more deconstructive than constructive.
quoteZh: 用19世纪的药方治疗21世纪美国的重病，特朗普并没有为现有困境开辟“第三条道路”，其政策主张更多是解构而非建构式的。

glossary.explanation: A term widely used in Chinese official and academic writing for popular uprisings, such as those in post-Soviet states, which are described as externally promoted attempts at regime change.

Here the market-oriented economic doctrine associated with Reagan and Thatcher (privatization, market liberalization, minimal budgets). The authors also extend it to political and cultural liberalization.
The American norm of avoiding language and practices seen as offensive to minority groups. The authors treat it as the cultural expression of pluralism that Trump opposes.

t: Serious ideological deviations of the CPSU under Gorbachev and their profound lessons
zh: 戈尔巴乔夫时期苏共意识形态的严重偏差及深刻教训
source: Marxist Studies (马克思主义研究), 2016 no. 11
paras: Why did the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) lose control of ideology under Gorbachev, and what follows from that for ruling socialist parties? Tang and Zhao argue that Gorbachev's "humane and democratic socialism", together with "democratization", "openness" (glasnost) and "pluralism", turned reform into a change of direction. In their account, the Party abandoned Marxism's guiding position in the ideological sphere, and this was an important cause of the Party's collapse and the Soviet Union's disintegration.

The article, published in Marxist Studies in 2016, has two parts. The first describes ideological deviation in three areas: the guiding ideology, public opinion and the media, and social culture including foreign relations. The second draws four lessons for socialist countries today. The authors rely on Soviet-era speeches, memoirs by Gorbachev, Ryzhkov and Ligachev, and Chinese and Western secondary studies.

On guiding ideology, the authors argue that abstract humanism, a misplaced theory of "alienation" and political pluralism replaced Marxism. They say this led to the removal of Article 6 of the constitution, multiparty politics, cadre purges and mass resignations from the Party, which the article puts at 4.2 million. On public opinion, they claim that a double standard on press freedom, the Nina Andreyeva affair, the rewriting of Soviet history and the 1990 press law produced historical nihilism and a media hostile to the Party. On culture and external relations, they contend that "returned literature", declassified archives and the destruction of history textbooks caused a crisis of national identity. They also argue that Gorbachev's priority of "universal human values" left the USSR defenceless against Western "peaceful evolution".

The authors draw four lessons. The ruling party must keep its leadership and the direction of reform, and must build socialist democracy step by step while curbing bureaucracy and privilege. Marxism must keep its guiding position, and the Party must firmly hold leadership of ideological work. Ideological work must innovate, including in how it manages the internet and new media. Socialist countries must also stay alert to Western ideological infiltration while drawing on other civilizations' achievements. Read the original if you want to see how Chinese Party scholars in 2016 interpreted the Soviet collapse as an ideological failure and used it to argue for ideological vigilance.
quoteEn: Fundamentally, the Soviet "reform" actively abandoned the guiding position of Marxism in the ideological sphere.
quoteZh: 从根本上看，苏联的“改革”主动放弃了马克思主义在意识形态领域的指导地位

glossary.zh: 人道的民主的社会主义
glossary.pinyin: réndào de mínzhǔ de shèhuì zhǔyì
glossary.explanation: Gorbachev's formula for his reform programme, adopted in the CPSU's 1990 28th Congress document. The authors treat it as a shift from scientific socialism to social democracy.
The Russian glasnost, a Gorbachev-era policy of loosening controls on information and debate. The authors read it as removing limits on criticism of Party history.
A term in Chinese Party discourse for alleged Western strategies of peacefully transforming socialist states through ideological and cultural infiltration.
In Chinese Party usage, a label for views that wholly negate the history and achievements of the revolution and of socialism.
The Party's work in guiding theory, media, propaganda, education and culture, which it regards as a core part of governance.

t: How "money-donor politics" took shape in the United States
zh: “金主政治”是如何形成的
paras: Ni Chunna takes up a question that, the author says, critics of American "money politics" rarely ask: how did the United States fall from its image as a "beacon of democracy" to become a model of "money-donor politics" (jinzhu zhengzhi)? Writing in 2016, after the "Democracy Spring" protests of April that year, Ni argues that campaign finance reform since the 1970s directly drove the change. In a struggle of more than forty years between Congress and the Supreme Court, the Court gradually overturned the limits Congress wrote into law.

The article follows this struggle chronologically. It starts with the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 and its 1974 amendments, passed after Watergate, and the Court's ruling in Buckley v. Valeo (1976). It then covers the rise of "soft money" and the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002, and the later rulings in Citizens United (2010) and McCutcheon (2014). A final section asks why reform failed, looking at the Supreme Court, the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Ni's central claim is that each reform produced a workaround, and each workaround was then validated or widened by the Court. Buckley allowed unlimited independent spending. Soft money, then "527 organisations" and super PACs, followed, and McCutcheon removed the aggregate limit on individual donations. Ni cites figures such as total presidential-election contributions rising from US$114 million in 1976 to US$1.38 billion in 2012, and argues that reform has in effect regressed to the situation before 1970. On the causes of failure, Ni points to three structural factors. First, justices serve for life and are appointed on a cycle unlike the electoral one, and Republican presidents have made far more appointments since the 1970s. Second, political polarisation and the filibuster make it hard for the Senate to reach the 60 votes needed. Third, a polarised, Republican-led House cannot compromise.

Ni concludes that life tenure for justices and congressional polarisation are the key reasons reform failed. Because these problems lie in the constitutional system, the author holds that only major political reform could resolve them, and that the United States will therefore sink deeper into money-donor politics. The article also notes defenders of the Court's rulings, such as Glenn Hubbard, but treats them as a minority view. Read the original if you want a detailed, source-heavy account of US campaign finance litigation and legislation from a Chinese critical perspective.
quoteEn: In this protracted tug-of-war of more than forty years between Congress and the Supreme Court, the legal provisions Congress enacted to regulate campaign finance were gradually overturned by the Supreme Court, ultimately sinking the American electoral system ever deeper into the abyss of "money-donor politics".
quoteZh: 在这场以国会和最高法院为对垒双方的长达40余年的漫长“拉锯战”中，国会制定的规制竞选资金的法律条款逐渐被最高法院推翻，最终导致了美国选举制度在“金主政治”的深渊中越陷越深。

glossary.literal: politics of the golden master / financial backers
glossary.explanation: A Chinese critical label for a political system in which wealthy donors hold decisive influence over candidates and policy. The article applies it to the United States.

t: How should we view the new changes in the Western capitalist world?
zh: 如何看待西方资本主义世界的新变化？
paras: Writing in early 2017, after the British referendum vote to leave the EU and Donald Trump's election as the 45th US president, Ding Yuanhong asks how these changes in the Western capitalist world should be understood. The short commentary argues that only class analysis can reveal their essence and likely course. It also warns against several labels commonly attached to these events.

The piece is organised in three parts. The first treats the referendum and the US election as signs of deep class antagonism between ordinary people and elites. The second examines the claim that a "reverse economic globalisation" is under way. The third considers whether "populism", "isolationism" and "protectionism" accurately describe Trump. Ding draws on US and British figures, including Richard Haass, Alan Greenspan, Barack Obama, Theresa May and Henry Kissinger.

Ding reads the divide as the product of the capitalist system under monopoly capitalism and as a sharpening of internal class struggle. As evidence the author cites a Pew survey (the US middle class falling from 62% of the population in the 1970s to 43%), household debt rising from $9,300 in 1980 to $65,000 in 2015, and the claim that half of American families cannot find $400 in cash. On globalisation, Ding holds that the post-Cold War version was unequal from the start and favoured the rich, multinationals, developed countries and above all the United States. Its problems, in this account, are self-generated, so it is wrong to call recent events "anti-globalisation". On populism, Ding notes the term's origin in nineteenth-century Russian narodnik currents criticised by Plekhanov and Lenin. The author says Western scholars now use it loosely for any opposition to elites. Trump, as a member of the monopoly bourgeoisie who rolled back Obama-era financial regulation to Wall Street's welcome, is not a true populist. Nor, Ding argues, has he abandoned US global hegemony, and protectionism is something Western states have always practised.

Ding concludes that Trump's "America First" rests on an "extreme national egoism", that he cannot resolve a division rooted in the system, and that his promises are limited by that system. The events are said to show a major crisis in Western capitalist society, which Chinese scholars should track closely from a Marxist standpoint. Read the original if you want a short example of how a senior Chinese diplomat applied class analysis to Brexit and Trump's election in 2017.
quoteEn: Only by using the method of class analysis can one grasp the essence of the changes now taking place in the Western capitalist world, understand their inner laws and accurately assess their prospects.
quoteZh: 对于西方资本主义世界正在发生的变化，只有用阶级分析的方法，才能洞悉其实质，掌握其内在规律，准确研判其前景。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist method that explains social and political events through the interests and conflicts of social classes. The article presents it as the only way to understand Western developments.
In the Leninist tradition, the stage of capitalism dominated by large monopolies and finance capital. The article uses it to characterise the contemporary United States and Britain.
Originally the term for the Russian narodnik movement of the nineteenth century. The author contrasts that sense with its current Western use against elite politics.

t: The current state of "new socialism" in Russia and an analysis of its causes
zh: 当前俄罗斯“新社会主义”的现状及其成因分析
paras: Writing in 2016, Chen Airu asks why ideas of "new socialism" and "socialism of the twenty-first century" are slowly returning in Russia, and what this return signals. The article argues that the revival has three layers of cause. The basic cause is the failure of neoliberal capitalist "reform" after 25 years. The main cause is the persistence of the Communist Party and other left-wing parties. The direct causes are Western "double standards" and pressure on Russia, and a "turn to the left" among intellectuals.

The article first sets out the record of post-Soviet capitalism: dependence on energy exports, polarisation of wealth, corruption and public dissatisfaction. It then surveys the programmes and writings of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), A Just Russia and a number of smaller communist and workers' parties. Finally it turns to intellectual life: the All-Russian association of scholars of socialist orientation, the "Socialism after Socialism" seminar, the "New Socialism" website, journals and monographs by authors such as Sulimov, Buzgalin and Slavin. Chen cites sociological data and opinion polls from the Levada Center, among other sources.

Chen's reasoning begins with the data. According to the article, 110 oligarchs controlled 35% of national wealth in 2014, and polls show that a plurality of Russians judge the 1990s reforms harmful. Chen then reports the CPRF leader Gennady Zyuganov's 2014 characterisation of Russian capitalism as reactionary, parasitic, oligarchic and comprador. In Chen's reading, left parties kept the socialist idea alive by pursuing justice in the line of Marx, Lenin and Stalin; without them the revival would not have appeared. Chen adds that the West's treatment of Russia, seen in the Ukraine crisis, pushed intellectuals to rethink capitalism, even though the 2016 Duma election still favoured United Russia because voters put territorial integrity first.

Chen concludes that the Russian trend ties the search for Russia's own path to the future direction of human society. The author holds that the left parties' and scholars' new interpretations of socialism deserve study as "stones from other hills" and could benefit the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The text is a sympathetic reading of Russian left-wing sources rather than an independent survey of Russian opinion. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist account of the Russian left and intellectual debate on socialism after 1991, with its sources and cited Russian authors.
quoteEn: The failure of Russia's neoliberal capitalist "reform" path is the fundamental cause of the slow return of the "new socialism" and "twenty-first-century socialism" currents in contemporary Russia.
quoteZh: 俄罗斯新自由资本主义“改革”路径失败是当代俄罗斯“新社会主义”“21世纪社会主义”思潮缓慢回潮的根本原因。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's current path and system, formulated from the reform era onward. Here the article suggests Russian debates may inform its development.

A label used by Russian left parties and scholars for renewed conceptions of socialism after the Soviet collapse, distinguishing them from Soviet-era understandings. It echoes a phrase also used in Latin America.
A term used by Russian parties such as A Just Russia and by scholars for post-Soviet interpretations of socialism. The article treats it as a social trend.
A Chinese idiom meaning that outside experience can help one improve one's own work. The author uses it to describe the value of Russian rethinking for China.

t: Fidel Castro's thought on intra-Party supervision in the Communist Party of Cuba and its lessons
zh: 古巴共产党党内监督思想及其启示
paras: This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in February 2017, asks what Fidel Castro's approach to supervision inside the Communist Party of Cuba consists of and what it offers the Communist Party of China. Tang argues that Castro, drawing on Marxism-Leninism and Cuban practice, developed a distinctive body of thought on intra-Party supervision, and that it carries lessons for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

The article sets out Castro's thought under three headings: ideological supervision, organisational supervision and institutional supervision. A final section draws three lessons for the Chinese Party.

On ideology, Tang reports that Castro treated ideas as the most powerful weapon against US ideological infiltration and domestic reactionary forces. He armed the Party with Marxism-Leninism and the thought of José Martí, screened new members for political consciousness, and set up Party schools for regular education. On organisation, Tang describes collective leadership with individual responsibility, internal democracy, differentiated scrutiny of leading cadres (stricter for higher rank), criticism and self-criticism, and grassroots branches as the front line of supervision. On institutions, Tang cites five Party statutes, regulations on grassroots organisations, admission and punishment, supervisory and appeals bodies, and a code of ethics for state cadres.

Tang concludes that the Chinese Party should make ideological supervision more thorough, raising the threshold for new members and enriching Party school training. It should also make organisational supervision more targeted, focusing on the "critical few" and improving criticism and self-criticism, and make institutional supervision more systematic by closing gaps in Party regulations built on the Party constitution. Read the original if you want a brief, officially aligned account of how Cuban Party supervision is presented to Chinese readers and how it is tied to Chinese Party-building debates in 2017.
quoteEn: The Party should further improve the intra-Party supervision system built on the Party constitution, classify the specific content of supervision, and build by category a targeted and practical body of supervisory regulations, so as to prevent gaps and loopholes in the system.
quoteZh: 要进一步完善以党章为基础的党内监督制度体系，对党内监督的具体内容进行归类，按类构建起针对性与实用性强的党内监督法规条例体系，有效预防党内监督存在制度空缺与漏洞。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan of the Xi Jinping leadership, prominent since about 2014, for strengthening discipline, supervision and anti-corruption work within the Communist Party of China.
A term for leading cadres, especially senior officials, whom Chinese Party discourse treats as the main targets of supervision because of their decision-making power.
A Leninist and Maoist method of Party life in which members openly criticise others and examine their own faults, presented as a means of internal supervision.

t: The positioning of the South African Communist Party's political strategy
zh: 南非共产党政治战略的定位
paras: This short commentary, published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 23 February 2017, asks how the South African Communist Party (SACP) positions itself politically after the 2008 financial crisis. Zheng distinguishes strategy from tactics. In Zheng's account, the SACP's strategy rests on the South African working class as its core support, while its tactics rely on taking part in government through the "tripartite governing alliance" with the African National Congress (ANC) and the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU).

The article has three parts. It first looks at the revisions to the Party constitution adopted at the 13th National Congress in July 2012. It then discusses how the SACP has consolidated the alliance since 1994 while keeping its independence. Finally, it sets out the Party's core policy agenda since the crisis, which Zheng groups under three heads: countering the crisis, sustainable development and environmental justice, and the fight against corruption.

Zheng reports that the new constitution stresses uniting the different strata of a working class that the SACP sees as increasingly divided, from skilled full-time workers to casual, informal and structurally unemployed ones. It also reaffirms democratic centralism and adds clauses on the Young Communist League and on neighbourhood ("branch") organisation. Within the alliance the ANC leads and the SACP acts as bearer of advanced ideas. Zheng says the SACP still voices criticism when decisions are mistaken, and cites its 2008 policy conference aim of becoming a party with decision-making power. On policy, Zheng reports that the SACP's five-year programme (2012–2017) targets monopoly finance and mining capital, calls for a state-led industrial policy and wants more social control of financial institutions. It also calls for renewable energy, land reform and public transport. It treats corruption as a threat to democracy, and Zheng cites a fall in South Africa's Transparency International ranking from 38th in 2001 to 72nd in 2013.

Zheng concludes that the 2008 crisis confirmed the SACP's view that capitalism is in a deep, systemic crisis, and this gave the Party an opening. Zheng cautions, however, that monopoly capital still controls key sectors and that the constitutional order and multiparty competition remain unchanged. In this reading the SACP must therefore work through the alliance, and the road to socialism will be long. Zheng judges that the Party has still raised its standing and influence. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese academic overview of the SACP's strategy, alliance politics and post-2008 policy priorities.
quoteEn: Of these, political strategy is the political foundation of the SACP's presence on the South African political stage, while political tactics are the political support through which it plays its role.
quoteZh: 其中，政治战略是南非共存在于南非政治舞台的政治基础，而政治策略是南非共发挥作用的政治依托。

glossary.explanation: The alliance of the ANC, the SACP and COSATU, which has underpinned the post-apartheid government in South Africa since 1994. The SACP and COSATU do not stand separately in elections but support the ANC.
A Leninist organisational principle combining discussion with binding unity of action, under which lower party bodies are subordinate to higher ones.

t: The 21st century is the century of the revival of world socialism
zh: 21世纪是世界社会主义复兴的世纪
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 14 March 2017
paras: Writing in March 2017, Lü Weizhou takes up the state of world socialism a quarter-century after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The author argues that, after a low point at the end of the twentieth century and nearly thirty years of recovery and adjustment, socialism is gradually reviving worldwide. Lü presents "the 21st century is the century of the revival of world socialism" as a growing consensus.

The short commentary opens with a sketch of socialism's history since 1516, then surveys five signs of revival: reforms in the remaining socialist states, the recovery of communist parties in capitalist countries, a variety of socialist currents, expanding contacts among socialist forces, and the role of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It closes with the obstacles ahead.

Lü treats the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics as the marker of a new upswing and the starting point of full revival, because it has shifted a badly unbalanced balance of forces between socialism and capitalism. Vietnam, Cuba and Laos held Party congresses in 2016, and the author cites their institutional strengths in crisis response and resource allocation. In capitalist countries, Lü reports over 120 communist parties with more than 8 million members, and electoral results in Greece, Cyprus and Japan. The author also lists market socialism, democratic socialism, eco-socialism and Latin American "21st-century socialism", and the European Left and international forums.

Lü cautions that the path is not smooth: capital still holds the offensive, class consciousness is uneven, ideological disunity persists, and populism is eroding the left's base. The author calls on left forces, communist parties included, to build strength, improve organization and innovate in their activities. Read the original if you want a brief, official-academic Chinese overview of how world socialism was assessed in 2017.
quoteEn: In a sense, the growing vitality of the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics has greatly encouraged foreign socialist and left-wing forces, and is both a sign of world socialism rising again and the starting point of its full revival.
quoteZh: 从某种意义上说,中国特色社会主义道路、理论、制度和文化活力的不断彰显,极大地鼓舞了国外社会主义及左翼力量的发展,是世界社会主义重新走向高潮的标志,也是世界社会主义实现全面振兴的起点。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path of socialist development since reform and opening up, combining Party leadership, a socialist system and a market-oriented economy.

t: The historical role of Mikhail Gorbachev
zh: 米·戈尔巴乔夫的历史角色
paras: This text is a Chinese translation of an article by the Russian author Vladimir Shveda (弗·施韦德). It asks how Mikhail Gorbachev's conduct as General Secretary and Soviet president should be judged. Shveda argues that his refusal to carry out the constitutional duties of the presidency, and his political deals with Western powers to "hand over" the USSR, were not stupidity but crime, and that he should face legal sanction. The piece opens with the February 2016 call by the Russian filmmaker Nikita Mikhalkov for the state to declare Gorbachev and Yeltsin criminals.

The article proceeds through five thematic sections: the Rust landing and the dissolution of the Warsaw Pact; Gorbachev's one-to-one talks with Western leaders; his violations of the Soviet constitution; his handling of ethnic conflicts in Sumgait, Tbilisi, Baku and Vilnius; and the Belovezha meeting of December 1991. Shveda draws on testimony from generals, KGB officials and Party figures, on Gorbachev's own interviews with Western press, and on the author's personal experience in Lithuania. Gorbachev's 0.51% vote in the 1996 presidential election is cited as popular verdict.

Shveda's central move is to treat each episode as a breach of specific constitutional articles obliging the president to guarantee sovereignty, territorial integrity, Soviet law and citizens' rights. On this reading, Gorbachev engineered the dismissal of military opponents after the Rust flight, accepted a small payment of 14 billion marks for the withdrawal from East Germany, and let Russia's 1990 sovereignty declaration pass unchallenged. He also failed to protect Soviet citizens in Lithuania and allegedly stalled a 1991 prosecutor's criminal case against him. A second move is the claim of secrecy: Gorbachev held private English-language talks at Reykjavik and Malta without records, and Shveda cites Kryuchkov and Gorbachev's own 1993 remarks as evidence of concessions made there.

Shveda concludes that Gorbachev built a system of personal power and then, by declining to order action against the Belovezha plotters despite the 1991 referendum result, let the state vanish, which in the author's words removed any need to answer for his deeds. The author dismisses Gorbachev as a permanent political failure who should await trial rather than comment on politics. Read the original if you want a stridently critical Russian account of Gorbachev, with its cited testimony and constitutional argument, as an example of how the Soviet collapse is interpreted in World Socialism Studies.
quoteEn: Gorbachev's conduct of this kind should not be interpreted as stupidity but as crime: the Soviet president failed to discharge properly his constitutional duty to guarantee the nation's security.
quoteZh: 戈尔巴乔夫的类似行为，不应解释为愚蠢，而是犯罪，即苏联总统未能以应有的方式履行其保障国家安全的宪法职责

t: The current international financial crisis as a systemic and total crisis of the contemporary imperialist economic system
zh: 当今国际金融危机是当代帝国主义经济体系性、总体性危机
paras: Writing in 2017, Luan Wenlian asks what the financial crisis that began in 2008 reveals about contemporary capitalism. The article argues that it is not merely a US crisis or a financial one, but a systemic and total crisis of contemporary imperialism. In Luan's account, capitalism has since the 1970s and 1980s entered a new stage dominated by fictitious financial capital and financial monopoly.

The article first sets out how the basic economic law of capitalism has changed form: from surplus-value production under free competition, to the law of monopoly profit, to extra monopoly profit and financial plunder under financialisation. It then covers the essential features of financial monopoly, new methods of exploitation and plunder, the global exploitation model built on financial hegemony, and the deepening of the gap between rich and poor.

Luan contends that financialisation leaves the capital–labour relation intact while shifting profit-making from production to circulation and speculation. Financial capital, the article says, now draws profit from workers' wages through housing credit, insurance, pension and health schemes, so that exploitation extends to consumption and to future generations. Internationally, developed countries relocate low-end manufacturing and keep core technology, intellectual property and the dollar's hegemony. After the dollar's break with gold in 1971, Luan holds, it was issued against fictitious capital and needs extra-economic power to sustain it. At home, income distribution tilts towards financial capital and a rentier stratum of shareholders and senior managers; Luan cites figures that put the fictitious part of Western economies at over 70 per cent and say multinationals control 40 per cent of world production.

Luan concludes that financialised capitalism is an unstable, increasingly polarised system in which financial, economic and currency crises will keep recurring. The article describes it as hostile to historical development and as sharpening imperialism's decay, parasitism and moribundity, and as having entered a period of decline since 2008. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Marxist political economy interprets financialisation and the 2008 crisis through the theory of monopoly capital and imperialism.
quoteEn: This is in fact a systemic and total crisis of contemporary imperialism.
quoteZh: 这实际上是当代帝国主义的体系性和总体性危机。

t: The current American debate on "socialism" and reflections on it
zh: 当前美国的“社会主义”论争及其思考
paras: Yu Haiqing asks what the revival of the word "socialism" in the United States since late 2015 amounts to. The occasion was Bernie Sanders's advocacy of "democratic socialism" and a "political revolution" in the Democratic primary. Yu argues that the opposing camps in the ensuing debate, mainstream opinion and the Communist Party USA (CPUSA), reflect in the end the developmental predicament of capitalism as it appears in real politics.

The article has three parts. The first sets out four mainstream readings of socialism. The second, the longest, reports a debate launched in January 2016 on the CPUSA's website People's World, opened by an article by Susan Webb. The third offers Yu's own reflections. Contributors discussed include John Bachtell, Rick Nagin, Pat Fry, Carl Davidson, Joel Wendland, Bill Fletcher and Emile Schepers.

In Yu's account, mainstream commentators equate socialism with nationalisation, the welfare state (a view held, by a poll the article cites, by 41 per cent of Americans), central planning, or the Soviet record. The CPUSA writers reject these equations. They define socialism as working-class power in a transitional class society with a mixed economy, and they add ecological, anti-racist, anti-sexist and human-rights dimensions. They also stress open-ended, varied paths and a long process of struggle. Wendland proposes "open-source socialism".
