Yu's own reflections run as follows. Sanders's programme and similar movements, such as the Trump phenomenon, Corbyn and Syriza, are reactions to an "organic crisis" of capitalism after 2008. Yu notes that these "socialisms" differ greatly from Marxist socialism, since they omit class relations and the replacement of the system, and Sanders never proposed abolishing private property. Communists' task is therefore to clarify socialism's meaning and to steer anti-capitalist movements onto a socialist track. Yu notes that the CPUSA's later support for Clinton and opposition to Trump drew doubts, and cites Nancy Fraser's call for a new left alliance. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist survey of how the CPUSA framed socialism during the 2016 US election cycle.
quoteEn: These many varieties of "socialism" differ greatly from Marxist socialism.
quoteZh: 这些形形色色的“社会主义”，与马克思主义的社会主义区别很大。

t: Fidel Castro's outstanding contributions to Cuba and to the development of world socialism
zh: 卡斯特罗对古巴和世界社会主义发展的卓越贡献
paras: Written after Fidel Castro's death on 25 November 2016, this article assesses his historical record. Mao Xianglin argues that Castro's contribution falls into three parts: his achievements for the Cuban people, the regional significance of the Cuban Revolution for Latin America, and his theoretical contribution to the development of world socialism.

The article is organised in three sections. The first lists four achievements within Cuba and illustrates Castro's personal conduct with episodes from his life. The second sets out four reasons why the revolution mattered internationally. The third surveys eleven strands of Castro's thought, from national independence to resistance to "peaceful evolution".

In Mao's account, the revolution carried out the most thorough social transformation in Cuban history: national independence, the end of class exploitation, a reorganised Communist Party (named as such in 1965) and a socialist system declared in 1961. Mao presents the survival of that system through the 1960s excesses, the mid-1980s "rectification" campaign and the crisis after Soviet aid ended as evidence of its vitality. Castro is portrayed as a model revolutionary who trusted the masses, opposed a personality cult, practised self-criticism, was strict with relatives and friends, and handed over office to Raúl Castro. Regionally, Mao calls the revolution the most thorough anti-dictatorship and anti-imperialist revolution in Latin America and the first to move from national-democratic struggle to socialism. Cuba's survival is also said to refute the claim that socialism suits only Eastern cultures. Mao holds that Castro upheld scientific socialism while adapting it to Cuban conditions, citing four Party-wide theoretical debates. Among his ideas Mao lists: globalisation as a historical law while neoliberal globalisation is rejected, the shaping of a "new man", Party and army building, free universal education and healthcare, and successful resistance to US efforts at "peaceful evolution".

Mao concludes that Cuba, one of five existing socialist states, offers experience in localising socialism that is useful to others, and that this owes much to Castro. His achievements, the article says, "will be recorded in history for ever". Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly and officially sympathetic assessment of Castro and of Cuban socialism, including its checklist of his ideas on the Party, education, health and anti-imperialism.
quoteEn: Over decades of leadership, Castro localised the theory of scientific socialism, continually explored and summed up lessons from revolutionary practice, put forward a series of brilliant ideas, and made outstanding contributions to enriching and developing Marxist scientific socialism.
quoteZh: 卡斯特罗在数十年的领导工作中，将科学社会主义理论本土化，从革命的实践中不断探索和总结，提出了一系列光辉的思想，为丰富和发展马克思主义的科学社会主义理论做出了卓越的贡献。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese Party discourse for alleged Western efforts to undermine socialist systems through ideological, cultural and political infiltration rather than force. Here the author applies it to US policy towards Cuba.
Adapting socialist theory and institutions to a country's own national conditions. The author uses it for Cuba in a way parallel to the Chinese idea of adapting Marxism to local conditions.
A campaign in Cuba in the mid-1980s to correct perceived flaws of the institutionalised system set up in the 1970s.
The idea of a person with socialist consciousness who rejects private-ownership attitudes. It is associated with Cuban revolutionary thought, including Che Guevara and Castro.

t: The Brexit referendum marks the beginning of the exhaustion of Western political and economic institutions
zh: 英国脱欧公投标志着西方政治经济体制开始衰竭
paras: Writing in 2017 about the 2016 British referendum on leaving the European Union, Ma Zhongcheng argues that it was essentially a depoliticised vote manipulated by capital, in which the mass media shaped public opinion while the political parties stayed ambiguous. Ma presents Brexit as a serious crisis of the global neoliberal order formed since the 1980s, a direct product of the global financial and economic crisis since 2007, and a desperate struggle of Thatcherism. In Ma's view it shows the comprehensive exhaustion of Western capitalist political institutions.

The article has four sections. The first examines how parties have become media-driven and how voting has become alienated. The second treats the referendum as a product of monopoly capital's shifting of social contradictions. The third traces the conflict between sterling and the dollar on one side and the euro on the other, using the EU financial transaction tax. The fourth considers the end of Gaullism and the geopolitical setting, drawing on Churchill, de Gaulle, Sarkozy, George Soros and Goldman Sachs.

Ma argues first that voting has been reduced to product marketing, citing the 1960 Kennedy–Nixon debates and Baran and Sweezy on advertising. Issues that matter to ordinary people, such as workers' rights and corporate taxation, were screened out, and many Leave voters reportedly regretted their choice. Second, Ma contends that after 2007 mainstream parties responded with further neoliberal austerity, and that the Conservatives and UKIP blamed the EU and immigrants to disguise class conflict. Third, Ma claims that British and American finance capital opposed EU regulation and the financial transaction tax, and that the EU, lacking unified political will, may be divided and defeated.

Ma concludes that a wave of exits would leave the EU an empty shell and produce the Atlantic community dependent on the United States that de Gaulle feared, which Ma sees as a setback for multipolarity and harmful to European workers and bourgeoisies alike. Ma holds that Europe's difficulties stem from adopting the Anglo-American model since the 1980s, after three decades of a mixed economy with state control of capital. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist reading of Brexit that links media, finance capital and transatlantic geopolitics.
quoteEn: The Brexit referendum was in essence a depoliticised political referendum manipulated by capital.
quoteZh: 此次英国脱欧公投本质上是一场由资本操纵的、去政治化的政治公投。

glossary.explanation: The political line associated with Charles de Gaulle, stressing French independence, a strong state and resistance to US hegemony. The article treats it as the guiding tradition behind European unity and as now largely ended.
The free-market policy programme of British prime minister Margaret Thatcher. The article treats Brexit as its last struggle.

t: The world system of financial imperialism will ultimately collapse
zh: 金融帝国主义世界体系终将走向崩溃
paras: Does the world system that finance capital has built since the 1980s and 1990s have a future? Zhang Quanjing answers that this "world system of financial imperialism" has not yet collapsed, but that its eventual collapse is an irreversible trend. The article rests this claim on what it calls the basic laws of social and historical development.

The article is a short theoretical essay in three parts. The first treats finance capital's control of the world system as the core of the age of financial imperialism. The second argues that parasitism and decay are the system's fundamental attributes. The third examines how the 2008 financial crisis and rising international economic conflict have sped up its decline. Zhang draws on Lenin's writing on imperialism, Engels on American politics, Madison, Thomas Piketty, the Japanese scholar Iwao Nakatani and figures on US election spending.

Zhang's central move is to treat financial imperialism as the current form of monopoly capitalism, in which the basic contradiction between socialised production and private ownership of the means of production remains unchanged. Following Lenin, the author holds that monopoly gives rise to finance capital through the fusion of banks and industry, and that the postwar Bretton Woods order under US leadership consolidated a system centred on finance capital. The author describes parasitism as control of the global economy by multinationals and developed countries, together with widening inequality, and describes decay as the manipulation of democracy by interest groups, citing 2012 US election spending of over 6 billion dollars. The 2008 crisis is attributed to the internationalisation of finance capital, US monetary policy and debt-fuelled consumption, and intensifying conflict among developed economies and between them and emerging economies such as China, India and Brazil. Zhang cites the rise in trade-remedy cases against China as evidence of that last conflict.

Zhang concludes that Marxist dialectics requires looking past the appearance of financial imperialism to its essence. The author calls on readers to remember that imperialism's reactionary nature never changes, especially when it appears in a friendly guise, and that it is bound to perish. The author also urges learning to struggle against it and affirms confidence in the victory of socialism and communism. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Chinese Marxist author applies Lenin's theory of imperialism to the post-2008 world economy.
quoteEn: The world system of financial imperialism has not yet collapsed, but the trend that it will eventually collapse is irreversible.
quoteZh: 金融帝国主义世界体系虽然还没有崩溃,但它终将走向崩溃这一趋势是不可逆转的。

t: The death of neoliberalism and the political crisis of the West
zh: 新自由主义的死亡与西方政治危机
paras: This is a Chinese translation of a commentary by the British writer Martin Jacques, first published in The Guardian in August 2016. Jacques argues that the 2007–2008 financial crisis began a deeper political crisis in the West, and that neoliberalism, though still dominant in politics and ideas, is dying. In his account, Brexit and the rise of Donald Trump are symptoms of this crisis. The Chinese journal's editors added a note written after Trump's election victory in November 2016.

The article moves from the crisis and the bailout of the banks to the origins of neoliberalism under Reagan and Thatcher in the late 1970s. It then covers rising inequality in the United States and Britain, the Brexit referendum, and the shifting attitudes of economists and political parties. The last third deals with Trump's programme of economic nationalism and foreign policy, and what it might mean for the United States.

Jacques makes three main moves. First, he holds that neoliberalism tilted resources towards capital and away from labour through deregulation, secretly negotiated trade deals such as the TPP and TTIP, and pressure on trade unions. He cites figures on stagnant or falling real incomes since the 1970s and notes that growth was twice as fast in the Keynesian era. Second, he reads the 'populist' revolts, including Brexit, Trump and Bernie Sanders, as the return of class to politics. He cautions that this is not the same as a labour movement and that working-class politics is unpredictable. Third, he treats Trump as a right-wing populist who breaks with both neoliberal globalization and the postwar foreign-policy consensus. Jacques also warns that a Trump presidency could bring authoritarian abuses, deep social division and a new era of protectionism.

Jacques concludes that the neoliberal era is ending, as social democracy did in the 1970s, even though it has not yet died. He notes that prominent economists such as Stiglitz, Krugman and Piketty, and even former believers such as Lawrence Summers, now criticise it. In his view, British media and political elites, including Labour and the Conservatives, lag behind. He expects resistance to 'hyper-globalization' to continue whether or not Trump wins. Read the original if you want a Western left-leaning interpretation of Brexit and Trump as products of neoliberal inequality, as a Chinese journal presented it in 2017.
quoteEn: We are witnessing the end of the neoliberal era: like social democracy in the 1970s, neoliberalism has entered decline and its end, and although it is not yet dead, it is barely alive.
quoteZh: 我们正在见证新自由主义时代的结束，正像20世纪70年代的社会民主主义一样，新自由主义已步入衰败终结中，但它还没有死，尽管已经奄奄一息了。

t: The South African Communist Party after the collapse of Soviet socialist power
zh: 苏联社会主义政权解体背景下的南非共产党
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by the South African scholar Gregory F. Houston (rendered in Chinese as 格里高利·F·休斯顿). It asks why socialism in South Africa has lasted more than a century and why the South African Communist Party (SACP) has survived the end of Soviet socialist power. Houston argues that the party's endurance rests on its historical alliance with the governing African National Congress (ANC), its record in the liberation struggle and wide popular support for socialism. He presents the SACP as one of the few communist parties worldwide that is allied with, or part of, a governing party.

The article is organised chronologically in five sections. It traces the origins of socialism among white immigrant miners after the 1886 Witwatersrand gold discovery and the founding of the Communist Party of South Africa in 1921. It then covers the party's relations with the ANC, with the Soviet Union and with the People's Republic of China, the effects of the Soviet and East European collapse, and the SACP's history since 1994. It ends with the party's present international orientation.

Houston's central line is that the SACP-ANC bond has deep roots. He cites the 1928 Comintern resolution on a 'native republic', which called for an alliance between the Communist Party and the national liberation movement. He also cites the ban on the party under the 1950 Suppression of Communism Act, which pushed the two organisations together again after about twenty years of discord, and the party's role in the armed struggle through Umkhonto we Sizwe. After 1990, he reports, about half of the SACP's Central Committee resigned and communists suffered a crisis of confidence in socialism's future. Even so, membership rose to 220,000 by 2015. Tensions with the ANC over the neoliberal GEAR framework in the Mandela era led many to see the party's role in the tripartite alliance as shrinking, though its leaders still sat in the ANC executive and in Zuma's cabinet.

Houston concludes that the SACP remains one of the few communist parties still gaining members, and that its ANC link gives it a way to influence government policy. He reports that the party sees its task as promoting international working-class solidarity and unity between workers and the urban and rural poor. It has built links through the African Left Network Forum and the São Paulo Forum, and has a bilateral agreement with the Communist Party of China providing for annual high-level delegation exchanges. Read the original if you want a historical overview of the SACP, its ties with the ANC, Moscow and Beijing, and its international outreach, as presented by a South African author in a Chinese journal.
quoteEn: Socialism has existed in South Africa for more than 100 years, and it still flourishes today!
quoteZh: 社会主义在南非已经存在了100多年，现在依然繁荣！

t: The historical evolution of socialist currents in Europe in the second half of the twentieth century
zh: 20世纪下半叶社会主义流派在欧洲的历史演进
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehuizhuyi), 2016 no. 3
paras: Lü Weizhou asks how socialist currents in Europe developed between the end of the Second World War and the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The article argues that the victory over fascism opened new space for socialism, and that the period saw both the expansion of older currents and the emergence of new ones. In Lü's account, world socialism became diverse, and European currents broke through geographical limits and moved from theory into practice.

The article is organised in two parts. The first examines three older currents that grew after 1945: democratic socialism and the social-democratic parties, market socialism, and Trotskyist socialism. The second turns to newer currents, briefly listing post-industrial socialism and feminist socialism, and then focusing on Eurocommunism and eco-socialism, which Lü regards as the most distinctly European and influential.

On democratic socialism, Lü traces the rebuilt Socialist International (1951) and its extension to the Third World, so that by 1983 it was a global body. Lü credits social-democratic governments with welfare and workers' participation, but holds that their basic positions differ essentially from those of communist parties committed to scientific socialism, and describes the International's Cold War anticommunism and its later strategy toward Eastern Europe. Market socialism is presented through Western models (Ward, Vanek, Nove) and Eastern European ones (Liberman, Brus, Sik, Kornai, Kardelj), with practical reforms in Yugoslavia and Hungary that Lü says ended in capitalist markets. Eurocommunism, centred on the Italian, Spanish and French parties, is described as a response to changes in Western capitalism and to flaws of the Soviet model, advocating a democratic, multiparty road to socialism. Eco-socialism arose from the green movement and shaped the programmes of other parties.

Lü concludes that the earlier pattern of 'one centre, one road, one model' in the international communist movement was broken. European socialist currents, in the author's view, therefore spread worldwide and increasingly tried to put their ideas into practice, which Lü credits with notable achievements for the socialist movement. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-academic survey of the main European socialist currents of 1945–1989, including how they are characterised and the thinkers associated with each.
quoteEn: In the second half of the twentieth century, the pattern of 'one centre, one road, one model' in the international communist movement was broken, and world socialism developed in diverse ways.
quoteZh: 20 世纪下半叶，国际共产主义运动中“一个中心”、“一条道路”、“一种模式”的局面被打破，世界社会主义呈现出多样化发展的态势。

glossary.explanation: The ideology of social-democratic parties and the Socialist International, favouring gradual reform within parliamentary democracy. Chinese scholarship usually distinguishes it sharply from scientific socialism.

A family of theories and reforms that seek to combine public ownership or worker self-management with market mechanisms. The article links it to debates on economic calculation and to reforms in Yugoslavia and Hungary.
A current of the 1970s in the Western European communist parties, chiefly Italian, Spanish and French, that stressed independence from Moscow and a democratic, multiparty road to socialism.
A current that blames capitalism for ecological crisis and seeks a socialist society in ecological balance. The article ties it to the green movement and green parties.
The term for the socialism founded by Marx and Engels, used in Chinese discourse as the standard against which other socialist currents are compared.

t: Frontier issues in recent research on the Soviet and East European upheavals
zh: 近年来苏东剧变研究中的前沿问题
source: Scientific Socialism (科学社会主义), 2016 no. 5
paras: Writing 25 years after the Soviet and East European upheavals, Li Ruiqin surveys recent Chinese scholarship on the subject. The review argues that research has become deeper, more detailed and more far-sighted, and that its basic purpose is to serve the ruling Party's building and socialism with Chinese characteristics. It identifies five areas it regards as the research frontier.

The five clusters are: the link between the lessons of the collapse and a country's fate; the rise of historical nihilism and other erroneous currents under Gorbachev; Russia's reassessment of Soviet history and its history textbooks; research on Marxism and socialism in present-day Russia; and the study of the upheavals in connection with socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li summarises studies in each area, often by describing what unnamed 'scholars' conclude, and draws on works edited by Li Shenming as well as Russian and Chinese reactions to them.

On causes, the review reports findings that Gorbachev's 'democratic, humane socialism' was the direct and main cause, and that historical nihilism served as its ideological tool. Other studies cited trace the collapse to the Soviet party's weak internal construction, formalism, bureaucracy and privilege, and ideological disorder, which explain why ordinary members did not defend the party. The review then describes Putin-era Russian efforts as it presents them: patriotic education programmes, a 2016 unified history textbook drawn up under presidential instruction, and a rejection of nihilism about the Soviet past. It also notes that Marxist methods and 'new socialist' currents persist in Russia, though socialist parties lack power.

Li concludes that the lessons point to maintaining Marxism's leading position in ideology, advancing inner-Party democracy and tying core socialist values to popular interests. The review also reports scholars' view that the central lesson for China is to reform in good time rather than refuse, delay or patch up reforms. It says the study of the upheavals remains a major long-term topic for the international communist movement. Read the original if you want a guide to the themes and works that Chinese Party-affiliated scholars treated as central to Soviet-collapse research around 2016.
quoteEn: Research on the Soviet and East European upheavals is a major long-term subject for the international communist movement, and the upheavals remain a warning close at hand for the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
quoteZh: 苏东剧变问题研究是国际共产主义运动事业长久的重大课题，苏东剧变也始终是中国特色社会主义事业的殷鉴不远。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese Party discourse for views that negate the Party's or socialism's historical record. It is used here for the denigration of Soviet history under Gorbachev.
The official name for China's current system and path, associated with reform and opening up since 1978.

glossary.literal: drastic change in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
glossary.explanation: The standard Chinese term for the collapse of ruling communist parties and the Soviet Union around 1989–1991.

t: World socialism in 2016: development and observations
zh: 2016世界社会主义发展与观察
source: China Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 29 December 2016
paras: Writing at the end of 2016 in the China Social Sciences Today, Cui Guitian offers a year-end survey of world socialism. The author's thesis is that 2016 was an eventful year in which socialism drew continued attention amid Western crises, the world communist movement kept recovering from its low point, and socialism developed in diverse forms, while the overall environment remained harsh.

The article is organised in four sections: the rising political profile of socialism; the movement's difficult progress among ruling parties, Western, post-socialist and developing-world communist parties; the variety of socialist currents; and the continuing difficulties. It moves through Vietnam, Cuba, Laos and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, then communist parties in France, Greece, Cyprus, the United States, Japan, Russia, the Czech lands, India, Nepal, South Africa and Brazil. It also covers social democrats, Latin American new left and Green parties.

Cui argues that the 2008 financial crisis showed that capitalism's basic contradictions remain unresolved. In the author's account, the 2016 Brexit vote, Donald Trump's election and the Italian referendum produced a "political tornado" that exposed capitalism's defects, while Western promotion of "universal values" and neo-liberalism brought new disorder. Cui also points to closer cooperation among communist and workers' parties, such as the 18th international meeting in Hanoi, and to the author's view that socialism with Chinese characteristics, through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, has advanced world socialism. The article reports party membership and vote figures, including growth in the South African and Brazilian parties and losses for the Russian party. Cui names three main troubles: difficulties for ruling and non-ruling communist parties, the rightward drift of social democratic parties, and setbacks for the Latin American left.

Cui concludes that world socialism is moving forward in a broader trend of recovery despite pressures. The author calls for firm socialist conviction, a strategic and tolerant attitude towards the diversity of socialisms, and, on the basis of principle, closer exchanges among socialist forces to deepen mutual understanding. Read the original if you want a compact, data-rich overview of how a Chinese scholar of contemporary socialism assessed the state of communist and left parties worldwide at the end of 2016.
quoteEn: World socialism is currently advancing within a broad trend of recovery and flourishing; although it still faces many challenges and pressures, we must still hold firmly to socialist faith and ideals.
quoteZh: 当前世界社会主义正在复苏繁荣的大势下前进，虽然世界社会主义发展仍然面临诸多的挑战和压力，但我们依然要坚定社会主义信念和理想

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping's leadership since 2012, covering anti-corruption campaigns and tighter Party discipline and organisation.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path of combining Marxism with China's conditions, in use since the 1980s.

t: The proposal of the principle of "consultation and consensus"
st: An important contribution of the Communist Party of China to the development of the international communist movement
zh: “协商一致”原则的提出
zhSub: 中国共产党对国际共运发展的一个重要贡献
paras: How should communist parties settle disagreements when none of them has authority over the others? Nie Yunlin argues that the Communist Party of China (CPC) under Mao Zedong answered this during the serious divisions of the 1950s and 1960s by proposing "consultation and consensus" (xieshang yizhi). In Nie's account, this was an important CPC contribution to unity and cooperation in the international communist movement.

The article moves in four steps. It first narrates the 1957 Moscow conference of ruling communist and workers' parties and the drafting of the Moscow Declaration. It then turns to Deng Xiaoping's three trips to Moscow in 1960, culminating in the 81-party meeting. A third section sets out the content of the principle, and a fourth assesses its significance, drawing on the First, Second and Third Internationals and on the present-day International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties.

Nie reads the principle as having four parts. Its nature is democratic persuasion rather than coercion. Its procedure is consultation on draft documents before and during meetings. Its precondition is an atmosphere of equality. Its outcome is that agreed points go into the document and disputed ones are left out. Nie contrasts the 1957 meeting, where Khrushchev accepted this approach and the declaration passed unanimously, with 1960, when Deng rejected majority rule and "father-son party" relations and the Soviet side refused consultation. In Nie's telling the 1960 statement was only a grudging compromise that deepened the split. Nie argues that majority rule and subordination of lower to higher bodies cannot apply among independent, equal parties, so consensus is the only workable route. Nie also contends that the CPC went beyond earlier practice: the First and Second Internationals used consultation informally, the Third relied on hierarchical democratic centralism, and Mao raised consultation from a method to a binding principle.

Nie concludes that the principle restores a democratic tradition, was first formulated as a principle by the CPC, and complements the norms of independence, equality, mutual respect and non-interference. It helps manage differences in a diverse world socialist movement. Nie notes that the international meetings of communist and workers' parties have applied it, issuing a press communiqué rather than forcing through a joint statement when consensus failed. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of Sino-Soviet disputes over inter-party relations and of how the CPC frames its own role in them.
quoteEn: Consultation and consensus is a gradual process, a process of continuous development, a process that keeps deepening.
quoteZh: 协商一致是一个渐进的过程，是一个持续发展的过程，是一个不断深化的过程。

glossary.explanation: A principle for settling differences among communist parties through equal discussion, so that only points of agreement are written into joint documents. The article presents it as proposed by Mao Zedong and the CPC around the 1957 Moscow conference.
A pejorative phrase from the Sino-Soviet dispute. It describes a hierarchical relationship in which one party treats others as subordinates. The article applies it to the CPSU under Khrushchev.
The organisational principle of Leninist parties: minority submits to majority, lower bodies to higher ones, and the whole party to the centre.

t: The fragmentation of Italy's communist parties and prospects for their development
zh: 论意大利共产主义政党的碎片化困境与发展前景
paras: Italy's Communist Party was once the strongest in Western Europe, yet it dissolved in 1991 and its successors have since splintered. Li Kaixuan asks why Italian communist organisations now form a fragmented "two weak, three small" pattern and whether they can recover. The article argues that fragmentation stems from abandoning democratic centralism and from ideological confusion and political vacillation. It treats Italy as a window onto the wider difficulties of Western European communist parties.

The article first maps the current landscape. It covers the declining Party of Communist Refoundation, the new Italian Communist Party (formed in June 2016 from the Party of Italian Communists), and three smaller groups: the Trotskyist Workers' Communist Party, the Communist Party (Marxist-Leninist) and the Communist Network. Li draws on membership figures from the parties' websites and from a December 2015 talk at the Academy of Marxism by an Italian communist official. A second section analyses causes, and a third examines attempts at reunification and external challenges.

Li's first main claim is organisational. Refoundation, in Li's account, created two top posts, allowed organised factions and dropped democratic centralism, so internal disputes became public and triggered splits (1995, 1998, 2006, 2009). Li contrasts this with the old Party after the 1960s, which held together under a ban on factionalism and under Berlinguer's leadership. The second claim is ideological: the parties never settled how to combine Marxism with Italian political reality. Their swings between joining centre-left governments and opposing them, and the 2008–2009 split over abandoning communist identity, are cited as evidence.

Li reviews the Party of Italian Communists' plan, from 2014, to rebuild a single communist party. The plan drew interest from about a fifth of Refoundation members but fell well short of its targets, and Li doubts it could solve fragmentation without a shared answer on Marxism and Italian conditions. Li also warns of two outside threats. One is Left Ecology Freedom, which Li describes as de-Marxified and which draws on the same voters. The other is the Five Star Movement, whose notion of "the people" Li sees as dissolving class mobilisation. Li calls on the communists to take both seriously. Read the original if you want a detailed, Chinese-academic account of Italian communist party splits, membership figures and strategic debates after 1991.
quoteEn: The future prospects for revival of Italy's communist parties depend largely on whether Italian communists can properly solve the question of how to combine Marxism effectively with Italy's political and social reality.
quoteZh: 意大利共产主义政党未来的复兴前景，很大程度上取决于意大利共产党人是否能够恰当地解决如何将马克思主义与意大利的政治社会现实有效结合的问题。

glossary.explanation: A Leninist organisational principle combining open internal discussion with unified action once a decision is taken. Li treats it as a key safeguard against factional splits.

t: Facing dissolution: the decline of Russia's "de-Stalinization" organisations
st: An analysis of the legal threat to the Memorial association
zh: 面临被解散：俄罗斯“去斯大林化”组织败落史透视
source: Internal Manuscripts of Chinese Social Sciences (Zhongguo shehui kexue neibu wengao), 2015 no. 3
paras: Writing in 2015, Li Ruiqin asks why Memorial, Russia's oldest and largest "de-Stalinization" organisation, has repeatedly faced dissolution since the Ministry of Justice sued it in the Supreme Court in September 2014. This came only three years after a 2011 state project on commemorating the victims of totalitarian regimes, which Memorial helped to shape. Li argues that the case reflects the decline of de-Stalinization in Russia, and that its causes lie in Vladimir Putin's outlook, the Ukraine crisis and Russian society's view of Stalin.

The article has four parts. It first describes Memorial, founded in 1989 on Andrei Sakharov's initiative, its human rights centre, its "Returning the Names" event and allied museums, and then the course of the lawsuit from 2014 to January 2015. It next traces three waves of de-Stalinization, under Khrushchev, under Gorbachev and Yeltsin, and from 2009 under Medvedev. It then examines Russians' contradictory views of Stalin, using Levada Centre polls, and sets out five reasons behind the dissolution crisis.

Li characterises all three waves as top-down, historically nihilist, aimed at courting the West, unrewarded by it and lacking a social base. Polls cited show roughly half of Russians rating Stalin positively, mostly because of the Great Patriotic War and industrialisation, while about a third reject him. Li attributes the crisis to Putin's more favourable view of Stalin, which in Li's account explains why the 2011 project stalled, to the collapse of Russia–West relations after Ukraine, and to a new public stance of "against repression but not against Stalin". The large-scale commemoration of the 70th anniversary of victory in the Second World War is also said to make de-Stalinization unsustainable. Li also reads Western and Ukrainian equations of Hitlerism and Stalinism as hostile pressure.

Li concludes that the delays in dissolving Memorial show the matter's complexity, since westernised intellectuals and foreign human rights bodies resist it, while the Ministry of Justice continues slowly towards its goal. Li describes the "fifth column" of westernised elites promoting historical nihilism as capable of making trouble for a time but destined to fail. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar framed the Memorial case in 2015 and the debate over Stalin in Russia.
quoteEn: "De-Stalinization was first put forward by the West, and it is also the permanent basis on which the West attacks the Soviet Union and Russia."
quoteZh: “去斯大林化”是西方最先提出的，也是西方攻击苏联和俄罗斯的永恒基础。

glossary.explanation: The process of dismantling the political and ideological system and the personality cult built under Stalin, beginning with Khrushchev's 1956 secret speech. The author treats it as a negation of Stalin and of Soviet history.
A term used in Chinese Party discourse for views that are seen as denying or distorting the history of the Soviet Union or the Communist Party. The author applies it to de-Stalinization.

t: The diverse features of contemporary Russian socialist parties
zh: 当代俄罗斯社会主义党派的多样化特征
paras: Writing in 2015, Li Ruiqin asks how the socialist parties that emerged after the collapse of the Soviet Union differ from one another, and what role they play in Russia today. The article argues that Russian socialism is plural: the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF) is the leading force, A Just Russia represents a rising democratic-socialist wing, and a range of smaller parties form a broader left front.

The article compares the CPRF, the All-Union Communist Party of Bolsheviks, the Russian Communist Workers' Party, A Just Russia, the Russian Socialist Movement and other small parties. It does so under six headings: guiding ideology, social base, goals for a "new socialism", political role under legal struggle, attitudes to religion, and the overall position and prospects of the Marxist-Leninist parties. It draws on party programmes, membership figures, election results and 2015 opinion polls.

Li contends that the Marxist-Leninist parties have a unified ideology that continues the Soviet party tradition. A Just Russia and the Russian Socialist Party are described as abstract and democratic-socialist, while the Russian Socialist Movement mixes many left currents. The CPRF's "socialism of the twenty-first century" is said to build on Soviet socialism, whereas the similar-sounding slogan of A Just Russia rejects Soviet history and Marxism-Leninism. All parties work within the law, but the CPRF's opposition is selective, and the CPRF is shown as an ageing party: retirees make up 43.64% of its members. Li notes that the CPRF's liberal stance on religion, which allows believers into the party, may help it to broaden its base. Li regards this as only an expedient that could erode the party's purity.

Li concludes that the CPRF and other Marxist-Leninist parties are indispensable but have no immediate chance of power. In the polls cited, United Russia scores about 57–60% against about 6–7% for the CPRF, and the objective conditions Lenin set for revolution are absent. The author calls for theoretical innovation, better party-building, unity among dozens of fragmented parties and a broad left front pursuing power mainly through parliament, without wholly abandoning non-peaceful means if circumstances require. Read the original if you want a detailed comparative survey of post-Soviet Russian left parties, with membership and polling data, as seen by a Chinese Marxist scholar writing in 2015.
quoteEn: Overall, all of Russia's socialist parties carry out their work within a legal framework.
quoteZh: 总体看来，俄罗斯各社会主义政党均在合法框架下开展工作。

glossary.explanation: A slogan adopted by the CPRF at its 13th Congress (2008) for a renewed socialism that builds on Soviet experience; A Just Russia uses a similar label with a different meaning.
Parties that take Marxism-Leninism as their guiding ideology and keep the Soviet communist tradition, such as the CPRF and the All-Union Communist Party of Bolsheviks.

keywords: Communist Party of the Russian Federation

t: What the evolution of threat perceptions in Russia's national security strategies reveals about the essence of US hegemonism
zh: 从俄国家安全战略威胁因素的演变看美霸权主义本质
source: Trends in World Socialism Studies (世界社会主义研究动态), 2016 no. 95
paras: Writing in 2016, Li Ruiqin asks why the West, which Russia once sought to join even at the cost of the Soviet state's collapse, was named in Russia's 2015 national security strategy as the main threat, with the United States and NATO treated as adversaries. The article argues that the cause lies neither in Russia's adherence to so-called universal values nor in its social system. In Li's account, the one real cause is a US global strategy of hegemonism and a unipolar world, which tolerates no challenger.

The article traces Russia's four security documents since 1991: the 1997 and 2000 National Security Concepts, the 2009 strategy to 2020 and the 2015 strategy to 2020. Each is tied to a turning point: NATO's eastward expansion and the cooling of the Yeltsin-era 'honeymoon', the Kosovo crisis of 1998, the 2008 South Ossetia conflict and the 2014 Ukraine crisis. A final section draws five general lessons from this record.

Li reads the sequence as a gradual loss of illusions. In 1997 Moscow still located its main threats inside the country and avoided naming NATO as a target; in 2000 it dropped that formula. In 2009, under Medvedev, it sought reconciliation, including the third wave of 'de-Stalinisation', but the Ukraine crisis and Western sanctions wiped out these concessions. The 2015 strategy then names US pressure, NATO's advance, missile defence and support for the Ukrainian 'coup' as threats. Li concludes that democracy, freedom and human rights serve as tools of intervention, that US judgments of other states are self-interested, and that Russia's strength made it an obstacle whatever its values.

Drawing on Mao Zedong and Putin, Li concludes that conciliation and concession bring only temporary calm and that hegemonism must be met without compromise. Li links Russia's experience to Western talk of a 'China threat' and to US human rights reports on China, and calls for continued progress on socialism with Chinese characteristics, the Chinese Dream and a moderately prosperous society. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist researcher in 2016 used Russian security documents to argue against Western universal values and for firm resistance to US hegemonism.
quoteEn: There is only one essential cause: the United States holds to a hegemonist global strategy and the goal of a unipolar world, and cannot tolerate any country that challenges or obstructs it.
quoteZh: 本质原因只有一个，美国秉持霸权主义的全球战略、单极世界目标，容不得任何国家对其有所挑战和障碍。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's current system and path, associated with the reform era since Deng Xiaoping. It is the central formula of Chinese Communist Party ideology.
A slogan popularised by Xi Jinping from 2012, referring to national rejuvenation, prosperity and strength.
A long-standing Chinese goal of general, moderate prosperity, used in Party planning as a target for national development.
Values such as democracy, freedom and human rights presented as applying to all societies. Official Chinese discourse often criticises the term as a vehicle for Western ideological influence.

t: Laos: lifting the veil of mystery and welcoming new opportunities for development
zh: 老挝：掀开神秘面纱，迎接发展新机遇
paras: Writing in late 2016, as Vientiane hosted the East Asia leaders' meetings, Pan introduces Laos to a general readership as a once-quiet Buddhist country now drawn into diplomacy and politics. The article's thesis is that Laos' wartime history, three decades of renewal and opening up, and closer ties with China together place it at a point of new development opportunity.

The piece is a magazine-style overview in three parts. It first recounts the Ho Chi Minh Trail and the American bombing of Laos, then turns to Laos' foreign relations, especially with Vietnam and China. It then traces the Lao People's Revolutionary Party's line from 1975 to its Tenth Congress in January 2016 and lists the achievements and problems of the renewal period.

Pan argues that the Trail, which the author says carried Chinese and other aid to southern Vietnam, bound China, Laos and Vietnam in revolutionary friendship. The author cites the claim that the US dropped four billion pounds of bombs on Laos in 1964–1973, and notes that unexploded ordnance still kills and maims. On the Party's line, Pan reads the shifting definition of Laos' stage of development, from 1991 to 2006, as a flexible strategy that allows market mechanisms to be used while leaving room for theoretical manoeuvre. For the renewal record, the article cites figures from a Lao scholar: growth above 7.5% a year in 2006–2015, GDP per capita rising from 114 to 1,913 US dollars, and poverty at 6.59% in 2015.

Pan acknowledges that Laos remains at a low level of development and faces a widening wealth gap, social instability and moral decline among Party cadres. The author adds that the Party must guard against "peaceful evolution". Pan expects the Belt and Road Initiative to be linked with Laos' strategy of turning a landlocked country into a land-linked one. Lao scholars, who once drew mainly on Vietnam, now want to learn from China on Party-building, the market–government relationship and poverty, which Pan sees as room for cooperation. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese view of Laos' history, Party line and relations with China and Vietnam as of 2016.
quoteEn: The Lao Party's adjustment of how it defines the country's stage of development is in fact a more flexible strategy for advancing reform, aimed at making full use of market mechanisms and the like to develop the economy while leaving some room for manoeuvre in theory.
quoteZh: 老党对本国发展阶段定位的调整，实际上是为推进改革而采取的更加灵活的策略，目的是充分利用市场机制等来发展本国经济，并在理论上留下一定的回旋空间。

glossary.explanation: A China-led initiative launched in 2013 to build infrastructure and economic links across Asia, Europe and Africa.
The reform line adopted by the Lao People's Revolutionary Party at its Fourth Congress in 1986, comparable to Vietnam's Doi Moi and China's reform and opening up.
A term in communist-party discourse for the alleged strategy of Western powers to undermine socialist systems through non-military means such as culture, ideology and economic ties.
A network of secret supply routes, partly through Laos and Cambodia, used from 1959 to supply forces in South Vietnam during the Vietnam War.

t: Trends and prospects of left-wing governments in Latin America
zh: 拉美左翼执政动向及前景
authors: Research Centre for the Theoretical System of Socialism with Chinese Characteristics, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 24 November 2016, p. 5
paras: Writing in late 2016, after the defeat of Argentina's left-wing governing party in November 2015, this newspaper commentary asks whether the cycle of left-wing government in Latin America is ending and what that means. The article argues that the left and right alternation, the so-called "pendulum effect", is essentially a regulatory mechanism developed within the capitalist framework to secure political stability and economic development. On that basis, it contends that the current left cycle may be ending but that the left is unlikely to disappear.

The piece covers three waves of left-wing government since the early twentieth century: the early 1900s (Batlle y Ordóñez, Billinghurst, Yrigoyen), the 1940s–60s (Cárdenas, Perón, Vargas) and the post-1999 wave that began with Chávez. It then assesses the nature of the contemporary left, explains why it keeps returning, and reviews the latest developments in Argentina, Brazil, Venezuela, Ecuador and Bolivia. It closes with an outlook for the region.

The author's central claim is that the ruling left parties are not proletarian parties but the left wing of the bourgeois camp. Only Cuba, with the Communist Party of Cuba, counts as a socialist state, and the "socialism of the twenty-first century" proclaimed elsewhere amounts to "change within the system". The author describes a recurring trade-off: the left stresses distribution, political mobilisation and participation but neglects growth and order, while the right does the reverse. The left's resilience is traced to five factors: representative democracy, the shift from elite to mass politics, ideological guidance from socialist thought and the experience of China and Cuba, deep inequality, and the failure of either camp to resolve growth versus distribution.

The author expects Latin American politics to alternate between left and right, with right or centre-right governments possibly becoming more numerous for some time. Several left governments still hold office into 2018–2020, so a decline is not a collapse. Right-wing governments may be politically closer to the West but more open to economic and trade cooperation, which the author flags as relevant to China–Latin America relations. Read the original if you want a concise 2016 Chinese academic assessment of the "pink tide" and its class character, as framed from a Marxist perspective.
quoteEn: Therefore, whether a government is left-wing or right-wing, in essence it is capitalism's self-regulation and development.
quoteZh: 因此,不管是左翼政府还是右翼政府,本质都是资本主义的自我调控与发展。

t: The essence of capitalist financialization
zh: 资本主义金融化的本质
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 29 November 2016
paras: Writing in 2016, Luan asks what lies at the core of the financialization of capitalism, the stage that she says emerged in the 1970s and 1980s when monopoly capitalism came to be dominated by fictitious financial capital. The author's thesis is that its essence lies in monopoly financial capital using financial means to seize enormous profits and plunder the world's wealth.

This short newspaper commentary is organised under three headings: financialization as a new form of exploitation, finance's detachment from its role of serving the real economy, and the hegemonic rule of monopoly financial capital. It draws on Marx's concepts of surplus value and monopoly profit, and on examples such as mergers and acquisitions, debt, futures and options, and household financial products.

Luan argues that the absolute law of surplus-value production, which became monopoly profit under monopoly capitalism, now takes the form of excess profit extracted through financial instruments, including leveraged trading and bubble creation. Finance increasingly serves its own expansion, in the author's account, through shareholder-value maximization and speculation. This hinders productive forces, spreads indebtedness to the state, and tilts distribution towards finance and senior managers. Luan adds that capital now also financializes workers' income through housing credit, health and pension insurance, so that exploitation is joined to consumption.

The author concludes that financialization sharpens the contradictions between a small financial oligarchy and working people at home and abroad. In this reading, Western financial crises are a necessary product of capitalism's basic contradiction, and financial hegemony over markets, pricing and rating agencies exposes the historical limits of capitalism. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how a CASS Marxist scholar interpreted financialization in 2016 through the framework of monopoly capitalism.
quoteEn: The financial sector increasingly departs from its function of serving production and serves its own self-expansion, which suppresses its role in promoting the development of productive forces and makes obstructing and destroying them the dominant tendency.
quoteZh: 金融部门日益脱离为生产服务的职能，服务于自身增殖，这就抑制了其促进生产力发展的作用，使阻碍和破坏生产力成为主导。

t: The economic outlook for advanced capitalist countries is bleak
zh: 发达资本主义国家的经济发展前景黯淡
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2016, no. 20), Huang Zhenqi and Huang Haiyan ask what lies ahead for the economies of the advanced capitalist countries over the next five years and beyond. They open from the 13th Five-Year Plan's call for all-round opening up, which in their view requires close attention to the external environment. Their thesis is that capitalism has entered a stage of domination by "fictitious financial capital", that this stage sharpens capitalism's basic contradiction, and that recovery from the 2008 crisis is therefore weak and a new crisis is possible.

The article has three sections. The first defines the new stage, which the authors date from the 1980s, and lists four factors behind the swelling of fictitious capital. The second sets out how this stage intensifies the basic contradiction of capitalism. The third examines why the major developed economies have recovered so feebly more than seven years after 2008, using data on the United States, Japan and the euro area.

The authors define fictitious financial capital as capital detached from the real economy and produced by circulation alone, such as over-issued paper money and securities. They cite figures such as 2012 securities and bond trading of over 600 trillion dollars, ten times trade in goods and services. For them the causes are deindustrialisation through industrial relocation, financial deregulation (the end of dollar convertibility, Reagan and Thatcher, the 1999 repeal of Glass–Steagall), globalisation and information technology. Their account of the consequences runs through unequal distribution, three great asset bubbles (Japan, the dot-com boom, US housing), surging public and private debt, and protest such as Occupy Wall Street. In the third section they argue that toxic assets are slow to clear, that austerity under sovereign-debt crises holds back growth, and that bail-outs go to big financial institutions while small firms lack credit. They cite US growth averaging 1.8% a year after the crisis.

The authors conclude that quantitative easing, ultra-low interest rates and widening inequality have fed new bubbles, so developed countries face renewed risk of financial crisis and recession. They cite an IMF warning and a similar warning from the former Bank of England governor Mervyn King. They urge China to study the possible effects of a new international crisis on its economy and finance and to prepare policy responses in advance. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese policy researchers in 2016 used the concept of fictitious financial capital to explain Western stagnation and to argue for contingency planning.
quoteEn: After more than thirty years of evolution, the financial sector no longer mainly finances the real economy but increasingly finances itself, using money to extract more money.
quoteZh: 经过近30多年的演变，金融业不再主要是为实体经济融资，而更多的是为自身融资，用钱来套取更多的钱。

glossary.explanation: A term, building on Marx's notion of fictitious capital, for financial capital detached from production and generated through circulation, such as excess paper money and securities. The authors treat it as defining a new stage of capitalism since the 1980s.
China's national economic and social development plan for 2016–2020. The article cites its call for all-round opening up.
The decline of manufacturing's share of output and employment in advanced economies. The authors link it to the export of low- and mid-range industry to developing countries.
In Marxist theory, the contradiction between socialised production and private appropriation. The authors argue that financial domination sharpens it.

t: Why populism keeps growing in Europe and the United States
zh: 民粹主义何以在欧美愈演愈烈
paras: Writing in spring 2016, Shi asks why populism has become ever stronger in Europe and the United States. The commentary argues that populist parties and candidates are a concentrated expression of social contradictions in Western countries, driven by economic hardship, inequality and the growing dominance of elites.

The article first surveys Europe since the 2008 financial crisis. It describes the rise of right-wing populist parties in France, Austria and Germany, and of left-wing populism in southern Europe, notably Syriza in Greece and Podemos in Spain. It then turns to Donald Trump's campaign in the 2016 US primaries as a further case.

Shi identifies two main causes. The first is mass unemployment and an uncertain economic outlook, with the EU economy still stuck near its pre-2008 level. The second is extreme inequality of income and wealth, for which Shi cites Thomas Piketty and the gap between the 1% and the 99%. Populism's core, in Shi's account, is putting the people first against elite domination. Western democratic politics, Shi says, has become more elitist and captured by interest groups and big capital, leaving ordinary people to speak only through their votes. Establishment politicians have lost the ability to set political agendas, while anti-establishment figures voice popular sentiment.

Shi concludes that the many "Trumps" across Europe and America are leading and changing the future model and form of politics. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese international-relations scholar read the rise of Western populism in 2016.
quoteEn: The populist phenomenon in European and American politics is a concentrated expression of the social contradictions within each country.
quoteZh: 欧美政治中的民粹主义现象是各国社会矛盾的集中体现。

t: The roots of the rise of populism in contemporary Europe
zh: 民粹主义在当代欧洲兴起的根源
paras: Why did populist parties surge across Europe after the financial crisis? Writing in 2016, Li Kaixuan argues that the surge has economic and political roots. Economically, it comes from the clash between global free-market expansion and the bounded national welfare state. Politically, it comes from the defects of representative democracy, the EU's democratic deficit and a crisis of representation among mainstream parties. Li adds that populism should not be dismissed as simply reactionary or foolish.

The article opens with the electoral breakthroughs of populist parties since 2012, among them Syriza in Greece, the National Front in France, UKIP in Britain, the Freedom Party in Austria, Podemos in Spain and the Five Star Movement in Italy. It then sorts European populism into types: right-wing (neoliberal and national populism), left-wing, and "issue" populism, which Li locates mainly in Italy. Two sections follow, on economic and on political roots, and a short conclusion extends the point beyond Europe.

Li's first move uses Karl Polanyi's "double movement": market expansion provokes social counter-pressure, and the European welfare state is such a limit on the market. Li says that capital flight, economic restructuring and free movement of labour erode its fiscal base. In north-western Europe, workers fall back on exclusive national boundaries to protect their welfare privileges, which Li reads in the Brexit vote and the Austrian result. In southern Europe, austerity imposed by the "troika" of the EU, the IMF and the European Central Bank fuelled left-wing populism. The second move is political. Li says that representation dilutes or distorts popular will, and that recall and referendum rights are hard to use in practice. The EU's economic powers outrun its accountability. Mainstream parties have become catch-all parties chasing the median voter, and the decline of the western European communist parties after the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe left their voters without representatives.

Li concludes that populism's appeal rests less on the persuasiveness of its programmes than on the poor democratic performance of mainstream parties. Their interests are narrow, and their ability to keep promises and resolve crises is weakening. Li also notes that the interest conflicts caused by globalisation affect every country drawn into it. Populism may therefore become a problem all countries must guard against, though Li holds that solutions must be sought within specific political and social settings. Read the original if you want a concise 2016 Chinese scholarly typology of European populism and its explanation through Polanyi's double movement and the crisis of party representation.
quoteEn: Populism has become an irresistible "temptation" for ordinary people probably not because its actual claims are so convincing, but because of the poor democratic performance of mainstream parties.
quoteZh: 民粹主义之所以成为一种对普通民众难以抵御的“诱惑”，恐怕并非因为其实际主张多么地令人信服，而在于主流政党在民主绩效上的糟糕表现

glossary.explanation: Karl Polanyi's concept, in The Great Transformation, of market expansion being met by a counter-movement from society seeking protection. The article uses it to explain the link between free markets and welfare-state defence.
The nickname for the European Commission, the European Central Bank and the IMF, which oversaw austerity programmes in debtor eurozone countries such as Greece.
The criticism that EU institutions hold wide powers while citizens of the member states have limited means to oversee or restrain them.

t: The populist turn of extremist parties in the West and its warnings
zh: 西方极端政党民粹化及警示
paras: Writing in 2016, Chai Shangjin asks why extreme left and right parties have risen across the West, and what this means for China. The article argues that Western party systems are fragmenting and politics is turning populist. In Chai's account, extremist parties exploit public discontent after the financial crisis. The author says China has little political ground for populism but must guard against its spillover effects.

The article has three parts. The first surveys cases. On the left it covers Syriza in Greece, Podemos in Spain, the New Anticapitalist Party in France, Italy's Five Star Movement and Jeremy Corbyn's election as Labour leader. On the right it covers France's National Front, the US Tea Party and Donald Trump, and parties in Hungary and Poland. The second part gives four causes. The third part draws lessons for China.

On causes, Chai names four. Economic stagnation, unemployment and insecurity feed discontent. Capitalist globalization sharpens competition among workers and revives national and racial conflict. A rigid, polarised multiparty system pushes politicians to compete in promising welfare and opposing rivals for opposition's sake. New online media amplify populist politics. Chai says extremist parties respect democratic rules only in appearance, and in fact favour a strong state and leader. The author also holds that these parties win because their slogans attract voters, not because of their own capability.

For China, Chai calls for three kinds of vigilance. The first is to recognise populism's real presence and political harm, since social polarisation, resentment of officials and the rich, and the wealth gap feed it. The second is to watch Western populist nationalism turning into trade protectionism that harms Chinese interests, including steel anti-dumping measures and obstruction of the Belt and Road Initiative. The third is to stop online political participation from becoming an outlet for populist venting, which Chai says hostile political forces could use to pressure the Party and government. Read the original if you want a Chinese official-think-tank reading of Western populism in 2016 and the domestic security concerns it was used to raise.
quoteEn: Populism not only fails to bring democracy but also hijacks public opinion, assaults the rational democratic political order and triggers the spread of extremism.
quoteZh: 民粹主义不仅不能带来民主，而且会挟持民意，冲击理性民主政治秩序，引发极端主义泛滥。

glossary.explanation: China's international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative, launched by Xi Jinping in 2013.

t: Lessons of the Soviet Union's political reform and democratization
zh: 苏联政治改革与民主化的教训
paras: Writing in 2016, the 25th anniversary of the Soviet collapse, Zhang Shuhua asks what the failure of Soviet political reform under Gorbachev teaches. The article's thesis is that the Soviet Union dissolved because the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) degenerated in its final years. In Zhang's account, Gorbachev's "restructuring" and "democratization" accelerated and triggered that process.

The article is organised around three questions, each posed as a choice: whether to hold to or change the path of political development, whether to uphold or abandon Party leadership, and whether to perfect or demolish the political system. Zhang draws on Lenin's remarks on democracy, statements by Gorbachev and Yakovlev, and comments from Western figures such as Nixon and Brzezinski. Zhang also cites membership figures, counts of informal organizations and ethnic-conflict statistics.

Zhang argues first that Soviet leaders, under Western "peaceful evolution" and having lost their faith, turned reform into a change of direction towards social democracy. Second, the CPSU was weakened from within, marginalized, split along national lines, stripped of its constitutional leadership role (Article 6) and finally abandoned by Gorbachev himself. Third, the system's three foundations (Party leadership, Soviet power and the union state) were dismantled, which in Zhang's reading produced political chaos, ethnic conflict and the state's collapse. Zhang says the result was oligarchic capitalism, not democracy.

Zhang concludes that reform must be the socialist system's self-improvement, keep a socialist orientation and proceed under Party leadership. Political reform, Zhang adds, must serve stability, ethnic unity, political democracy and efficiency, and requires a correct view of democracy. The article closes by contrasting the CPSU's fate with the Communist Party of China, which it says has held to the Four-sphere Confidence and handled reform, development and stability well. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese Marxist scholars in 2016 interpreted the Soviet collapse and drew lessons from it.
quoteEn: Reform is the self-improvement of the socialist system; it must adhere to the socialist direction and be carried out under the leadership of the Party.
quoteZh: 改革是社会主义制度的自我完善，必须坚持社会主义方向，必须在党的领导下进行。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese political discourse for alleged Western strategies of using political, cultural and ideological pressure, not force, to transform socialist states into capitalist ones.
An official formulation of confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The article uses an earlier three-plus-one version of this phrasing.

t: World socialism in the twenty-first century: new configuration, new features, new trends
zh: 21世纪的世界社会主义：新格局、新特征、新趋势
paras: Writing in the inaugural year of the journal World Socialism Studies (2016), which the author marks as the 500th anniversary of world socialism since Thomas More's Utopia (1516), Jiang Hui asks what the condition and prospects of world socialism are in the twenty-first century. The article's thesis is that the twentieth century was defined by the rise of the socialist movement, while the twenty-first is the century in which world socialism moves towards revival, with China as its main pillar.

The article is organised in three parts. The first compares the balance between world capitalism and world socialism after three capitalist crises: 1929, 1973 and 2008. The second sets out four new features of twenty-first-century socialism. The third discusses new problems, strategies and trends, framed as four pairs of relationships that must be kept in unity.

Jiang argues that after 2008 capitalism is on the defensive and entering a long-cycle decline, while socialism, though still in the trough that followed the Soviet and East European collapse, has entered an upswing anchored in socialism with Chinese characteristics. The four features are: socialism winning wider institutional advantages over capitalism; China becoming the mainstay and banner of world socialism, without the hegemonic 'great party, great state' posture of the Soviet Union; a historic turning point in the balance of forces as China's economy overtakes that of the United States; and a new yardstick for judging socialism, combining the number of socialist states with how far socialist ideals are realised. Looking ahead, Jiang says socialism must unite the national and the international, the local and the world-historical, working-class movements and broader mass movements, and social development with ecological civilization.

Jiang concludes that the capitalist crisis offers world socialism a rare opportunity, but that turning possibility into necessity will require long and arduous struggle by socialists and progressive forces worldwide. The article ends with the confident claim that the twenty-first century is the century of world socialism's revival. Read the original if you want an example of how a leading Chinese scholar of scientific socialism, writing in 2016, periodises the contest between capitalism and socialism and presents China's place in it.
quoteEn: Twenty-first-century world socialism is by no means a gradually vanishing 'local communism'; its development and revival can be achieved only as a 'world-historical' undertaking.
quoteZh: 21世纪的世界社会主义绝不是逐渐消失的“地域性的共产主义”，其发展振兴只有作为“世界历史性”的事业存在才有可能实现。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path, system and theory of socialism since reform and opening up, associated with Deng Xiaoping. The article treats it as the banner of world socialism.
An official concept of building a society in harmony with nature, made part of the 'five-sphere integrated plan' for socialism with Chinese characteristics.

t: Why we should believe in communism
zh: 我们为什么要信仰共产主义
paras: Published in Beijing Daily on 27 June 2016, in a special issue marking the 95th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China, this commentary asks why Party members should hold communism as a faith. The author, Jing Li, argues that communist belief is the Party's 'spiritual calcium' and the source of its drive. Jing Li offers four reasons for holding it.

The piece opens with the Party's growth from a small group in 1921 to more than 87 million members, then restates Xi Jinping's call for confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The four reasons are presented as sections: communism as a rational vision, as a lofty value, as a practical cause, and as the Party's core competitiveness. A closing section gives short accounts of Ren Bishi, Peng Pai, Fang Zhimin and Chen Shiju as examples of steadfast belief.

Jing Li contrasts religious expression of hope for a better future, which locates it in the afterlife, with rational expression. Within the rational tradition, the author places Marx above Confucian datong ideals, Plato, Thomas More and the utopian socialists, because Marx derived the future from the laws of history. On values, the author says Marx's 'free development of each' differs from 'universal values', which are said to serve only some people and to remain bound to capital and private property. The author also holds that class struggle is only a phased means and that socialism with Chinese characteristics, at the primary stage of socialism, is part of the communist cause. Citing Marx's late writing on Russia and the 'Kaufman Gorge', Jing Li says China is moving into socialism without a fully developed capitalism while absorbing capitalism's positive results.

The article concludes that ideals decide success or failure and that communist belief gives the Party its core competitiveness. As evidence it cites Party membership figures, China's growth and poverty reduction, and the claim that the Nationalists lacked a guiding purpose. It also cites Xi Jinping's five tiers of ideals, from communism down to the people's expectations of a better life, to show that ideal and reality are united. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-press commentary in 2016 presented communist belief to Party members, including its use of martyr narratives and its contrasts with religion and Western 'universal values'.
quoteEn: Communism is an extremely beautiful rational vision of humankind.
quoteZh: 共产主义是人类极其美好的理性愿景。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era, combining Marxism with China's conditions.
An official thesis, formalised in the 1980s, that China is at an early and long stage of socialist development.

t: The international financial crisis and new developments in state monopoly capitalism
zh: 国际金融危机与国家垄断资本主义新发展
paras: Writing in 2016 in Red Flag Manuscripts (Hongqi Wengao), Liu Ru asks what the 2008 global financial and economic crisis has done to the structure of contemporary capitalism. The article argues that the crisis rooted in the basic contradiction of capitalism, brought down neoliberalism, and pushed advanced countries back to Keynesianism and state intervention. In Liu's account, this deepened state monopoly capitalism without changing the essence of monopoly capitalism, so that Lenin's theory of imperialism remains valid.

The piece has three parts. The first traces the origins of the crisis and the bankruptcy of neoliberalism, setting it against the cycle from classical economics to the Great Depression, Keynesianism and the stagflation of the 1970s. The second describes three post-crisis developments in state monopoly capitalism: the return of Keynesianism, the growth of state-owned capital, and stronger macroeconomic regulation. The third turns to debates on the stage of contemporary capitalism.

Liu contends that neoliberal policies of privatization, loose market controls and weak financial supervision produced financialization, asset bubbles and hidden overproduction, which sharpened capitalism's basic contradiction. When the housing bubble burst, the crisis spread from the financial sector to the real economy and from developed to developing countries. Liu presents Keynesianism as the theoretical basis of state monopoly capitalism because it keeps the market but adds government intervention. As evidence, Liu cites US Treasury stakes of 79.9 per cent in Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and 36 per cent in Citigroup, the 700 billion dollar rescue plan, the 787 billion dollar stimulus, quantitative easing, a 750 billion euro EU rescue and sweeping US financial regulatory reform.

Liu concludes that, despite about ten scholarly views on the stage of contemporary capitalism, it has not moved beyond state monopoly capitalism, and that neoliberalism's failure confirms Lenin's theory of imperialism as the foundation for understanding it. Liu adds that state monopoly capitalism will not exhaust capitalist development, and that productive forces and relations of production will keep moving towards a higher degree of socialization. Read the original if you want an example of how a Party journal in 2016 used Lenin's theory of imperialism to interpret the post-2008 crisis and Western state intervention.
quoteEn: The facts once again show that the essence of monopoly capitalism has not changed and that Lenin's theory of imperialism has not become outdated.
quoteZh: 事实再一次表明，垄断资本主义的实质并没有改变，列宁的帝国主义论并没有过时。

glossary.explanation: A concept in the Leninist tradition for the fusion of the state with private monopoly capital, in which state power and ownership are used to serve monopoly interests. Chinese writers treat it as the characteristic stage of contemporary capitalism.

Lenin's account of imperialism as the monopoly stage of capitalism, set out in Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1917). Chinese Marxist writers often treat it as the basic framework for analysing modern capitalism.
In Marxist political economy, the contradiction between the social character of production and private appropriation. It is held to be the root of periodic economic crises.
The economic school following John Maynard Keynes that advocates government demand management and intervention. Liu treats it as the theoretical basis of state monopoly capitalism.

t: "Democracy Spring" and capital's control over democracy
zh: “民主之春”与资本对民主的控制
paras: Writing in 2016, Tong Dezhi examines the "Democracy Spring" protests held in Washington in April 2016. The article asks what kind of movement this was, what it demanded and where it might lead. Tong's answer is that it is aimed at the core flaw of American democracy: the control of democratic politics by capital.

The piece first describes the march from Philadelphia to the Capitol, the sit-ins that followed and the arrest of more than 1,400 people. It places the movement in a line running from the Selma march and Black Lives Matter to Occupy Wall Street in 2011. It then turns to the movement's demands and tactics.

Tong argues that elections are increasingly dominated by wealthy donors, which undermines the principle of one person, one vote. To show that this is widely recognised, the author cites Michael Walzer, Anthony Arblaster, Jacques Derrida and David Schweickart. Schweickart's seven channels of money's influence include lobbying, media campaigns, bribery and campaign financing. On the movement's side, Tong notes an "empowerment plus disruption" strategy, reform bills, and a declaration calling for voting-rights protection and the reversal of Citizens United.

Tong concludes that the movement's immediate target is money politics and corrupt elections, and its ultimate aim is democracy that serves the people. Tong also stresses that Congress answered with silence and arrests. Read the original if you want a Chinese academic account of the 2016 protests and of how Western critics of money in politics were used to frame them.
quoteEn: The movement's demands are very clear: promote democracy and fight corruption. Its direct goal is to oppose money politics and corrupt elections, and its ultimate goal is to realise the popular character of democracy.
quoteZh: 这一运动的诉求非常明显，那就是兴民主、反腐败，其直接目标是反对金钱政治和腐败选举，最终的目标是实现民主的人民性。

t: The clash of ideas and social crisis behind Brexit
zh: 英国脱欧背后的观念较量与社会危机
paras: Writing in October 2016, after the British referendum on leaving the European Union, Tang Jian asks what Brexit reveals about the philosophy of history that underpins globalisation. The article argues that Brexit, together with Donald Trump's rise in the United States, challenges Francis Fukuyama's "end of history" thesis. In Tang's reading, the Anglo-Saxon model of liberal democracy is not a perfected universal form but one imperfect path of human development that can itself degenerate.

The piece begins with Fukuyama and the way his thesis became the intellectual background of globalisation advocacy. It then examines three readings of Brexit: the globalist view that treats Leave as backward and closed, the generational explanation (young Remainers versus old Leavers), and the nationalist view that Brexit means a return to imperial glory and "splendid isolation". It goes on to discuss Mark Monmonier's How to Lie with Maps, Karl Polanyi, and Alexandre Kojève's reading of the end of history.

Tang's central move is to say that both camps think in binary terms and turn Brexit into a contest of positions rather than an "event" with gains for some and losses for others. The generational account, in Tang's view, fails because today's elderly voters were the young who voted to stay in the European Communities in 1975. The nostalgic account also fails, since Britain once balanced the continent from a position of strength, whereas a weakened Britain loses influence by leaving. Tang adds that globalisation has produced rising non-Western powers, clashes of civilisations, migration and identity problems, and job and welfare losses in Britain and America. Elites who dismiss voters as a "mob" ignore Polanyi's point that society protects itself when it is damaged.

Tang concludes that globalisation cannot and will not mean Anglo-Americanisation, and that Brexit does not mean a return to the past either.
