Drawing on Kojève, Tang urges managing the positive and negative effects of events rather than imagining an end point, and recognising that every development path can contribute something universal. Anglo-American society is to be surpassed, not treated as an object of faith. Read the original if you want a short Chinese commentary from 2016 that uses Brexit to criticise the end-of-history thesis and binary debate about globalisation.
quoteEn: Globalisation cannot and will not be Anglo-Americanisation.
quoteZh: 全球化不能也不会是英美化。

t: China and world socialism
zh: 中国与世界社会主义
paras: Tian Xinming asks what socialism with Chinese characteristics means for world socialism. The article's answer has two sides. The concrete path, theoretical system and institutions of Chinese socialism grew out of China's national conditions and cannot be copied elsewhere. Yet the principle of integrating Marxism's universal truth with concrete national realities, together with the 'living soul' of Mao Zedong Thought, has validity beyond China.

The article deals only with the second aspect of the China–socialism relationship, the world significance of Chinese theory and practice. It has four parts: the rejection of wholesale transplanting of experience; the universal applicability of the 'integration' principle; the universality of the three basic aspects of Mao Zedong Thought's living soul; and what China's practice shows about the general trend of history and what new problems it poses. Tian draws throughout on Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Party resolutions and Lenin's remarks on the general and the particular.

Tian argues that the Party's own history of struggle against dogmatism, which treated Comintern resolutions and Soviet experience as sacred, shows that other countries must decide for themselves which Chinese experience suits them. The author then contends that the 'integration' principle is itself a basic principle of Marxism. Marxism's basic tenets reflect general laws, while every country's conditions are particular, so the principle holds beyond China. In the same way, seeking truth from facts, the mass line and independence and self-reliance are described as standpoints and methods, not conclusions tied to a given stage or country. Tian points to Deng Xiaoping's presentation of self-reliance and seeking truth from facts to foreign visitors as evidence for this reading.

Tian concludes that China's persistence with socialism, as a country with a fifth of the world's population, supports the Marxist view of historical direction after the Soviet collapse. Tian also stresses that China faces unresolved problems, including keeping public ownership dominant, preventing corruption among officials, upholding Marxist guidance in ideology, and avoiding polarisation of wealth. In Tian's view, China meets these problems first as a front-runner, so its successes and failures are a resource for world socialism. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist argument, grounded in Mao and Deng, on what is and is not exportable from China's experience.
quoteEn: Integrating the universal truth of Marxism with China's concrete realities is the Party's most important and also its most universal experience, an ideological principle whose truth and applicability extend beyond a single country.
quoteZh: 把马克思主义的普遍真理同中国具体实际相结合，是中国共产党最重要的同时也是最具有普遍性的经验，是一条具有超出一国范围的普遍真理性和适用性的思想原则。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path since reform and opening up, which the article describes as a unity of path, theoretical system and institutions.

glossary.zh: 毛泽东思想的活的灵魂
glossary.pinyin: Máo Zédōng sīxiǎng de huó de línghún
glossary.en: living soul of Mao Zedong Thought
glossary.explanation: A formulation from the 1981 Party resolution on history, naming three basic aspects: seeking truth from facts, the mass line, and independence and self-reliance.
The Party's ideological line, which Mao and Deng presented as a Chinese formulation of dialectical and historical materialism.
The Party's basic work method of serving and relying on the masses and of going 'from the masses, to the masses'.
A founding principle of the Party and the People's Republic: China's affairs must be decided by the Chinese people, without copying foreign models.

keywords: integration of Marxism with Chinese reality

t: Japanese socialism still has to find its way
zh: 日本社会主义的实现仍需摸索
paras: This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in January 2016, asks what the Japanese Communist Party's turn to parliamentary struggle means for the prospects of socialism in Japan. Shi argues that the party has shifted from a revolutionary tradition to work within the capitalist framework. The author warns that it risks mistaking small improvements in welfare for the realisation of socialism.

The article begins with the party's position as one of seven parties in the Japanese Diet and its unchanged goal of socialism and communism since 1922. It then looks at Miyamoto-era successor Fuwa Tetsuzo's 2003 proposal on Japan's path in the twenty-first century and the programme revision that followed. It ends with Fuwa's 2014 theory of the "three inevitabilities" of the growth of the subject of social change.

Shi reports that in 2003 the party deleted phrases such as "establishing workers' power" and "people's revolution" from its programme. It now seeks democratic reform within existing capitalism, through a united front of workers, citizens, farmers and others. The author credits this approach with gains such as free medical care for some age groups and higher relief payments. Shi argues, however, that the party is a non-governing parliamentary party with very limited influence under continuous bourgeois rule. In Shi's view, treating temporary welfare gains as a sign that socialism is arriving is the "infantile disorder" of utopian socialists.

Shi concludes that the shift from revolutionary thinking to parliamentary struggle poses serious ideological and political challenges for Japanese communists. They must keep the socialist goal firmly in mind and constantly examine themselves. Read the original if you want a brief, critical Chinese view of the Japanese Communist Party's post-2003 strategy.
quoteEn: This theoretical infantile disorder of the utopian socialists needs to be guarded against.
quoteZh: 这种空想社会主义者的理论幼稚病，需要引起警惕。

t: World socialism is now entering a period of seeking revival
zh: 当前世界社会主义正进入谋求振兴期
paras: Writing in 2016, Jiang Hui asks where world socialism stands some twenty-five years after the Soviet and East European upheavals. The article argues that since the early twenty-first century it has emerged from its trough and entered a period of seeking revival through development and change. Jiang holds that this period brings rare opportunities as well as severe challenges, and that socialism with Chinese characteristics is its brightest spot, its benchmark and its mainstay.

The article begins by describing how communist parties survived the crisis after the Soviet collapse: some dissolved, renamed themselves or became social-democratic, while others persisted. Jiang cites statistics of roughly 130 parties worldwide that keep the communist name or Marxist character, with about 103 million members, of whom more than 88 million are in the Communist Party of China. It then sorts these parties into four types: ruling parties in existing socialist countries, parties in developed capitalist countries, parties in the former Soviet and East European region, and parties in developing countries. Jiang also mentions non-communist left currents such as Latin American 'twenty-first-century socialism', market socialism and eco-socialism. A section on opportunities and challenges follows, and the article closes with three conclusions.

Jiang lists six favourable conditions: the weakening of neo-liberal dominance in the wake of the capitalist crisis, the vindication of socialist criticism and the revived interest in Marx, the recovery and maturing of socialist forces, closer cooperation among left parties, more objective lessons drawn from the Soviet collapse, and China's achievements as a local high tide within a general ebb. Against these stand four difficulties. Capitalism remains stronger than socialism, communist parties are marginalised in Western politics, they lead social movements only weakly, and the global working class remains 'in itself', without a global class consciousness. Jiang therefore warns that crisis does not automatically produce socialist revolution, and that the idea of a single decisive blow is an infantile error. He argues that contemporary capitalism, now in an international monopoly stage, regulates and innovates well beyond the capitalism of Marx's day.

Jiang concludes that world socialism will remain at a general low ebb for a considerable time, and that preparations are needed for long-term cooperation and struggle between the two social systems. He calls on China to concentrate on its own affairs, building comprehensive national strength and improving living standards, invoking Deng Xiaoping's and Xi Jinping's statements about the growing influence of China's path. In his view, world socialism's revival depends on the development of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Party scholar in 2016 surveyed the global communist movement, with membership figures and a typology of parties, and tied its prospects to China.
quoteEn: As long as socialism with Chinese characteristics develops, the revival of world socialism will not be empty talk.
quoteZh: 只要中国特色社会主义发展起来，世界社会主义的振兴就不是空话。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path of combining socialism with China's conditions, associated with the reform era since the late 1970s. The article treats it as the mainstay of world socialism.
The Chinese expression for the collapse of Soviet and East European communist regimes around 1989–1991. Chinese scholarship treats it as the main setback for world socialism.
A field in Chinese scholarship covering socialist states, communist and left parties, and socialist currents worldwide, also called the international communist movement.

t: Left-wing governments in Latin America face severe challenges
zh: 拉美左翼政权面临严峻挑战
paras: Writing in late 2015, Xu Shicheng asks why the Latin American left, which rose to power from 1999 onwards, now faces what the article calls a severe challenge. Xu argues that after roughly a cycle in office, left-wing and centre-left governments are under pressure from economic slowdown, corruption, domestic opposition, internal divisions and external interference. Xu judges Venezuela and Brazil to be the most exposed.

The piece opens by tracing the left's rise. Xu attributes it to the failure of traditional ruling parties and of neoliberal reform, beginning with Hugo Chávez's election in Venezuela in 1999 and followed by victories in Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Bolivia, Ecuador, Nicaragua, El Salvador and Peru. It then assesses these governments' record in politics, economics, social policy and foreign policy, before setting out five challenges and the left's responses.

In the article's account, left governments won broad support through new constitutions, participatory democracy, nationalisations such as Bolivia's 2006 energy measure, anti-poverty programmes in Brazil and Venezuela, and regional bodies such as ALBA, UNASUR and CELAC. Xu then cites falling commodity prices and regional growth dropping from 2.9% in 2012 to a forecast negative figure in 2015, with Brazil and Venezuela hit hardest. Austerity, scandals such as Brazil's state oil company affair, and protests followed. Xu adds that right-wing forces still hold major cities, that coalitions and parties are split (for example the Workers' Party over its 'rightward turn', and the landless movement over unfulfilled land promises), and that the United States funds opposition groups and pursues 'colour revolution'.

Xu notes that left parties recognise these threats. Examples include the 'Latin American Progressive Meetings' in Quito and the 21st São Paulo Forum in Mexico City (2015), whose final statement stressed left unity against imperialism and oligarchies. Xu sees Mauricio Macri's victory in Argentina in November 2015 as swinging the regional pendulum to the centre-right, and flags Venezuela's 6 December parliamentary election as the next test. Read the original if you want a concise, Chinese-academic overview of the state of the Latin American left at the end of the 'pink tide' cycle, with country-level figures and the author's framing of US involvement.
quoteEn: At present, left-wing governments in Latin America face severe challenges.
quoteZh: 目前拉美左翼政府面临严峻挑战。

t: International eco-socialism regards China as an "experimental field"
zh: 国际生态社会主义将中国视为 “实验场”
paras: Xu Chongwen introduces eco-socialism, a current of thought that emerged amid Europe's green movements, and asks how its adherents view China. Xu argues that eco-socialists trace the ecological crisis to the capitalist system and see its solution in replacing capitalism with socialism. On this basis, the article says, they regard China as an "experimental field" of eco-socialism and expect it to lead and set an example globally.

The short piece begins with the origins of eco-socialism after the 1970s and its distinction from other ecologisms. It then surveys the visions of socialism held by Michael Löwy, André Gorz and Joel Kovel, and discusses the rise and decline of ecocentrism. It ends with Saral Sarkar's criticism of the Soviet model and his hopes for China.

Xu's central contrast is that most ecologists blame science, technology and industrialisation, whereas eco-socialists blame capitalism. Ecocentrism, which Xu describes as an overcorrection against anthropocentrism, dominated global ecologism before the 1990s with its anti-growth, anti-technology stance. Xu says European eco-socialists since 1990 have returned to anthropocentrism, holding that the problem lies in a capitalist way of treating nature rather than in human mastery of it. Citing Sarkar's 1997 book, Xu reports that he sees Soviet bureaucratic socialism as having failed on ecological limits. Sarkar judges that China has a greater chance of success than other countries if its leadership accepts genuine eco-socialism, because of its socialist market economy, family planning policy and emphasis on happiness with fewer material goods.

Xu says Sarkar's views differ from those of Marxists but that his expectations of China deserve affirmation. Xu points to the 18th Party Congress (2012), which placed ecological civilization within the five-sphere overall plan and set the goal of a beautiful China, as evidence of the Party's resolve. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese official-academic account of how eco-socialist thinkers are presented as viewing China.
quoteEn: In fact, the cause of ecological problems is not human domination of nature, but the capitalist way in which humans treat nature.
quoteZh: 实际上，引起生态问题的原因并不是人对自然的支配，而是人类对待自然的资本主义方式。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese policy concept, elevated at the 18th Party Congress (2012), that aims to integrate environmental protection into economic, political, cultural and social development.
The official framework adopted at the 18th Party Congress (2012) that coordinates economic, political, cultural, social and ecological development.
The official description of China's economic system since the early 1990s, combining market mechanisms with public ownership and state guidance.
A slogan from the 18th Party Congress (2012) expressing the goal of a cleaner, ecologically sound country.

t: Changing the marginalisation of Marxism
zh: 改变马克思主义被边缘化的状况
paras: Why is Marxism being pushed to the margins in a socialist country, and how can this be reversed? Writing in Beijing Daily in 2016, Chen Xianda takes up Xi Jinping's remark at the symposium on philosophy and social sciences that Marxism has been marginalised, hollowed out and reduced to a label in some fields. Chen argues that the phenomenon is no accident. It follows from international conditions and from the social changes of reform and opening up, and it can be corrected only by holding firm to two economic principles and by improving governance and theoretical work.

Chen opens from personal experience. The author recalls studying at Fudan and Renmin University in the early years of the People's Republic, when Marxist courses were prestigious and rarely questioned, and contrasts this with today's classrooms, forums and publications. The article then moves through three sections: the causes of marginalisation, the economic principles that must be upheld, and the social disorders now blamed on the system. It closes with practical demands for ideological work in universities.

Chen names external causes: the upheavals in Eastern Europe, the Soviet collapse, the ebb of world socialist revolution and Western ideological infiltration. The internal causes are the shift from a single public ownership to multiple ownership forms and from a planned to a market economy, which Chen says breeds diverging interests and pluralised values. Chen holds that the public sector must remain dominant and that the market economy must be socialist in substance, not "socialism plus a market economy". A purely market logic, the author warns, would push the humanities and Marxism aside. On corruption, the wealth gap and moral decline, Chen distinguishes the basic system (zhi) from governance (zhi), citing Liu Zongyuan's remark that the fault lay in the people, not in the system. The system is sound, in Chen's view, but governance of the market is inadequate, and young people's doubts about Marxism stem from resentment at such disorders, not from reading Marxist texts.

Chen calls for lawful, effective management of the ideological sphere, higher standards of Marxist research and propaganda, and a higher political standing for Marxist theorists, who should see themselves as fighters on the theoretical front. Chen also proposes judging Marxist scholars by whether they address China's real problems, not by counting books and articles, and warns that without changing these evaluation standards marginalisation will persist. Read the original if you want a senior Chinese Marxist philosopher's 2016 diagnosis of why Marxism is losing ground in universities and what institutional remedies the author proposes.
quoteEn: The four characters for "socialism" are the lifeline.
quoteZh: “社会主义”这四个字是生命线。

glossary.explanation: The policy course launched in 1978 that introduced market reforms and opened China to foreign trade and investment.

t: Diverse explorations out of the trough
st: The "five crests" in the revival of world socialism
zh: 走出低谷的多样探索
zhSub: 世界社会主义回暖潮流中的“五个潮头”
paras: Writing in 2016, more than twenty years after the collapse of the Soviet Union and the upheavals in Eastern Europe (1991), Wang Dong asks what trends and currents are now visible in world socialism. The author's overall judgement is that, helped by the general crisis of capitalism in the age of economic globalisation, contemporary world socialism has left its lowest point and is exploring diverse new paths suited to a new era and to national conditions. Wang identifies five "crests" in this warming tide.

The short article is organised as a survey of five currents: ecological socialism responding to the global ecological crisis; calls for socialist justice in the face of polarisation; the search for twenty-first-century socialism in Latin America; calls for a socialist revival in Russia and other Commonwealth of Independent States countries; and Vietnam's exploration of a path of renewal (đổi mới). Each section gives a brief account of figures and events, drawing on interviews, books and leaders' statements.

On ecology, Wang reports the view that the ecological crisis is rooted not in science and technology but in the internal contradictions of the capitalist mode of production, with its drive for maximum profit, and notes that ecosocialists influence politics in Europe and the Americas. On justice, Wang points to the worldwide debate around Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014) after the 2008 financial crisis, and cites David Harvey's view that Piketty's data are valuable but his explanation and remedies are flawed, so that Marx or a modern equivalent is still needed. For Latin America, Wang summarises the proposals of Ecuador's Rafael Correa ("modern socialism" combining market and state) and Bolivia's Evo Morales ("good socialism" based on shared, harmonious living), after Hugo Chávez's death in 2013. In Russia, Wang cites the Moscow philosopher A. Bagaturia's 2015 call to analyse the Soviet collapse with classical Marxism and to create new theory, while in Vietnam the discussion centres on Ho Chi Minh Thought, which combines national and class struggle and patriotism with internationalism.

Wang concludes that these currents show socialism recovering through varied paths rather than a single model, and presents the capitalist crisis as the common background. The text is a brief overview and offers no extended theoretical argument or evaluation of the cases. Read the original if you want a compact, 2016 Chinese-language snapshot of how a Chinese scholar framed the revival of world socialism, with pointers to figures such as Correa, Morales, Harvey and Bagaturia.
quoteEn: Contemporary world socialism has already emerged from its lowest point and is exploring diverse new paths suited to a new era and to new national conditions.
quoteZh: 当代世界社会主义已经走出最低谷，正在探索适应新时代、新国情的多样化新道路。

t: Chinese experience deepens Sino-Russian inter-party relations
zh: 中国经验深化中俄党际关系
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 31 March 2016
paras: Writing in a newspaper commentary in 2016, Li Yazhou examines how the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (CPRF), successor to the Soviet Communist Party, views socialism with Chinese characteristics. Li argues that the CPRF, led by Gennady Zyuganov, holds China's experience in high regard and actively seeks to learn from it, which in turn strengthens ties with the Communist Party of China, formally established in 1995.

The article draws on statements and writings by Zyuganov and other CPRF figures, notably Central Presidium member Vladimir Vichmanov. It is organised under four headings: praise for China's achievements, China as a pole of a multipolar world, the uniqueness of China's reform experience, and expectations for the "Chinese Dream". It also lists CPRF delegations to China, including Zyuganov's visits in 1995, 2004, 2006 and 2014 and a youth delegation in 2013.

Li reports that the CPRF contrasts Russia's capitalist reforms, which it says brought the economy near collapse, with China's reform and opening up under Party leadership. In Li's account, Zyuganov holds that China's Party character as vanguard of both the working class and the whole nation offers lessons for Russian communists, and that Russia should maintain close ties with China for reasons of economic complementarity and resistance to global hegemonism. Vichmanov is said to defend Deng Xiaoping Theory against charges that Chinese communists have abandoned Marxism. Zyuganov also lists problems China must manage, including growth, political stability and avoiding a Soviet-style collapse.

Li concludes that the CPRF expects to deepen relations with the Communist Party of China, to promote friendly Sino-Russian state relations, and to remain optimistic about the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, officially oriented account of how the CPRF's praise for China is presented in Chinese Party-affiliated media.
quoteEn: China's reform experience is unique; Russia's reformers should study the speeches of the Chinese Communist Party's leaders and read the Selected Works of Deng Xiaoping carefully to understand China's successful experience.
quoteZh: 中国的改革经验是独一无二的，俄罗斯的改革者应该学习中国共产党领导人的讲话，应当认真读一读《邓小平文选》，了解中国成功的经验。

glossary.explanation: The official name for China's path of combining Marxism with Chinese conditions, associated with the reform era beginning under Deng Xiaoping.
The policy launched in 1978 of economic reform and opening to the outside world.
A slogan promoted by Xi Jinping from 2012 that centres on national rejuvenation and national prosperity.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: An official goal of restoring China's national strength and international standing.
The body of ideas associated with Deng Xiaoping's reform-era leadership, written into the Party constitution in 1997 as a guiding ideology.

keywords: Communist Party of the Russian Federation

t: Tactical success and strategic impasse: the world socialist movement since the 2008 financial crisis
zh: 战役成功与战略困局：2008年金融危机以来的世界社会主义运动发展态势
source: Marxist Studies (马克思主义研究), 2015 no. 10
paras: Writing in Marxist Studies in 2015, Nie Yunlin asks why the 2008 financial crisis, which put capitalism "in the dock of history", did not produce a resurgence of the world socialist movement. The article's answer is that communist parties in capitalist countries won a "campaign-level" (tactical) success but no strategic victory. They remain marginalised in political life, and the movement is still at a low ebb.

The article has two parts. The first reviews what communist parties in capitalist countries did after 2008 and why their gains were limited, drawing on speeches by delegates to the 11th International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties. The second sets out six problems that Nie says the parties must solve to break the strategic impasse. These are internal division, "left" and right deviations, democratic centralism, class and mass bases, left alliances, and the constraints of the bourgeois political system.

Nie credits the parties with analysing the crisis theoretically, joining strikes and protests, voting against crisis-shifting policies in parliament, and strengthening party-building and international cooperation. Membership stabilised or grew in some parties, for example the Communist Party of India (Marxist), which kept more than a million members. The limits are attributed to the legacy of the Soviet and East European collapse, welfare systems that blunted workers' political consciousness, weak capacity for innovation, and sectarian splits. Nie cites the number of rival communist parties in Britain, India, Turkey and Russia. The author argues that parties which kept democratic centralism, such as those of India (Marxist), Japan and Portugal, recovered strength, while those that dropped it, such as the French, Spanish and Italian Refoundation parties, declined. Nie adds that, in the author's account, the parties have lost their ties to trade unions, struggle to win over the middle classes, and are hemmed in by electoral, two-party and separation-of-powers arrangements.

Nie concludes that the crisis-era success is comparable to the Defence of Huangyangjie in the Jinggangshan period: a single battle won, with a long struggle still ahead. The task of the post-crisis period is to explore socialist paths suited to each country, and the most pressing step is for each party to resolve its own internal problems. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-affiliated scholar's assessment of Western communist parties after 2008, including the argument for democratic centralism and against both "left" and right deviations.
quoteEn: Correct theory and strategy are the lifeblood of the Party.
quoteZh: 正确的理论与策略是党的生命。

glossary.explanation: The organisational principle of Leninist parties, combining discussion and election with binding discipline once decisions are taken. The article defends it as essential for communist parties while acknowledging excessive concentration of power in the past.

glossary.zh: 共产党和工人党国际会议
glossary.en: International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties
glossary.explanation: An annual gathering of communist and workers' parties from many countries. The article draws on delegates' speeches at the 11th meeting.

t: Foreign scholarship on the communist movements of twentieth-century Southeast Asia: a review
zh: 国外关于20世纪东南亚共产主义运动的研究述评
paras: This is a literature review of foreign research, mostly in English with a little in French, on the communist movements that spread across Southeast Asia from the early twentieth century to the 1980s. Liu and Shi treat these movements as part of both regional history and the rise and decline of international communism in Asia. They note that the movements were shaped by anti-colonial struggle, the war against Japan and the Cold War, and that armed communist struggles largely ended only in the late 1980s.

The review moves from regional and international perspectives to country studies. It covers the early Cold War works of the 1950s, studies of the 1960s and 1970s, and Singapore-based volumes of the 1980s. It then turns to Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, to Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines, and finally to Burma and Thailand. For each country it lists major monographs, memoirs, document collections and doctoral theses.

Liu and Shi highlight several clusters of work. On Vietnam, they point to historical studies (McAlister, Turner, Pike, Duiker), research on the Vietnamese Workers' Party's position between China and the USSR, and comparisons of British counter-insurgency in Malaya with the American effort in South Vietnam. On Laos and Cambodia, they note work on the Pathet Lao's dependence on Vietnam and the attention given to the Khmer Rouge. For Malaya they distinguish participants' accounts, such as Chin Peng's memoir, from scholarly studies. Their remarks on Indonesia concern the 1948 Madiun uprising and the 1965 destruction of the party, and on the Philippines the studies by participants and journalists. On Burma they note Lintner's history and the document collections. On Thailand they note studies of the party's Maoist orientation and of China's role in its armed struggle.

The authors' overall assessment is that this scholarship was clearly shaped by the course of the Cold War in Asia and relied mostly on government publications and press reports. They add that studies from the angle of the international communist movement are comparatively few, and they point to useful reference materials such as FBIS broadcast translations and the Hoover Institution's yearbook. The review mainly surveys and describes and does not set out a new programme of research. Read the original if you need a bibliographic guide, organised by country, to English-language scholarship on Southeast Asian communist parties and their links with the Comintern, the Soviet Union and China.
quoteEn: On the whole, these studies were clearly influenced by the development of the Cold War situation in Asia, and most of the sources they used were government publications and press reports.
quoteZh: 总的来说，这些研究明显受到亚洲冷战形势发展的影响，使用的资料大多是政府出版物和新闻报道。

glossary.explanation: The Lao communist-led movement that fought for power in Laos and took control in 1975. It worked in close alliance with Vietnamese communists.
The Cambodian communist movement led by Pol Pot, which ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979. The review notes the attention given to its mass killings.
The September 1948 revolt by the Indonesian Communist Party, put down by the Indonesian Republic's government. The review counts it as the party's second devastating blow.

t: How the social-democratic welfare state transcends and falls short of liberalism and its individualism
zh: 社会民主主义福利国家对自由主义及其个人主义的超越和局限
paras: Writing in Zhejiang Social Sciences in 2016, Zhu Xuhong asks whether the post-war social-democratic welfare state, especially in the Nordic countries, moves beyond liberalism, individualism and capitalism, or remains within them. The article's answer is double. The welfare state shows a real critical and transcending relation to liberalism, but this is non-institutional and confined to the capitalist framework. Zhu concludes that the welfare state is not a socialist state.

The article begins with the origins of the term, from Bismarck's Germany to Attlee's Britain in 1948, and with Esping-Andersen's three types of welfare state. Zhu focuses on the social-democratic (Nordic) type, with Sweden as its showcase. It then sets out the model's features (mixed economy, full employment, fair distribution, social welfare and security) and its reported achievements in lower poverty, social stability and reported happiness.

Zhu first argues that social-democratic values mark a break with liberalism and individualism. These are an 'active' view of freedom that uses state power, equality of outcome as well as opportunity, a principle of mutual aid, economic planning and expanded public ownership, weaker bourgeois rights, and stronger workers' co-determination. Zhu also reads neoliberal hostility to the welfare state as evidence of this transcendence. The article then turns to the limits. Zhu argues that social democrats retreated from public ownership of the means of production to regulating distribution, with Swedish theorists and party congresses holding that ownership matters less than how firms are run. The article cites figures showing that over 90 per cent of Swedish productive assets are privately held. It cites Swedish interlocutors who call Sweden capitalist and describe its model as 'welfare capitalism'.

Zhu concludes that the welfare state is a capitalist system with more socialist elements than before, in income distribution, economic democracy and social security. At most it shows that capitalism can serve public welfare better than once thought. The article treats the social-democratic equation of socialism with welfare policy as a retreat on the core question of ownership. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's assessment of Nordic social democracy, drawing on many Chinese-language sources and Swedish interviews, and an account of why the author denies it the label socialist.
quoteEn: The welfare state is not a socialist state.
quoteZh: 福利国家不是社会主义国家。

glossary.explanation: A reformist current that seeks to move towards socialism by parliamentary means and welfare policy. In Chinese Marxist scholarship it is usually distinguished from scientific socialism and assessed critically.
The article's term for a capitalist economy with extensive state redistribution and regulation, which it sees as the true nature of the Nordic welfare state.

glossary.en: public ownership of the means of production
glossary.explanation: The ownership basis that Marxist theory takes to define a socialist economic system. The article uses it as its main test of whether a state is socialist.

glossary.literal: joint decision by labour and capital
glossary.explanation: Arrangements, especially in Germany and Sweden, by which workers and employers share decision-making in firms. The article counts them as strengthening workers' democratic rights.

t: An analysis of the Communist Party of the Russian Federation and its youth problem
zh: 俄共及其青年问题探析
paras: Writing in 2016 in China Youth Studies, Cao Peng asks why the Communist Party of the Russian Federation (KPRF), heir to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU), is losing its young people. The article argues that the party's shrinking strength and ageing membership reflect a severe youth problem. Cao traces it to outdated youth policy, the lack of a leadership-replacement mechanism, factional strife and weak implementation by party organisations, and adds pressure from rival parties.

The article first contrasts the CPSU, with roughly 19 million members in 1987, with the KPRF, which Cao says had fewer than 160,000 members by January 2013 and about 130,000 by 2014. It then presents age data: in 2013, by Cao's figures, 10.79 per cent of members were under 30 and 62.76 per cent over 50, so the party is nicknamed a 'party of the old'. Five causes of youth loss follow, and the article ends with five lessons for communist parties.

Cao argues that the 2008 programme speaks of youth only in general, abstract terms and never says what 'renewed socialism' would offer young Russians raised under capitalism. Leadership for life, symbolised by Gennady Zyuganov's unchallenged position since 1993, is said to block promotion and keep stale working methods. Splits between 2000 and 2004 and later infighting damaged the party's image and diverted young members to a rival faction. Cao adds that central youth policy, though announced in 2005 and 2008, was not carried out by local organisations. The party's declining power in the Duma, young people's resistance to its ideology, and competition from Putin, United Russia's 'Young Guard' and pro-government youth groups are also named.

Cao draws five lessons: treat young people as the foundation of party building; keep pace with the times; rejuvenate membership and cadres through real succession mechanisms; preserve unity and the party's image; and make socialism appeal to the young by linking their demands with Marxist ideas, which Cao calls 'the youthification of socialism'. Read the original if you study the post-Soviet communist movement, party ageing, or how Chinese scholars draw lessons for party-youth relations from the Russian case.
quoteEn: If a communist party is to survive and develop, it must win the support of young people, because they are the party's future and the foundation of its cause's prosperity.
quoteZh: 一个共产主义的政党要想生存和发展，就必须得到青年的支持与拥护，因为青年就是党的未来，是党的事业兴旺和发达的基础。
keywords: Communist Party of the Russian Federation

t: The current state of socialist parties in Asia, Africa and Latin America and the reasons for it
zh: 亚非拉地区社会党发展现状及其原因
source: Problems of Contemporary World Socialism (Dangdai shijie shehuizhuyi wenti), 2016 no. 1
paras: Writing in early 2016, Xiang Wenhua surveys the socialist parties of Asia, Africa and Latin America and asks why they have multiplied so quickly. The article reports more than 100 such parties, 31 of which govern alone or take part in government. It argues that they are guided mainly by social democracy or democratic socialism, and that their rise rests fundamentally on the replacement of earlier development models in the region.

The study counts parties that belong to the Socialist International (85), parties that claim social-democratic or democratic-socialist principles without belonging (for example five in Central Asia), and eleven parties suspended in 2014 for unpaid dues. Part one describes the present situation: the parties' origins by period, their governing status as of January 2016, their ideology and policies, and uneven development across regions (25 parties in Asia, 45 in Africa, 31 in Latin America). Part two gives five explanations for the growth.

Xiang finds that most of these parties are still in opposition. Most declare social democracy rather than democratic socialism, which the author reads as an abandonment of the aim of replacing capitalism. Many also keep other ideologies such as nationalism, populism or a 'middle way', so they are less uniform than their West European counterparts. The causes the author gives are the political vacuum left when radical socialist and communist parties declined after the Cold War, and the example of the British Labour Party, Nordic parties and successful governing parties such as Mauritius's Labour Party. Further causes are Socialist International recruitment and the European education of leaders such as Nehru and Senghor. The central explanation is the failure of four models: radical socialism, village-community socialism, populism and neoliberalism. The author cites falling per capita GDP, rising poverty and widening inequality, and presents social democracy as a way to pursue efficiency while keeping equality and justice.

Xiang concedes that opportunism, such as seeking foreign aid or influence, also played a part, but holds that the substitution of development models is the root cause. The article notes that the parties' momentum has weakened while their influence has not, and calls for continued tracking research. Read the original if you want a detailed, country-by-country inventory of social-democratic parties in the Global South, or a Chinese academic account of why left parties turned to social democracy after 1989.
quoteEn: In any case, the fundamental reason why socialist parties have been able to develop in these three continents lies in the replacement of the region's models of social development.
quoteZh: 但无论如何，社会党在这三大洲得以发展的根本原因，在于该地区社会发展模式的替代。

glossary.explanation: The worldwide association of social-democratic, socialist and labour parties, founded in 1951 and long centred on European parties. It later recruited members from Asia, Africa and Latin America.

In this article, the aim of promoting socialist ideals within democratic institutions and eventually replacing capitalism. Chinese scholarship usually distinguishes it from the Marxist-Leninist tradition.
Here, the position that capitalism should be made more humane through welfare states and social insurance. The author treats it as accepting the capitalist system.
The author's label for the Soviet-style model adopted by left parties in power, marked by comprehensive state intervention and priority for state-owned enterprises.
A model adopted in some sub-Saharan African states. It stressed restoring traditional rural communities and collectivising agriculture.

t: The German Left Party sees China as the most important birthplace of "Socialism 3.0"
zh: 德国左翼党认为中国是“社会主义3.0”最重要的诞生地
paras: This piece reports a lecture given on 24 May (2016) at the invitation of the Party Research Centre of the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau. The speaker was Charles (Charle) Bri, a senior researcher at the Left Party's Rosa Luxemburg Foundation in Germany; the name is given only in Chinese transliteration (夏尔·布里). Titled "The Third Wave of Socialism", the lecture holds that the Soviet collapse 25 years earlier did not end socialism but opened a third wave, "Socialism 3.0", and that China is its most important birthplace.

Zhang's report follows the lecture's three-part structure. It first outlines two earlier waves: 1789–1917 and 1917–1991. It then sets out two features of the third wave, which began in 1991. Finally it turns to the crisis of modern capitalism and to China's place in the future of socialism.

In the speaker's account, the first wave produced the main socialist currents, with Marxism giving them a scientific basis. The second wave ran from the October Revolution to the Soviet collapse and included the Chinese revolution and Western social-democratic welfare states. It failed because the Soviet model stagnated, social democracy could not contain accumulation, and neoliberalism put both on the defensive. For the third wave, the speaker says an alternative to capitalism must be a learning, "polycentric" society, neither bureaucratically centralised like the Soviet system nor competition-driven like the American one. It must also foster a new, harmonious civilisation that balances humans with nature and work with leisure. Capitalism, the speaker argues, has largely fulfilled its mission, which Marx called a "temporary necessity". It now faces ecological, identity, political-legitimacy and international-security crises, while the movements opposing it lack a convincing alternative.

The speaker cites Perry Anderson's remark that the twenty-first century will be shaped by Chinese revolutionary events, as the twentieth was by the Soviet ones. The speaker links China's "Socialism 3.0" to the post-1978 learning process, theoretical innovation and the Chinese Dream, which joins modern civilisation to China's traditional culture. Five conditions are listed for a socialist association: ecological productive forces, diverse forms of ownership, bodies for political consultation, a culture of solidarity, and a peaceful international system. If these are met, the speaker says, the twenty-first century could be a century of global socialism. Read the original if you want to see how a Left Party thinker, as presented in a Party journal in 2016, periodises socialism and places China within it.
quoteEn: The Soviet collapse was not, as many believed in 1991, the end of socialism, but can be seen as the moment of birth of "Socialism 3.0".
quoteZh: 苏联的解体并非像许多人在1991年所认为的那样，是社会主义的终结，而是可被视为“社会主义3.0”的诞生时刻。

glossary.explanation: A slogan introduced by Xi Jinping in 2012 that stands for national rejuvenation and prosperity. In this piece it is said to join modern civilisation with China's traditional culture.
A Chinese state institution that translates Marxist classics and Party documents and studies theory. Its Party Research Centre invited the speaker.

t: The evolution of Marxism in Cuba and its lessons
zh: 马克思主义在古巴的演进及启示
source: Scientific Socialism (科学社会主义), 2016 no. 3
paras: Li Jianguo, writing in 2016, treats Cuba as the only socialist country outside Asia and asks what the development of Marxism there can teach the effort to understand the laws governing the adaptation of Marxism to the Chinese context. The article argues that Cuba's path, shaped by its particular national conditions, offers lessons on theory, reform and popular support.

The piece has four parts. It first describes Cuba's national conditions: its status as a US dependency before 1959, the long US blockade afterwards, and a strong popular sense of independence. It then divides the history of Marxism in Cuba into five stages, from the democratic revolution (1944–1959) to the reforms of the post-Soviet "special period". A third part summarises Cuban theoretical results, and a fourth draws three lessons.

In Li's account, Cuba's early "revolutionary offensive" of 1968 broke with reality, and the country then copied the Soviet model from 1971 to 1989, which deepened its economic dependence. After the collapse of the Soviet bloc, Cuba turned to building "socialism with Cuban characteristics" and made José Martí's thought, alongside Marxism-Leninism, the Party's guiding ideology in 1991. Li reports that Cuba sees the essence of socialism as national independence and the welfare of the people, avoids the word "reform", keeps a planned economy, and opens to the outside world only on conditions. Li also notes that Cuba has not yet raised economic construction to the level of socialism's essence, and that Cuba judges the present to be an era of two social systems in struggle.

Li draws three lessons: hold to Marxism-Leninism, Martí's thought and socialism as the theoretical and institutional foundation; carry out steady reform to "update" the socialist model while limiting social costs; and protect the fundamental interests of the people, citing free healthcare and education, subsidies and clean conduct among Party cadres. Li treats popular trust in the Party as the key to Cuba's survival under internal and external pressure and as the feature other socialist states should most learn from. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's 2016 overview of Cuban socialism's stages and its supposed relevance for China and other socialist countries.
quoteEn: Cuba has its own distinctive understanding of the essence of socialism, namely national independence and benefit for the people.
quoteZh: 古巴对社会主义的本质有着自己独特的认识，那就是国家独立和为民造福。

glossary.zh: 有古巴特色的社会主义
glossary.explanation: Cuba's slogan, adopted after 1990, for building socialism suited to its own conditions. It echoes the Chinese phrase "socialism with Chinese characteristics".

t: The Latin American left in retreat: causes of the 2015–2016 setbacks and the case against declaring its death
zh: 日本马克思主义经济学者眼中的全球危机
paras: Writing in spring 2016, the author asks why left-wing governments in Latin America have suffered successive blows in the preceding six months, and whether the left is now in lasting decline. The answer is that the setbacks are real and have deep domestic and external causes, but that the left is neither dead nor dying. The article contends that the region's political pendulum has swung right and may swing back towards the centre-left after policy adjustment.

The piece opens with a country-by-country account of the swing to the right. It covers the election of Mauricio Macri in Argentina (November 2015), the opposition's two-thirds victory in Venezuela's National Assembly (December 2015) and the ensuing clash with President Maduro, the impeachment vote against Dilma Rousseff in Brazil's lower house (April 2016), Evo Morales's referendum defeat in Bolivia, and Rafael Correa's decision not to stand again in Ecuador. It then lists five causes, and closes with evidence of the left's continuing strength.

The author's five causes are as follows. First, the end of the commodity-export boom, which the article says slowed growth, forced austerity and left governments exposed after they failed to diversify their economies. Second, fragmented ruling coalitions and factional parties, with Brazil's Workers' Party and its coalition partner the PMDB as the main case. Third, corruption scandals that undermined the left's anti-corruption credentials and fuelled protest, often led by a new middle class. Fourth, what the author describes as US interference through funding of opposition groups, support for colour revolution tactics and sanctions on Venezuela. Fifth, rising right-wing strength in cities, provinces and a largely right-leaning media.

In rebutting claims that the left has died, the author points to the Cuban Communist Party's Seventh Congress (April 2016), to left governments still in office in many countries, and to the strength of the Peronists in Argentina and of left parties in Mexico and Peru. Persistent inequality and social conflict, together with the left's record on poverty, education, health and regional integration, are said to give it a solid base. The author concludes that, if left parties reflect on their errors, the pendulum may swing back, and ends with a remark by former Uruguayan president Mujica that the left should learn and return. Read the original if you want a concise 2016 Chinese overview of the Latin American left's reversals, with figures on the economy and elections.
quoteEn: It is true that the Latin American left has suffered setbacks and is tending towards an ebb, but it has not died, nor is it "on its last gasp".
quoteZh: 的确，拉美左翼受挫、趋于低潮，但拉美左翼并没有死亡，也没有“奄奄一息”。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Chinese official and academic writing for popular uprisings said to be promoted from abroad to change governments, modelled on events in post-Soviet states. Authors using it usually attribute such movements to Western, especially US, backing.

t: The global crisis in the eyes of Japanese Marxist economists
zh: 日本马克思主义经济学者眼中的全球危机
source: Political Economy Review (Zhengzhi jingjixue pinglun), 2016 no. 4
paras: Writing in 2016, Watanabe Masao and Tan Xiaojun survey how Japanese Marxist economists have interpreted the global financial crisis that began in 2008 and the subsequent eurozone debt crisis. The article is a review of the three main schools of Japanese Marxist economics: the orthodox school, the Uno school and the regulation school. The authors present the schools' views and conclude that the orthodox account is the most penetrating.

The article is organised around two kinds of understanding that Japanese scholars bring to the crisis: a 'stage' view of contemporary capitalism, and a 'current situation' view of the crisis itself. The first section draws on reports given by Kitahara Isamu (orthodox), Ito Makoto (Uno) and Yamada Toshio (regulation) at a 1995 conference. The second section treats each school's analysis of the post-2008 crisis, mainly through Imura Kiyoko, Ito Makoto (with Kaneko Masaru) and Yamada. A short conclusion compares them.

Imura, the orthodox representative, argues that capitalism underwent a 'degeneration' in the 1970s, after the end of dollar–gold convertibility and the turn to neoliberal policy. She holds that this produced speculative financial activity detached from the real economy, and that the eurozone sovereign-debt crisis followed from European states' pursuit of a finance-based national strategy and from banks' purchase of sovereign debt. Ito sees a return of liberal market competition and reads the crisis as a modern form of Marx's 'second type' of monetary panic, with workers facing a double exploitation through consumer credit. Yamada reads the crisis as structural, a shift from Fordism to a finance-led growth model driven by asset prices that collapsed in 2008, and sorts national economies into seven types.

The authors find three points of agreement: the crisis dates from the 1970s transition, it reflects a shift from production-led to finance-led capitalism, and its core is financial movement independent of real capital. They see differences in method. In their judgement Imura's treatment is more comprehensive and persuasive, while Ito's and Yamada's are narrower and one-sided, though still useful as other angles. They also call Ito's three factors for avoiding collapse nearly impossible to realise. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language overview of Japanese Marxist crisis theory and a mainland scholar's evaluation of its schools.
quoteEn: It is not hard to see from the views of the various schools that the orthodox school's understanding of this crisis is deeper, more thorough and more accurate, while the other schools' views, though one-sided, offer different perspectives for understanding this global economic crisis.
quoteZh: 从上述各学派的观点中不难看出，正统派对这场危机的认识具有更为深刻、透彻的特点，把握得也更为准确，而其他学派的观点虽然比较片面，但也为我们了解这场全球经济危机提供了不同的思考视角。

t: Research on foreign communist parties
st: Comparing domestic and overseas scholarship, and ways forward
zh: 国外共产党研究
zhSub: 域内外比较与推进路径
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 28 January 2016
paras: Writing in a Chinese Academy of Social Sciences newspaper in January 2016, Yu asks how Chinese research on foreign communist parties differs from Western research, and what Chinese scholars can learn. The field, Yu notes, was marginalised after the Soviet collapse and is now drawing renewed Western attention with the partial revival of the European radical left. Yu argues that comparison with overseas work can widen Chinese scholars' horizons and open new lines of inquiry.

The short piece has two parts. The first compares domestic and overseas scholarship on four points: perspective, scope, themes and analytical framework. The second sets out three proposed paths for Chinese research.

Yu says Chinese studies usually treat foreign communist parties within the international communist movement and as separate cases. Western scholars treat them as parties within a party system and as one family within the radical left, and they ask what the parties do, for example in relation to European integration, trade unions and social movements. Western work also uses interdisciplinary methods, such as mathematical models of radical-left electoral support. Chinese work, in Yu's account, relies largely on internet sources, offers little fieldwork, tends to describe single cases in depth, and is only beginning to use the radical-left concept, with some confusion.

Yu calls for Chinese scholars to draw on overseas findings, to move beyond detailed case description to the realities of contemporary capitalism and the future of the world socialist movement, and to develop comparative, general theory. Yu says this should build on existing strengths. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese assessment, from 2016, of the gaps in domestic scholarship on foreign communist parties.
quoteEn: Foreign scholars attend not only to the communist parties' "left-wing character" but even more to their "party character", stressing that they are "real political actors" who take part in competition and bear its pressures.
quoteZh: 国外学者不仅关注共产党的“左翼性”，更重视其“政党性”，强调它们是参与并承受竞争压力的“现实的政治行为者”。

glossary.explanation: A Western political-science category covering communist and other parties to the left of social democracy. Yu says Chinese scholars have only recently begun to use it, and not consistently.
The framework within which Chinese scholarship traditionally studies foreign communist parties, as part of the worldwide history of communism and socialism.

t: The Western "Marx fever" and its lessons
zh: 西方“马克思热”及其启示
paras: Writing in the People's Daily in February 2016, Cui asks what the renewed Western interest in Marx since the 2008 international financial crisis shows. The article argues that Marxism, long treated in Western mainstream opinion as a heterodoxy confined to marginal academic and left-wing circles, is again drawing attention because the crisis exposed contradictions capitalism cannot overcome. In Cui's view, this offers evidence of the truth of Marxism.

The commentary is a short survey of signs of this "Marx fever". It covers mainstream media coverage, book sales, protest slogans, university courses, statements by Western scholars, and study groups and sites devoted to Marx. It ends with a reference to Deng Xiaoping's remarks in the early 1990s.

Cui's evidence is descriptive. The Guardian, The Times, the Financial Times and Time are said to have given Marx prominent space, and slogans such as "Marx was right!" are reported from Wall Street and German streets. Terry Eagleton's Why Marx Was Right (2011), Elmar Altvater's essay and David Harvey's work on capitalism's contradictions are presented as scholarly defences of Marxism or calls to "return to Marx". Cui also cites Germany's "Marx evening school", Harvey's Capital reading group and visitor numbers at Marx's birthplace museum in Trier.

Cui concludes that this revival supports Deng Xiaoping's early-1990s prediction, made when the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe had left many pessimistic, that more people would come to endorse Marxism "because Marxism is a science". The Western trend is therefore taken as indirect confirmation of Marxism's truth in the contemporary world. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Party newspaper in 2016 used Western interest in Marx to affirm Marxism's validity.
quoteEn: The "Marx fever" that arose in the West after the international financial crisis confirms, from one angle, Comrade Deng Xiaoping's foresight, and also confirms the truth of Marxism in the contemporary world.
quoteZh: 国际金融危机爆发后在西方兴起的“马克思热”，从一个侧面佐证了邓小平同志的远见卓识，也佐证了马克思主义在当代世界的真理性。

t: The new vision of civilisation in Western Marxist research
zh: 西方马克思主义研究的新文明构想
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 28 April 2016
paras: Writing in a 2016 newspaper commentary, Che Yuling asks where human civilisation should go after the Enlightenment, whose legacy the author links to technological over-extension, nihilism, consumerism, environmental degradation and moral decline. Che argues that contemporary Western Marxists offer a constructive answer: a new type of civilisation that overcomes the defects of modern civilisation and avoids resource depletion, ecological damage and spiritual crisis.

The piece has three parts. It first sets out the features of a new civilisation as Marx describes them, then the claim that the network era calls for one, and finally the Marxist route to realising it. It draws on ecological Marxism, historical-geographical materialism, David Harvey and István Mészáros, and ends with a note on China.

Che reads Marx as treating all social formations up to capitalism as 'prehistory', after which a truly human history begins in communism centred on the all-round development of the human being, not on the economy. Contemporary ecological Marxists and historical-geographical materialists draw three features from this: the liberation of both humans and nature, a 'co-existence' that goes beyond the nation-state, and a meaningful, poetic life. Che adds that Harvey's 'time-space compression' and the rise of network-based 'space economy' have made capital global, uneven in development and culturally corrosive. Following Marx's view that 'the real barrier of capitalist production is capital itself', Che argues that capital's expansion into every field shrinks its own profit space. Mészáros's 'structural crisis' is cited as showing that 'going beyond capital' is the only option.

Che concludes that China's Scientific Outlook on Development and its ecological civilisation drive already show the new civilisation Marx envisaged. In this reading, Chinese practice and Marxist theory confirm each other, and Western Marxist visions of a new civilisation have real relevance. Read the original if you want a short, officially aligned Chinese introduction to how Western Marxist ecological and spatial theories are used to support the idea of a new civilisation.
quoteEn: Clearly, Marx had already defined the fundamental feature of the new civilisation: a new social formation that is not centred on the economy but puts people first and differs from rule by capital.
quoteZh: 显然，马克思已经明确了新文明的根本特征，即不以经济为中心，而是以人为本、有别于资本主宰的新的社会形态。

glossary.explanation: A guiding concept promoted by the Party leadership in the early 2000s under Hu Jintao. It stresses people-centred, coordinated and sustainable development.
An official Chinese policy concept that makes environmental protection and sustainable development part of the country's overall development goals.
The tradition of Marxist thought outside the Soviet orbit. In Chinese usage the label is sometimes applied loosely to contemporary Western Marxists such as Harvey and Mészáros.

t: Latin American Marxism since 1909
st: Transcending "Eurocentrism" and "Indo-American exceptionalism"
zh: 1909年以来的拉美马克思主义
zhSub: 对“欧洲中心主义”与“拉美例外论”的超越
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by the French Marxist sociologist and philosopher Michael Löwy (given in the Chinese text as M. Roy), part of a series on Latin American Marxism since 1909. Löwy argues that two opposed errors have haunted Marxism in Latin America: Eurocentrism, which mechanically transplants the European nineteenth-century pattern of development, and "Indo-American exceptionalism", which treats Latin American particularity as absolute and Marxism as a purely European theory. The creative path, he holds, lies in a dialectical unity of the universal and the particular.

The article is a historical survey from the introduction of Marxism by European immigrants in the late nineteenth century to the 1970s and early 1980s. It moves through the Second International's parties, the communist parties of the 1920s, the Stalinisation of the 1930s, the post-war debates on economic history, the Cuban Revolution, Castroism, the Central American revolutions and liberation theology. Figures discussed include Julio Antonio Mella, José Carlos Mariátegui, Vittorio Codovilla, Sergio Bagú, Caio Prado Jr., Silvio Frondizi, Che Guevara, Gunder Frank and Gustavo Gutiérrez.

Löwy contends that both errors, despite their opposition, reach the same conclusion: that socialism does not suit Latin America. He offers Haya de la Torre's APRA as the exceptionalist case and Stalinist stage theory, calling for an anti-feudal bourgeois-democratic revolution, as the Eurocentric one. Against both he sets thinkers who argued that colonial and dependent capitalism, not feudalism, shaped the region, that the national bourgeoisie is weak and subordinate to imperialism, and that revolution must therefore be socialist. Mariátegui is presented as the strongest example of the synthesis, combining internationalism with indigenous communal traditions. Löwy treats the Cuban Revolution as a turning point that broke the Eurocentric and Stalinist hold and revived the "original communism" of the 1920s.

Löwy concludes that the successes of Latin American Marxism came when it joined general principles to regional realities. He also notes the limits of guerrilla voluntarism and the new weight of radical Christianity, which he says should now be seen as an organic part of revolutionary movements. He ends by endorsing Mariátegui's call for unity among socialist currents without giving up their theoretical differences. Read the original if you want a compact, sympathetic overview of Latin American Marxist currents and their disputes over stages of revolution, dependency and the Latin American revolutionary tradition.
quoteEn: The correct path for the creative development of Latin American Marxism lies in handling the two errors dialectically and transcending them, that is, in seeking a dialectical unity between the universal and the particular.
quoteZh: 拉美马克思主义的创造性发展的正确之途，就显现为对二者的辩证处理与超越，即在普遍性与特殊性之间追寻辩证统一。

t: Marxist movements in Africa
zh: 非洲的马克思主义运动
paras: Is there a distinctive African contribution to Marxist thought? The article, credited to Glaser and published in Marxism and Reality in 2014, notes that many African Marxist-Leninist leaders flatly denied it. After the first wave of post-independence "African socialism", they insisted on a single universal Marxism-Leninism. The author argues that African Marxism was not without original contributions, and that African socialism should be counted as an independent contribution to it.

The article moves from African socialism to the later Marxist-Leninist regimes. It begins with Pan-Africanism, W.E.B. DuBois, George Padmore, Kwame Nkrumah, Sékou Touré and Julius Nyerere. It then covers Soviet theories of a "non-capitalist" path and three routes by which Marxism reached Africa: colonial contacts, multi-ethnic urban milieux, and the communist bloc. Further sections treat military coups, guerrilla "people's war" and Amilcar Cabral, and the exceptional cases of South Africa and Ethiopia. The article closes with the decline of African Marxism after 1989–91.

The author makes three main moves. First, the regimes were not mere Soviet creations: Marxist governments often kept Western links, and their authoritarianism is attributed to home-grown African Leninism. Glaser defends the military regimes against critics who doubted their sincerity, but also doubts that guerrilla movements were more democratic or more committed to socialism. Second, the author lists genuine innovations. These include Siad Barre's attempt to combine Marxism with Islam, the Eritrean and Tigrayan fronts' positions on national self-determination, Touré's mass-party experiments, and Madagascar's limited multiparty system. Third, the author explains the failures. External causes were underdevelopment, war and Cold War pressures. Internal causes were impatience, forced rural policies, alienation of society, and a Leninist idea of participation as mobilisation towards goals set by the ruling party, not as free choice among competing projects.

Glaser concludes that African socialism and Marxism were short-lived, with most regimes liberalising from the mid-1980s and renouncing Marxism in 1990–91. The turn to representative democracy at least lets citizens remove bad rulers, but the author says dependence on the IMF and World Bank has narrowed real choice and that the new capitalism is no panacea. Socialists and social democrats should avoid neoliberal traps, learn from the negative lessons of African Marxism, and may still need Marxism to analyse new class inequalities. Read the original if you want a detailed comparative survey of African socialist and Marxist regimes, from Ghana and Guinea to Ethiopia and Madagascar, and an assessment of why they failed.
quoteEn: On the whole, we hold that African Marxism is not entirely lacking in original contributions.
quoteZh: 总体上说，我们要论述非洲的马克思主义并不完全缺少其原创贡献。

t: The method of ecological Marxism
zh: 生态马克思主义的方法
source: Studies in Contemporary Chinese Marxist Philosophy, 2015, no. 4 (cumulative series)
paras: This text is a Chinese version of a conference paper by Hannah Holleman (the name is rendered in Chinese in the source). It asks what methodology underlies the strengths of what John Bellamy Foster calls the "third stage" of ecosocialist research. Holleman argues that the revival of ecological Marxism comes from strict adherence to Marx's own method, which she holds is still a powerful tool for social change.

The paper first sketches three stages of ecosocialism since the 1980s. The first grafted Marx onto existing green theory, assuming Marx offered no ecological foundation. The second returned to Marx's materialist and naturalist roots, though Holleman, following Foster, calls it simplified, idealised and moralising. The third restores Marx's radical materialist critique and dialectics. The paper then sets out five features of Marx's method and briefly surveys recent applications, such as a study of oceans and fisheries, before ending with a conclusion on ecological civilization.

The five features are: embracing materialism, using abstraction critically, applying dialectics, attending to historical specificity, and linking ethical and political change to critical social analysis. Holleman, drawing on Sweezy, Lewontin and Levins, and York and Mancus, contends that abstraction must be chosen to fit the problem and tested against historical evidence. Dialectics, she says, steers between reductionism and an undifferentiated holism that treats everything as "one". She presents Marx's account of labour as a metabolic process between humans and nature as the historical and ecological base of this method. Citing Mészáros, she argues that ethics cannot replace a thorough critique of politics.

In the conclusion Holleman proposes that the method be used to assess the aims and strategies of any movement, including those that call themselves socialist, since ideological slogans may diverge from practice. She names three conditions for a worthwhile struggle: material and political equality, an end to all forms of oppression and exploitation, and a society in which rational regulation governs the human relation to nature. She contrasts this with romantic green ideas and with ecological modernization theory. Whether the goal is called ecological civilization or something else, she holds that critical social analysis is needed to overcome obstacles. Read the original if you want a compact statement of the methodological foundations of the Monthly Review school of ecological Marxism, as presented to a Chinese audience interested in ecological civilization.
quoteEn: The revival of ecological Marxism owes much to strict adherence to Marx's methodological orientation and to building its own theory on Marx's methodology.
quoteZh: 生态马克思主义的复兴，在很大程度上得益于严格遵守马克思的方法论取向，得益于根据马克思的方法论来建构自己的理论。

glossary.explanation: A concept promoted in Chinese official discourse since the 2000s, referring to a form of development that integrates environmental protection into economic and social life. The conference for which the paper was written took it as its theme.

t: The European refugee crisis and the predicament of "universal values"
zh: 欧洲难民危机与“普世价值”的困境
paras: Writing in early 2016, Zhang Weiwei takes up the refugee influx into Europe since 2015 and argues that it is directly linked to the "universal values" the West promoted in the Middle East. In Zhang's account, the crisis exposes paradoxes and dilemmas in the idea of "universal values" itself. Europe's early celebration of the "Arab Spring" has, the author says, turned within five years into alarm.

The commentary has three parts. The first describes the "arrogance" of promoting "freedom", "democracy" and "human rights" as universal, and recounts two waves of Western-backed "democratization" in the Middle East: the post-2003 Iraq war and "Greater Middle East" plan, and the uprisings from 2011. The second sets out four paradoxes revealed by the crisis. The third draws lessons for China and the world.

Zhang traces the arrogance to a view of history in which the Western model is the end point of human development, reinforced by a missionary tradition. The four paradoxes are as follows. These values were detached from the conditions of Middle Eastern societies and left sectarian, ethnic and economic problems unsolved or worse. Western democratic politics, in which politicians answer to their own voters, works against the human rights of outsiders, as shown by border fences and EU disputes over quotas. The values struggle to accommodate multiculturalism, which Cameron and Merkel had already declared a failure. Abstract principles give way to concrete national interests, including among EU states and in the United States' reluctance to take in refugees.

Zhang concludes that Chinese people should always ask why of any value claimed to be universal, and that the crisis shows the significance of persisting with socialism with Chinese characteristics. The author predicts that the West's discursive hegemony will decline, and calls on China, as a responsible major country, to offer ideas of its own, such as "peace and development", which Zhang holds are preconditions for freedom, democracy and human rights. Read the original if you want an example of how a prominent Chinese commentator in a Party journal framed the refugee crisis as a critique of Western "universal values" in 2016.
quoteEn: Without "peace", "freedom", "democracy" and "human rights" will be hard to sustain; without "development", how fragile "freedom", "democracy" and "human rights" will be!
quoteZh: 没有“和平”，“自由”、“民主”、“人权”将难以维系；没有“发展”，“自由”、“民主”、“人权”将是何等的脆弱！

glossary.explanation: The idea that values such as freedom, democracy and human rights apply to all societies. In Chinese official discourse the term is often criticised as a vehicle for Western ideological influence.
The official name for China's current political and economic path, associated with the reform era since the late 1970s.
The power to set the terms and concepts of international debate. Chinese commentators use it to criticise Western dominance in global narratives.
A formula used in Chinese official foreign-policy discourse since the 1980s, describing them as the main themes of the era.

t: New trends in Vietnam's foreign strategy after the 12th Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam
zh: 越共十二大之后越南外交战略的新趋向
paras: Writing in late 2016, Pan Jin'e asks what new ideas the 12th National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam (January 2016) introduced into Vietnam's external strategy and where Vietnamese foreign policy is heading. The article's answer is that Vietnam will keep diplomacy in the service of national interest, integrate actively into the international community, stress economic development while balancing the major powers, and pursue a pragmatic line of "both cooperation and struggle".

The article first sets out the Congress report's foreign-policy line and the eight main tasks the Party assigned for the next five years, drawing on the Central Propaganda Department's explanatory materials. It then reviews the practice of the new leadership: the April 2016 changes in office, Prime Minister Nguyen Xuan Phuc's visits to Russia, Japan and China, Barack Obama's visit, reactions to the South China Sea arbitration ruling, and the August 2016 foreign affairs conference. It ends with five trends it expects in coming years, drawing on Vietnam's first Diplomatic Blue Book (2015).

Pan argues that Vietnam's diplomacy is, first, anchored in securing a peaceful environment and external resources for economic growth, with economic integration as its core task. Second, it follows an independent, diversified and multilateral line built on non-aligned "partnerships" and the "three nos" (no military alliances, no foreign bases, no reliance on one country against another). Third, it balances the great powers while treating each differently: Japan is welcomed, the United States is both courted and guarded against "peaceful evolution", Russia is a traditional friend with limited economic potential, and China is a close but disputed partner. Pan reads Party General Secretary Nguyen Phu Trong's stress on absolute obedience to unified Party leadership as a sign of disagreement within the leadership, including over China policy.

Pan concludes that Vietnam's foreign affairs face instability, citing divisions within the leadership, the South China Sea dispute and what the author calls threats of subversion. Uncertainty over the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP), which the new National Assembly did not ratify as planned, adds to this. Pan expects Vietnam to keep developing economic ties with China while its China policy may prove unstable or inconsistent, which the author says demands more careful handling of China–Vietnam relations. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's reading of Vietnamese foreign policy in 2016 and of the Vietnamese sources on which it relies.
quoteEn: In its external relations Vietnam will place still clearer emphasis on national interest as the highest standard, uphold the values of "national interest above all" and "no absolute friends and no absolute enemies", and adopt a more flexible, case-by-case pragmatic approach.
quoteZh: 越南在对外关系中将更加明确强调把国家利益作为最高标准，奉行“国家利益至上”“没有绝对的朋友也没有绝对的敌人”的价值观，采取相机抉择更加灵活多变的务实策略。

glossary.explanation: A formula in the Vietnamese Party's foreign-policy line, applied even to a single country across different issues. Partners and adversaries are defined by their stance on Vietnam's sovereignty and can change category.
A term used in communist-party discourse for alleged Western efforts to undermine socialist systems through non-military means such as ideology, culture and economic pressure.
Vietnam's declared defence-policy stance: no military alliances, no foreign military bases on its soil, and no reliance on one country against another.

t: Drawing lessons from the loss of the Soviet Union's socialist institutional advantages
zh: 深刻认识苏联社会主义制度优势丧失的教训
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Wang Rui asks why the Soviet Union lost the advantages of its socialist system and, in the end, the system itself. The article holds that after strong early achievements, Soviet socialist construction slowed from the 1970s and the system's advantages drained away. From the mid-1980s, Wang argues, reform turned from upholding and improving socialism into a wholesale negation of it, producing economic and social crisis and collapse.

The article is organised around four causes, each presented as the loss of one pillar that the system's advantages depend on: a theoretical foundation, institutional support, a material guarantee and a leading core. It moves chronologically through the Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev periods. Each section ends with a lesson for present-day socialist countries, and a short conclusion draws on Deng Xiaoping.

Wang argues first that ideology moved from rigidity under Brezhnev to outright betrayal under Gorbachev. Dogmatic Marxism-Leninism, the heavy-handed treatment of intellectual disputes and then Gorbachev's "openness" and pluralism are said to have eroded belief and let bourgeois liberalisation spread. Second, after the 19th Party Conference (1988), reform veered off course: Stalin was wholly repudiated, tens of thousands of "informal organisations" arose, nationalist separatism grew, and power shifted from the Party to the soviets, ending the Party's leadership. Third, Wang says that high-speed, poor-quality growth, a lopsided economy and low consumption left the Soviet Union falling behind the United States and the West, fuelling discontent.
