Fourth, the Party lost its vanguard character and purity: a privileged bureaucracy distanced itself from the people, and Wang lists five changes in the Party's nature, guiding ideology, goals, status and organisational principle (democratic centralism).

Wang concludes that the Soviet collapse does not show Marxism-Leninism to be outdated or socialism itself to be flawed, only that the Soviet model had defects. China, the article says, must study this lesson to avoid repeating it. Wang calls for upholding Marxism as the guiding ideology while innovating, reforming without abandoning socialism's basic principles and system, raising productivity with attention to quality and living standards, and keeping the Party close to the people. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Party journal summarised the causes of Soviet collapse in 2016 and the lessons it drew for China.
quoteEn: The disintegration of the Soviet Union does not prove that Marxism-Leninism is outdated or that the socialist system itself is flawed; it only proves that the Soviet model of socialism had defects and malpractices.
quoteZh: 苏联的解体并不能证明马克思列宁主义已经过时，或者社会主义制度本身有问题，而只是证明苏联社会主义模式存在缺陷和弊端。

glossary.explanation: The Leninist organisational principle of Communist parties, combining discussion and election with binding discipline and obedience to higher bodies. The article says the late Soviet Party stressed democracy and played down centralism.
Standard Chinese Party terms for the Party's role as the leading force of the working class and for its freedom from corruption and ideological dilution.
A Chinese Party term for the spread of Western liberal political ideas, seen as undermining socialist leadership and ideology.

t: What was Dimitrov's attitude to the Xi'an Incident?
st: A query on Pantsov's biography of Mao Zedong
zh: 季米特洛夫对西安事变的态度究竟如何
zhSub: 对潘佐夫著《毛泽东传》的一点质疑
source: Chinese Reading Weekly (Zhonghua dushu bao), 2 March 2016
paras: Li Yibin takes issue with one passage in Alexander Pantsov's biography of Mao Zedong, whose Chinese edition has drawn wide attention because it draws on declassified Soviet archives. The article asks how Georgi Dimitrov, General Secretary of the Comintern, actually viewed the Xi'an Incident of December 1936. Li argues that Dimitrov opposed the incident, as Stalin did, and that Pantsov's claim that he was delighted by it rests on a misreading of a source.

The piece is a short critical note, first published in the Chinese Reading Weekly (Zhonghua dushu bao) in March 2016. It first sketches Dimitrov's career and his role in Comintern work on China. It then sets out Comintern documents and Dimitrov's diary entries from August and December 1936, followed by the Soviet strategic situation and the diary entry that Li believes Pantsov misread.

Li's evidence runs in three steps. First, Dimitrov distrusted Zhang Xueliang even before the incident: a telegram of August 1936 told the Chinese Communist Party not to trust him, and after the incident Dimitrov wrote to Stalin suspecting Communist involvement. Second, Li explains Soviet hostility by the memory of Zhang Zuolin's 1927 raid on the Soviet embassy and the killing of Li Dazhao, and above all by Stalin's strategy of backing Chiang Kai-shek against Japan while Germany and Japan threatened the USSR. On this account Dimitrov, a Soviet citizen, could not have diverged from Stalin; his late-night telephone exchange with Stalin on 14 December and the meetings that produced the telegram urging a peaceful settlement show the two in agreement. Third, Li traces the error to Dimitrov's diary entry for 13 December. In it, the favourable, optimistic assessment of Zhang comes from Stomonyakov, the deputy foreign commissar who brought the news, not from Dimitrov himself.

Li concludes that Pantsov mistook one speaker for another, a case of "putting Zhang's hat on Li", and that this distorted the historical record. He also notes that Zhou Enlai later called the Comintern's depiction of Zhang as a tool of Japan completely wrong. Read the original if you work on Comintern–CCP relations, the Xi'an Incident or Pantsov's use of Soviet archives and want to see a specific source-critical objection with its citations.
quoteEn: It is quite clear that, in using this entry from Dimitrov's diary, Pantsov mistook words spoken by Stomonyakov for words spoken by Dimitrov.
quoteZh: 很显然，潘佐夫在使用季米特洛夫日记中的这条史料时，误把斯托马尼亚科夫说的话当成了是季米特洛夫说的。

glossary.explanation: The detention of Chiang Kai-shek at Xi'an on 12 December 1936 by Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng, who pressed him to end the civil war against the Communists and resist Japan. It was settled peacefully and led to a united front against Japan.
The Communist International, founded in 1919 and dissolved in 1943, which coordinated communist parties worldwide under Soviet leadership, including the Chinese Communist Party.

t: Never let go of the banner of communism
zh: 共产主义这面旗帜什么时候都不能丢
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in March 2016, Chen Shuguang responds to what the author calls the "theory of communism's remoteness", the view that communism is illusory and unreachable. Chen takes up Xi Jinping's remarks since the 18th Party Congress (2012) that communism is not as simple as "potatoes stewed with beef" yet is not a mirage. The article argues that communism is the spiritual banner of Communists and must never be abandoned.

Chen first reconstructs three lines of reasoning behind the sceptical view: communism concerns only a distant future; "distribution according to need" is unbelievable; and the collapse of the socialist bloc and China's present problems refute the ideal. The commentary answers these in three sections. They deal with communism as both a social system and a movement, with the essence of communism, and with setbacks and the gap between ideal and reality.

Chen's central move is to treat communism as a "totality" with three dimensions: a system, a doctrine and a real movement. Citing Marx and Engels's definition of communism as the real movement that abolishes the present state of things, Chen says Chinese revolution, socialist construction and reform are all continuations of that movement. Features such as the leading role of the working class, public ownership and common prosperity are described as communist elements accumulating within socialism. Second, Chen argues that the essence of communism, as Marx and Engels describe it in three ways, is the free and all-round development of each individual, not the literal wording of "distribution according to need". The concrete shape of the distant future, Chen holds, should be left to future practice. Third, Chen attributes the Soviet and East European collapse to departing from Marxism, and says the failure of one socialist model is not the failure of socialism.

Chen concludes that the gap between ideal and reality is normal, and that the way forward is to reform reality towards the ideal rather than abandon the ideal to suit reality. The article says China's problems, such as inequality, corruption and pollution, are either growing pains, results of departing from Marxist principles, or costs of practice. Chen holds that socialism with Chinese characteristics keeps the basic principles of scientific socialism and the banner of communism, and that, so long as exploitation and oppression exist, communism remains a banner for justice and liberation. Read the original if you want an example of how a 2016 official-press commentary defends the communist ideal against scepticism inside and outside the Party.
quoteEn: The way out lies in changing reality to approach the ideal, not in negating the ideal to suit reality.
quoteZh: 问题的出路在于改造现实以趋向理想，而不是否定理想以迎合现实。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism, developed since reform and opening up began in the late 1970s. The article says it is socialism first and keeps the basic principles of scientific socialism.
The goal of prosperity shared by all, rather than a few getting rich. The article lists it among the communist elements within socialism.

t: New Youth and the spread of Marxism in China
zh: 《新青年》与马克思主义在中国的传播
paras: Yin Yungong asks how the journal New Youth became the main Chinese vehicle for propagating Marxism-Leninism. The author argues that it did so only after a winding process of understanding, in which the journal and its founder Chen Duxiu moved from a shallow, eclectic view of socialism to a firm commitment to Marxism.

The short newspaper article first notes earlier, fragmentary mentions of Marx's ideas in Wanguo Gongbao (1889), Zhejiang Chao (1903) and Minbao (1906). It then follows New Youth, founded as Youth Magazine in 1915, through its early issues, the reader correspondence of 1916, the impact of the October Revolution, the Marxism-focused issues of 1919, the Labour Day special issue of May 1920, and the journal's adoption as a Party organ in September 1920.

Yin shows that in 1915 Chen Duxiu knew the origins and main ideas of Marxism but treated socialism as just one of several Western intellectual tools, and the journal profiled no Marxist figures. When a reader urged the journal to promote socialism, an editorial reply said socialism could wait in China because industry was undeveloped. For Yin, the turning point came with Li Dazhao's 1918 articles praising the October Revolution and the concentrated Marxist issues of 1919. The Labour Day issue is presented as a milestone in joining Marxism to the Chinese workers' movement and as the start of the adaptation of Marxism-Leninism to China. Yin adds that the May Fourth Movement prepared the ground for spread among ordinary people.

Yin concludes that New Youth deserves great credit for choosing the best ideological weapon for the Chinese nation, and presents Chen Duxiu's shift from radical democrat to Marxist as a classic case for Chinese intellectuals. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of the journal's path toward Marxism, with quotations from Chen Duxiu's 1915 essay and the 1916 reader exchange.
quoteEn: Chen Duxiu's shift from radical democracy to Marxism, from man of letters to Marxist believer, from shallow belief to deep belief, became a classic specimen for China's intellectual circles.
quoteZh: 陈独秀从激进的民主主义转向马克思主义、从文人学者转为马克思主义信徒——从浅信到深信，成为中国知识界的经典标本。

t: Deng Zhongxia's thought on the policies and tactics of the working-class struggle
zh: 邓中夏关于工人阶级斗争政策和策略的思想
paras: This short commentary, originally published in Guangming Daily on 26 April 2016, examines how Deng Zhongxia, an early Party leader and labour-movement organiser, thought about policy and tactics in the workers' movement. Xu argues that Deng came to see policy and tactics as decisive for the movement's success or failure, and that his ideas remain a notable part of the Party's early theoretical legacy.

Xu first sketches Deng's practical record: the Changxindian workers' movement, the Beijing–Hankou railway movement, the Shanghai Japanese cotton-mill strike and the Guangdong–Hong Kong general strike. The article then takes up four themes: the importance of policy and tactics, building a broad united front, concentrating blows on the main enemy, and combining economic with political struggle.

Xu reports that after the failure of the Beijing–Hankou railway strike Deng concluded that the small Chinese proletariat could not defeat powerful enemies alone. He therefore called for worker–peasant and wider alliances, and blamed the May Thirtieth Movement's failure on the proletariat's isolation. During the Guangdong–Hong Kong strike, Deng urged dropping the slogan of opposing all imperialisms in favour of a policy aimed at Britain alone, with permits for non-British goods. In Deng's own assessment, this kept Guangdong's merchants neutral and split the imperialist front. Deng also opposed both purely economic struggle and political slogans that ignore workers' material interests.

Xu concludes that Deng treated these tactics as the core of leading the workers' movement. In Deng's view, the final aim of all workers' struggle is the complete liberation of labour, yet struggles for better pay and conditions should be pursued even under capitalism. Read the original if you want a brief overview of Deng Zhongxia's tactical thinking, as presented in a Chinese Party-oriented account of early labour history.
quoteEn: Although Deng Zhongxia did not formulate it in such a high-level generalisation, in organising and leading the workers' movement he gradually came to see that policy and tactics were the key issue determining its success or failure.
quoteZh: 邓中夏虽然没有作出这样的高度概括，但他在组织和领导工人运动中逐步认识到政策和策略是关系到工人运动成败的关键问题。

t: Marx and Proudhonism
zh: 马克思与蒲鲁东主义
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in 2016, Yang Hongyuan asks what the long entanglement between Marx and Proudhonism reveals about the intellectual revolution Marx achieved. Yang argues that Marx's theory should be assessed comparatively, and that his twenty-year critique of Proudhonism has both historical value and present relevance.
The short commentary has three parts. It first reconstructs Proudhonism itself, then traces Marx's shift from praise to systematic polemic, and finally draws lessons for today.

Yang rejects the usual labels for Proudhon (petty-bourgeois socialism, reformism, anarchism) as too simple. Proudhonism, in Yang's account, was an ambitious system of serial dialectics, social economics and a theory of social revolution, rooted in the clash between advanced ideas and France's backward small-peasant economy. Marx's verdict of petty-bourgeois socialism is judged accurate. Marx first welcomed Proudhon's examination of private property, then criticised his Hegelian method and his substitution of economic categories for revolution. Yang holds that the critique let Marx integrate historical materialism, political economy and socialist doctrine. It did not remove Proudhon's influence among workers, because slogans such as "property is theft" were easier for poorly educated workers to grasp than theory. Yang adds that Capital, volume 1 (1867) eventually brought wide acceptance of Marx's doctrine.

Yang concludes that profound theory survives the test of history, and that Proudhonism persists because the world-wide development of productive forces that communism requires is not yet achieved. Current theories advocating class conciliation, small private property with equal distribution, anarchy or opposition to the dictatorship of the proletariat are said to share its spirit. Yang calls for using Marx's methods and tactics against them. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese statement of how Marx's critique of Proudhon is used to address present-day ideas.
quoteEn: Profound thought and scientific theory can stand undefeated only if they withstand the test of history and the tempering of time.
quoteZh: 深邃的思想和科学的理论只有经得起历史的检验与时间的锤炼方能立于不败之地。

glossary.explanation: A Marxist term for working-class political rule in the transition to communism. In Chinese official usage it remains a basic principle of the state.

t: The "self-transformation" of the privileged stratum in the collapse of the CPSU and its warnings
zh: 苏共垮台中特权阶层的“自我蜕变”及其警示
paras: Guo Yanlin asks why a party with more than 70 years of history and over 20 million members, the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU), collapsed. The article argues that, among many contributing causes, a decisive one was the growth of privilege and corruption inside the Party, which hardened into a vested-interest, bureaucratic stratum. In Guo's reading, the collapse was to a large extent the "self-transformation" of this privileged stratum rather than the work of anti-communists from outside.

The article has three parts. It first traces how the privileged stratum formed, from Lenin's struggle against bureaucracy through the Stalin, Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev periods. It then sets out four political harms of privilege and corruption. Finally it draws five warnings for the Chinese Communist Party, written in 2016 in the context of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party.

Guo's central claim is that the privileged officials, who controlled key posts and enjoyed special housing, supply and education benefits, used Gorbachev-era reforms to convert administrative control into legal private ownership. The author cites a 1995 Russian survey in which 74–75 per cent of the political elite and 61 per cent of the economic elite came from the Soviet cadre corps. Guo also cites David Kotz: around 1990 only 5–20 per cent of the Soviet public favoured capitalism, but about 76.7 per cent of an elite of roughly 100,000 did. The harms listed are loss of ideological appeal, a crisis of trust between Party and people, the spread of unwritten rules such as bribery and the sale of posts, and the elite's role as vanguard of capitalist restoration.

Guo calls for a long-term, continuous campaign against privilege during the primary stage of socialism. The proposals are to strengthen ideals and convictions and oppose historical nihilism, never to use privilege as a tool of political order, to reform supervision and discipline inspection so that officials dare not, cannot and do not want to be corrupt, and to treat close ties with the people as the basis of anti-privilege work. Read the original if you want an official Chinese interpretation, published in 2016, of the Soviet collapse as a story of elite degeneration, and of the lessons the author draws for Party discipline.
quoteEn: It can be said that the main force that brought down the CPSU was not anti-communists, but the privileged and corrupt elements within the CPSU itself.
quoteZh: 可以说，搞垮苏共的主要力量并不是反共分子，而是苏共党内的特权腐败分子。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan promoted since the 18th Party Congress (2012) under Xi Jinping, covering discipline, anti-corruption and Party-building.
An official thesis that China is at an early stage of socialism, expected to last a long historical period; it was formalised in the 1980s.
In official usage, a label for views that denigrate or distort the history of the Party and of socialism.

glossary.pinyin: bù gǎn fǔ, bù néng fǔ, bù xiǎng fǔ
glossary.en: dare not, cannot and do not want to be corrupt
glossary.explanation: A formula in official anti-corruption discourse describing deterrence, institutional constraint and ideological conviction as three layers of prevention.

t: The historical facts of Lenin's defence and consolidation of Party unity must not be distorted
zh: 列宁维护和巩固党的统一的历史事实不容歪曲
paras: Yuan Xiuli takes up the long-running charge that Lenin's draft resolution "On Party Unity", adopted by the Tenth Congress of the Russian Communist Party (Bolsheviks) in March 1921, was a weapon in factional struggle. In the article's account, critics have presented it as a tool for crushing opposition, protecting one-party rule and expressing Lenin's "autocratic thinking". Yuan argues that this reading contradicts both Lenin's thought and the historical record, and that the resolution aimed to safeguard the unity of the Bolshevik Party under exceptional conditions.

Writing in Hongqi Wengao in 2016, Yuan reconstructs the circumstances of 1921 and relies heavily on Lenin's own speeches at the congress, quoted from the Chinese edition of his Collected Works. The article is organised in three sections: defending Party unity, consolidating Party leadership, and securing the most urgent task of economic construction. It focuses on the "Workers' Opposition" and the "Democratic Centralism" group.

Yuan's central move is to read the resolution as a call for unity rather than an attack. The article stresses that Lenin acknowledged the opposition groups' valid criticisms of bureaucracy, and that the congress elected four of their members to the Central Committee and asked them to withdraw their resignations. In Yuan's telling, these groups then drifted towards syndicalism and anarchism: they demanded an all-Russian congress of producers to run the economy and put trade unions above the Party. They also distributed pamphlets and held separate meetings. Yuan adds that, after the Kronstadt rebellion of February 1921 and amid economic ruin, the dispute over the unions' role became what Lenin called an "excessive luxury". The Workers' Opposition's "leftist" resistance to the New Economic Policy is said to have obstructed the economic recovery the Party urgently needed.

Yuan concludes that Lenin's leadership resolved these disagreements, preserved unity, strengthened Party leadership and gave the New Economic Policy a firm political and organisational guarantee. The article also notes Lenin's warning that the NEP was an "unprecedentedly difficult retreat", which demanded stronger conviction and discipline from the Party. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-theory journal in China defended the 1921 resolution against its critics, and which of Lenin's statements it uses to do so.
quoteEn: Maintaining the unity of the Party and achieving unity of will in the proletarian vanguard is the basic condition for guaranteeing the victory of the dictatorship of the proletariat.
quoteZh: 保持党的统一和实现无产阶级先锋队意志的统一是保证无产阶级专政胜利的基本条件。

glossary.explanation: A faction within the Russian Communist Party around 1920–21 that wanted trade unions to run the economy. The Tenth Congress condemned it as a syndicalist deviation.
Another opposition group in the Bolshevik Party of the early 1920s that criticised bureaucratic centralisation. The article treats it alongside the Workers' Opposition.
The policy introduced in Soviet Russia in 1921 to replace War Communism. It allowed limited private trade and a market in agricultural produce.

t: Warnings from the Soviet collapse for building Marxist ruling parties
zh: 苏联解体对马克思主义执政党建设的警示
paras: More than twenty years after the Soviet Union dissolved, debate over its causes continues, with scholars pointing to nationalities, loss of belief, reform, or the federal state form. Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Xue Yan accepts that many causes were at work but contends that the Soviet Communist Party's flaws as a ruling party were what ultimately brought the collapse. The article draws from this lessons for how socialist countries should strengthen Marxist ruling parties.

The piece is a short commentary organised in six numbered sections. Each takes one failing of the Soviet party and sets it beside the stance of the Communist Party of China: guiding ideology, the succession of leaders, privilege and corruption, error correction, control over reform, and international relations. Xue draws on Soviet figures such as Ryzhkov, Bolkin and Titarenko, and on statements by Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping.

Xue's central claim is that the Soviet leadership gradually drifted from Marxism-Leninism, and that by Gorbachev's time the party's 1991 self-definition had shifted to "universal human values" and "humane, democratic socialism". Xue ties this to a missing mechanism for the regular replacement of leaders, which allowed a privileged stratum to form and, in the author's account, to become the main beneficiary of the collapse. The author adds that the party lacked the capacity to correct errors and to steer reform, which was driven by leaders' whims and then by a change of direction. Xue also argues that the party failed to guard against Western "peaceful evolution", citing Margaret Thatcher's remark that the West helped promote Gorbachev.

Xue concludes that China must keep Marxism as its guiding thought, build sound systems for selecting and replacing leaders, keep up anti-corruption work, and be willing to face and correct mistakes. The article also calls for firm control over the direction of reform and long-term vigilance against peaceful evolution while reform and opening up continues. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party-affiliated scholarship in 2016 drew lessons from the Soviet collapse for Party building.
quoteEn: One could even say that it was precisely the problems and defects in the Soviet Communist Party's building of itself as a ruling party that led to the final disintegration of the Soviet Union.
quoteZh: 甚至可以说，正是苏共在执政党建设方面的问题和缺陷导致了苏联的最终解体。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese Communist Party discourse for alleged Western efforts to bring about the transformation of socialist states through ideological, cultural and economic influence rather than force.
The policy course launched in China in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, introducing market-oriented economic reforms and opening to the outside world.

t: The turn in social values seen through the revival of social consciousness in Russia
zh: 从俄罗斯社会意识回潮看社会价值转向
paras: Writing in 2016, Wu Huixin asks what a series of ideological "revivals" in post-Soviet Russia reveal about changing social values. The article argues that as Russia has emerged from the disorder produced by the collapse of the Soviet system, a number of earlier ideas have returned to public life. In Wu's reading, these are the result of social change and signal a shift in value positions towards the pragmatic and the concrete.

The first part surveys seven revivals, drawing mostly on polls by the All-Russian Centre for the Study of Public Opinion (VTsIOM). They are the proposed restoration of the title "Hero of Labour" (support rising from 67% to 81% between 2012 and 2013); the rewriting of history textbooks; renewed ideas of national unity; a harsher reassessment of Gorbachev's reforms; the rehabilitation of patriotism; the return of collectivism; and a more measured assessment of Marxism. The second part analyses the value shifts behind these events.

Wu argues that value positions follow the interests of the subject, and that the post-1991 collapse of values mirrored a disordered social reality. The recent turn, in the author's account, has four features: a return to "the people" (renxing) as the standpoint, drawing on the class basis of values; a return to practical reality, seen in valuing hard work, patriotism and an honest view of history; renewed firmness in inherited national values such as collectivism; and a return to objectivity, citing Marx's claim that social being determines consciousness. Values are also becoming more concrete, which Wu sees in three ways: they are group-oriented, rooted in the village community; they are basic, centred on the family; and they are moral, since Wu holds that moral values and economic development move in the same direction.

Wu concludes that Russia's changing positions come from reflection on history, inheritance of tradition and respect for reality. The author judges the wave of revivals to be progressive in essence, pragmatic in value terms, and so far only preliminary results that are "worth looking forward to". Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist ethicist's interpretation of Russian opinion data on Soviet legacies, collectivism and patriotism, with the source polls cited in full.
quoteEn: In any case, the series of ideological revivals now appearing in Russian society are progressive in essence and pragmatic in value judgement, and their results are preliminary and promising.
quoteZh: 无论如何，当前俄罗斯社会出现的系列思想回潮事件在本质上是具有进步性的，在价值判断上是务实的，其结果是初步的和令人期待的。

glossary.explanation: A Soviet honorary title awarded to outstanding workers. Its proposed restoration in Russia is one of the revivals the article discusses.
A Marxist-Leninist criterion that values and policies should reflect the standpoint and interests of the working people. The author treats it as the basis of Soviet-era values and of their return.

t: Sharp changes in the political landscape of Latin America: causes, impact and prospects
zh: 拉美国家政治格局发生急剧变化：原因、影响和前景
paras: Writing in 2016, Xu Shicheng asks why left-wing governments in Latin America have suffered a run of setbacks in the preceding six months, and whether the left will keep declining. Xu argues that the political pendulum has swung to the right and that the left has entered an ebb tide. The article nonetheless rejects claims that the Latin American left is dead or dying, and expects a swing back towards the centre-left after a period of policy adjustment.

The article first documents the shift country by country. It covers the right's victory in Argentina (Macri, November 2015), the opposition's two-thirds majority in Venezuela's National Assembly (December 2015) and the ensuing conflict with Maduro's government, and the impeachment vote against Dilma Rousseff in Brazil (April 2016). It also covers Evo Morales's referendum defeat in Bolivia and Rafael Correa's decision not to stand again in Ecuador. It then lists five causes and ends with the case that the left remains alive.

Xu names five causes. The first is economic: falling commodity prices ended the export boom, forcing austerity and cuts to social programmes that left newly middle-class people at risk of falling back into poverty. Xu adds that governments failed to diversify their economies and that some policies were too radical, such as nationalising non-essential firms. The second is political: fragmented ruling coalitions and factionalised ruling parties, as with Brazil's PMDB and Venezuela's PSUV. The third is corruption, which Xu says often triggers protests. The fourth and fifth are US interference, including funding for opposition groups and sanctions on Venezuela, and the growing strength of right-wing forces and right-leaning media.

Xu concludes that the left still governs in Cuba, Brazil, Venezuela, Bolivia, Ecuador, Nicaragua, Chile, Uruguay and El Salvador. It also keeps real strength in Argentina, Mexico and Peru. In Xu's view, deep inequality and social tension sustain the left's social base, and its achievements against neoliberalism, in poverty reduction, education, health care and regional integration should not be dismissed wholesale. Xu cites Uruguay's former president José Mujica on the pendulum of history, and holds that the left's prospects are bright if it reflects seriously on its own problems. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic assessment, written in 2016, of the Latin American left's reverses, with country-level figures and a defence of the left's prospects.
quoteEn: The Latin American left has suffered setbacks and is tending towards an ebb tide, but it has not died, nor is it "on its last breath".
quoteZh: 拉美左翼受挫、趋于低潮，但拉美左翼并没有死亡，也没有“奄奄一息”。

t: The Vietnamese Communist Party's 12th Congress and the "nine relationships" of renewal
zh: 越共十二大提出革新发展“九大关系”
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 31 March 2016, p. 5
paras: This short commentary, written in 2016, reports on the 12th National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV), held on 20–28 January 2016 at the thirtieth anniversary of Vietnam's renewal (Doi Moi). Pan Jin'e argues that the congress set the direction of economic renewal for 2016–2020 around building and perfecting a socialist-oriented market economy, and that the "nine relationships" it asks the Party to handle show problems similar to China's.

The article has three parts. It first traces the Party's changing theory of economic reform since 1986, then sets out the congress's targets and reform measures for the next five years, and finally lists the nine relationships and comments on Vietnam's deepening international integration.

On theory, Pan describes a move from a Soviet-style centrally planned economy to the "socialist-oriented market economy", step by step from the 6th Congress (1986) to the 9th (2001) and the 2008 resolution that treated the market economy as a means of building socialism rather than as capitalism. The 12th Congress added the word "perfecting" and, as Pan reports, a Vietnamese theorist names five sources of socialist orientation: state management under the rule of law, Party leadership, the people's mastery, suitable relations of production, and social progress and equity. Pan then reports the congress's targets, including annual growth of 6.5–7% and GDP per capita of 3,200–3,500 US dollars by 2020, and its plans for state-owned enterprises, collective, private and foreign-invested firms. These include share-based restructuring of state firms, separating commercial from political and public-interest tasks, and encouraging private capital.

Pan notes that the nine relationships put stability and reform first. The new pair, the state and the market, in Pan's reading borrows from the Third Plenum of the 18th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party (2013). Pan also observes that Vietnam signed the Trans-Pacific Partnership in January 2016. Pan holds that the agreement's demands on trade unions, state-owned enterprises and freedom of association will affect the CPV's control and Vietnam's future path, and that the report makes both opportunities and challenges plain. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese scholarly summary of the CPV's 12th Congress economic line and its parallels with Chinese reform discourse.
quoteEn: The Vietnamese Communist Party will continue to give first priority to handling the relationship between reform and stability, and attaches great importance to economic construction.
quoteZh: 越共将继续把处理好改革和稳定的关系放在首要位置，十分重视经济建设

glossary.explanation: The Chinese rendering of Vietnam's Doi Moi, the reform programme launched by the CPV at its 6th Congress in 1986 to move from central planning toward a multi-sector market economy.

glossary.zh: 社会主义定向的市场经济
glossary.pinyin: shèhuì zhǔyì dìngxiàng de shìchǎng jīngjì
glossary.explanation: The CPV's official description of its economic model, formally adopted in 2001. It combines market mechanisms with Party leadership and a leading role for the state sector.
The nine pairs of relationships the 12th CPV Congress said must be handled in future renewal, including those between stability and development and between the state and the market.

t: If poor, cultivate oneself; if successful, benefit the whole world
st: Value pursuits and the notion of righteousness and interest in Chinese diplomatic culture
zh: 穷则独善其身，达则兼济天下
zhSub: 中国外交文化的价值追求与义利观念
source: Renmin Luntan (People's Tribune), Academic Frontier, August 2016 (second half)
paras: Writing in 2016, Pan Jin'e asks what values underlie Chinese diplomacy. The starting point is Xi Jinping's September 2015 speech at the UN's 70th anniversary summit, where he pledged that China would keep to the principle of 'giving equal weight to righteousness and interests, with righteousness first'. Pan argues that the speech reflects the foreign-policy thinking of the new leadership. In the article's account it inherits traditional Chinese diplomatic culture and the ideas of earlier leaders, and develops them for present conditions.

The article is organised around two strands of Confucian thought. The first is the view of righteousness and interest (yi and li), which Pan traces through Chinese foreign aid from the Mao era to Xi. The second is the idea of 'harmony without uniformity', which Pan links to the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence and to Deng Xiaoping's and Jiang Zemin's views on peace, development and multipolarity. It also covers Hu Jintao's 2005 'harmonious world' speech and Xi's concept of a community with a shared future for mankind.

Pan holds that the 'correct approach to righteousness and interest', which Xi put forward in 2013, continues what every generation of leaders practised. As evidence the article cites declassified figures: aid to more than 110 countries and regions before 1976, and total aid spending of 41.181 billion yuan by 1985. It also cites Hu Jintao's debt relief for Africa and Xi's pledges of a South–South cooperation assistance fund and the Belt and Road Initiative. On the second strand, Pan reads the community with a shared future for mankind, along with calls for equality among states and respect for each country's chosen path, as an extension of Confucian ideas on conduct.

Pan concludes that, across periods, the Mencian ideal of cultivating oneself when poor and benefiting all under heaven when successful runs through Chinese diplomacy. Pan adds that this ideal overlaps with the Party's guiding ideology, namely Marxist internationalism and the communist goal of human liberation. In Pan's view, combining the two yields a distinctive diplomatic culture with Chinese characteristics. Read the original if you want an example of how Chinese scholars in 2016 grounded official foreign-policy language in Confucian tradition and the history of foreign aid.
quoteEn: Reviewing the diplomatic thinking and policies of Chinese leaders in every period, one finds that the traditional value 'if poor, cultivate oneself; if successful, benefit the whole world' runs through them all, and this is precisely the value pursuit of China's external relations.
quoteZh: 回顾和总结各个时期中国领导人的外交思想和政策措施，可以发现，“穷则独善其身，达则兼济天下”⑥的传统价值理念贯穿始终，而这正是中国对外交往的价值追求

glossary.explanation: A Confucian way of weighing moral principle (yi) against material benefit (li). Xi Jinping invoked a 'correct view' of it in 2013 as a guide for China's dealings with developing and neighbouring countries.
A saying attributed to Confucius, in the Analects, that people can coexist in harmony without simply agreeing. Chinese leaders have applied it to relations among states and civilisations.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept central to Xi Jinping's foreign-policy discourse. It calls for cooperation and shared development among states on the basis of equality and mutual respect.
Hu Jintao's foreign-policy concept, set out in his 2005 UN speech. It envisages lasting peace and common prosperity, with multilateralism and respect for civilisational diversity.

Principles of mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence. They were jointly advocated by China, India and Burma in the 1950s.
A Chinese initiative launched in 2013 to build economic cooperation and infrastructure links along land and maritime 'Silk Road' routes.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: The direction of Vietnam's Đổi Mới as seen from the 12th Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam
zh: 从越共十二大看越南革新的走向
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (当代世界与社会主义), 2016 no. 1
paras: Writing in early 2016, shortly after the 12th National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) held in Hanoi on 20–28 January 2016, Pan Jin'e asks why the Congress kept the over-70 Nguyen Phu Trong as General Secretary rather than choosing the widely tipped Prime Minister Nguyen Tan Dung. The article also asks what this means for China–Vietnam relations and where Vietnam's renovation (Đổi Mới, in Chinese 革新) is heading. Pan argues that the Congress reaffirmed a socialist-oriented path, while behind apparent stability the personnel outcome reflected struggle and compromise among forces inside the Party.

The article first traces preparation of the political report, including Pan's own 2015 interviews in Vietnam and the publication of draft documents for public comment. It then reviews the draft's assessment of 30 years of renovation, its lessons and the "nine relationships" to be managed. Further sections analyse the personnel changes and new election rules, and Vietnam's defence, security and foreign policy. A short conclusion looks at internal and external challenges.

Pan's core argument has three parts. First, comparing the draft report with Nguyen Phu Trong's delivered report, and the 2015 draft with the 11th Congress theme, Pan sees more emphasis on building a "pure and strong" Party, on socialist democracy and on defending the homeland. The foreign-policy passages were notably softened: the delivered text and Foreign Minister Pham Binh Minh's speech dropped formulas such as "cooperation and struggle", and stressed managing differences over the South China Sea. Second, Pan describes the 2014 Party election rules, the age limits, the vote that denied Nguyen Tan Dung a Central Committee seat, and the 2015 Referendum Law, which Pan sees as adding pressure on one-party rule. Third, Pan points to Western ideological currents, corruption, "peaceful evolution" and Vietnam's commitment to the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) as threats to Party stability. Pan also notes that the "government and market" relationship appears to borrow from the Third Plenum of the 18th CPC Central Committee (2013).

Pan concludes that the Congress ensured continuity and a transfer of power, but that the new leadership faces a heavy test. Pan suggests it is unclear whether Trong will serve the full term. Pan reads the public statements of Vietnamese officials as signals of friendlier cooperation with China. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's detailed account of the 12th CPV Congress documents, the new Party election procedures and the shift in Vietnam's foreign-policy wording.
quoteEn: It can be seen that the problems Vietnam's renovation currently encounters, and the ways of resolving them, are very similar to those of our country.
quoteZh: 可见，越南革新当前所遇到的问题和解决思路与我国非常相似。

glossary.explanation: The Chinese rendering of Đổi Mới, the reform programme launched by the Communist Party of Vietnam in 1986 that introduced a market economy under Party leadership.
A term used in communist-party discourse for alleged Western efforts to undermine socialist systems by non-military, ideological and cultural means.
The Party's supreme body, held every five years, which elects the Central Committee and approves the political report.

t: Rereading Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism
zh: 重读列宁《帝国主义是资本主义的最高阶段》
paras: Writing in 2016, a century after Lenin's Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, Li Jie asks what the book still explains. The article argues that two long-running developments are both anticipated in Lenin's analysis. The first is capitalism's move from free competition to financial monopoly at the start of the twentieth century. The second is the decline of contemporary capitalism at the start of the twenty-first, marked by the rise of socialism with Chinese characteristics and by emerging countries entering modernity by non-capitalist means.

The piece is a short essay in two numbered parts. The first summarises Lenin's account of imperialism as the inevitable product of capitalist free competition, with page references to the Selected Works of Lenin. The second takes up socialism with Chinese characteristics as a further option beyond capitalist modernization. It ends with a brief judgement on the lasting value of Lenin's book.

Li reconstructs Lenin's logic in six steps: concentration of production produces monopoly; monopoly produces finance capital; ownership of capital separates from its productive use; surplus capital is exported; and finance capital leads to the direct partition of the world. Li holds that today's capitalist world still moves according to this logic, including in the financial crisis that began in 2008, where reforms against monopoly keep giving way to higher levels of monopoly. The author reads this as a self-expanding finance capital heading towards self-destruction. In the second part, Li says capital's overseas expansion awakened national independence movements and a search for modernization. Li argues that Western models, whether the British Commonwealth model or the Washington Consensus, lead only to the "middle-income trap", privatization and electoral disorder. Socialism with Chinese characteristics, in Li's account, combines reform and opening up, the Two Unwaverings and a decisive role for the market with public ownership in the main position, Party leadership and opposition to privatization and "constitutional democracy".

Li concludes that the greatness of Lenin's book does not depend on whether particular specific claims still hold. It rests, in Li's view, on its disclosure of objective and lasting laws of capitalism and socialism. Li adds that Marx's and Lenin's laws of capitalist and imperialist demise will arrive however long they take. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a 2016 Party-journal essay links Lenin's theory of imperialism to the case for the Chinese development path.
quoteEn: For the broad range of developing countries, the essence of the success of socialism with Chinese characteristics is that, beyond capitalist modernization, it offers a realistic option of achieving modernization by non-capitalist means.
quoteZh: 中国特色社会主义的成功，对于广大发展中国家来说，其实质是在资本主义现代化之外，提供了通过非资本主义方式实现现代化的现实选择。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era. It combines Party leadership and public ownership in the main position with market mechanisms.
The official formula of unwaveringly consolidating and developing the public sector and unwaveringly encouraging, supporting and guiding the non-public sector.
The policy of domestic economic reform and opening to the outside world, begun in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.
A concept from development economics for economies that stall after reaching middle-income levels. The author cites it as a result of following Western-designed paths.
A set of market-liberalising policy prescriptions associated with Washington-based institutions from the 1980s. Chinese writers often cite it as the model of Western-dictated development.

t: Rethinking the lessons of the Soviet collapse
zh: 对苏联解体教训的再认识
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, Lin Yanhu and Feng Yanli ask why a superpower disappeared 'without a single shot' and what China should learn from it. They argue that the main cause was the Soviet Communist Party leadership's abandonment of Marxism as its guiding ideology and of its socialist and communist ideals. In their view the collapse was a historical tragedy but not a failure of socialism, and it did not alter the historical law by which socialism replaces capitalism.

The article has two parts. The first seeks a comprehensive understanding of the collapse, in three sub-sections: abandoning Marxism as the root cause, the persistence of the historical law despite the collapse, and the collapse as a national disaster and a tragedy for world socialism. The second part draws three lessons for China: consolidating Marxism's ideological position, strengthening Marxist discourse power and national cultural soft power, and holding firm to the Four-sphere Confidence.

On causes, the authors hold that under Gorbachev's 'new thinking' the Party pursued political 'pluralism', economic privatisation and the 'de-ideologisation' of culture and foreign relations. They call this a reversal of socialism, in substance a copy of capitalism, which produced confusion and a loss of popular cohesion. They answer Brzezinski and Fukuyama by arguing that capitalism's internal contradictions, wealth concentration and the post-2008 crisis and protest movements point to its decline. To show the human cost, they cite falling output, wars in six former republics, rising inequality in Russia and a fall in life expectancy. Their lessons call for 'one guiding ideology over many' and for resisting historical nihilism and Western infiltration. They also call for promoting socialist core values, grounding Marxist discourse in the people's interests and cultural 'going out', and building China's own academic discourse.

The authors conclude that China must study the Soviet case closely and hold firmly to Marxist belief, socialism with Chinese characteristics and the communist ideal. They quote Xi Jinping's 1 July 2016 speech on confidence in the path, theory, system and culture, and argue that only the Four-sphere Confidence can carry the Party through a complex international and domestic situation. Read the original if you want a concise example of mid-2016 official-academic Chinese framing of the Soviet collapse as an ideological lesson, with the statistics and policy conclusions the authors draw.
quoteEn: The Soviet collapse was merely a setback in the course of the world socialist movement; the downfall of the CPSU neither will nor can change the historical law by which socialism replaces capitalism.
quoteZh: 苏联解体只是世界社会主义运动过程中的一次挫折，苏共亡党不会也不可能改变社会主义代替资本主义的历史规律。

glossary.explanation: A formula in Party discourse, in full form confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. The cultural element was added in 2016 by Xi Jinping.
The official name for the path, theory and system the Chinese Communist Party has pursued since reform and opening up began in the late 1970s.

The capacity to shape the concepts and narratives through which a society or the international community understands issues. Chinese official and academic writing often treats it as part of ideological security and soft power.
In Party usage, a label for views that question or negate the official account of the Party's and socialism's history. Official writers present it as an ideological threat.
A twelve-word set of values promoted since the 18th Party Congress (2012), at national, social and individual levels, as the core of official ideology.

t: The development of the world socialist movement in China
zh: 世界社会主义运动发展在中国
paras: Reviewing the year 2015, Liu Hanfeng and Guan Yongqian ask how research and practice on world socialism developed in China and what trends follow for the movement. They argue that world socialism is in a phase of revival since the financial crisis, and that China is one of its main forces. In their account, the development of the theoretical system of socialism with Chinese characteristics supplies experience for refining scientific socialism.

The article is a year-in-review survey. It first describes the advance of world socialism studies in China in 2015, including a series of academic forums and the first World Marxism Congress hosted by Peking University. It then tracks the main research hotspots among Chinese scholars, and closes with the basic trends facing the movement. It reports the views of many named scholars, among them Deng Chundong, Nie Yunlin, Yan Zhimin, Wang Weiguang, Li Junru and Yan Shuhan, as well as a Vietnamese and a US voice.

The authors start from the cyclical-crisis logic of capitalism, citing Kondratiev's long waves and Ernest Mandel. They hold that the crisis has opened a new opportunity for socialism. Chinese scholars, they report, describe a "new normal" of world socialism: diversity of paths, independent exploration by each party, peaceful coexistence and competition between the two social systems, and an end to a single model. The Four Comprehensives are presented as the latest achievement of socialism with Chinese characteristics, including the first Party-history call for full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. The authors also treat ideological struggle as a standing task: they say the West uses peaceful evolution and "colour revolutions", and quote Wang Weiguang that holding the discourse power of Marxism is the most reliable weapon.

The authors conclude that difficult economic recovery in the US and Europe, together with the refugee crisis, objectively favours the movement. They say socialism with Chinese characteristics is gaining wide recognition and leading theoretical and practical innovation. They expect confidence in its path, theory and system to grow and to unite the Party's cause, the Chinese nation's cause and that of world socialism. Read the original if you want a compact record of how Chinese scholars framed world socialism and the Four Comprehensives in 2015.
quoteEn: Socialism with Chinese characteristics has not only made an outstanding contribution to world economic development, but is also increasingly becoming the leader of innovation in socialist theory and practice.
quoteZh: 中国特色社会主义不仅对世界经济发展作出了突出贡献，也日益成为社会主义理论与实践创新的引领者。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's line of socialist development since reform and opening up. It is presented as Marxism adapted to China's conditions.

A strategic framework put forward by Xi Jinping around 2014–2015. It covers building a moderately prosperous society in all respects, deepening reform, advancing rule of law and strictly governing the Party.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: The official name for the Party's drive for stricter discipline and anti-corruption within its own ranks, tied to the leadership under Xi Jinping.
A phrase popularised by Xi Jinping from 2014 for China's slower but steadier economic growth. Here Chinese scholars extend it to describe a new stable state of world socialism.
The term used in Chinese official and academic discourse for popular uprisings in post-Soviet and other states that it presents as Western-instigated regime change.

t: The evolution of Marxism in Cuba and its lessons
zh: 马克思主义在古巴的演进及启示
source: Scientific Socialism (科学社会主义), 2016 no. 3
paras: Cuba is, in the author's words, the only existing socialist country outside Asia, and Li Jianguo argues that the course of Marxism there offers lessons for understanding the regularities of adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Writing in 2016, Li contends that Cuban socialism rests on a distinctive national situation and has survived through steady reform, loyalty to Marxism-Leninism and José Martí's thought, and the protection of the people's basic interests.

The article has four parts. It first describes Cuba's national conditions: its status as a US dependency before 1959, the long US blockade afterwards, and a strong popular commitment to independence. It then divides Cuba's history into five stages, from the democratic revolution (1944–59) through the socialist revolution, the search for a path of construction, the period of copying the Soviet model, and the reforms of the post-Soviet 'special period'. A third part sets out Cuban theoretical outcomes, and a fourth draws three lessons.

Li's central claim is that Cuban Marxism grew out of national circumstances. The author describes Cuba as defining socialism's essence as national independence and the people's welfare, and as having adopted Martí's thought as the Party's guiding ideology at the Fourth Party Congress (1991). Li treats the 1968 'revolutionary offensive' and the later wholesale copying of the Soviet model as errors that detached policy from national conditions. After the Soviet collapse, Cuba pursued 'socialism with Cuban characteristics' and cautious reform, retaining planning, limiting foreign capital and private business, and avoiding the word 'reform' itself. Li also notes that Cuba holds that the world is still an age of two social systems and two classes, and rejects neoliberal globalisation.

Li draws three lessons: uphold Marxism-Leninism, Martí's thought and socialism as the theoretical and institutional foundation; carry out steady reform and opening up to 'update' the socialist model; and protect the people's fundamental interests. In this account, free healthcare and education, subsidies, low unemployment and clean conduct by Party cadres explain why the people trust the Party and why Cuba has survived internal and external pressure. Li presents this as the most valuable point for other socialist countries. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic overview of Cuba's socialist trajectory, written in 2016 around the Seventh Congress of the Cuban Communist Party and from a Chinese viewpoint.
quoteEn: For Cuba, socialism means independence and opposition to the United States; without socialism there would be nothing of Cuba as it is today.
quoteZh: 对古巴而言，社会主义意味着独立和反美，没有社会主义就没有古巴今天的一切。

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: The official formula for applying Marxism's basic principles to China's concrete conditions and developing them. The 2016 article uses the shorter 'Sinicization of Marxism' idea.

glossary.zh: 有古巴特色的社会主义
glossary.explanation: Formula adopted by Cuba in 1990, after the Soviet collapse, to signal a path suited to its own conditions. It echoes the Chinese phrase 'socialism with Chinese characteristics'.
The policy of economic reform and engagement with the outside world launched in China in 1978. The article applies the term to Cuba's own cautious reforms.

t: Rethinking the lessons of the Soviet collapse
zh: 对苏联解体教训的再认识
paras: Writing in 2016, Lin Yanhu and Feng Yanli revisit the collapse of the Soviet Union and the fall of the Soviet Communist Party. They argue that the main cause was the top leadership's abandonment of Marxism as its guiding ideology and of socialist and communist ideals. In their view the collapse was a historical tragedy but not a failure of socialism, and it does not alter the historical law by which socialism replaces capitalism.

The article has two parts. The first sets out how the collapse should be understood: its root cause, its place in the long course of the world socialist movement, and its human and political costs. The second draws three lessons for China: consolidating Marxism's position in ideology, strengthening the discourse power of Marxism, and holding to the Four-sphere Confidence.

On the cause, the authors hold that Gorbachev's "new thinking" amounted to a capitalist reform. They name three features: political "pluralism" that ended Marxism's leading position, privatisation and a rapid move from planning to the market, and "de-ideologisation" in culture and foreign policy. They say the collapse brought economic decline, wars in some republics, wider inequality in Russia and a fall in the number of socialist states from 15 to 5. On the lessons, they claim that losing discourse power opens the way for subverting a socialist ideology. They call for core socialist values to build consensus, for resistance to historical nihilism and to Western ideological infiltration, and for a Marxist discourse system anchored in the people's interests.

The authors conclude that China must study the Soviet case closely and keep Marxism as the guiding ideology of socialism with Chinese characteristics. They also call for a Marxist-led academic discourse in the humanities and social sciences, and for firm confidence in China's path, theory, system and culture. They present this confidence as the safeguard against the dangers of a complex international and domestic situation. Read the original if you want an example of how Party-aligned scholarship drew ideological lessons from the Soviet collapse for China in 2016.
quoteEn: That the Soviet collapse was a historical tragedy is an undeniable fact, but it does not equal the failure of socialism, nor can it change the historical law by which socialism replaces capitalism.
quoteZh: 苏联解体是历史悲剧，这是不能否认的事实，但苏联解体不等于社会主义的失败，也不可能改变社会主义代替资本主义的历史发展规律。

glossary.explanation: A formula promoted under Xi Jinping: confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. It is used to call for ideological firmness.
The official name for China's model of socialism since the reform era, combining Party leadership with a market-oriented economy.
The capacity to set the terms of public and intellectual debate. In Chinese official writing it is treated as a matter of ideological security.
In Party usage, a label for views seen as denying or disparaging the Party's history and the socialist record, including that of the Soviet Union.
A set of 24 characters in 12 values at the national, social and individual levels, promoted officially since the 18th Party Congress (2012).

t: Profound lessons from the CPSU's ideological work
zh: 苏共意识形态工作的深刻教训
paras: Writing on the 25th anniversary of the dissolution of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) and the collapse of the USSR, Jiang Hong asks why Soviet ideological work failed. The author treats the gradual loosening and final collapse of the ideological front as one important factor among several in the Soviet defeat. Jiang argues that the failure resulted from the interaction of subjective and objective, internal and external, and political and socio-economic causes, and that it ultimately lay in a failure to unite Party spirit with the people's character.

The article is a short commentary in Red Flag Manuscripts that examines the Soviet record from Lenin through Khrushchev, Brezhnev, Andropov and Gorbachev. It is organised into five numbered sections: dogmatic treatment of Marxism, the loss of belief among top leaders, the isolation of propaganda work, heavy-handed control of currents of thought, and great-power chauvinist foreign policy. A closing section draws these threads together.

Jiang's main claim is that the CPSU turned Marxism into a closed textbook system, beginning with Stalin's 1938 text, which lost its capacity for innovation and became a tool for policies that violated the laws of productive-force development. Top leaders then lost their Marxist faith and communist ideals, and the Party became, in the author's words, a special-interest group detached from the people. Propaganda was separated from culture and from people's everyday concerns, such as shortages and unequal distribution, and remained dogmatic, coercive preaching. Jiang adds that suppressing underground publications through the KGB and the offence of 'ideological subversion' only spread Western ideas and damaged the Party's image, while Soviet hegemonism towards other socialist states and parties, and the invasion of Afghanistan, weakened its ideological leadership from outside.

Jiang concludes that a ruling communist party which abandons the unity of Party spirit and the people's character loses its ideological ground and then its power. In the author's account, the CPSU drifted from serving the people, and its ideology lost its correctness and scientific character, ending in 'the Party's fall as its people fell away'. The lesson drawn is implicitly for today's ruling communist parties. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese Party-affiliated scholars in 2016 explained the Soviet ideological collapse as a warning for the present.
quoteEn: In the final analysis, the failure of the CPSU's ideological work lay in its failure to understand and handle correctly the unity of Party spirit and the people's character.
quoteZh: 说到底，苏共意识形态工作的失败，归根结底在于没有正确认识和处理党性与人民性的统一。

glossary.en: Party spirit and the people's character
glossary.explanation: A pairing in Chinese Party ideology: the Party's class-based loyalty and discipline, and its orientation towards the interests of the broad masses. Official discourse holds that the two must be unified.
The Party's work of propaganda, theoretical education and control of the media and culture, intended to secure the leading position of Marxism and the Party's authority over public thought.
A Chinese Communist term for a dominant state treating smaller states and parties as subordinate. Beijing used it in criticising Soviet conduct towards other socialist countries.

t: The German Left Party sees China as the most important birthplace of "Socialism 3.0"
st: A report on Charles (Charles) Bully's lecture "The Third Wave of Socialism"
zh: 德国左翼党认为中国是“社会主义3.0”最重要的诞生地
paras: This short report, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, summarises a lecture given on 24 May at the invitation of the Party Studies Centre of the Central Compilation and Translation Bureau. The speaker was a senior researcher of the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, linked to Germany's Left Party; the report gives his name in Chinese transliteration as Xia'er Buli (夏尔·布里). The lecture, titled "The Third Wave of Socialism", argues that 25 years after the Soviet collapse socialism must be re-examined across the period from 1789 to the twenty-first century. In the speaker's view, the Soviet collapse opened a third wave, "Socialism 3.0", and China is its most important place of birth.

The report follows the lecture in three parts. The first sketches the first wave (1789–1917) and the second (1917–1991). The second part sets out two features of the third wave, which the speaker dates from 1991. The third part addresses the multiple crises of modern capitalism and China's place in the future of socialism.

As reported, the first wave produced reformist, anarchist and revolutionary-vanguard currents, with Marxism seeking to give them a scientific basis. The second wave saw the October Revolution, the Chinese revolution of 1949 and Western social-democratic welfare states, but all of these proved unstable and were overtaken by the neoliberal turn. For the third wave, the speaker holds that an alternative to capitalism must be a learning society, neither bureaucratically centralised like the Soviet system nor competition-driven like the United States, and organised as a "polycentric" mixed system with plural ownership. It must also help to create a new, "harmonious" civilisation that rebalances humans with nature and with society and relies more on broad democratic participation and consensus.

The speaker describes capitalism as facing ecological, identity, political-legitimacy and international-security crises, with opposing movements lacking a convincing alternative. Citing Perry Anderson, he expects the twenty-first century to be shaped by Chinese revolutionary events, as the twentieth was by Soviet ones. He lists five preconditions for socialist association, from ecologically friendly high productivity to a peaceful international order, and says "Socialism 3.0" must prove it can advance them. Read the original if you want a brief Chinese-language record of how a German left-wing researcher framed China's place in world socialism for a Chinese audience in 2016.
quoteEn: The collapse of the Soviet Union was not, as many believed in 1991, the end of socialism, but can be seen as the moment of birth of "Socialism 3.0".
quoteZh: 苏联的解体并非像许多人在1991年所认为的那样，是社会主义的终结，而是可被视为“社会主义3.0”的诞生时刻。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese state body that translates and studies Marxist classics and Party documents, and that hosted the lecture.

t: Review of foreign research on the communist movements of twentieth-century Southeast Asia
zh: 国外关于20世纪东南亚共产主义运动的研究述评
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehuizhuyi), 2015 no. 6
paras: This is a literature review of foreign scholarship on the communist movements that, from the early twentieth century to the 1980s, spread across almost every Southeast Asian country. Liu and Shi treat these movements as part of the region's national histories and as a manifestation of the rise and fall of the international communist movement in Asia. They note that the research they collected is mainly in English, with a little in French, and that it has been shaped throughout by Cold War conditions in Asia.

The review is organised in four parts. The first covers regional and international perspectives, from 1950s American works such as Jack H. Brimmell's study of Southeast Asian communism through to studies of Soviet and Chinese policy. The second turns to Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia, and the third to Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines. The fourth deals with Burma and Thailand. Within each country the authors group books by theme, by source base and by the author's position, whether scholar, journalist, participant or defector.

The authors identify several patterns. Regional studies relied largely on government publications and press reports, supplemented by the FBIS bulletins translating communist radio broadcasts and by the Hoover Institution's yearbook. On Vietnam, they distinguish party histories, studies of the Vietnamese Workers' Party's position between Beijing and Moscow, and comparisons of British counter-insurgency in Malaya with the American effort in South Vietnam. On Laos, works stress Vietnamese support for the Pathet Lao. On Cambodia, attention centres on the Khmer Rouge and the genocide of 1975–78. For Malaya, accounts by participants, notably Chin Peng's memoirs, are set against scholars' assessments. Studies of Thailand and Burma examine, among other things, how far Maoist strategy suited local conditions and what role China played.

Liu and Shi present the survey as an overview of how foreign scholars have followed these movements from the late 1940s onward, rather than proposing a new thesis of their own. They record the varied source bases, including captured documents, interviews with defectors and documentary compilations, and the differing national trajectories. These range from the Indonesian party's three devastating blows to the Burmese party's collapse in the late 1980s. Read the original if you need a country-by-country bibliographic guide to English-language work on Southeast Asian communism, with notes on each book's sources and arguments.
quoteEn: Since the Cold War spread to Asia, foreign scholars have kept watching the communist movements of Southeast Asia, and research from regional, international and country-specific perspectives has produced many results.
quoteZh: 自冷战扩展到亚洲以来，国外学者一直关注东南亚共产主义运动，从地区、国际和国别的视角进行的研究取得了许多成果。

t: The Vietnamese Communist Party's 12th Congress and its "nine relationships" for renovation
zh: 越共十二大提出革新发展“九大关系”
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 31 March 2016
paras: Writing in March 2016, Pan Jin'e reports on the 12th National Congress of the Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV), held on 20–28 January 2016, thirty years after the start of renovation (doi moi). The article argues that the Congress's political report and its 2016–2020 socio-economic development strategy set the goal of building and perfecting a socialist-oriented market economy, and fixed the targets and direction of economic renovation for the next five years.

The piece is a short newspaper commentary in four parts. It traces how the CPV's theoretical understanding of economic reform evolved from 1986 to 2016, summarises the Congress's definition of the socialist-oriented market economy, lists the targets and sector-by-sector reform plans for 2016–2020, and closes with the "nine relationships" that the report says must be handled well.

Pan shows a progression from a Soviet-style centralised planned economy, through "commodity economy" formulations in 1989, 1991 and 1996, to the formal concept of a socialist-oriented market economy at the 9th Congress (2001). The 2008 resolution is quoted as saying the market economy is not identical with capitalism and is a means of building socialism. The 12th Congress added the word "perfecting" and, as Vietnamese theorists read it, anchors the socialist orientation in five features, including management by a socialist law-governed state, Party leadership and the people's mastery. The Congress sets targets such as 6.5–7 per cent annual growth and per capita GDP of 3,200–3,500 US dollars by 2020, and orders state-owned enterprise equitisation, support for private firms and more selective foreign investment.

Pan notes that the nine relationships put stability and reform first. The state–market relationship is an addition to the eight relationships summarised at the 11th Congress, which Pan sees as borrowing from the Third Plenum of the 18th CPC Central Committee (2013) and as showing that Vietnam's economic problems resemble China's. Pan adds that Vietnam's signing of the US-led Trans-Pacific Partnership in January 2016 will, in the author's view, affect the Party's control and Vietnam's future path, given its demands on trade unions, state enterprises and freedom of association. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese overview of the CPV's 2016 economic line and how a Chinese scholar compares it with China's reform agenda.
quoteEn: In sum, the development opportunities Vietnam faces after the 12th Congress are plain to see in the report, and the challenges it faces leap off the page as well.
quoteZh: 总之，越南在十二大后所面临的发展机遇在报告中一览无余，所面临的挑战也在报告中跃于纸上。

glossary.explanation: The Chinese rendering of Vietnam's doi moi, the reform process launched by the Communist Party of Vietnam at its 6th Congress in 1986, which moved away from central planning towards a market-based economy.

glossary.zh: 社会主义定向的市场经济
glossary.pinyin: shèhuì zhǔyì dìngxiàng de shìchǎng jīngjì
glossary.literal: market economy with a socialist orientation
glossary.explanation: The CPV's official description of its economic model, formally adopted in 2001. It treats the market as a means to build socialism under Party leadership and with a leading role for the state sector.
The CPV's term for a state governed by law under socialism, listed in the report as one of the elements of the market economy's socialist orientation.

t: Cuba's Seventh Party Congress "updates" the socialist model
st: A compilation of international news agency reports on Raúl Castro's opening speech, April 2016
zh: 古共七大“更新”社会主义模式
paras: This is a compilation of foreign wire and press reports, republished in Cankao Xiaoxi on 18 April 2016, on the opening of the Seventh Congress of the Communist Party of Cuba (PCC) on 16 April 2016. The reports (EFE, AFP, Prensa Latina, AP, Reuters, Die Zeit and Deutsche Welle) cover the roughly two-and-a-half-hour speech by First Secretary Raúl Castro. They present it as a reaffirmation of one-party socialism together with an economic "update" of the model, and no single author advances a thesis.

The text is arranged under four headings: the pledge not to return to capitalism; criticism of bureaucracy as an obstacle to development; the renewal of the top leadership; and a pragmatic stance on relations with the United States. Each section collects short agency dispatches, and some close with background from Deutsche Welle on how Party congresses work.

On the economy, the reports quote Castro as saying the constitution will be amended to incorporate the "update" begun five years earlier and to define the scope of state and private activity. State enterprise remains the main economic form, ownership and wealth are not to be concentrated, and shock therapy and neoliberal privatisation will not be allowed. AP and Die Zeit report that he conceded that only 21 per cent of the 313 guidelines approved in 2011 had been implemented. They add that he blamed bureaucracy and "old thinking", and listed import dependence, slow growth, the dual currency and weak farm output as problems. On succession, Castro proposed age limits of 60 for entering the Central Committee and 70 for top leaders, on top of the two-term limit from 2011. He said he would step down in 2018.

On foreign affairs, Castro says Cuba is committed to "civilized coexistence" with the United States but warns that Washington's goals are unchanged and only its methods differ. He also urges unity among Latin American left-wing governments against a possible neoliberal return. The reports present this as a congress balancing continuity of the political system, pragmatic economic adjustment and generational change. Read the original if you want a quick, multi-source digest of how the foreign press reported Cuba's 2016 Party congress, including Castro's self-criticism, the succession rules and his wariness towards the US.
quoteEn: Raúl also stressed that the existence of private ownership in Cuba does not mean the "reconstruction of capitalism".
quoteZh: 劳尔也强调，私有制在古巴的存在并不意味着“重建资本主义”。

t: North Korea will keep to its established course
st: A reading of Kim Jong Un's work report to the Seventh Congress of the Workers' Party of Korea
zh: 朝鲜将沿既定路线走下去
source: International Herald Leader (Guoji Xianqu Daobao), 13–19 May 2016
paras: Writing in International Herald Leader in May 2016, Gao Haorong reads the work report that Kim Jong Un delivered to the Seventh Congress of the Workers' Party of Korea, the first congress in 36 years (opened 6 May 2016). Gao treats the report, published in full by North Korean media on 8 May, as the best guide to the country's direction. The commentary's thesis is that North Korea will continue along its established line.

The piece, a short commentary, follows the structure of the report of more than 70,000 characters. It first covers the retrospective on the 36 years since the Sixth Congress (1980). It then turns to the five tasks Kim set for the future. The remaining sections deal with Korean unification and with nuclear status.

Gao reports that Kim attributes the achievements to three things: defending socialism while world socialism suffered setbacks, becoming a political, ideological and military power with nuclear weapons, and solving the succession of the revolutionary cause. In Gao's reading, pairing a severe environment with these successes serves to affirm Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il as eternal leaders and the Juche idea and military-first politics as the Party's unchangeable guiding ideology. The five tasks are the Kim Il Sung–Kim Jong Il-ization of the whole society (the priority), and building powers in science and technology, in the economy, in culture, and in political and military strength. Gao sees the new emphasis on self-reliance as a response to international sanctions. Gao also notes the first national economic plan in many years, a 2016–2020 five-year strategy, with electric power named as its precondition. Kim restates the federal formula for unification and proposes talks between the two Koreas' military authorities. According to Gao, South Korea's Unification Ministry rejected this as propaganda, so Gao expects no early dialogue. On nuclear weapons, Kim calls North Korea a responsible nuclear state and pledges to strengthen its deterrent, while keeping a no-first-use position. Gao concludes that denuclearisation looks more remote and that sanctions alone cannot resolve the issue.

Gao concludes that the congress, which made Kim chairman of the Workers' Party, opens the "Kim Jong Un era" proper, with goals set across political, economic, military and cultural fields. The strongest impression is continuity. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese media interpretation of the 2016 Party congress report and of how Chinese commentators assessed North Korea's nuclear and unification stance at that time.
quoteEn: North Korea will continue along its established line.
quoteZh: 朝鲜将继续沿着既定路线走下去。

glossary.explanation: The official ideology of North Korea, associated with Kim Il Sung, stressing national self-reliance and independence in politics, economy and defence.
North Korea's policy, developed under Kim Jong Il, that gives priority to the military in state affairs and resource allocation.
The ideological formula, in the Workers' Party of Korea's usage, for the ideas of its two late leaders. The report calls for remoulding all of society according to it.
A proposal put forward by Kim Il Sung at the Sixth Congress (1980) for unifying the Korean peninsula as a federation.

t: Currents of socialism in Europe in the second half of the twentieth century
st: From the end of the Second World War to the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
zh: “左翼党”与联邦德国的左翼政治
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehui zhuyi), 2016 no. 3
paras: This article traces how currents of socialism developed in Europe from the end of the Second World War to the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. It argues that the victory over fascism, and the establishment of people's democratic regimes in eight Eastern European states, opened a period in which world socialism grew stronger and more diverse.
