In the author's account, European socialist currents both expanded beyond Europe and moved from theory into practice.

The text has two main parts. The first examines three currents that predated 1945: democratic socialism and the social democratic parties, market socialism, and Trotskyist socialism. The second turns to newer currents, namely eco-socialism, Eurocommunism, post-industrial socialism and feminist socialism, and concentrates on the first two as the most distinctly European and influential.

On democratic socialism, the author describes the refounding of the Socialist International in Frankfurt in 1951 and its growth into a global body, with 50 full members by 1983, 22 of them European. Social democratic governments are credited with welfare and workers' participation gains, but the author insists that their basic positions differ essentially from those of communist parties, citing Cold War anti-communism and the 1989 Declaration of Principles. Market socialism is traced from Benjamin Ward's 1958 Illyrian model to reform designs by Liberman, Brus, Sik, Kornai and Kardelj, and to practice in Yugoslavia and Hungary. The author says these experiments ended in capitalist market economies because the models were imperfect. Eurocommunism, led by the Italian, Spanish and French parties, is presented as a response to changes in Western capitalism and to the Soviet model, especially after the Prague Spring. Its core was a democratic, multiparty road to socialism, and it declined from the mid-1980s. Eco-socialism arose from the green movement, with the West German Greens (founded 1980) winning 5.6 per cent and 27 seats in 1983, and it influenced the Social Democratic Party's programme.

The author concludes that in this period the pattern of 'one centre, one path, one model' in the communist movement broke down. Two features marked European socialist currents: they overcame geographical limits and spread to the Third World, and they moved beyond theory to try to put their ideas into practice. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly survey of Western European socialist currents, with names, dates and organisations, and of how they were characterised for readers in China in 2016.
quoteEn: Overall, in the second half of the twentieth century the situation of 'one centre, one path, one model' in the international communist movement was broken, and world socialism developed in increasingly diverse ways.
quoteZh: 总体上看，20 世纪下半叶，国际共产主义运动中“一个中心”、“一条道路”、“一种模式”的局面被打破，世界社会主义呈现出多样化发展的态势。

glossary.explanation: In Chinese scholarship this term usually denotes the ideology of the Western European social democratic parties and the Socialist International. It is generally treated as distinct from the scientific socialism of communist parties.
A family of theories and reform models that combine socialist ownership or worker self-management with market mechanisms. It was debated in the West and tried in Yugoslavia and Hungary.
A current of the 1970s associated mainly with the Italian, Spanish and French communist parties. It favoured a democratic, multiparty road to socialism independent of Moscow.
A current that attributes the ecological crisis to capitalism and seeks to combine ecological balance with socialism. It emerged from the green movements and green parties of the 1960s–80s.

glossary.en: the upheavals in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
glossary.explanation: The standard Chinese term for the collapse of ruling communist parties in the USSR and Eastern Europe around 1989–91.

t: Die Linke and left politics in the Federal Republic of Germany
zh: “左翼党”与联邦德国的左翼政治
source: Peking University Marxism Studies (Beida Makesizhuyi Yanjiu), vol. 4
paras: This is a Chinese translation of a text by Gregor Gysi, a leading figure of Germany's Die Linke (The Left) and chair of its Bundestag group, apparently delivered as a talk to a Chinese audience. Gysi presents what he calls the party's character as a left-socialist force and sets out where it stands among Germany's left parties. His thesis is that Die Linke is distinct from both social democracy and Soviet-style communism, and that the left remains divided for lasting structural reasons.

The text has three parts. The first places Die Linke in the European family of 'left-socialist' parties and explains its origins in Germany's division. The second compares the three left-of-centre parties in the Federal Republic: the Social Democrats, the Greens and Die Linke. The third takes up three problems Gysi says the left must tackle: the crisis of neoliberalism, international politics, and the link between social justice and ecological transformation.

Gysi argues that Western capitalism built mass prosperity and democracy partly under pressure from competition with the Soviet bloc. In his account, once that rivalry ended, neoliberalism took over, social democrats embraced it, and a 'representation deficit' opened that new left parties filled. Die Linke arose from the 2007 merger of the PDS, successor to the East German ruling party, and the WASG, a western left-social-democratic group. Gysi says it has dropped dogmatic Marxism, though Marx's theory is still needed to analyse crisis. He holds that the three parties differ over state bureaucracy, over NATO and relations with the United States, and over how far to pursue ecological change. He criticises Western policy in the Ukraine crisis and the response to the euro crisis. He says ecological transformation requires job security and global solidarity, including the development rights of countries such as China and India.

Gysi concludes that a single united left party is unlikely in the foreseeable future, though cooperation is possible, especially at local and state level. He hopes the Social Democrats will regain a will to power and move away from neoliberal thinking. He describes Die Linke's aim as overcoming capitalism through an expanded parliamentary democracy, an ecological mode of production and a classless society of free individuals, without drawing utopian blueprints. Read the original if you want a German left leader's own account of Die Linke's identity, its relations with the SPD and Greens, and its positions on the euro crisis, NATO and Ukraine, as presented to a Chinese readership.
quoteEn: Our goal is to build a classless society in which individual freedom is the precondition and condition of freedom for all.
quoteZh: 我们的目标是建立一个没有阶级的社会，在这样一个社会里，个人自由是所有人自由的前提和条件。

t: The historical evolution of the communist movement in Nepal
zh: 尼泊尔共产主义运动的历史演进探析
paras: Writing in 2015, Yuan Qun and Zhang Lifeng ask how Nepal's communist movement has developed over its 66 years, and what that history implies for its prospects. They argue that the movement has grown from a weak left-wing current into a politically significant force. Since the 1980s, the authors say, its main parties have adjusted their strategy to domestic and international change in search of a path suited to Nepal. The authors present it as a typical case within today's international communist movement.

The article is organised chronologically in four parts. It begins with the rise of the movement from 1947 to 1954, amid opposition to the Rana family's autocracy, followed by the split and regrouping of the movement from the late 1950s to the 1990s. It then covers the movement's turn towards peaceful and parliamentary politics, and ends with an assessment of its achievements and problems. The account follows the proliferation of party factions, such as the CPN (Unified Marxist-Leninist) and the CPN (Maoist), and the mergers and splits between them.

The authors' central argument is that the movement moved from armed struggle towards multi-party politics. They trace this in the CPN (UML)'s 1993 programme of "People's Multi-party Democracy", and in the Maoists' later move from the "People's War" launched in 1996 to accepting multi-party democracy in the 2000s. They credit this shift with the first communist-led government (1994) and with the abolition of the monarchy in 2008. They then identify three problems that hold the movement back. First, the rivalry between the two largest parties, the UML and the Maoists, weakens its overall strength, since each party puts its own immediate interests above the movement's long-term interest. Second, the authors describe an ideological degeneration, citing the Maoists' abandonment of the land policy and of the army, and the UML's replacement of class struggle with nationalism. They link this to election losses in 2008 and 2013. Third, factionalism has produced repeated splits, which the authors attribute to both external factors (the Sino-Soviet split, Chinese reform, Indian influence) and internal disputes.

The authors conclude that the movement is an important political force in Nepal and a bright spot in a still depressed international communist movement. They also argue that whether it can resolve inter-party antagonism, ideological decline and factionalism will largely decide its future. Read the original if you want a detailed chronology of Nepal's communist parties, their splits and mergers, and a Chinese academic assessment of the movement's problems as of 2015.
quoteEn: Factionalism has put personal and small-group interests above the interests of the party and of the communist movement, damaging party unity and obstructing the movement's further development.
quoteZh: 宗派主义使个人利益、小团体利益超越了党的利益、共产主义运动的利益，影响了党的团结，也阻碍了共产主义运动的进一步发展。

glossary.explanation: The political programme adopted by the CPN (UML) at its fifth congress in 1993. It accepts multi-party politics and a peaceful, gradual transition to socialism, and in the authors' view it laid the theoretical ground for the parliamentary path.
A protracted rural armed struggle on the Chinese model. The Nepali Maoists launched it in 1996 to seize power, and it ended with the 2006 peace agreement.

t: The "self-degeneration" of the privileged stratum in the collapse of the CPSU and its warnings
zh: 苏共垮台中特权阶层的“自我蜕变”及其警示
paras: Writing in 2016, Guo Yanlin asks what role privilege and corruption played in the collapse of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU). The article argues that, among the many factors behind the fall of a party of more than 70 years and over 20 million members, a major one was that the CPSU never escaped the "cyclical trap" of history. In Guo's account, a privileged bureaucratic stratum emerged inside the Party, and its "self-degeneration" did more than any anti-communist force to bring the Party and the state down.

The article has three parts. The first traces how the stratum formed, from Lenin's struggle against bureaucratism through the Stalin, Khrushchev, Brezhnev and Gorbachev periods. The second sets out four political harms of privilege and corruption. The third draws five lessons for the Chinese Communist Party. Guo relies on Lenin, Deng Xiaoping, memoirs by Arbatov and Ryzhkov, a 1995 survey by the Russian Academy of Sciences, and David Kotz's study of Soviet elite opinion.

Guo's central claim is that the stratum moved from enjoying privileges to converting power into property. Under Gorbachev's reforms, officials privatised profitable state enterprises and turned control into ownership. The article cites a 1995 survey showing that 74–75 per cent of the political elite around the Russian president and government, and 61 per cent of the economic elite, came from the Soviet cadre corps. It also cites Kotz's finding that about 80 per cent of ordinary people wanted to keep socialism, while 76.7 per cent of a roughly 100,000-strong elite favoured capitalism. The four harms Guo lists are weakened ideological appeal, a crisis of trust between Party and people, broken discipline with the rise of unwritten rules and the sale of office, and the elite's role as vanguard of capitalist restoration.

Guo draws five warnings for China. Anti-privilege work must be long-term during the primary stage of socialism, and must be part of full and rigorous self-governance of the Party. Leading cadres who lose their ideals and form vested-interest groups must be dealt with. Privilege must never become a tool for maintaining political order. Intra-Party supervision must be strengthened, with Deng Xiaoping's stress on institutions cited in support. Close ties between Party and people must anchor the campaign. Read the original if you want a Chinese Party-affiliated reading of the Soviet collapse, used in 2016 to justify the anti-corruption campaign.
quoteEn: It can be said that the main force that brought down the CPSU was not anti-communists but the privileged and corrupt elements inside the Party.
quoteZh: 可以说，搞垮苏共的主要力量并不是反共分子，而是苏共党内的特权腐败分子。

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping's leadership, which gained prominence after 2012 and covers anti-corruption work, discipline and Party-building.
The official characterisation of China's present stage of development, adopted in the 1980s. It is said to last a long historical period.

t: Lies and truth about the Soviet economic crisis
st: Based on Kara-Murza's analysis
zh: 苏联经济危机的谎言与真相
zhSub: 基于卡拉-穆尔扎的分析
paras: Did the Soviet economy collapse in the late 1970s and early 1980s, before Gorbachev took over? Kang Yanru, drawing on the Russian scholar Sergei Kara-Murza, rejects this widely accepted view, which treats the Soviet Union's dissolution as the result of a crisis of the 'Soviet system' that could not be reformed. The article, published in 2016, argues that the Soviet economy showed no sign of crisis before 1985 and that Gorbachev's reforms and de-Sovietising decisions produced the economic deterioration and collapse.

The article has three parts. The first examines who produced and spread the 'lie' of a pre-reform crisis, citing Yakovlev, the reform theorist Boris Nayshul and the Western Sovietologists David Cohen, Ellman and Kontorovich. The second sets Soviet economic data from before and after 1985 side by side. The third reviews the basic condition of the national economy and tests the claim that the Soviet economy was oriented towards raw-material exports.

Kang reports Kara-Murza's argument that the first stage of Gorbachev's reform dismantled the financial system and the consumer market. The 1987 Law on State Enterprises allowed non-cash money to be converted into cash, foreign trade was decentralised, and cooperatives sold goods abroad. Enterprises kept more profit and raised incomes without matching output. The article cites rising budget deficits, internal debt and external debt, and falling gold reserves, all after 1985. It also reports figures showing balanced investment, production and consumption growth before 1989 and steady industrial growth from 1950 to 1990. On the 'raw-material' claim, it cites 1989 data in which processed goods made up 77% of the Russian Federation's exports, and 1988 data in which fuel and electricity exports equalled 3.2% of Soviet gross national product. On this basis it dismisses the claim that the United States depressed oil prices and so ended the USSR. It presents Russia's present raw-material dependence as a product of the reforms.

Kang concludes, following Kara-Murza, that the crisis dates from the 1987–1990 policy decisions and that the Soviet economy was not inefficient or uncompetitive. The article warns that the loss of critical analysis, and the failure of intellectuals to rebut these claims for over twenty years, is the greatest threat to Russia's development. Read the original if you want a Chinese-language account of Russian arguments against the 'inevitable collapse' thesis, with the economic statistics Kara-Murza uses.
quoteEn: In fact, Russia's current backward, raw-material-based economy is not an inheritance from history but a product of the reforms, the result of the de-industrialisation of the Soviet economy.
quoteZh: 实际上当前俄罗斯落后的原料型经济不是对历史的继承，而是改革的产物，是苏联经济非工业化的结果。

t: For the liberation of workers and peoples, for socialism: an assessment of the 17th International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties
zh: 为了工人和人民的解放，为了社会主义
zhSub: 第17次共产党和工人党国际会议评析
paras: This is a report and assessment of the 17th International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties, hosted by the Communist Party of Turkey in Istanbul from 30 October to 1 November 2015. Yu and Zhou, four of whose research-centre colleagues attended as scholarly observers, say 104 delegates from 58 parties in 48 countries took part. The theme was strengthening the working-class struggle against capitalist exploitation, imperialist war and fascism. The meeting adopted a working-group document, admitted the Workers' Party of Austria and issued a press release.

The report follows the meeting's themes in seven sections. It covers the delegates' view that capitalism's structural crisis continues, and their account of regional turmoil and terrorism. It then turns to popular protest movements and their immaturity, the experience of mass struggle and party-building, and the position of socialist countries. It ends with joint action proposals and the authors' own commentary. Most of the material is drawn from speeches by named delegates from Portugal, India, Greece, Brazil, Ireland, Belgium, Croatia, Turkey, Iraq and other parties.

According to the authors, most parties held that the post-2008 crisis was unresolved and that imperialism was the root of terrorism and instability. Delegates pointed to economic plunder, political and financial backing for extremist groups, military intervention and divisive propaganda. Protest movements, including anti-austerity campaigns, struggles in Latin America and West Asia, and resistance to the EU, were judged immature. Delegates blamed bourgeois ideology, the rise of the far right, unprepared working-class parties and repression of communists. Parties differed on tactics: the Communist Parties of Greece and Turkey stressed separation from opportunism, while the Portuguese, Indian (Marxist), Lebanese and Iraqi parties favoured broad anti-imperialist alliances. Some, including the Brazilian party, again called for a new Communist International. Speakers from the Chinese, Vietnamese, Cuban and Lao parties described their paths, and the Croatian party defended the view that China is socialist.

Yu and Zhou conclude that the meeting has become an established platform for exchange and solidarity. They say it showed a spirit of 'consultative democracy' and took a step towards institutionalisation by adopting rules for the working group. They also list difficulties: few parties able to host, an eight-minute speaking limit that left theory shallow, difficulty reaching consensus, weak follow-through between meetings, and some parties' loss of confidence. Whether the meeting can play a larger role in the world socialist movement, they say, remains to be seen. Read the original if you want a detailed, party-by-party account of positions at this 2015 gathering and of how Chinese scholars assessed it.
quoteEn: After years of development, the International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties has become a platform for exchange among communist and workers' parties and a major event in their political life.
quoteZh: 共产党和工人党国际会议经过多年的发展，已经成为各国共产党和工人党相互交流的一个平台，是世界各国共产党和工人党政治生活中的一件大事。

glossary.explanation: A term in Chinese political discourse for decision-making through discussion among different actors to reach consensus. The authors use it to describe the consensus-seeking procedure of the meeting.

keywords: International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties

t: The spectre of the "Maoist movement"
zh: “毛主义运动”的幽灵
paras: Wang Hui asks why Maoist movements in South Asia, which he calls a spectre present everywhere yet rarely spoken of, are so largely absent from contemporary thought and media. The text began as his preface to Wang Jing's study of the Communist Party of India (Maoist), published in 2016. Wang Hui argues that these movements are a "spectacle" in an age of financialised capitalism, because they openly claim descent from twentieth-century revolution, especially the Chinese one, and still treat land, caste and national independence as central questions.

The article has three parts. The first sets the Maoist movements against the post-1989 "end of history" climate and the Occupy-style protests, and discusses the Indian Maoists, the Subaltern Studies school and Arundhati Roy's reporting. The second examines the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) through four problems: people's democracy versus parliamentary democracy, army reform, land and peasants, and the constitution and federalism. The third considers the "low-intensity war" waged against such movements, their internal divisions, a comparison with Venezuela, and the Belt and Road Initiative. Wang notes that he knows little about Maoist movements in Peru, Colombia, the Philippines and Turkey.

Wang contends that the movements' scale, endurance and intensity far exceed those of the Occupy protests, which he describes as short-lived and built on urban middle-class interests. In Nepal, he argues, the Maoist leader Prachanda's belief that people's democracy could be merged with multiparty parliamentary politics was wishful thinking. Wang compares the dispute over the People's Liberation Army and the land reforms with the Guomindang's 1945 demand for "nationalisation of the army". He also compares the movement's setbacks with its inability to produce a leadership with strategic vision and a mature theory. He sets this against Chávez, who relied on charisma because his party was weak. He also describes a US-designed "low-intensity war" of information control, blockade, intelligence and decapitation of leaders, which he says widens the technological gap between ruling classes and revolutionary forces.

Wang concludes that simply repeating past paths has no future, but that basic values must be kept while strategies are rethought for the twenty-first century, in political forms that serve the majority. He argues that studying South Asia and Latin America can also illuminate the history of the Chinese Revolution. He adds that the Belt and Road Initiative can succeed only if the poor and their political movements are included and China's domestic development model is readjusted. Read the original if you want a Chinese left-intellectual reading of Nepal's Maoists and South Asian Maoism, and of their bearing on China's international strategy.
quoteEn: The Maoist movement is a "spectacle" not because it is rare or small, but because we have grown used to viewing our world through the lens of the "end of history", even many who explicitly reject that thesis.
quoteZh: “毛主义运动”之为“奇观”，并非由于其罕见或规模弱小，而是因为我们已经习惯于在“历史终结论”的视野中观察我们置身的世界，即便对于许多明确拒绝“历史终结论”的人而言也是如此。

glossary.explanation: China's international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative, launched in 2013. Wang links its success in South Asia to the interests of the region's poorest people.

A revolutionary-socialist model of democracy, drawn here from Mao Zedong's On New Democracy, in which the revolutionary side keeps political, military and cultural leadership. The article treats it as distinct from parliamentary democracy.
A school of South Asian historiography that began with studies of peasant movements. Wang argues that its second generation turned to postcolonial questions and away from Maoist-style movements.
A US military doctrine of long, combined military, political, economic and psychological warfare. Wang says it was used against guerrilla movements in the Third World.

t: Revisiting why the Soviet Union chose a heavy-industry development strategy under Stalin
st: Refuting false charges imposed on Stalin
zh: 斯大林时期苏联选择重工业发展战略原因再探讨
zhSub: 驳强加在斯大林头上的不实之词
paras: Why did the Soviet Union under Stalin adopt an industrialisation strategy centred on heavy industry? Yuan takes issue with the view, associated with Zuo Fengrong, that Stalin deliberately exaggerated the danger of Western armed intervention and overstated the war threat to justify his policies. Yuan argues that the hostility of the capitalist powers in the 1920s was real and sustained, that Stalin's assessment of it was grounded in events, and that the heavy-industry strategy was a correct choice for the time.

The article has three parts. The first reviews the attitudes and actions of Britain, the United States and the capitalist states acting jointly towards the USSR in the 1920s. The second traces how Stalin's judgement of the international situation changed from 1924 to 1928. The third offers five evaluative points on Stalin's intentions and decisions. Yuan draws on Stalin's writings and on Chinese, Soviet and Western scholarship, including Kissinger, Service and Paterson.

Yuan lists a series of incidents: the Curzon ultimatum (1923), the forged "Zinoviev letter" (1924), the raid on the Soviet embassy in Beijing, the raid on Arcos, the assassination of the Soviet envoy Voikov in Warsaw, and Britain's break of relations in 1927. Yuan adds the American policy of non-recognition, the Dawes Plan, and the Locarno and Kellogg–Briand pacts, which Yuan reads as instruments of isolation or of an anti-Soviet front. Stalin, on this account, moved from optimism in 1924–26 to the conclusion in 1927 that these events were not isolated and that the danger of war was growing. Yuan holds that Stalin wanted to postpone war and preserve peace, that his basic aim was the state's survival and security, and that he judged Soviet strength soberly. Siege and hostility produced a strong sense of crisis, and a USSR left as an agrarian appendage of the capitalist world would be defenceless. Hence the author calls the planned economy, heavy-industry-centred industrialisation and collectivisation a necessary response.

Yuan concludes that analysing Stalin's errors is legitimate and necessary, but only with an objective and comprehensive view of the external pressures he faced. The author maintains that Stalin's decisions secured the survival of the first socialist state and showed the vitality of socialism. Read the original if you want to see how a Chinese Marxist scholar defends Stalin's industrialisation strategy by pointing to the international environment, and how the article assembles the 1920s diplomatic record to support that case.
quoteEn: Capitalist encirclement and hostility gave Stalin a strong sense of isolation and crisis, and this was the direct reason he urgently pushed forward national industrialisation and agricultural collectivisation at home.
quoteZh: 资本主义的包围和敌对使斯大林形成了强烈的孤岛意识和危机意识，这是促使斯大林急切地在国内开展国家工业化和农业集体化的直接原因。

t: World socialism is now entering a period of seeking revival
zh: 当前世界社会主义正进入谋求振兴期
paras: Writing in 2016, Jiang Hui asks where world socialism stands some twenty-five years after the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. The article argues that, amid a new crisis of capitalism, world socialism has emerged from its trough and entered a period of seeking revival. Jiang holds that this development refutes claims of capitalism's final triumph and the "end of history", while cautioning that the movement as a whole will remain at a low ebb for a long time.

The article first traces how communist parties survived the post-1991 shock through crisis, regrouping and renewal. It then gives figures: parties in over 100 countries, about 100.3 million members in total, of which the Communist Party of China accounts for over 88 million. Jiang sorts these parties into four types: ruling parties in existing socialist countries; parties in developed capitalist countries such as Japan, France, Italy and Greece; parties in the former Soviet and East European region; and parties in developing countries such as India, South Africa and Nepal. Other left currents, including Venezuela's "socialism of the twenty-first century", market socialism and eco-socialism, are noted briefly.

Jiang lists six favourable conditions: the weakening of neoliberal and right-wing dominance, the vindication of socialist critiques of capitalism (seen in the "Marx fever"), the recovery of left forces, closer left cooperation, more objective lessons drawn from the Soviet collapse, and the achievements of socialism with Chinese characteristics. Four challenges are set against them. Capitalism remains stronger than socialism, communist parties are marginalised in crisis-hit Western states, their leadership of social movements is weak, and the global working class remains "in itself" without a global class consciousness. From these Jiang draws a key distinction: Marxist principles on crisis and revolution still apply, but crisis does not automatically bring revolutionary upsurge, and expecting a single decisive blow is called "infantile".

Jiang concludes that capitalism, now at the stage of international monopoly capitalism, retains strong self-regulating and innovative capacity. Socialism should therefore prepare for long-term cooperation and struggle between the two systems. The author describes socialism with Chinese characteristics as the brightest spot and mainstay of world socialism. China is urged to concentrate on its own development, balancing "keeping a low profile" with "getting things done", because world socialism's revival depends on that success. Read the original if you want a 2016 official-academic assessment of the global communist movement, with membership figures and a typology of parties.
quoteEn: As long as socialism with Chinese characteristics develops, the revival of world socialism is not an empty phrase.
quoteZh: 只要中国特色社会主义发展起来，世界社会主义的振兴就不是空话。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the path, system and theory of socialism pursued by the Communist Party of China since the reform era, associated with Deng Xiaoping.

glossary.literal: hide one's brightness and nurture obscurity
glossary.explanation: A phrase associated with Deng Xiaoping's foreign policy guidance, advising restraint in international affairs while building national strength. It is often paired with "getting things done" (有所作为).

glossary.en: the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
glossary.literal: drastic upheaval in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
glossary.explanation: The standard Chinese term for the fall of Soviet-bloc communist regimes around 1989–1991.
Francis Fukuyama's thesis that Western liberal democracy is the final form of human government, which the author rejects.

t: Lenin's October Revolution as a "great revolution"
st: On the controversy sparked by quoting Putin's remarks out of context
zh: 列宁领导的十月革命是“伟大的革命”
zhSub: 评对普京讲话断章取义引发的争论
paras: In January 2016 reports circulated online that Vladimir Putin had negatively assessed Lenin, saying Lenin's ideas had led to the Soviet collapse like a nuclear bomb placed under the building of Russia. Wu Enyuan argues that these reports quoted Putin selectively and distorted what he said. In Wu's account, Putin criticised specific Leninist ideas, not Lenin's thought as a whole.

The commentary, published in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2016, first reconstructs Putin's remarks of 21 and 25 January. It then turns to three questions: how Putin assesses the Soviet system, how he treats Soviet history and historical figures in earlier statements, and what causes of the Soviet collapse are being debated.

Wu reports that Putin explained the "mine" as the dispute between Lenin and Stalin over the structure of the new state. Lenin favoured equal republics with a right of secession, which Putin considered mistaken, but Putin also praised planned economy, health care, education and industrialisation as achievements of the Communist Party. Wu adds that Putin said he still keeps his Party card, and that he has repeatedly warned against blackening the national past. Wu also cites a 2014 history-textbook commission view that the October Revolution and civil war can be called a "great revolution".

Wu notes that the day after Putin spoke, Security Council secretary Nikolai Patrushev gave a front-page interview. In it he blamed Gorbachev's policy errors as the main cause of the collapse. Wu reads this as both a gloss on Putin's remarks and a pointed answer to the scholarly debate over whether historical or immediate factors weighed more. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's defence of Lenin's standing, framed through Putin's 2016 remarks and Russian official statements.
quoteEn: It is clear that Putin here was not rejecting all of Lenin's thought.
quoteZh: 很明显，普京这里并不是对列宁全部思想的否定。

t: Discursive power and organizational power in the contemporary world socialist movement
st: A rereading of the Communist Manifesto
zh: 当代世界社会主义运动中的话语权和组织权
paras: Zhang Wenmu rereads the Communist Manifesto to ask how the world socialist movement can rebuild its "discursive power" (huayuquan) and "organizational power" (zuzhiquan) after the setbacks of the late twentieth century. Writing in 2016, Zhang argues that the world has entered an age of financial imperialism, that a new upsurge of socialism is already on the horizon, and that socialists must use organization to win the contest over discourse.

The article, an excerpt from a longer piece, first characterises financial imperialism as the most decayed stage of capitalism. It then surveys signs of an approaching socialist upsurge, among them Occupy Wall Street, student protests in Britain, the rhetoric of John McDonnell and Bernie Sanders, and Tony Blair's apology over Iraq. It closes with three proposals: strengthen international proletarian unity, build a broad international united front, and uphold scientific socialism.

Zhang holds that since Nixon ended the dollar's gold link and tied it to oil, the dollar has rested on petrodollars and foreign wars rather than national labour. Marx's circuit M–C–M′ has become, in Zhang's formula, M–War–M′. Finance capital, in this account, has no homeland and now exploits industrial capitalists and the whole of humanity, so it is producing its own gravediggers at unprecedented speed. Against Western finance capital's media power, Zhang calls for organizational strength and, following Lenin's What Is to Be Done?, for positive education or "inculcation" (guanshu) rather than entertainment-led propaganda. Zhang also says that the socialist state is the movement's strongest organization. The article defines the main enemy as Wall Street finance capital rather than the American nation or its national capital. It names "democratic socialism" of the Bernstein–Gorbachev type as the most dangerous internal threat, and it defends the dictatorship of the proletariat, citing Deng Xiaoping's 1992 talks.

Zhang concludes that drawing on the lessons of socialism's earlier defeats, organizing the working class internationally and holding to Marxism-Leninism are preconditions for the coming upsurge. Zhang warns that China, nearer than ever to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, also faces greater risk of a Soviet-style collapse if it dilutes people's democratic dictatorship and the Four Cardinal Principles. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Marxist scholar reads financial imperialism, ideological struggle and the Soviet collapse in 2016, with its many contemporary references.
quoteEn: The international socialist movement needs to use organizational power to win discursive power, to advance the proletarian struggle in an organized and comprehensive way, and to build an international united front that can include industrial capital, so as to prepare in advance for the coming of a new socialist upsurge.
quoteZh: 国际社会主义运动需要用组织权争取话语权，有组织地全面推进无产阶级的斗争，建立可以涵盖工业资本的国际统一战线，为社会主义新高潮的来临提前做好准备。

glossary.explanation: The capacity to shape public narratives and set the terms of ideological debate. It is widely used in Chinese political writing on media and ideology.
Zhang's term for a movement's capacity to organize and unite its forces, above all through the party and the socialist state.

Lenin's idea, taken from Kautsky, that socialist consciousness has to be brought to workers from outside their spontaneous struggle. In Chinese usage it also means direct, systematic ideological education.
A principle of the Chinese state: democracy for the people and dictatorship over enemies. Deng Xiaoping presented it as the Chinese form of the dictatorship of the proletariat.
Principles announced by Deng Xiaoping in 1979: the socialist road, the people's democratic dictatorship, the leadership of the Communist Party, and Marxism-Leninism and Mao Zedong Thought.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central official goal of the Chinese Communist Party, widely used since the early 2010s, of restoring China's national strength and international standing.

t: Diverse explorations out of the trough: the "five currents" in the revival of world socialism
zh: 走出低谷的多样探索——世界社会主义回暖潮流中的“五个潮头”
paras: Writing in 2016, Wang Dong asks what has happened to world socialism in the two decades since the collapse of the Soviet Union and the upheavals in Eastern Europe (1991), which he treats as its lowest point. His overall judgement is that, drawing on the general crisis of capitalism in the age of economic globalization, contemporary world socialism has left its deepest trough. In his account it is now exploring varied new paths suited to a new era and to national conditions.

The short commentary singles out five currents within this recovery. These are eco-socialism, calls for a socialism of justice in response to polarisation, Latin America's twenty-first-century socialism, appeals for socialist revival in Russia and the CIS countries, and Vietnam's path of renewal. Each section gives a brief portrait, usually built around one representative figure or event.

On eco-socialism, Wang reports the view that the ecological crisis is rooted not in science and technology but in the capitalist mode of production and its drive for maximum profit, and cites a 2015 interview with Communist Party USA chairman John Bachtell. On justice, he points to the worldwide debate over Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014) and to David Harvey's verdict that Piketty's data are valuable but his explanation and remedies are flawed, so that Marx or a modern equivalent is still needed. For Latin America he sets out Rafael Correa's 'modern socialism' (2014) and Evo Morales's 'good socialism', and he presents the Russian philosopher A. Bagaturia and Vietnamese theorists on Ho Chi Minh Thought as evidence that socialist ideas persist and adapt.

Wang concludes that these currents show socialism renewing itself in different forms in different places, rather than disappearing after 1991. He also notes Bagaturia's repeated visits to China and his interest in socialism with Chinese characteristics, though the article does not develop this into a wider argument. Read the original if you want a compact 2016 Chinese overview of which foreign socialist trends and figures a Peking University philosopher regarded as signs of recovery.
quoteEn: Contemporary world socialism has already emerged from its lowest trough and is exploring diversified new paths suited to the new era and to new national conditions.
quoteZh: 当代世界社会主义已经走出最低谷，正在探索适应新时代、新国情的多样化新道路。

glossary.explanation: The official term for China's path since reform and opening up, combining Marxism with China's conditions. Here it appears only in the article's passing mention of Bagaturia's interest in it.
The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism, developed since the late 1970s. The article mentions it only in passing.
A current of thought that blames the ecological crisis on capitalism's profit-driven logic and seeks a socialist alternative.
A label associated with Hugo Chávez and other Latin American leaders for new socialist projects since the late 1990s.

t: The "new socialism" movement in Latin America: problems and prospects
zh: 拉美“新社会主义”运动：问题与前景
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (中国社会科学报), 25 February 2016, p. 5
paras: Writing in 2016, Jin Chengwei examines the wave of "new socialism" that has emerged in Latin America since the late 1990s and distinguishes it from the "twentieth-century socialism" of the traditional communist parties. The article asks why this current arose, what it advocates and practises, and what challenges and prospects it faces. Jin's thesis is that it is an exploratory, non-Soviet attempt to transcend capitalism and neoliberalism that still has considerable vitality despite mounting difficulties.

The piece is a short newspaper commentary in three parts. It first sets out four background conditions, then surveys the doctrines and policies of four representative cases: Venezuela's and Ecuador's "socialism of the twenty-first century", Bolivia's "communitarian socialism" and Brazil's "labour socialism". It closes with the challenges these movements face and eight judgements on their character and outlook. Each case is summarised under political, economic, social and international headings.

On origins, Jin points to the shock of the Soviet and East European collapse, which opened intellectual space for left-wing thinkers to look beyond the Soviet model. Jin also cites repeated economic crises since the 1980s, the failure of neoliberalism, and the third wave of democratisation, which gave the left a legitimate political stage. On character, Jin notes that scholars disagree over whether this is socialism at all, and that the answer depends on whether the term is used narrowly or broadly. Jin's own view is that it is not scientific socialism, but it is an exploration of a socialist nature and a new attempt different from the Soviet model. Jin also stresses its inclusiveness, its acceptance of winning power through elections, and its emphasis on regional integration and international cooperation.

Jin lists the main challenges: building a coherent theoretical system, reducing dependence on charismatic leaders, strengthening party organisation, resisting corruption, keeping left unity, overcoming economic difficulties, answering popular discontent and countering domestic and foreign opponents. Although the governing parties involved face greater uncertainty, Jin concludes that the movement retains strong vitality and room to develop as an alternative to neoliberalism and capitalism in Latin America's specific conditions. Finding effective responses to these challenges is, in Jin's words, the urgent task. Read the original if you want a compact Chinese-language overview of how a Party School scholar classifies and assesses Latin America's twenty-first-century socialist experiments.
quoteEn: It can be said that Latin America's "new socialism", although not scientific socialism, is an exploration of a socialist nature and a new socialist attempt different from the Soviet model.
quoteZh: 可以说，拉美“新社会主义”虽然不是科学社会主义，但是具有社会主义性质的探索，是不同于苏联模式的社会主义新尝试。

glossary.explanation: The term for the socialism theorised by Marx and Engels, set against utopian socialism. In Chinese academic writing it is the standard benchmark for judging whether other socialist currents are fully Marxist.
The label used by Venezuela and Ecuador for their own socialist projects. It presents them as new, humanistic and distinct from Soviet-style socialism.
The Bolivian version of new socialism, based on community, reciprocity, solidarity and harmony with nature. Some politicians call it "Bolivarian Indian socialism".
The label for the Brazilian Workers' Party's socialist outlook. Some scholars call it "democratic and sustainable socialism".

glossary.en: the Soviet and East European collapse
glossary.literal: drastic change in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe
glossary.explanation: The standard Chinese term for the end of Soviet-bloc socialist rule around 1989–1991.

t: China–Vietnam economic and trade cooperation under new conditions: alignment and development
zh: 新形势条件下中越经贸合作：对接与发展
source: Party and Government Studies (Dangzheng yanjiu), 2016 no. 1
paras: Writing in early 2016, Pan and Qin ask how China and Vietnam can deepen economic and trade cooperation in a changed domestic and international setting. They argue that Xi Jinping's state visit to Vietnam in November 2015 gave this cooperation fresh momentum, and that the two countries' development strategies can be aligned to turn new opportunities into mutual gain while managing the challenges.

The article has four parts. It first reviews the visit and the political framework it set, including the proposed China–Vietnam 'community with a shared future'. It then describes the features of bilateral trade, investment and tourism since normalisation in 1991, and sets out the opportunities and challenges created by the Belt and Road Initiative, Vietnam's reform record and its entry into the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP). A last part considers what China–Vietnam ties mean for China–ASEAN cooperation.

The authors present trade as growing fast and as strongly complementary. They cite Chinese customs figures of 36 million dollars in 1991 rising to 83.6 billion in 2014, with Vietnam exporting tropical farm and mineral products and importing machinery and manufactures. They also credit cultural similarity and warming political ties. Problems they list are Vietnam's large deficit, complaints about the quality of Chinese goods and contracting work, and media amplification of these issues. Their central proposal is to link the Belt and Road Initiative, backed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, with Vietnam's 'two corridors and one economic circle' plans to ease Vietnam's infrastructure bottleneck. The authors see TPP as bringing both opportunity and risk for Vietnam, including pressure on state enterprises and financial instability.

Pan and Qin make four recommendations: Vietnamese infrastructure planning using Belt and Road mechanisms; industrial and capacity cooperation, with Chinese firms investing in Vietnam to fill supply-chain gaps and reduce the deficit; cross-border economic cooperation zones; and financial cooperation, including a currency swap agreement. They also urge better media guidance. They conclude that stronger bilateral ties would help China–ASEAN free trade area upgrading, the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and China's neighbourhood diplomacy. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly view of China–Vietnam economic relations around 2015, with trade and investment figures and concrete policy proposals.
quoteEn: It can thus be said that political relations are a powerful booster of the development of the two countries' economic and trade relations.
quoteZh: 可见，政治关系可以说是两国经贸关系发展的强大助力器。

glossary.explanation: A Chinese initiative announced in 2013 to build overland and maritime connectivity, trade and investment links with countries along the old Silk Road routes.
A foreign-policy concept promoted by Xi Jinping, applied here to China–Vietnam and China–ASEAN relations, stressing shared interests and joint development.

glossary.en: two corridors and one economic circle
glossary.explanation: A plan proposed by Vietnam in 2004 for the Kunming–Hanoi–Haiphong and Nanning–Lang Son–Hanoi corridors and the Gulf of Tonkin economic circle.

t: Difficulties and reconstruction of China–Vietnam relations: a methodological reflection
zh: 中越关系的困境与重构：一个方法论的思考
paras: Writing in Party Politics Research in early 2016, Pan Jin'e asks why China–Vietnam relations, which developed rapidly after normalisation in 1991, have fluctuated since about 2006–2007, and how they might be put on a stable footing. The article is framed as a methodological proposal rather than a finished analysis. Pan suggests that relations should be rebuilt on a culturally grounded sense of shared identity, using three schools of international relations theory.

The opening section recalls the framework guiding bilateral ties: the 1999 sixteen-character guideline, the 2005 "four goods" spirit and the 2008 comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership, together with Xi Jinping's 2015 visit to Vietnam. Pan stresses that Vietnam matters to China as a fellow Party-led socialist state and as a link in neighbourhood diplomacy and the Belt and Road Initiative. A literature review then sorts existing work into three groups: histories of the tributary relationship and of the modern "comrades plus brothers" era; tracking studies of post-normalisation ties by Chinese and Vietnamese scholars; and studies using general international relations theory, including Brantly Womack on asymmetry, Alexander Wendt's constructivism and Qin Yaqing's relational theory.

Pan observes that Chinese research on the recent period is scarce, partly because the topic is treated as sensitive, and that Vietnamese scholars increasingly view China's rise with unease. No joint Chinese–Vietnamese studies exist. In Pan's account, the two countries' relationship has passed through four identities: tributary hierarchy, "comrades plus brothers", hostility in the late 1970s and 1980s, and ordinary state-to-state relations. The post-2007 fluctuations are attributed to changed national statuses that the bilateral framework did not adjust to; imbalance then built up and was triggered by territorial disputes that inflame nationalism. Pan argues that constructivism, which treats identity as the basis of interests, suits this problem. Because Vietnam's line follows Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought, "comrades plus brothers" is described as a red line that can only be given new content.

Pan proposes a new-type relationship combining solidarity based on the socialist system, consensus drawing on positive elements of Confucian culture and the tributary past, and win-win cooperation under modern international norms. The proposed method is a joint team of Chinese and Vietnamese scholars with expertise in history, international relations, Party and government studies and media, using documents, fieldwork, questionnaires and interviews, with results acceptable to both sides and then adopted officially. Read the original if you want a short Chinese scholarly agenda on China–Vietnam relations, with a review of Chinese and Vietnamese literature, rather than a detailed empirical study.
quoteEn: As long as Vietnam upholds Communist Party leadership and the socialist road, its foreign policy line will remain essentially unchanged, that is, guided by Marxism-Leninism and Ho Chi Minh Thought, and Ho Chi Minh long ago defined China–Vietnam relations as "comrades plus brothers".
quoteZh: 在越南坚持共产党的领导走社会主义道路的前提下，越南外交路线将“万变不离其宗”，即坚持以马列主义和胡志明思想为指导思想，而胡志明早已把中越两国关系定位为“同志加兄弟”。

glossary.explanation: China's international infrastructure and economic cooperation initiative, announced by Xi Jinping in 2013.
A formula attributed to Ho Chi Minh describing the close revolutionary and fraternal ties between the Chinese and Vietnamese parties and peoples.
The formula agreed by Chinese and Vietnamese leaders in 1999: long-term stability, orientation to the future, good-neighbourly friendship, comprehensive cooperation.

glossary.zh: 全面战略合作伙伴关系
glossary.explanation: The highest-level bilateral partnership label between China and Vietnam, agreed in the 2008 joint statement.
The hierarchical imperial-era order in which neighbouring states such as Vietnam sent tribute to the Chinese court in return for recognition.

t: Paths to socialism
st: Part two of "The prospects of socialism: painful reality and historical opportunity"
zh: 通向社会主义的途径
paras: This is a Chinese translation, by Yang Weimin of the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences, of the second half of an article first published in January 2015 in the Russian journal 21st Century Marxism. The Russian author, a former deputy chairman of the State Duma and an economist, asks how a transition from capitalism to socialism can still be achieved in Russia and elsewhere. The author argues that only revolution can change a socio-economic formation, that peaceful routes are now largely closed in Russia, and that the left must organise mass action, win control of the media and study past revolutionary experience.

The text opens with a call to act rather than wait, then moves through five sections. It treats revolution as a way of resolving acute class contradictions, and it reads the Soviet road to socialism through the October Revolution, the civil war and the 1990s. It then asks whether socialist revolution has reached its limit and what opportunities remain. Finally it examines the left's weaknesses, the role of mass media, and the lessons of Bolshevik preparation before 1917.

The author holds that revolution means the passage from one social formation to another, and that bloodshed belongs to the methods used, not to its essence. On this reading October 1917 was largely peaceful, and the violence that followed came from foreign intervention and from the resistance of the old classes. Post-Soviet capitalism is called a counter-revolution. Rigged elections and police repression, in the author's account, have made a parliamentary road to socialism in Russia practically impossible. The author also faults communist, socialist and social-democratic parties for opportunism, for failing to lead the anti-capitalist protests in Europe, and for misreading the media as a weapon through which the bourgeoisie shapes public consciousness.

The author concludes that the left must unite on the basis of Marxism and represent working people's interests, and that it must break the ruling class's monopoly over the mass media. The left should also study the long Bolshevik preparation, which included decades of propaganda, organisation and tactical reconnaissance of the masses. Today's Russian opposition is said to lack strategic aims, and the author argues that resistance must appear in the squares as well as at the ballot box. Read the original if you want a Russian communist-oriented view of revolution, the Soviet collapse and left strategy, written with strong polemical language and sweeping claims about the United States and the West.
quoteEn: The people's resistance to capitalism must be realised not only at election time but also in the squares.
quoteZh: 人民反抗资本主义，不仅应该落实在选举时，还必须体现在广场上。

t: The state of mind of CPSU grass-roots organisations and members before the Soviet collapse
zh: 苏联解体前苏共基层党组织与党员思想状况分析
paras: Why did the roughly 16.5 million members of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) not publicly rise to defend the Party when it was suspended and the USSR dissolved? Li Yan and Zhang Shuhua take up this question, prompted by a Chinese commentator's remark that no one in the Party proved a "real man". They argue that the members' silence was real but has been misread. In their account it had historical and objective causes, as well as members' dissatisfaction with corrupt officials and a mistaken reform line, and it was not the whole story, since many members protested in other ways.

The article draws on memoirs by Roy Medvedev, Valery Boldin and Anatoly Chernyaev, and on archival letters from Russian state archives. It also uses 1989–1991 Party statistics on membership losses and dissolved organisations. It begins with the apparent calm in Moscow in August–November 1991. It then sets out five reasons for the silence, turns to forms of resistance, and ends with lessons for a ruling party.

The five reasons are as follows. Democratic centralism had become a formality, so rank-and-file members had no real say in the Party's fate. The ranks were impure, because of the excesses of the purges and the later "excessive stability" and office-selling under Brezhnev. Ideological attacks on Stalin and Soviet history, from Khrushchev's "de-Stalinisation" to Gorbachev's glasnost, left members disoriented. Privilege and corruption alienated members from officials. Finally, Gorbachev's multi-party reforms turned the CPSU into a "parliamentary party", one of hundreds. The authors report Party membership falling from about 19.49 million in early 1989 to 16.52 million in January 1991, and a collapse of workplace organisations. They read the mass resignations, protest letters, public calls for Gorbachev's resignation, the suicides of veterans such as Marshal Akhromeyev, and members who kept paying dues as forms of resistance that were suppressed.

The authors conclude that the collapse was not directly the grass roots' responsibility, but that a ruling party rests on active grass-roots organisations and a correct line. They draw five lessons. The ruling party should balance democracy and centralism and follow the mass line. It should govern itself rigorously and keep its cadres pure. It should keep a correct ideological direction and reject historical nihilism. Its cadres should be self-disciplined and free of privilege. Democracy and multi-party supervision should be kept within limits. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly reading of the CPSU's final years, built on archival letters and Party statistics, and its lessons for Party-building.
quoteEn: When the fate of the Party and state was decided by a few elites, the \"calm\" of rank-and-file members looked like indifference, but was more often a matter of not being informed or being powerless.
quoteZh: 当党和国家的命运取决于部分精英时，基层党员的“平静”看似冷漠，更多的则是不知情或无能为力。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Chinese Party discourse for the wholesale negation of a socialist country's history and its leaders. The article applies it to the Soviet criticism of Stalin and of the Soviet past.
The Leninist organisational principle of free discussion followed by unified action and subordination to higher bodies. The article argues that in the late CPSU it had become a formality.
A Maoist method of leadership: gather the views of the masses, concentrate them into policy and return to the masses. The article presents it as an answer to bureaucratism.

t: China must be highly vigilant against and guard against "colour revolutions"
zh: 必须高度警惕和防范“颜色革命”
paras: Writing in 2016, Zhou Xiaobing takes up the wave of "colour revolutions" that have toppled governments in a series of countries. Zhou argues that these are not spontaneous popular movements but regime-change operations directed by the United States, and that China must be highly vigilant against them. The piece appeared in the Party journal Red Flag Manuscripts.

The article has three parts. The first sets out what Zhou presents as the regularities of colour revolutions, defined as coups carried out through non-violent "street politics". The second argues that every case is manipulated by, and serves the interests of, the United States, drawing on examples from Eastern Europe, the former Soviet Union and North Africa. The third turns to prevention in China and lists basic measures.

Zhou distinguishes two types: those that turn socialist states into capitalist ones, which Zhou equates with "peaceful evolution", and those that install pro-US governments in capitalist states. Both, Zhou says, follow four steps: shaping opinion against the government, building opposition organisations through NGOs and then parties, choosing a charismatic pro-American leader, and using an incident or election to launch street protests under the banner of democracy. Zhou argues that Washington prefers this route to war because it is cheaper and wins wider acceptance, and cites funding figures and training workshops for opposition cadres in several countries. Democracy, in this reading, is only a pretext.

For China, Zhou calls for strengthening the instruments of dictatorship, in the form of the people's democratic dictatorship, against a small number of liberal agitators. Zhou also calls for four preventive measures: strengthening Marxist guidance in ideology, keeping leadership at every level in the hands of Marxists, consolidating the Party's mass base, and upholding the dominant position of public ownership. Zhou also urges strict control of Western-funded NGOs and education in a Marxist view of democracy. Read the original if you want to see how a Party-journal author of 2016 framed colour revolutions as a US-led strategy and what domestic countermeasures were proposed.
quoteEn: It can be said that in the so-called "colour revolution", ideological work is the foundation, organising an opposition led by prominent figures is the key, sudden incidents are the opportunity to exploit, and the goal is to establish a pro-American regime.
quoteZh: 可以说，所谓“颜色革命”，意识形态工作是基础，组织有头面人物带领的反对派是关键，突发事件是可以利用的时机，目标是建立亲美政权。

glossary.explanation: A label for non-violent mass movements, often marked by a colour or flower, that overthrew governments in places such as Georgia, Ukraine and Kyrgyzstan. Chinese official writing generally treats them as externally engineered subversion.
A Chinese term for the alleged Western strategy of using non-military means, such as ideology and cultural exchange, to turn socialist states towards capitalism.

The constitutional description of China's state system, with democracy for the people and dictatorship over designated enemies. Deng Xiaoping used it as the Chinese form of the dictatorship of the proletariat.
Mass demonstrations, rallies, strikes and occupations of public space used to pressure a government. The article treats it as the final step of a colour revolution.

t: The current development and role of the middle class around the world
zh: 当前中产阶级在世界各国的发展状况及作用
paras: Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts (2016, no. 3), Li Changjiu asks how the middle class is faring worldwide and what role it plays. The author notes that there is still no agreed definition, but says countries share a consensus: the middle class is a main force in scientific and technological innovation and a backbone and "stabiliser" of economic and social development. Li's thesis is that the middle class is shrinking in Western countries but growing in developing ones, where the main challenge is the "middle-income trap".

The article has two parts. The first surveys the United States, Germany, France, Britain and Japan, drawing on official statistics, polls and Western commentators such as George Friedman and Joseph Stiglitz. The second turns to developing countries and emerging economies, citing projections from the World Bank, the UN Development Programme and the African Development Bank, and then examines South Korea as a case of escaping the trap.

For the West, Li cites figures that the US middle-class share of national income fell from 53.2% in 1968 to 45.7% in 2012. German middle-class population share fell from 66.5% to 61.5% between 2000 and 2009, and French middle-class households are described as squeezed by compulsory spending. Li reports that Stiglitz blames the polarisation on institutional factors, namely the combination of market speculation and political manoeuvring, and that Friedman sees the decline as a threat to US power. For the developing world, the article cites World Bank data that Asia's middle class tripled between 1990 and 2005, and projections of strong growth in Asia-Pacific and Africa. It then reports a 2012 World Bank and State Council Development Research Centre study finding that, of 101 middle-income economies in the 1960s and 1970s, only a dozen or so had reached high income by 2008.

Li concludes, following the economists cited, that the middle-income trap is essentially a problem of economic development, avoidable through sustained, high-quality growth and rising incomes. South Korea is presented as the model: heavy investment in education and R&D, and thirty years of five-year plans that, in the article's figures, raised per capita GNP from 87 to 6,316 US dollars between 1962 and 1991. The lesson Li draws is that correct government policy combined with popular innovation and effort can avoid the trap. Read the original if you want a compact, data-led Chinese state-media overview of middle-class trends abroad and of how the middle-income trap was framed in 2016.
quoteEn: The valuable experience South Korea offers emerging countries is that, if the government adopts correct policies and relies on the people's innovation and striving, the so-called "middle-income trap" can be avoided.
quoteZh: 韩国为新兴国家提供的宝贵经验是，如果政府采取正确政策、依靠群众的创新和奋斗，所谓“中等收入陷阱”是能够避免的。

glossary.explanation: A concept from development economics, used in World Bank-related literature, describing economies that reach middle-income status but then stall and fail to reach high income. It became a common reference in Chinese policy debate.
A Chinese Communist Party theoretical journal, published by the People's Daily organisation, that carries commentary and policy-oriented analysis.

t: What new changes have taken place in contemporary capitalism
zh: 当代资本主义发生哪些新变化
paras: Writing in a newspaper commentary in 2015, Tang Zhengdong asks how contemporary capitalism's new features should be understood and how Western scholars' accounts of them should be read. Tang argues that the changes are real but cannot be grasped by empirical description. They must be read through historical materialism, which shows that capitalism's social form remains capitalist beneath altered material and technical forms.

The piece moves from the limits of single-factor explanations (labour, production technology, finance, consumption, globalization) to the question of which concepts should name the new stage. It compares "state monopoly capitalism" and "international monopoly capitalism" with "post-industrial society", "post-Fordism" and similar labels. It then sketches a research programme and ends with a statement on the Four-sphere Confidence.

Tang first holds that each partial explanation sees only one element and so concludes that Western capitalism is in good shape. In their view, post-Fordist flexible production also brought lower social welfare and sharper class conflict. Facts are themselves constructed by social power, and even political or historical analyses that expose this stay empirical unless they explain the historical basis of the power struggle. Tang says Western left scholars have largely given up historical materialist method. Second, Tang says Marx used "capitalism" in terms of both a technical and a social paradigm of production, the social one being more important and tied to the contradictions of social relations. Concepts such as "post-Fordism", which stress technique, cannot capture this, and stretching them to describe the whole post-1970s era leads into neoliberal ideology. Western scholarship therefore shows two features. One is empiricism. The other is utopianism: supporters exaggerate the merits of the free market, while critics either build idealised pictures of freedom or abstract one element from social relations to imagine emancipation.

Tang calls for study to start from the labour process and relations of production. Tang concedes that notions such as "immaterial labour" are fashionable but holds that the social form of both remains capitalist. Analysis should then extend to consumption, ideology, globalization and spatialization, where Western scholars have produced work that is "interesting" but not necessarily "profound". Tang proposes dissecting this work's limits to deepen understanding of capitalism's inner contradictions. Tang concludes that such critical reading should strengthen confidence in the path, theory and system of socialism with Chinese characteristics, given China's achievements. Read the original if you want a short example of how a Chinese philosopher frames Western theories of contemporary capitalism as empiricist and utopian.
quoteEn: But \"interesting\" is not necessarily \"profound\".
quoteZh: 但“有意思”并不一定“深刻”。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's model of socialism since the reform era. It is presented as Marxism adapted to China's conditions.

An official formula calling for confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics. This 2015 article names only the first three, which were the earlier version of the formula.

Marx and Engels's theory that social change is explained by the development of productive forces and relations of production. The author uses it as the standard against which Western accounts are judged.

A term for the shift from standardised mass production to flexible production, associated with the period after the 1970s. The author argues it describes a technical paradigm and is wrongly stretched to characterise the whole era.

t: Where is the Western left heading? The condition and prospects of the left in the twenty-first century
st: The Latin American left's rise, record in office and present challenges
zh: 西方左翼何去何从？——21世纪西方左翼的状况与前景
paras: Writing at the end of 2015, Jiang Hui asks what has become of the left in Latin America after roughly fifteen years of governing. Despite the title's reference to the Western left, the article deals only with Latin America. Jiang argues that the region's left rose by offering alternatives to neoliberalism and achieved real gains, but now faces serious challenges, with Venezuela and Brazil under the greatest pressure.

The article has three parts. It first traces the left's rise from Hugo Chávez's election in Venezuela in 1999 to governments of the left or centre-left in more than ten countries, including Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Chile, Bolivia, Ecuador and Nicaragua. It then assesses these governments' politics, economics, social policy and foreign policy. Finally it sets out five challenges and notes how the left is responding. It ends with the Argentine presidential election of November 2015 and the upcoming Venezuelan parliamentary vote.

Jiang credits the left with new or revised constitutions and participatory democracy, nationalisation of key sectors such as Bolivia's oil and gas in 2006, and poverty-reduction programmes. In Brazil, the author says, these programmes lifted nearly 40 million people out of poverty. The left also pursued regional integration through ALBA, UNASUR and CELAC, and several governments proposed their own socialisms, such as '21st-century socialism'. Jiang then lists five problems. Growth has slowed as commodity prices fell, forcing austerity and protests. Corruption scandals, especially in Brazil, have hurt support. Conservative opposition is strong in many cities and legislatures. Divisions exist within ruling coalitions, within left parties and between parties and new social movements. Finally, Jiang says the United States interferes, citing National Endowment for Democracy funding and sanctions on Venezuelan officials.

Jiang concludes that left governments are aware of these challenges and are responding. The article points to the Quito 'Latin American Progressive Meetings' of 2014 and 2015 and to the São Paulo Forum's 21st meeting in Mexico City, which stressed left unity. It reads Mauricio Macri's victory in Argentina as shifting the region's political pendulum towards the centre-right and as a blow to other left governments. Read the original if you want a Chinese specialist's 2015 assessment of the Latin American left's record, its difficulties and its view of US involvement.
quoteEn: Social conflict and protest in Latin American countries are becoming normalised and more varied, and the newly emerged middle class, dissatisfied with the status quo, often takes the leading role in the protests.
quoteZh: 拉美国家社会冲突和抗议趋于常态化和多样化，而对现状不满的新兴中产阶级常常成为抗议的主角。

glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Hugo Chávez in Venezuela and taken up in Ecuador, describing a socialist project distinct from both neoliberal capitalism and twentieth-century state socialism.

t: Where is the Western left heading? The condition and prospects of the Western left in the twenty-first century
zh: 西方左翼何去何从？——21世纪西方左翼的状况与前景
source: Foreign Social Sciences (Guowai shehui kexue), 2015 no. 3
paras: Writing in 2015, Jiang Hui asks what has become of the Western left since the collapse of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, and where it can go after the 2008 financial–economic crisis. Jiang argues that the crisis has opened a rare historic opportunity, but that the left has not been able to use it. Its future depends on how far it achieves a genuine "negation of the negation", meaning a sublation of its own past rather than a simple return to the old left.

The article has three parts. The first divides the left's course since 1990 into three phases: retreat (1990–1995), a rightward turn (1996–2007), and a partial return (2008–2014). The second diagnoses the left's present difficulties. The third names four relationships the left must handle if it is to renew itself.

In the diagnosis, Jiang says the left has "heaven's timing" (capitalism and the right are discredited) but lacks "human harmony". Centre-left parties lost elections, communist parties stayed marginal, and far-right parties took up part of the discontent. Jiang lists four problems: a lost identity, inadequate theoretical and strategic preparation, criticism without constructive programmes, and fragmentation despite efforts at unity. For the way forward, Jiang stresses four relationships: the left and socialism, which should form a "great left" led by the socialist movement; the left and class struggle, where the working class remains the main force; electoral politics and mass movements, which are in a standing paradox; and national against global activity.

Jiang concludes that the left should neither return to its earlier form nor settle for turning back a few steps. It should build a new left and a hopeful socialism suited to the post-crisis situation. For Jiang, this requires a socialist orientation, a class basis, a balance between parliamentary and extra-parliamentary struggle, and an international outlook, since socialism is national in form and international in content. Read the original if you want a Chinese Marxist scholar's periodisation and assessment of the Western left after 1990, written from the standpoint of the study of scientific socialism.
quoteEn: The left movement and the socialist movement should be \"natural allies\".
quoteZh: 左翼运动与社会主义运动应该是“天然的同盟军”。

t: Luxemburg and the violence of global capitalism
zh: 卢森堡与全球资本主义暴力
paras: This short essay on Rosa Luxemburg (1871–1919) asks what her theory of imperialism, set out in The Accumulation of Capital (1913), still tells us about global capitalism. The author argues that her account of capital's dependence on non-capitalist societies, and of the violence this entails, has proved largely prescient and applies to developed economies as well as colonised ones. The text appears to be a Chinese rendering of an English-language piece; no author is named, and the translator is given as Lu Yingchun.

The essay opens with a portrait of Luxemburg as a writer, her humour, her taste for plain theoretical prose and her immersion in the work on accumulation. It then summarises her economic analysis, her criticism of Volume II of Marx's Capital, and her survey of pre-capitalist economies. Next it lists the cases she examined, including the ruin of English peasants, the destruction of Native Americans, the enslavement of Africans, and colonial assaults on Algeria, India, China and South Africa. The final sections turn to her views on international loans, militarism and the First World War.

The author identifies three features that set Luxemburg apart from Hilferding, Bukharin and Lenin. First, because workers receive less value than they create, capitalists face underconsumption and must expand into non-capitalist regions for markets, raw materials and labour. Capital thus lives by destroying those regions, and accumulation would eventually stall. Second, she treats imperialism not as capitalism's 'highest stage' but as present from primitive accumulation onwards. Third, she shows an anthropological sensitivity to the cultures that expansion destroys. The author adds that this penetration now reaches family life, friendship, creativity and gender in advanced economies. The author also notes that capital's drive to accumulate has, contrary to Luxemburg's expectation, weakened socialist revolution rather than provoking it.

The author concludes that, whatever the criticisms of the book, Luxemburg's analysis is highly plausible and has been borne out. The essay cites Joan Robinson, who found the book more prescient than the orthodox theorists of its day. It also credits Luxemburg with foreseeing foreign investment and aid, the role of international lenders, and arms spending as a field of accumulation paid for by workers. The author adds that her words resonate in the twentieth century and in present-day globalisation. Read the original if you want a brief, sympathetic introduction to Luxemburg's theory of imperialism and its contemporary relevance, as presented in a Chinese-language outlet.
quoteEn: The view that capitalism is more complex and variable than Luxemburg recognised is open to question.
quoteZh: 资本主义比卢森堡认识的更为复杂更为多变这一观点[8]是值得商榷的。

t: Has winter arrived for the Latin American left?
zh: 拉美左翼的冬天来临了吗？
paras: Writing in early 2016, after electoral defeats for the left in Argentina and Venezuela, this unsigned commentary asks whether Latin America's left is entering a period of decline. The article answers that it is not necessarily doing so: setbacks for left-wing parties, it argues, do not amount to a victory for neoliberalism.

The piece has three parts. It first describes how neoliberal reform from the 1980s produced the conditions for the left's rise from 1999, beginning with Hugo Chávez's election in Venezuela. It then reviews the record of left and centre-left governments in politics, the economy, social policy and foreign relations. Finally it turns to the recent reverses and to how they should be read.

The author cites figures to argue that neoliberalism brought slower growth, higher unemployment, a wider gap between rich and poor, and a larger poor population. Left governments, in this account, wrote new constitutions, nationalised key sectors, ran anti-poverty programmes (Brazil's, for example, are said to have lifted some 40 million people out of poverty) and promoted regional integration through bodies such as ALBA, UNASUR and CELAC. The recent downturn is attributed to falling commodity prices, an unreformed export-based growth model, austerity measures and corruption within left parties. The author nonetheless contends that the opposition's Venezuelan parliamentary win was largely a punishment of the governing party. Polls are cited showing majority support for the Bolivarian social programmes and over two-thirds opposition to privatising state oil and electricity companies, and the author says right-wing candidates have had to present themselves in the language of Chávez and Kirchner.

The article concludes that defeated left forces are mobilising people in streets and neighbourhoods to defend the gains of the Bolivarian revolution against a coming right-wing offensive. It closes by quoting that history is made by the masses rather than in parliaments. Read the original if you want a brief, sympathetic Chinese-language account of how the Latin American left's 2015 reverses were interpreted on a Chinese Marxist platform.
quoteEn: In sum, the setbacks of the Latin American left do not necessarily mean a victory for neoliberalism.
quoteZh: 总而言之，拉美左翼的挫败并不一定意味着新自由主义的胜利。

t: The financial crisis as an opportunity for the revival of world socialism
zh: 金融危机为世界社会主义复兴提供契机
paras: This commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today, takes up the claims that socialism has "ended" and that China is about to "collapse".
