Lü argues that the global financial crisis of 2008 has turned these claims against their authors. In the article's account, what is actually ending is the "end of socialism" thesis and the "China collapse" thesis, while capitalism declines and world socialism, though not yet out of its trough, partly recovers.

The article has four parts. It first traces the origins of the "end of socialism" and "China collapse" arguments, from the late 1980s to the early 2010s. It then examines the institutional difficulties of capitalism after the crisis, and the signs of revival in world socialism. It closes with a warning that a new round of such predictions is under way and with proposals for how China should respond. Figures discussed include Nixon, Brzezinski, Fukuyama, Gordon Chang and David Shambaugh, with Derrida, Huntington and several investors cited as critics.

Lü's central move is to treat the "China collapse" thesis as a form of the "end of socialism" thesis, aimed at discrediting socialism and flattering capitalism. The sharpest rebuttal, in this reading, comes from the real development of the two systems. Lü says the crisis exposed capitalism's instability, parasitism and decay, and that it ended the myth of an "eternal" capitalism, citing Fukuyama's own remark that the crisis shows capitalism's inherent instability. Lü then points to three signs of socialist revival: renewed interest in Marx and socialist alternatives, stronger communist and left parties in Greece, Portugal, Spain, Latin America and elsewhere, and the rising standing of socialism with Chinese characteristics, as China was first to recover economically.

Writing in 2015, Lü warns that China's entry into a period of "new normal" growth and "tackling tough problems" in reform invites fresh predictions of collapse. Lü calls for deepening reform and opening up, advancing the Scientific Outlook on Development, building the material basis for the Chinese Dream, and keeping strategic resolve through firm communist ideals. Read the original if you want an example of how a CASS scholar answered Western "end of history" and "China collapse" arguments in the mid-2010s.
quoteEn: The gradual decline of capitalism and the gradual revival of socialism since this crisis eloquently show that what some Western scholars have declared "ended" is not socialism but the "end of socialism" thesis, and what they have predicted would "collapse" is not China but the "China collapse" thesis.
quoteZh: 此次危机以来资本主义的日渐衰落和社会主义的逐步复兴雄辩地表明：一些西方学者所倡导的“终结”的不是社会主义，而是“社会主义终结论”，所预言的“崩溃”的不是中国，而是“中国崩溃论”。

glossary.literal: theory of the end of socialism
glossary.explanation: The argument, widespread after the Soviet and East European upheavals, that socialism has failed historically. Chinese writers often link it to Fukuyama's "end of history".
A label used in China for Western predictions that China's economic, political or social system will collapse. Chinese commentators generally treat it as a hostile argument.
A guiding concept of the Hu Jintao era, written into the Party constitution in 2007. It stresses people-centred, coordinated and sustainable development.
A slogan associated with Xi Jinping since 2012, which equates the dream with the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
An official term from 2014 for China's shift from high-speed to medium-high-speed growth, with a change in growth model.

t: Distinguishing the epoch from the theme of the epoch
zh: 对时代和时代主题的辨析
paras: Li Shenming takes up a question of strategic judgement: what is the nature of the present epoch, and how does it relate to the 'theme of the epoch'? Starting from Xi Jinping's call for overall and long-term thinking in deepening reform, Li argues that the epoch and its theme must be kept apart. In Li's view, the present epoch is still the epoch of finance imperialism that Lenin described, and 'peace and development' is only the theme of a phase within it, not the name of a new epoch.

The article has two parts. The first defines the epoch and its theme through Marx, Engels and Lenin, who in Li's reading identify epochs by the class at their centre. Li subdivides the bourgeois epoch into commercial capitalism, industrial capitalism and finance imperialism. The second part traces how Deng Xiaoping and later Party documents spoke of peace and development, reviews Lenin's account of imperialism, and applies it to the post-Cold War world, including the 2008 financial crisis. Li also cites statements by Mao Zedong, Deng, Chen Yun, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi to show continuity of judgement.

Li's central claim is that the epoch's nature determines its theme and not the reverse. The epoch is the deeper level, and themes are changing outward forms of its basic contradiction between international bourgeoisie and international proletariat. Lenin's three basic contradictions, Li says, have changed in form but are unresolved. On this basis Li proposes a 'two-sided' judgement: finance imperialism is still strong and at the centre, yet it is relatively declining while the proletariat rises, within a long and winding transition from capitalism to socialism. Li objects to colleagues who equate the 'epoch of peace and development' with the theme, noting that wars have continued and that the length of war or peace cannot define an epoch.

Li concludes that misjudging the epoch could lead either to blind optimism and an attempt to skip over the finance-imperialist stage, which Li calls 'left-wing' infantile disorder, or to a loss of confidence in socialism and communism, even the fate of the Soviet Union. Li holds that Deng enriched the Marxist idea of the theme without denying the imperialist character of the era. The article argues that the correct judgement underpins the Party's long-term strategy. Read the original if you want to see how a senior academic voice defends Lenin's theory of imperialism against the idea of an 'epoch of peace and development'.
quoteEn: Fundamentally, it is the epoch that determines the characteristics of the epoch, not the characteristics of the epoch that determine the epoch.
quoteZh: 从根本上说，是时代决定时代特征，而不是时代特征决定时代。

glossary.explanation: In Chinese Party discourse, the main issue or struggle that defines a given period within a larger historical epoch. Since the 1980s official documents have named 'peace and development' as the present theme.

Formula for the main international issues, associated with Deng Xiaoping's remarks of the 1980s and written into Party Congress reports from the 13th (1987) onwards. It replaced the earlier 'war and revolution' formula.
Li's term for what he takes Lenin's 'imperialism' to mean: the rule of finance capital as the highest stage of capitalism.
A dialectical method of weighing both aspects of a contradiction. Here it means seeing both the continuing strength of finance imperialism and its relative decline.

t: Economic financialization will inevitably intensify economic and social turmoil in capitalism
zh: 经济金融化必将加剧资本主义经济社会动荡
paras: Writing in 2015, Xing Wenzeng asks whether the financial reforms adopted after the 2008 global financial crisis have checked the financialization of capitalist economies. The article's answer is no: financialization remains a defining feature of capitalism, and the author argues that it will inevitably deepen economic turmoil and social crisis in the future.

The article has three parts. The first traces how financialization became a central feature of capitalism from the 1970s and how it prepared crises. The second surveys the regulatory measures taken by the United States, the EU, Britain, Japan and Germany after 2008 and assesses their results. The third looks ahead to three consequences: a continuing split between the real and the virtual economy, more channels for large-scale financial crises, and sharper class conflict.

Xing explains financialization as a response to falling profit rates and stagnation in the 1970s, helped by neoliberal deregulation. The author cites figures on the growth of financial assets, derivatives and financial-sector profits. On the post-crisis reforms, including the Dodd–Frank Act, new supervisory bodies, oversight of rating agencies and limits on executive pay, Xing argues that the effect was limited. The evidence offered is record bank profits, over-the-counter derivatives growing roughly eightfold between 1998 and 2012, shadow banking above 73 trillion dollars in 2013, and rising concentration among large banks. Re-industrialization drives in the West, the author says, have barely raised manufacturing's share of GDP or employment. Xing adds that financial innovation gives capital new ways to extract surplus value, and cites the post-2008 workers' movements in Europe and elsewhere, with slogans such as ending the capitalist system, as signs of widening class antagonism.

Xing concludes that capitalist states' policies, which the article describes as taking from the poor to give to the rich, make financialization more severe. The author predicts a deeper crisis of capitalist accumulation, greater global class confrontation and unavoidable social crisis. Read the original if you want an example of how a Chinese Marxist economist in 2015 used data on derivatives, shadow banking and post-crisis regulation to argue for capitalism's structural instability.
quoteEn: Economic financialization has strengthened the power of financial capital as never before, aggravated the disconnect between the virtual and the real economy, and made the hollowing-out of capitalist economies serious.
quoteZh: 经济金融化空前强化了金融资本的力量，加剧了虚拟经济与实体经济之间的脱节，也使资本主义国家经济空心化现象严重。

glossary.explanation: The growing weight of finance, financial assets and financial profits in an economy, including in non-financial firms. The article treats it as a defining feature of capitalism since the 1970s.
A term in Chinese economic writing for financial activity detached from the production of goods and services, such as speculation and derivatives. It is contrasted with the real economy (实体经济).

t: The genealogy, present state and future of the world socialist movement
st: Popular movements toward socialism: their unity and diversity
zh: 世界社会主义运动的谱系、现状与未来
orig: Monthly Review, June 2014 ("Popular Movements Toward Socialism: Their Unity and Diversity")
source: Marxism Studies (马克思主义研究), 2015 no. 10
paras: This text is a Chinese edited translation of an article by the Egyptian Marxist economist Samir Amin, first published in Monthly Review in June 2014. Amin treats socialism/communism as a stage of civilisation superior to capitalism. He uses "movements toward socialism" for all mass movements that resist capitalism. His thesis is that such movements advance only if they recognise their differences and still act together.

The article first sketches the French Revolution's values of liberty, equality and fraternity, which Amin says capitalism can accept but never realise. It then traces three lineages of the movement: the capitalist centre, the semi-periphery, and the periphery. The centre runs from French socialism and the First and Second Internationals to postwar social democracy. The semi-periphery is the Leninist line, from Russia to Soviet "state socialism". The periphery runs from the Taiping movement to Mao Zedong, India, Africa and Latin America. The last sections turn to the future and to the "second rise" of the Global South.

Amin's central claim is that the relation between unity and diversity has decided the fate of each lineage. He argues that the Second Internationals' ideal of a single workers' party and mass unions led to revisionism. Revisionism, he says, rested on prosperity built on imperialist plunder, and left European parties merely social-liberal. Lenin inherited the one-class, one-party idea, and the Third International later subordinated strategy to Soviet needs. Amin credits Mao and the Chinese communists with moving beyond Leninism, and says China's management of unity and diversity explains its stability and legitimacy. He treats Vietnam and Cuba as comparable successes, and the Latin American governments and Indian communists as unresolved or failed cases. He holds that class analysis must not be simplified and must separate major from minor differences.

Amin proposes that radical left forces in the imperialist centre nationalise monopoly property and democratise and socialise its management, setting common goals for each stage. On the periphery, he says, they must identify the components of their social alliance and its shared goals. He rejects multiparty elections as a formula for "true democracy" and calls for "sovereign projects" built from below, including moving away from financial globalisation and the dollar, and geopolitical alliances to restrain US military control. Read the original if you want a Marxist account, from the Global South, of how socialist movements have divided and what he thinks they should do next.
quoteEn: Resolving the two does not mean negating one of them, but turning their opposition into complementarity.
quoteZh: 解决这两者并不是要求否定其中一个，而是要将两者的对立转化为互补。

t: Humanity's advance towards socialism is an irresistible movement
zh: 人类走向社会主义是一种不可抗拒的运动
orig: Marxism of the 21st Century (Russian journal), January 2015
paras: This is a Chinese translation of an article by a Russian economist and former State Duma deputy chairman, first published in a Russian journal in January 2015. The author starts from the question whether humanity will still see socialism and treats it as settled: socialism is the future stage of civilisation. The real question, in the author's view, is how long capitalism can hold back human progress. The thesis is that movement towards socialism is irresistible, but its timing depends on subjective factors that are currently poorly prepared.

The article has five sections. It first separates the objective and subjective conditions of socialism, then asks whether modern capitalism is already ripe for transition. It next lists five features of capitalist 'decay', explains why socialism has not arrived sooner, and ends with a critical assessment of the socialist and democratic movements, including the Soviet collapse and the situation in post-Soviet Russia.

The author argues that objective conditions supply only the material basis for social reconstruction. History is made by social-economic subjects: states, governments, politicians, theorists and the mass media, driven by class struggle. The author defends Lenin's thesis of capitalist 'decay' and cites war, hunger, spiritual impoverishment, unemployment, the corruption of work ethics and youth drug addiction. Economic crises, ecological threat, monopoly and the 'fascisation' of state conduct are also listed. Socialism has not yet replaced capitalism because the subjective side is weak: trade unions have been bought off, communist and workers' parties disarmed, genuine Marxist theorists are few, and no leader of the stature of Marx, Lenin, Castro or Chávez exists. The author also blames the Soviet collapse on the ruling class's mismanagement, dogmatism and passive waiting rather than on economic causes, and attributes anti-socialist pressure to the global elite, naming Bilderberg and 'world government'.

The author concludes that the best remedy for anti-socialist and anti-communist sentiment is serious study of socialist thought worldwide and of socialist practice, including the Soviet experience. The author calls for new socialist theory under present conditions and urges the unity of the left opposition. Read the original if you want a Russian left-wing view, published in China in 2015, of the Soviet collapse, the subjective conditions of socialism and the crisis of the communist movement.
quoteEn: The best 'medicine' for curing anti-socialist and anti-communist sentiment is to study seriously socialist thought around the world and the socialist practice of socialist countries, including the Soviet Union.
quoteZh: 医治反社会主义、反共产主义情绪的最好“良药”，是认真研究世界各国的社会主义思想，以及社会主义各国包括苏联在内的社会主义实践。

t: Tactical success and strategic impasse: the world socialist movement since the 2008 financial crisis
zh: 战役成功与战略困局：2008年金融危机以来的世界社会主义运动发展态势
paras: Did the 2008 financial crisis revive the world socialist movement? Nie Yunlin argues that it produced only a limited result. Communist parties in capitalist countries won what the author calls a campaign-level ("战役性") success, but the movement remains at a low ebb, these parties are still marginalised in political life, and no strategic victory has been achieved.

The article has two parts. The first reviews what communist parties did after 2008 and why the hoped-for upsurge did not come, drawing largely on speeches at the 11th International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties. The second sets out six tasks that the author says these parties must resolve to escape their strategic impasse, using examples from Britain, India, Turkey, Russia, France, Spain, Italy, Brazil, South Africa and Nepal.

In Nie's account, the parties analysed the crisis theoretically, joined strikes and protests, voted against crisis-shifting policies in parliaments and strengthened their own organisation. Some held or raised their membership, for example the Communist Party of India (Marxist) with over a million members. The article attributes the lack of a strategic breakthrough to four causes cited by delegates: the lingering effects of the Soviet and East European collapse, welfare systems that dulled workers' political consciousness, weak capacity for self-renewal, and sectarian splits. The six tasks are: overcoming fragmentation; avoiding both "left" dogmatism and rightist abandonment of Marxist principles; upholding and reforming democratic centralism; consolidating the class base and widening mass support, especially among trade unions and the middle strata; sustaining left alliances; and breaking out of the constraints of capitalist political systems. Nie claims that parties which kept democratic centralism have recovered, while those which dropped it, such as the French, Spanish and Italian parties, have declined.

Nie concludes that the post-crisis period opens a long new journey in which each party must find a socialist path suited to its own country. The author likens the crisis-era gains to the defence of Huangyangjie in the Jinggangshan period of the Chinese revolution, a battle won before the war was decided. The most pressing step, Nie says, is to solve the parties' internal problems. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholar's assessment of Western communist parties after 2008, and of their organisational and strategic dilemmas, based on party delegates' own statements.
quoteEn: The campaign-level success of communist parties in capitalist countries during the financial crisis is merely comparable to the victory in the defence of Huangyangjie during our Jinggangshan struggle.
quoteZh: 资本主义国家共产党在金融危机时期的战役成功，仅相当于我们井冈山斗争时期黄洋界保卫战的胜利

glossary.explanation: The organisational principle of Leninist parties, combining discussion and election within the party with binding decisions and discipline once a decision is taken. The article treats it as essential to communist parties, while admitting past excesses of centralisation.
The social groups between the working class and the capitalist class. The article treats them as politically unstable and as a key target of communist alliance policy.

glossary.zh: 共产党和工人党国际会议
glossary.en: International Meeting of Communist and Workers' Parties
glossary.explanation: An annual gathering of communist and workers' parties from many countries. The article draws on delegates' speeches at the 11th meeting (2009).

t: An analysis of the ideological state of CPSU grass-roots organisations and members before the Soviet collapse
zh: 苏联解体前苏共基层党组织与党员思想状况分析
paras: Why did the roughly ten million rank-and-file members of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) not act when the Party was dissolved and the USSR collapsed? Writing in Red Flag Manuscripts in 2015, the author takes up a question often put by commentators who read their calm as indifference. The thesis is that the silence came from structural and ideological causes, not apathy, and that some members did resist.

The author draws on interviews with veteran Party members conducted during a 2014 research visit to Russia, and on archives, letters and documents read there. The article has three parts: five reasons for the silence, examples of protest within it, and the historical lessons. It also uses memoirs by Roy Medvedev, Valery Boldin and Chernyaev.

The first part argues that Lenin's priority of democracy within centralism was gradually reversed. Power concentrated in a bureaucratic pyramid, so grass-roots members could only obey, stay silent or write complaint letters. The author adds four further causes. The cadre ranks were swollen by careerists. Khrushchev's and especially Gorbachev's ideological policies of glasnost and the criticism of Stalin spread what the author calls historical nihilism. Elite privilege and corruption alienated members. Gorbachev's political reforms, including multiparty competition, weakened Party leadership and set off mass resignations in 1990–91. The second part cites the teacher Nina Andreyeva's 1988 letter, the deputy Sarie Umalatova's call for Gorbachev to resign, and suicides of figures such as Marshal Akhromeyev. The author reads these as despairing protest and argues that the crowds outside the Party headquarters in August 1991 did not speak for ordinary members.

The author concludes that the collapse is not directly attributable to grass-roots members. Even so, a ruling party rests on vital grass-roots organisations, and these were disrupted once Gorbachev abandoned the Party's leading role and the socialist path, while privilege and corruption cost the Party public support. The article's lesson is that a ruling party must hold to a correct political line, to Marxist principles and to socialism. It must also keep strict organisational and political discipline and serve the people in practice. Read the original if you want a Chinese scholarly account of the Soviet collapse that centres on ordinary Party members, with archival and memoir material.
quoteEn: When the fate of the Party and the state depended on a section of the elite, the grass-roots members' "calm" looked like indifference, but was more often ignorance of the real situation or helplessness.
quoteZh: 当党和国家的命运取决于部分精英时，基层党员的“平静”看似冷漠，更多的则是不知实情或者“无奈”。

glossary.explanation: A term used in Chinese Party discourse for what it sees as the wholesale negation of a socialist state's or Party's history. It is typically applied to critical reassessments of Soviet and Chinese Communist history.
Gorbachev's policy of greater openness in media and public debate from the mid-1980s. The author treats it as the channel through which the Party's own history was attacked.

t: Marxist movements in Africa
zh: 非洲的马克思主义运动
orig: Daryl Glaser and David M. Walker (eds), Twentieth Century Marxism: A Global Introduction (Routledge, 2007), chapter 7
source: Marxism and Reality (马克思主义与现实), 2014 no. 4
paras: This text is a Chinese translation, with some abridgement, of a chapter by Daryl Glaser from Twentieth Century Marxism: A Global Introduction (Routledge, 2007). It asks whether Africa made an original contribution to Marxist thought, a claim many African Marxist leaders themselves rejected. Glaser answers that it did, even though the ruling Marxist-Leninists after the 1970s insisted on a single universal model.

The chapter surveys "African socialism" of the independence era (Nkrumah, Touré, Nyerere) and the Marxist-Leninist regimes that followed. It traces how Marxism reached Africa through colonial links, urban multi-ethnic milieus and the Soviet bloc. It then compares routes to power: military coups (Ethiopia, Benin, Madagascar, Somalia), people's war (Cabral, FRELIMO, the MPLA), and the special cases of South Africa and Ethiopia. It closes with the decline of these movements around 1990.

Glaser argues that Marxism in Africa did not arrive merely as a Soviet import. African Marxist governments often kept channels open to the West, and their authoritarianism was largely home-grown. The author also defends military Marxists and guerrilla movements against critics who dismissed them as insincere. Original contributions are identified in Siad Barre's attempted synthesis of Marxism and Islam, the national-question positions of the Eritrean and Tigrayan liberation fronts, Touré's mass-party experiments and Madagascar's limited multiparty system.

In Glaser's account, failure stemmed from both external and internal causes. External causes were underdevelopment, war, Cold War pressures and debt. Internal causes were impatience, overambitious planning, coercion of the peasantry, hostility to wider society and a "participatory" democracy that served mobilisation behind goals the ruling party had set. Glaser sees the shift to representative democracy after 1990 as valuable but constrained by the IMF and World Bank. Future socialists and social democrats, the author says, must learn from the negative lessons of African socialism and Marxism and may still need Marxism to analyse new class inequalities. Read the original if you study African socialism, Cabral or the global spread of Leninism and want a critical comparative overview.
quoteEn: But it is plainly wrong to assume that Africa's Marxist movements adopted Marxist policies in order to secure the protection of Soviet or Cuban armed forces.
quoteZh: 但是，如果假定非洲的马克思主义运动采用了马克思主义政策以保护苏联武装力量或古巴军队，那么显然是错误的。

t: Latin America: left-wing progressive governments urgently need strategic planning
zh: 拉丁美洲：左翼进步政府急需战略规划
source: Contemporary World and Socialism (Dangdai shijie yu shehuizhuyi), 2014 no. 3
paras: This is a Chinese translation (compiled and translated by Wang Jin) of a report by the Cuban scholar Roberto Regalado, a professor at the University of Havana. Writing in 2014, fifteen years after Hugo Chávez's first election victory, Regalado asks whether Latin America's more than ten left-wing progressive governments will build a new society or become part of fully developed capitalist rule. He holds that both outcomes remain possible and depend on several factors, including the governments' awareness of and capacity to create a new emancipatory paradigm.

The report analyses four external factors and five continental processes that shaped the region's left after 1989. It then surveys changes within the left and the ideological debates over a new paradigm. The external factors are the transnational concentration of capital known as globalisation, the neoliberal onslaught of the 1980s, the collapse of the Soviet and East European socialist bloc in 1989–1991, and the adoption of neoliberal doctrine by West European social democracy in the late 1990s.

Regalado's central argument is that the left's electoral rise rested on three positive factors: the accumulated effect of earlier popular struggles, the human rights movement, and the organisational capacity built up in the fight against neoliberalism. He adds one negative factor, the acceptance of a "new world order". He distinguishes two groups of governments. Venezuela, Bolivia and Ecuador came to power as neoliberal systems collapsed, whereas Brazil and Uruguay did so through long political accumulation by the Workers' Party and the Broad Front. He sees the governments facing growing threats since 2009. These are defeat or overthrow by US imperialism and the local right (he cites Honduras in 2009), erosion of popular support, or a combination of the two.

On ideology, Regalado describes three phases since 1989: the discrediting of revolutionary ideas, a revival of critical analysis without a new paradigm, and, since 2006, the return of socialism through Chávez's "socialism of the twenty-first century". Alongside it he sets the Indigenous idea of "good living" (buen vivir). He concludes that Marxist positions take part in the debate but do not decisively shape any government's policy. Policy and the search for a new paradigm run in parallel, and he says this gap brings growing risks. Read the original if you want a Cuban Marxist's 2014 assessment of Latin America's left-wing governments, their threats and their ideological debates.
quoteEn: The policies of Latin America's left-wing progressive governments run in parallel with the search for a new emancipatory paradigm; in other words, there is a gap between theory and practice.
quoteZh: 拉美左翼进步政府的政策同对新解放范式的探索是并行的，换句话说，二者之间存在理论和实践的差距。

t: Beware of the so-called "pan-socialism"
zh: 警惕所谓“泛社会主义”
paras: Zhou Xincheng takes issue with a new concept, "pan-socialism" (fan shehuizhuyi), which he says was put forward by a research unit. As Zhou describes it, the idea treats democratic socialism, ecological socialism and petty-bourgeois socialism alike as members of one "socialist family" that deserves tolerance and unity. Zhou reads this as a way of saying that democratic socialism should no longer be criticised. He argues that it is wrong and dangerous, because democratic socialism is not socialism at all but a form of capitalism.

The piece opens with the historical origins of the word "socialism" and the many currents that claimed it, which Zhou lists as feudal, petty-bourgeois, utopian and bourgeois socialism. It then sets out the basic principles of scientific socialism and the difference between those principles and the concrete forms in which they are realised. After that it turns to democratic socialism, and Zhou takes its three main definitions of socialism in turn: "ethical", "welfare" and "functional" socialism. The article ends with a note on how the Party should relate to socialist parties.

Zhou's central claim is that the test of socialism is whether a movement upholds the basic principles of scientific socialism. He cites Xi Jinping's remark that "if they are lost, it is no longer socialism". For Zhou these principles are Communist Party leadership, the dictatorship of the proletariat, public ownership of the means of production, distribution according to work, and Marxism as guiding ideology. Different "models" of socialism, he says, differ only in how these principles are realised, so a current that rejects them cannot count as a model. Zhou answers each democratic-socialist definition from Marx, Lenin, Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping. He treats democracy as class-bound and rejects "pure democracy". He treats welfare as a distribution policy that, in his reading, repeats the Lassallean error criticised in the Critique of the Gotha Programme, because it leaves ownership untouched. Workers' participation in management, he adds, leaves the bourgeoisie in power. Two tests decide the question: who owns the means of production, and who holds state power.

Zhou concludes that democratic socialism is a model of capitalism, not of socialism. In capitalist countries he casts it as a doctor at capitalism's sickbed, and in socialist countries as a bridge to capitalism. He holds that muddying this boundary raises the question of which banner to raise and which road to take. He also separates the nature of socialist parties from inter-party relations. Citing a 1956 Party document, he calls for united-front work with their left and centre while keeping the class boundary clear, and he warns that blurring it is now the greater risk. Read the original if you want a representative Chinese Marxist case, dated 2015, for drawing a hard line between scientific socialism and social democracy.
quoteEn: Democratic socialism is not a model of socialism, but a model of capitalism.
quoteZh: 民主社会主义不是社会主义的一种模式，而是资本主义的一种模式。

glossary.explanation: A term the author says was proposed in a research report, holding that all currents calling themselves socialist belong to one family. The author rejects it.
In Chinese Party discourse, the social-democratic current of Western socialist parties. Official writings usually criticise it as reformist and non-Marxist.
The socialist theory founded by Marx and Engels on historical materialism and the theory of surplus value, set against utopian and other earlier socialisms.

t: The history, present state and future of Germany's Left Party
zh: 德国左翼党的历史、现状及未来
paras: Writing after the German federal election of September 2013, Liu Hui asks how a young party formed by merger has become Germany's third-largest force yet remains unable to enter a governing coalition. The article's answer is that the Left Party's rising influence is real, but its East German legacy, its radical positions and its internal divisions keep other parties from working with it. Liu nonetheless judges the prospects positive and argues that coalition government is attainable if the party adjusts.

The article has three parts. It first traces the party's origins from the East German ruling Socialist Unity Party, through its 1989 reorganisation as the Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), to the 2005–2007 merger with the Labour and Social Justice Party (WASG) led by Oskar Lafontaine. It then describes the present party: its membership (about 69,500, of whom 37.3 per cent are women), its two co-chairs, Katja Kipping and Bernd Riexinger, and its election results of 8.7 per cent in 2005, 11.9 per cent in 2009 and 8.6 per cent in 2013. A final section considers its future.

Liu credits the party with four roles: opposing war and military intervention (for example over Syria), promoting environmental protection, defending social fairness through demands such as a national minimum wage, and advancing the interests of women and children. Against this the article sets two main problems. One is disunity: the party combines two organisations with different histories, its factions lack discipline, and its strength lies far more in the East than the West. The other is the refusal of the Social Democrats and Greens to form a coalition with it. Liu attributes that refusal to history (the party's perceived inheritance from the East German ruling party), to its hard line against aid to eurozone crisis states, and to its demand to abolish NATO and break with US hegemony, which Liu describes as an ideologically tinged position.

Liu proposes four steps: learn from past elections and keep up the party's work on peace, ecology and social justice; consolidate its Eastern base while tailoring policy and slogans to Western voters; play a constructive role in the European Left Party; and combine firmness of principle with tactical flexibility, toning down radical language so that a red–green–red alliance with the Social Democrats and Greens becomes possible. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese-language overview of the Left Party's origins, its 2013 election position and one scholar's assessment of its coalition prospects.
quoteEn: However, opinion within the party has become disordered, even without organisation or discipline, so that differing views cannot be unified and in the end the party's decisions are hard to bring to agreement.
quoteZh: 但是，党内意见出现无序化，甚至是没有组织，没有纪律，致使党内不同意见无法统一，最后使该党的决策难以达成一致。
